en: (2) Sandhi: For the convenience of word search, internal and external [sandhis are applied].
Vowel sandhis are decomposed by ^; for example, *viśeṣokti* < *viśeṣa + ukti*, and *ca iti* < *ca + iti*.
*horāṇyaḥ* < *horāṇyaḥ*,
*ko'pi* < *kaḥ api*;
consonantal sandhis are retained.
(3) Compound Words:
The members of compound words are occasionally separated by a caret (^), though this is not consistently applied.
(4) Other variants for the portion beginning with * are provided in [ ].
1. The Chapter on Initiation (*upanayanādhyāyaḥ*).
Victorious is the Sun, the progenitor of the world, the soul of the universe, the natural ornament of the sky,
honored by a garland of a thousand rays resembling molten gold.
Having observed that the meaning of this extensive treatise, as spoken by the First Sage, is unerring,
I am now intent upon explaining it clearly through a composition that is neither too concise nor too prolix.
1.03ab/ "This was composed by a sage"—if that is why it is ancient and good, rather than being merely composed by a human;
1.03cd/ then since the meaning is the same, what special claim can there be for [the Veda] on the grounds of a difference in syllables when it lacks a mantra?
If, according to what was proclaimed by Pitāmaha (Brahmā), the day of the son of the Earth (Mars) does not bring auspiciousness—
or if it is said that Tuesday is unfavorable— what distinction is there here between the effects produced for humans and for gods?
Having observed the extensive body of literature issued from Brahmā downwards, I have therefore undertaken this work in brief, as it is being composed in due order; hence my enthusiasm.

1.06ab/ Indeed, this was darkness; therein, within the golden egg of the waters, there arose Brahmā, the creator of the universe, whose eyes were the sun and the moon. 1.06cd/ [He dwelt] upon the fragment of heaven and earth within that cosmic egg.

1.07ab/ Kapila declared that *pradhāna* is the [cause] of this universe, consisting of substance and so forth; Kaṇabhuj [declared] time to be its cause. 1.07cd/ Some have proclaimed *svabhāva*, while others have proclaimed *karman*.
1.08ab/ Therefore, enough with this excessive elaboration; the determination of the meaning of these incidental discussions is already very extensive.
1.08cd/ Here, I shall state the determination regarding the auxiliary branches of the science of astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra).
1.09a The science of luminaries (jyotiḥśāstra), which has manifold branches as its subject matter and is established upon three divisions (skandhas),

is called by the sages "Saṃhitā" when it brings about a complete presentation of that [science]. 1.09c Within this division, that which concerns the motion of the planets through calculation is designated as "Tantra."
1.09d The determination of the limbs other than the horā has been declared; this is another, the third chapter.
1.10ab/ The retrograde, prograde, heliacal setting, and rising of the star-planets have been described by me in the Karaṇa.
1.10cd/ Furthermore, the matters pertaining to the horā, along with birth, journeys, and marriages, have been explained previously in detail.
Having set aside questions and counter-questions, digressions in discourse, matters of little utility,
and the conjunctions of planets, as well as all trivialities, I shall explain the essential meaning with its full significance.
Chapter on the Yearly Sūtra:
Now, therefore, we shall explain the Sūtra of the Yearly [Astronomer].
In this regard, the yearly [astronomer] should be of noble birth, pleasing to behold, modest in dress, truthful in speech, free from envy, and impartial.

His bodily joints were well-knit and developed; he was complete in all parts, with beautiful hands, feet, nails, eyes, chin, teeth, ears, forehead, eyebrows, and head; he possessed a magnificent physique and a deep, noble voice.
For generally, both virtues and defects follow the form of the body.

2. (2) In that regard, the qualities [of the teacher] are as follows: he is pure, skillful, bold, eloquent, possessed of quick-wittedness, knowledgeable of place and time, virtuous, not timid before an assembly, not to be overcome by fellow students, dexterous, free from vices, proficient in the rites of pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), and sorcery (*abhicāra*), as well as in bathing and spells (*vidyā*), devoted to the worship of the wise, observances (*vrata*), and fasting, having produced power through independent wonders, and speaking only when questioned.

Except by divine providence, one may become a knower of the meaning of the treatises on planetary mathematics (*gaṇita*), compendiums (*saṃhitā*), and horoscopy (*horā*). Among these, in the five established systems (*siddhāntas*)— namely those of Pauliśa, Romaka, Vāsiṣṭha, Saura, and Paitāmaha— there is [the calculation of] the yuga,
year, solstice, season, month, fortnight, day-and-night, watch (*yāma*), hour (*muhūrta*), *nāḍī*, *vināḍī*, breath (*prāṇa*), *truṭi*, and the various subdivisions beginning with *truṭi*.
He is the knower of time and the field;
he is one who understands the causes for the occurrence of intercalary months and omitted days among the four measures of time— the solar, the civil, the sidereal, and the lunar—
and who discerns the commencement and cessation of the lords of the sixty-year cycle, the yugas, the years, the months, the days, and the hours.
2. (6) He is skilled in demonstrating the suitability or unsuitability of the solar and other systems of measurement, whether they be similar or dissimilar;

(7) and despite differences in established doctrines (*siddhānta*), he is an expert in understanding the causes of the swift, slow, southern, northern, apogee, and perigee motions of the sun and other planets through direct observation—such as the occurrence of the equinoctial line at the end of the solstices (*ayana*) and the rising of degrees—and through the correspondence between shadow, water-clocks, visual observation, and calculation.

2.(9) He is skilled in the eclipses of the sun and moon, including the timing of their commencement and release, the cardinal directions, the duration, the obscuration, the color, and the prognostications; as well as future planetary conjunctions and conflicts. 2.(10) He is proficient in the individual revolutions of the planets, the measurement of their celestial orbits (*yojana-kakṣyā*), and the determination of the *yojanas* for each respective sphere. 2.(11) He is expert in the calculations of space and time, such as the revolution and configuration of the terrestrial sphere and the stellar mansions (*bhagaṇa*), the gnomon (*akṣa*), the plumb line (*avalambaka*), the diameter of the day, the half-ascensional difference (*cara-dala*), the time, the rising of the zodiacal signs, shadows, the calculation of *nāḍīs*, and so forth.

2.(12) One who knows the tantras becomes a speaker whose essence of speech is produced by the realization of various challenges, questions, and distinctions; he is like gold that has been further purified through the processes of rubbing on a touchstone, heating, and refining—so too is the speaker of this scripture [which is like gold] when it has been thoroughly cleansed.
And it is said:
2.01ab/ He does not cause [the meaning] to be understood when it is obstructed, nor does he answer even a single question when asked;
2.01cd/ nor does he explain it to his disciples—how can such a person be known as one who knows the meaning of the treatise?
2.02ab/ A text that has one meaning and the ignorant author who composes it otherwise—
2.02cd/ that man, having approached his grandfather, praises him with the manner of a courtesan.

2.03ab/ When the treatise is thoroughly understood, when the ascendant is known through the shadow and the water-clock (ghaṭīyantra), and when the meaning of the horās is firmly established, the speech of the astrologer is never barren. 2.03cd/ [The speech of the teacher is not fruitless.]
2.04a Even a man crossing the ocean might, by the power of the wind's velocity, sometimes reach the far shore;
2.04b but not so [the shore] of this great ocean known as Time and the Person (kālapuruṣa).
2.04d Even one who is not a seer might perhaps reach the further shore even with the mind.

2.(13) Furthermore, in the *Horāśāstra*, there is the inclusion of the strengths and weaknesses of the planets regarding the signs (*rāśi*), periods (*horā*), decans (*dreṣkāṇa*), ninth-parts (*navāṃśaka*), twelfth-parts (*dvādaśabhāga*), and thirtieth-parts (*triṃśadbhāga*);

the determination of the various types of planetary strength through direction (*dik*), position (*sthāna*), time (*kāla*), and motion (*ceṣṭā*); the inclusion of [the analysis of] nature (*prakṛti*), elements (*dhātu*), substances (*dravya*), caste (*jāti*), and actions (*ceṣṭā*);

and [the treatment of] conception (*niṣeka*), the time of birth (*janmakāla*), causing forgetfulness (*vismāpana*), prognostication (*pratyayādeśa*), sudden death (*sadyomaraṇa*), the allotment of lifespan (*āyurdāya*), major and minor periods (*daśā-antardaśā*), the *aṣṭakavarga*, royal yogas (*rājayoga*), lunar yogas (*candrayoga*), dual-planetary yogas (*dvigrahādiyoga*), and the *nābhasa* yogas, etc.

And the fruits of the yogas, the observation of the nature of the physical basis (*āśrayabhāva*), the points of departure (*niryāṇa*), the movements (*gati*), and the signs of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness at the time of questions; the [astrological factors for] rites such as marriage; and furthermore, in relation to military expeditions (*yātrā*): the lunar day (*tithi*), the day (*divasa*), the karaṇa, the asterism (*nakṣatra*), the muhūrta, the ascendant (*vilagna*), the yoga, bodily tremors, dreams, victory-baths, planetary sacrifices (*grahayajña*), communal offerings (*gaṇayāga*), the fire-linga, the gestures of elephants and horses, the rumors and activities of the army, the planets, the six measures of policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), the means (*upāya*), auspicious and inauspicious omens (*śakuna*), the encampment of the troops, and the types of terrain.
"The employment of fiery spies, secret agents, envoys, and forest-dwellers at the appropriate time, as well as the means for seizing an enemy's fort—this has been stated by the teachers.
It is as if spread throughout the world, as if inscribed, and as if poured into the heart of the intellect. (2.05ab)
2.05cd/ For one whose treatise is accompanied by its constituent parts (*sabhagaṇa*), his instructions are not fruitless.
2.(15) And he becomes one who has mastered the *saṃhitā* and is a contemplator of fate (astrologer).
2.(16) In this regard, these are the topics of the *saṃhitā*:

2.(17.1) the movements of the planets beginning with the Sun, and among those, [the analysis] by means of their natural and modified states, dimensions, color, rays, luster, configuration, setting, rising, paths, deviations from the path, retrograde motion, direct motion, conjunctions with lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), and the courses of the planets, and so forth.
The movement of Agastya in various regions according to the division of the asterisms and the tortoise diagram;
the movement of the Seven Sages; and the planetary divisions.

The array of constellations, the conjunctions of planets, planetary battles, planetary meetings, the results of planetary rain-showers, the characteristics of the womb, and the yogas of Rohiṇī, Svātī, and Āṣāḍhā.

Immediate rainfall; the blooming of flowers and creepers; halos surrounding the sun and moon; portents such as the *parigha* meteor; winds; meteors; conflagrations in the quarters; earthquakes; the colors of the twilight (*saṃdhyārāga*); cities of the Gandharvas; dust storms; thunderbolts; the value of offerings (*argha*); the growth of crops; the staff of Indra (*indravajra*); the rainbow; the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*); the science of bodily marks (*aṅgavidyā*); the science of crows (*vāyasavidyā*); the inner wheel (*antaracakra*); the wheel of wild animals (*mṛgacakra*); the wheel of dogs (*śvacakra*); the wheel of wind (*vātacakra*); the characteristics of palaces; the characteristics of images; their consecration (*pratiṣṭhāpana*); the life-span of trees (*vṛkṣāyurveda*); the northern bolt (*udagārgala*); the lustration rite (*nīrājana*); the *khañjanaka* bird; and the pacification of portents (*utpātaśānti*).
The characteristics of peacocks, variegated blankets, swords, silk cloths, cocks, tortoises, cows, goats, horses, elephants, men, and women;
the consideration of the harem, the characteristics of baskets, the examination of shoes, the cutting of clothes, the handles of fly-whisks, beds, seats, and jewels;
the characteristics of lamps, and the auspicious and inauspicious signs based on tooth-sticks and so forth, as well as the general omens of the world.
For each individual and for each moment regarding the king, the astrologer must remain intent upon his task without distraction;
yet, it is not possible for him alone to discern the omens day and night. Therefore, the astrologer, being well-supported, should employ four other experts in that same field.
In that regard, one person should observe the eastern and southeastern directions;
another should observe the southern and southwestern directions; likewise, [others should observe] the western, northwestern, northern, and northeastern directions.
This is because omens such as the falling of meteors and so forth will quickly pass away.
The results [of these] arise from the perception of their shapes, colors, moisture, dimensions, and so forth, as well as from the influence of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and other factors.
One who is skilled in all the primary and secondary limbs [of astrology], and has reached the ultimate mastery of *horā* and calculation (*gaṇita*), [is a true astrologer]. 2.06ab.
2.06cd/ That king who does not pay honor goes to destruction.
2.07 Even those who have taken refuge in the forest, being free from the sense of "mine" and devoid of possessions,
even they inquire of one who is skilled in the movements of the luminaries.
Just as a night without a lamp, or as a sky without the sun, so a king who does not observe the year wanders like a blind man on a path.
2.09ab/ The muhūrta, lunar day, asterism, seasons, and likewise the two solstices—
2.09cd/ all these would indeed be without foundation if there were no astrologer.

2.10ab/ Therefore, a king who desires victory, fame, prosperity, enjoyments, and the highest good must employ a learned astrologer as his leader. 2.10cd/ [He must do so] by one who intensely seeks these very things.
2.11ab/ One who desires prosperity should not dwell in a country where the king does not follow the annual calendar (i.e., lacks regular administration).
2.11cd/ For where he acts as an eye, there no evil exists.
2.12ab/ And one who recites the *Sāṃvatsara* does not fall into the hells;
2.12cd/ the astrologer attains a firm station in the world of Brahmā.
2.13ab That twice-born man who knows this entire [work] both in its wording and in its meaning, 2.13cd shall be the first to eat at a *śrāddha*, honored as a purifier of the assembly.
2.14ab For the Yavanas are indeed Mlecchas; yet among them, this scripture remains perfectly established.
2.14cd / Even they are honored like sages; how much more so a twice-born man who knows the destiny of the gods?
One who has been commissioned based on reasons such as whispered instructions or the influence of sorcery,
and who is not consulted in all matters, is not a knower of fate.
2.16ab/ He who, without even knowing the science, claims the status of an astrologer—
2.16cd/ that sinful indicator of constellations should be known as a defiler of the assembly.
He who mocks one who has pointed out a constellation or made a prediction goes to the Andhatāmisra hell together with those who resemble the stars.
Just as there might be a vow made for a clod of earth at a city gate, so it is.
2.17cd/ Likewise, that instruction which is given to the ignorant is considered to be true.
One who has been appointed to a position of high office through favoritism, who delights in talk that interrupts his duties,
and who is intoxicated by only a fragment of the scriptures— such a person should be abandoned by a king.
2.19ab/ But he who correctly understands the Hōrā, Gaṇita,
and Saṃhitā [sections of astrology], 2.19cd/ he, being honored by the king, should be accepted by one who desires victory.

2.20ab/ A thousand elephants and four times as many horses do not accomplish what a single astrologer, who knows the proper place and time, can achieve. 2.20cd/ [A single astrologer, knowing the place and time, achieves that which they do not.]
2.21ab/ Bad dreams, evil thoughts, harmful sights, and wicked deeds—
2.21cd/ these quickly go to destruction upon hearing the discourse of the Moon.

Neither the father, nor the mother, nor kinsmen, nor friends of the king desire his welfare as much as a trusted astrologer who knows the divine signs does, for the sake of increasing his own fame and that of the king together with his army.
Chapter 3: On the Motion of the Sun.
3.01ab: From the midpoint of Āśleṣā, the sun’s southern and northern solstices begin with Dhaniṣṭhā.
3.01cd: Surely this must have been so at some time, as it was stated in the ancient treatises.
3.02ab/ At present, the sun’s solstice begins with Cancer, and the other begins with Capricorn.
3.02cd/ The absence of what was stated is a modification; its manifestation is through direct observation and examination.
3.03ab/ By piercing a distant mark at sunrise or even at sunset, [one determines the north];
or by the marks of the entry and exit of the shadow upon a large circle for the thousand-rayed sun.
3.04ab/ Having not reached Capricorn, the Sun, turning back, destroys the southern region along with Yama.
3.04cd/ And having not reached Cancer, turning back, it destroys the northern region along with Indra.
Having passed the northern course and turned back, the sun brings security and the growth of crops;
likewise, when established in its natural state, it does so, but when its course is distorted, it causes fear.
3.06ab/ Except for the Tvaṣṭṛ-parvan, he makes the solar disc devoid of light.
3.06cd/ He destroys seven kings and the people through weapons, fire, and famine.
3.07ab/ There are thirty-three comets known as the Tāmasakīlakas, which are the sons of Rāhu.
3.07cd/ Having observed them according to their color, position, and shape when they appear in conjunction with the Sun, one should declare the results.
3.08ab/ And those [planets] situated in the solar disc produce evil results, while the benefics [situated] in the lunar disc [produce good].
3.08cd/ Even when situated in the moon's disc, the malefics take the forms of crows, headless trunks, and weapons.
3.09ab/ When these [planets] rise, the signs [of their influence] are turbid water, a sky shrouded in dust,
and a fierce wind that crushes mountains and tree-tops and carries pebbles.
3.10ab/ Trees bear fruit out of season, wild animals and birds appear agitated, and there are portents such as the burning of the quarters.
3.10cd/ Furthermore, in such a time, calamities such as thunderclaps and earthquakes occur.

3.11ab/ If the appearances of Śikhin, Kīlaka, and Rāhu do not have separate fruits [of their own], 3.11cd/ then one should declare the fruit of these, such as Ketu and the others, to be the same as that of their rising.
3.12ab/ In whichever region the [planets] situated in the solar disc become visible,
3.12cd/ in that very region the calamities of kings are to be recognized.
3.13 Even sages, their bodies withered by hunger and having abandoned the practice of righteous conduct,
come to foreign lands with great difficulty, their hair and hands devoid of flesh.
3.14ab/ Those whose wealth has been plundered by thieves, with eyes half-closed due to long-drawn sighs;
3.14cd/ being virtuous, their bodies are exhausted, and their vision is obstructed by tears born of grief.
3.15ab/ Emaciated and full of loathing, men oppressed by their own king or by a foreign army,
3.15cd/ proclaim their own king’s conduct as a deed committed in the past [or, according to another reading, as something previously rejected].
Even when clouds have formed within the womb [of the sky], they do not release abundant water;
rivers flow with diminished volume, and crops grow only here and there.
3.17ab/ When the Sun is situated in Daṇḍa, there is death for the king; in Kavandhasaṃsthāna, there shall be fear of disease.
3.17cd/ In Dhvāṅkṣa, there is fear of thieves; and when the Sun is in Kīlaka, there is famine.
3.18ab/ Pierced by [planets] in the form of royal insignia, such as the umbrella, banner, chowrie, and so forth, [the native becomes] a king.
3.18cd/ The Sun, when pierced by sparks, smoke, and so forth, causes him to become someone other than a king, while [pierced by] others, he destroys his people.
3.19ab/ One such [halo] causes famine; two or more lead to the destruction of the king.
3.19cd/ When the sun is pierced by these [halos] which are white, red, yellow, or black, it destroys [the people] corresponding to those colors.
3.20ab/ And since those great portents are seen to have arisen from the solar disc,
3.20cd/ by that very region does fear come upon the worlds.
3.21ab/ A copper-colored sun with its rays pointing upward destroys the commander-in-chief. 3.21cd/ A yellow one kills the king's son, while a white one slays the domestic priest.
Alternatively, if the sun’s rays are variegated or smoky and cause the earth to be agitated,
and if it does not quickly discharge water due to the falling of thieves' weapons, [there will be famine].
In the cold season, the sun is coppery or tawny; in spring, it has the luster of turmeric or saffron;
in summer, it is pale golden in color; and in the rainy season, it is white.
3.24ab/ In autumn, it is auspicious when it has the luster of the interior of a lotus; in winter, it is praised when it resembles blood.
3.24cd/ In the rainy season, it is a bestower of fortune when it is glossy, even if it resembles all other seasons.

3.25ab/ A dry, white [halo] destroys Brāhmaṇas; one with a reddish appearance destroys Kṣatriyas. 3.25cd/ A yellow [halo] destroys Vaiśyas; a black one destroys those other than these; while a glossy one brings auspiciousness.
3.26ab/ In summer, the sun being red causes fear; in the rainy season, being black, it brings about drought. 3.26cd/ In winter, the sun being yellow brings about the fear of disease before long.
3.27ab/ When its body is pierced by the rainbow of the gods, the thousand-rayed sun causes conflict with kings;
3.27cd/ but when its radiance is clear during the rainy season, it immediately brings rain.
3.28ab/ During the rainy season, one that has the luster of a *śirīṣa* flower brings rain immediately.
3.28cd/ One resembling a peacock feather does not produce water for twelve years.
3.29ab/ When the sun is dark-colored, there is danger from insects; when it resembles ashes, they declare there is danger from a foreign army.
3.29cd/ For whichever lunar mansion is pierced by a crack, the destruction of the king belonging to that [mansion] occurs.
3.30ab/ When the sun is situated in the vault of the sky resembling the blood of a hare, battles occur.
3.30cd/ If it resembles the moon, there is the death of a king, and another king soon arises.
3.31ab/ One resembling a jar causes death by hunger; one that is broken kills people [or kings]; one lacking luster brings fear.
3.31cd/ One in the form of an archway destroys the city; one resembling an umbrella leads to the destruction of the country.
3.32ab/ When the sun is trembling and rough, battles resemble a banner or a bow;
3.32cd/ if there is a black streak upon the sun, then the minister slays the king.
3.33ab/ When meteors, thunderbolts, and lightning strike the sun as it stands at either its rising or setting;
3.33cd/ one should know that there will then be the death of the king and the accession of another ruler.
3.34ab/ If the sun is surrounded by a halo every day at both twilights,
or if it sets red and rises red, it brings about another king.
3.35ab/ Covered by clouds resembling weapons during both twilights, it portends war;
3.35cd/ And appearing in forms like deer, buffaloes, birds, donkeys, and young camels, it brings fear.
3.36ab/ From the intense heat of the sun's rays, a constellation suffers great affliction;
3.36cd/ yet it subsequently becomes pure, like gold purified by the heat of fire.

3.37ab/ The sun-like comet (pratisūrya) causes drought when situated in the north; the water-causing one (jalakṛt), when situated in the south; and the wind-causing one (anilakṛt), when situated in both places.
3.37cd/ When situated above, it brings fear of water; when below, it destroys the king and the people.
If the sun, its body reddened by harsh dust, appears in the sky like blood, it will soon bring about the end of kings; or if it is black,
variegated, blue, and harsh, it causes the slaughter of people.
And at the onset of night and dawn, by the terrifying cries and sounds of birds and wild beasts.
3.39ab/ With a stainless body, a non-crooked orb, and clearly manifest, vast, pure, and long rays;
3.39cd/ Bearing an unaltered physical form, complexion, and marks, the sun brings auspiciousness to the world.
Chapter 4: On the Motion of the Moon 4.01ab.
Of the moon, which is always situated below the sun, one half becomes white by the rays of the sun;
4.01cd. the other half is dark due to its own shadow, like that of a water-jar placed in the sunlight.
The rays of the sun, concentrated in the moon which consists of water, dispel the nocturnal darkness, just as rays reflected within the surface of a mirror dispel the darkness inside a house.
Just as the moon, when leaving the solar orb, is followed by its white light from behind,
so too does the rising of the moon shine forth starting from below due to the influence of the sun.

4.04ab. Thus, day by day, due to its specific position relative to the sun, there is an increase in the whiteness of the moon. 4.04cd. This occurs in the afternoon on the western side, like [the light on] a water-jar. 4.05ab. The cool-rayed one [appears] when it has arrived at the region of Indra (Jyeṣṭhā) and the two Āṣāḍhās.
4.05cd/ To the south, it brings destruction to seeds, aquatic creatures, and forests, and causes fear of fire.
4.06ab/ When the Moon passes through Viśākhā and Anurādhā by its southern side, it is malefic.
4.06cd/ But when it passes through the middle of Pitrya (Maghā) and Viśākhā, it is auspicious.
4.07ab/ Six [nakṣatras] are future from Pauṣṇa (Revatī), and twelve from Raudra (Ārdrā) are joined with the middle [moon].
4.07cd/ The nine constellations beginning with Jyeṣṭhā are joined after the moon has passed them.
4.08ab/ When the horns are slightly elevated and there is breadth in the shape of a boat, it is so described.
4.08cd/ In that case, there is suffering for the boatmen, but there is welfare for all the world.
4.09ab/ If it is raised by half [a cubit], there is a plough-shaped mark; there is suffering for those who depend upon it.
4.09cd/ But if it is so without cause, there is affection for kings and an abundance of food.
4.10ab/ When the right tusk is half-raised, it is called the "defective plough" (duṣṭalāṅgala).
4.10cd/ It causes the death of the Pāṇḍya king and brings about the mobilization of armies.
4.11ab/ When the moon rises level [with the horizon], there shall be abundance of food, security, and rain, corresponding to the first day [of the lunar fortnight].
4.11cd/ When it rises like a staff, there is suffering for cattle, and the king here inflicts severe punishment.
4.12ab/ When the form is that of a bow, battles occur; however, when the string [is taut], victory belongs to them.
4.12cd/ A position known as "the yoke" (yuga), extending from south to north, portends an earthquake.
If the yoke alone is slightly elevated at its southern end, it is called "lying on its side";
it destroys caravan leaders and brings about a cessation of rain.
4.14ab/ If one horn of the moon should appear elevated while the other is turned downwards,
4.14cd/ being thus bent, it brings about famine and likewise causes the loss of cattle.
4.15ab/ A line that is uninterrupted on all sides and circular is called a *kuṇḍa*.
4.15cd/ In this [configuration], there is the loss of territory for regional kings (*māṇḍalika*) and sovereigns (*narapati*).
4.16ab/ Due to the absence of the previously mentioned positions, when the Moon is high in the north, it brings security, prosperity, and rain.
4.16cd/ But when the Moon is high in the south, it is indicated to cause famine and fear.
4.17ab/ Having seen the moon with only one horn, or else with its horn turned downward, or again as full and newly risen, one might fall from life. 4.17cd/ [One might fall from life.]
4.18ab/ The rule for its appearance has been stated; from this, the forms of the moon arise.
4.18cd/ A small [disc] is said to cause famine, while a large one brings about abundance.
4.19ab/ A comet with a middle-sized body is called Vajra; it brings fear of famine and causes agitation among kings.
4.19cd/ A comet shaped like a drum (mṛdaṅga) brings about security and abundance of food.
4.20ab/ A moon of broad form is to be known as leading to the increase of a king’s fortune;
4.20cd/ one that is thick brings about abundance of food, while one of slender form causes a dearth of grain.

4.21 When the Moon’s horn is struck by Mars, it destroys border regions and wicked kings; when struck by Yama (Saturn), it causes fear of weapons and famine; when struck by Mercury, it causes drought and scarcity;
when struck by Jupiter, it kills eminent kings; and when struck by Venus, it kills minor kings.
4.21d This result caused by the planets is curable during the bright fortnight; during the dark fortnight, it follows the stated tradition.
Divided by Śita, [the army] marched against the Magadhas, Yavanas, and Pulindas;
the Nepālas, Bhṛṅgis, Marukacchas, Surāṣṭras, and Madras;
and the Pañcālas, Kaikayas, Kulūtakas, and Puruṣādās.
It shall destroy even the people of Uśīnara for seven months.

4.23ab/ The moon, when conjoined with Jupiter, should scorch the Gāndhāras, Sauvīrakas, Sindhus, Kīras, grains, mountains, and the lords of the Draviḍas; 4.23cd/ as well as the twice-born and the ten months.

He shall slay the Trigarta kings along with their mounts, the Mālavas, the Kaulindas— the preeminent among the hosts— then the Śibis and the kings of Ayodhyā; he shall also slay the lords of the Kauravas, Matsyas, and Śuktyas, as well as the foremost of the nobility.
4.24d When the Moon has entered the sign of Mars, [the lifespan] is six months according to the Aryā rule.
The Moon, its orb pierced by the Sun, shall slay the Yaudheyas, the ministers, the Kauravas, the Prāgīśas, and the Arjunāyanas through affliction for ten months.
4.26ab/ The son of the Moon (Mercury) afflicts the Magadhas, Mathurā, and the banks of the Veṇā river.
4.26cd/ One should declare that the Kṛtayuga has begun elsewhere if [Mercury] emerges after piercing the Moon.
If the Moon is pierced by Ketu, it destroys security, health, and abundance;
it shall cause the destruction of those who live by weapons and bring great suffering to thieves.
4.28ab/ When the moon, already eclipsed, is struck by a meteor, 4.28cd/ then the king for whom [the moon] was situated at birth is struck down.
4.29ab/ Resembling ashes, rough, with a reddish form, cold-rayed, and deprived of its beams;
4.29cd/ dark-brown in body, cracked, or throbbing—it portends fear of famine, war, disease, and thieves.
4.30ab/ The moon, as white as frost, jasmine, water-lily, and crystal, has been raised high by the Daughter of the Mountain as if with great effort;
4.30cd/ that which shall appear for my welfare at night will bring welfare to the world.
4.31ab When the bright fortnight has begun to wax, the Brahmin and Kṣatriya castes increase, as do the subjects.
4.31cd When it wanes, there is decline; when it is equal, there is equality; and during the dark fortnight, all these results occur in the opposite manner.

4.32 If, white as a garland of night-lotuses and lotus stalks, the cool-rayed moon waxes or wanes according to the rule of the lunar days, yet maintains its unaltered course, orb, and conjunction with the rays, it brings victory to men.
Chapter 5: On the Motion of Rāhu.
5.01ab: It is said that this head of the Asura, though severed due to its extraordinary taste for nectar, 5.01cd:
was not abandoned by its vital breaths; some declare that it attained the status of a planet.
5.02ab/ It is said that the orb of the moon is not seen in the sky because of its blackness;
5.02cd/ except at the time of the new moon, due to the granting of a boon by the Lotus-born One.
5.03ab. Others teach that [Rāhu] has the form of a serpent, with its body divided into a head and a tail.
5.03cd. Others describe it as formless, consisting of darkness, and known by the name Saiṃhikeya.

5.04ab/ If Rāhu is corporeal and possesses motion, and if he is spherical in shape, how can he, whose movement is fixed, seize [the Sun and Moon] when they are separated by half the zodiac? 5.04cd/ [How does he seize them] when they are obstructed by half the circle of the asterisms?
5.05ab/ If its movement is indeed unrestricted, how can it be apprehended by number?
5.05cd/ Why does it not grasp [the object] from within, rather than through what are called its tail and mouth?
5.06ab/ But if, in the form of a lord of serpents, he seizes [the sky] with his tail or his mouth;
5.06cd/ why then does he not conceal the half of the stellar sphere situated between his mouth and his tail?
5.07ab/ If there should be two Rāhus when the moon has been eclipsed, or at its setting or rising;
5.07cd/ then the sun also is seen to be eclipsed by another [Rāhu] moving in the same path as that one.
5.08ab/ During its own eclipse, the moon enters the shadow of the earth; during the sun’s eclipse, the moon enters the sun.
5.08cd/ Therefore, the commencement of the eclipse occurs first for the moon from the west, and for the sun from the eastern half.
5.09ab/ Just as the clear shadow of a tree becomes long and extended on one side,
5.09cd/ so too, night after night, does it happen for the sun due to the obstruction of the earth.
5.10ab/ If the moon is in the seventh lunar mansion from the sun and has not yet passed to the north or south [of it], 5.10cd/ then the moon, facing eastward, enters the shadow of the earth.
5.11ab/ The moon, situated below, obscures the sun like a cloud when it has come together behind it.
5.11cd/ Therefore, the solar eclipse appears variously in different regions according to the observer's perspective.
The obscuration of the moon is great, and therefore its horns appear blunt when half-concealed;
that of the sun is small, and for this reason the sun appears with sharp horns.
5.13ab/ Thus has the cause of eclipses been described by the teachers who possess divine vision. 5.13cd/ It is the true nature of the scriptures that Rāhu is not the cause in this matter.
5.14ab/ That asura Rāhu—this boon was commanded for him by Brahmā: 5.14cd/ "At the time of an eclipse, you shall receive nourishment from the portion of the oblation offered to you."
5.15ab/ At that time, Rāhu is figuratively said to be present there; 5.15cd/ likewise, in calculation, the north-south motion of the Moon is also treated as such.

5.16ab/ By no means whatsoever is the perception [of a planet] known through its signs; for these signs occur even at other times, appearing as portents. 5.16cd/ They manifest even at other times, taking the form of omens.
5.17ab/ It is said that an eclipse cannot occur when there is a conjunction of five planets.
5.17cd/ Furthermore, the analogy of oil on water on the eighth lunar day should not be considered by the wise in this context.

5.18ab/ From the depression (avanati) of the sun, the eclipse and the direction are to be known; from the depression and the deflection (valana), the time [of the end of the eclipse] is determined. 5.18cd/ These have been explained by me in the Karaṇa [section] as occurring at the conclusion of the lunar day (tithi).
5.19ab/ The seven presiding deities of the parvas increase by six months in succession:
5.19cd/ They are to be known as Brahmā, Candra, Indra, Kubera, Varuṇa, Agni, and Yama.
5.20ab/ Under Brāhma, there is an increase in Brahmins, cattle, and prosperity, as well as security, health, and an abundance of crops.
5.20cd/ Similarly, under Saumya, there is the same, though with suffering for the learned and a lack of rain.
5.21ab. In the region of Indra (the east), there will be conflict with kings, a loss of autumnal crops, and no security.
5.21cd. In the region of Kubera (the north), there will be the destruction of wealth for the masters of riches, yet there will be an abundance of food.
5.22ab/ The Vāruṇa [wind] is inauspicious for the lord of the earth, but for others it brings security and an increase in crops.
5.22cd/ The Āgneya wind, known as Mitra, brings about the growth of crops, health, fearlessness, and water.
5.23ab/ It brings about the realm of Yama, drought, famine, and the destruction of crops.
5.23cd/ Whatever follows this is inauspicious; such a lunar day (parvan) brings hunger, death, and drought.
5.24ab/ When the lunar node (parvan) occurs outside its proper time, there is miscarriage of embryos and an outbreak of weapons.
5.24cd/ If it occurs too early, there is the loss of flowers and fruits, danger, and the destruction of crops.
5.25ab/ The result for times that are deficient or excessive has been stated because it is seen in the ancient treatises.
5.25cd/ For one who knows clear calculation, the time does not become otherwise in any way whatsoever.
5.26ab/ If there is an eclipse of both the sun and the moon in a single month, then the rulers of the earth,
5.26cd/ through the agitation of their own forces, go to destruction, and there is an excessive outbreak of weapons.
5.27ab/ When [the moon] rises or sets eclipsed, it brings about the destruction of autumnal grain and the lord of the earth.
5.27cd/ When both [lunar and solar eclipses] are total, they cause famine and pestilence, especially when aspected by malefic planets.

5.28ab / When half-risen and eclipsed, [the sun] destroys the deceitful and all sacrifices. 5.28cd / When risen at an improper time (*ayugābhyudita*), it destroys those who live by the sacred fires, those distinguished by their virtues, Brahmins, and those in the stages of life (*āśrama*).
5.29ab/ Farmers, heretics, merchants, Kṣatriyas, and army commanders [are affected] in the second portion.
5.29cd/ Artisans, Śūdras, and Mlecchas, along with their attendants, [are affected] in the third portion of the sky.

5.30ab. At midday, it destroys the king and the central region; the price of grain is auspicious. 5.30cd. In the fifth degree of its course, it kills grass-eaters, ministers, women of the inner apartments, and Vaiśyas.
5.31ab. In the sixth degree, it destroys women and Śūdras; at the time of setting, it destroys bandits and border regions.
5.31cd/ In whichever tenth-part (khāṃśa) liberation occurs, there is auspiciousness for those [planets] previously mentioned.

5.32ab. Rāhu, when seen in the northern course, destroys the twice-born and kings; in the southern course, he destroys Vaiśyas and Śūdras. 5.32cd. When seen in the north and so forth, moving clockwise, he destroys the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes.
5.33ab Standing in the intermediate directions, it portends the destruction of barbarians, marching armies, and those devoted to the sacrificial fire.
5.33cd Moving southward, it destroys aquatic creatures and elephants; moving northward, it is inauspicious for cattle.
5.34ab/ When the Daitya has arrived, he makes the earth filled with water in the east.
5.34cd/ In the west, he is indicated as causing the destruction of farmers, servants, and seeds.
5.35ab/ The Pāñcālas, Kaliṅgas, Śūrasenas, Kāmbojas, Uḍras, Kirātas, and those who subsist by the use of weapons;
5.35cd/ and those who live by the profession of fire—these suffer affliction when [the Sun] is situated in Aries.
5.36ab/ Cowherds, cattle, and then the cattle-owners, as well as those men who have attained high status;
5.36cd/ these suffer affliction when the Sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, or when the Moon is eclipsed by Vṛṣa.

5.37ab/ In Gemini, there are excellent women, kings, and royal mothers who are powerful and skilled in the arts; 5.37cd/ those born on the banks of the Yamunā, along with the Bāhlikas, the Matsyas, together with the people of Suhma.
In the Karkaṭa yoga, he afflicts the Ābhīras, Śabaras, Pahlavas, Mallas, Matsyas, Kurus, Śakas,
Pañcālas, and Vikalas, and he also destroys their food.

5.39ab. In Leo, [the Moon] destroys kings who resemble monarchs, those associated with the Pulinda tribes, the Mekalas, and forest-dwelling creatures. 5.39cd. But in the sixth sign, it destroys those devoted to agriculture, poetry, writing, and song, as well as the regions of Aśmaka, Tripura, and Śāli.
5.40ab/ The merchants from Tulādhara, Avantī, Aparānta, Daśārṇa, Maru, and Kacchapa;
5.40cd/ And those from Alinī, Udumbara, Madra, and Cola, along with the Drumas, the Yaudehas, the Viṣas, and the Āyudhīyas.
5.41ab/ In the Dhanvin [nakṣatra], one should slay the best ministers, excellent horses, the Videhas, the Mallas, the Pañcālas, physicians, and merchants who are skilled in uneven weapons.
5.41cd/ But in the Mṛga [nakṣatra], one should slay fish, ministers, families, low-born men, those skilled in spells and medicines, and elderly soldiers.
5.42ab. When Saturn enters Aquarius, it destroys those dwelling in the mountains, the westerners, the carriers of burdens, thieves, Ābhīras, Daradas, Āryas, Siṃhapurakas, as well as the Barbaras.

5.42cd. When it enters Pisces, it brings misfortune to those living on the seashore, those who deal in oceanic products, forest-dwellers, the wise, and those who subsist upon water; one should declare these results according to the instructions of the Kūrma[-vyūha].
5.43ab/ Leftward, rightward, licking, swallowing, obstructing, crushing, and ascending;
5.43cd/ Sniffed, middlemost, darkness, and the final—these are the ten types of swallowing.

5.44ab/ When the darkness moves to the left, the world becomes flooded with water, joyful, and free from fear; 5.44cd/ when it moves to the right, there is the destruction of subjects through the oppression of kings and thieves.
If that circle, which dispels darkness, is licked all around by a tongue,
then the earth there will have abundant water and all living beings will be filled with joy.
5.46ab/ When one-third, one-quarter, or even one-half [of the asterism] is seized, it is called "Devouring" (grasana).
5.46cd/ There is loss of wealth for the prosperous king, and suffering for the flourishing regions.
5.47ab/ Having grasped it at its extremities, one should remain with it condensed in the center as darkness.
5.47cd/ That is to be known as *nirodha* (cessation), which brings joy to all beings.
5.48ab. "Crushing" (*avamardana*) means that having completely covered [the enemy], if it remains for a long time;
5.48cd. then, like a mass of darkness, it destroys the principal kings and the principal regions.
5.49ab/ If, when an eclipse has occurred, darkness is seen again after having been momentarily covered;
5.49cd/ this is called "ascending," which, through mutual friction, brings fear to kings.
Like a mirror struck on one side by the breath of sighs mixed with tears, that [cloud] should be seen as "smelled"; it brings about abundant rain and the prosperity of the world.
If the disk, free from darkness, enters into the central darkness on all sides,
it causes the destruction of the central region and brings fear of abdominal diseases.

5.52ab/ In the border regions there will be an abundance [of grain], while in the center it will be very scarce; in the region called Tamontya, there will be fear of calamities regarding crops and fear of thieves. 5.52cd/ [In that same region,] there will be fear of thieves.
5.53ab/ When Rāhu is white, one should predict security, abundance of food, and affliction for the Brāhmaṇas.
5.53cd/ When it is fire-colored, there is danger from fire and suffering for those who live by the sacrificial fire.

5.54ab. If [the comet] is green, there will be an abundance of disease and the destruction of crops by calamities. 5.54cd. If it is tawny-brown, there will be the swift destruction of mobile beings, barbarians, and then famine.
5.55ab/ When [the halo] corresponds to the color of the dawn rays, there will be famine, drought, and affliction to birds.
5.55cd/ If it is smoky-grey, one should predict security, abundance, and meager rainfall.
5.56ab/ When it has the luster of a dove, crimson, tawny, or dark brown, fear of famine is to be predicted.
5.56cd/ A dove-colored [fire] brings disease to the Śūdras, as does one that is black in color.
5.57ab/ Having the luster of a pure, wish-fulfilling gem, it portends the destruction of Vaiśyas and brings about an abundance of food.
5.57cd/ If it is radiant, there is danger from fire; if it has the appearance of red ochre, there will be wars.
5.58ab/ One should predict a plague when [the moon] is green like a blade of dūrvā grass or even yellowish-brown.
5.58cd/ Rāhu, resembling a pāṭala flower, brings about the fear of a thunderbolt.
5.59ab/ If it has the appearance of dust or blood, it portends the destruction of the Kṣatriyas and of rain.
5.59cd/ If it bears the form of the morning sun, a lotus, or a divine bow (a rainbow), it portends the wrath of weapons.
5.60ab/ When Mercury is seen eclipsed, it portends the depletion of ghee, honey, and oil for kings.
5.60cd/ Mars [portends] the ravage of battle, the fury of fire, and fear of thieves.
5.61ab/ Venus causes the crushing of crops and various afflictions upon the earth.
5.61cd/ Saturn brings about drought, famine, and fear of thieves.
Whatever inauspiciousness has been declared regarding the observation of a planet, whether caused by its birth [in a sign] or its eclipse,
that is pacified when observed by the preceptor of the gods, just as a blazing fire is extinguished by water.

5.63ab/ When [the moon] is eclipsed by the signs [of portents] in sequence, the eclipse recurs after an increase of six months. 5.63cd/ [These signs are] wind, the fall of meteors, dust, earthquakes, darkness, and the falling of thunderbolts.
5.64ab/ When the son of the Earth (Mars) is eclipsed, the people of Āvantika, those dwelling on the banks of the Kāverī and Narmadā,
and the arrogant lords of men are afflicted.
5.65ab/ The wise man destroys the inner altar, the Sarayū river, Nepal, the eastern ocean, and the Śoṇa river; 5.65cd/ as well as women, kings, warriors, and princes, along with the learned.
5.66ab/ When Jupiter enters a state of eclipse (conjunction), there is the destruction of learned men, kings, ministers, elephants, and horses;
5.66cd/ as well as for those dwelling on the banks of the Indus and those residing in the northern direction.
When Rāhu enters the son of Bhṛgu (Venus), the Dāśerakas, Kaikayas, and Yadheyas,
as well as the people of Āryāvarta, the Śibis, and the groups of female ministers, are afflicted.
5.68ab/ When Saturn is in the sign of Scorpio, the Marubhavas, Puṣkaras, Saurāṣṭrikas, Dhātus, Arbudas, and Antyajanās;
5.68cd/ as well as those dwelling in the Gomanta and Pāriyātra mountains, quickly meet their destruction.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, he shall afflict the Magadhas who subsist on fire, the eastern rulers, the Kośalas, the Kalmāṣas,
and the Kāśīs together with the Śūrasenas;
furthermore, like darkness, he shall swiftly slay the king of the Kaliṅga country along with his ministers and servants.
When this is seen, it produces the distress of the Kṣatriyas, yet it brings security accompanied by abundant food.
5.70ab/ He shall destroy the people of Kaśmīra, Kośala, and Puṇḍra, as well as the Mṛgas and those of Aparāntaka.
5.70cd/ He who destroys those who drink Soma brings good rain in the north, and creates security and abundance of food.

5.71ab. In the month of Pauṣa, there will be oppression upon the twice-born and the kṣatriya class; the Kukuras known as the Saindhavas and the Videhas shall go to ruin. 5.71cd. Furthermore, one should expect scant rain, fear, and famine in this year.
But in the month of Māgha, Rāhu afflicts those devoted to their mothers and fathers, those of the Vasiṣṭha lineage,
those intent on sacred study and dharma, elephants, horses,
and the people of Vaṅga, Aṅga, and Kāśī.
And it brings about rain, which is desired by the people of the agricultural class.
The festival in the month of Phālguna causes suffering for the Vaṅgas, Aśmakas, Avantikas, and Mekalas;
it also brings hardship to those skilled in dance, to excellent crops, to beautiful women, to archers, to the kṣatriyas, and to ascetics.
In Caitrī (the month of Caitra), however, [one should worship] those devoted to painting, drawing, and song;
those who live by their appearance, those skilled in the Vedas, and those whose trade is gold;
as well as the people of Pauṇḍra, Oḍra, Kaikaya, and Aśmaka.
5.74d Here, the god of the immortals, raining down various [precipitations], touches one with heat.
5.75ab/ During an eclipse in the month of Vaiśākha, cotton, sesame, and mung beans go to ruin.
5.75cd/ The Ikṣvākus, Yaudheyas, Śakas, Kaliṅgas, and those with floods (or calamities) suffer; however, there will be plenty of food in this [year].
5.76ab/ When Jupiter is in Jyeṣṭhā, the wives of kings and Brahmins, the crops, the rains, and great assemblies [perish]; 5.76cd/ as do gentle men and the hosts of Niṣādas joined with the Sālvas.
5.77ab/ During the full moon festival of Āṣāḍha, if there is an overflow from wells, embankments, or rivers, and if crops of fruits and roots perish;
5.77cd/ one should declare that the Gāndhāras, Kāśmīras, Pulindas, and Cīnas will be slain, and that there will be rain within this region.

5.78a If the planet rains in Śrāvaṇa, it shall destroy the people of Kaśmīra along with the Pulindas, Cīnas, and Yavanas, as well as those born in Kurukṣetra; 5.78b it shall also destroy the Gāndhāras together with the inhabitants of Madhyadeśa.
5.78c Having abandoned these aforementioned regions, it shall likewise destroy the Kāmbojas and the single-hoofed animals during the autumn.
Elsewhere, it makes the land filled with men who are joyful due to abundant food.
5.79a The Asura destroys the Kaliṅgas, Vaṅgas, Magadhas, and Surāṣṭras; 5.79b the Mlecchas, Suvīras, Daradas, and Aśmakas; 5.79c and he destroys the embryos of women.
5.79d When [the moon] enters Bhādrapada, it brings about abundance of food.

He shall slay the Kambojas, Cīnas, and Yavanas along with the Śalyahṛts, as well as the inhabitants of Bāhlīka and the banks of the Sindhu; likewise, he shall destroy the Ānartas, Pauṇḍras, Bhiṣajas, and the Kirātas.
When the Asura is seen in the month of Āśvayuja, it brings about abundant prosperity.
5.81ab/ The divisions of the jaw, the belly, and the anus; twice each for vomiting and digestion;
5.81cd/ and the splitting at the middle and the end—these are the ten liberations of the Moon and the Sun.
5.82ab. In the southeast, there is the departure of the Moon, known as the "Splitting of the Right Jaw.
5.82cd. There will be the destruction of crops, facial diseases, oppression by the king, and good rain.
5.83ab/ Or, if the left jaw is fractured toward the northeast, it portends danger to the king and princes.
5.83cd/ One should know that there will be disease of the mouth, fear of weapons, and yet an abundance of food.

5.84ab/ If there is a piercing of the right side of the belly by the right flank, there will be liberation. 5.84cd/ There will be suffering for the king’s sons, and enemies from the south will launch an attack.
5.85ab/ But if Rāhu is situated on the northern path, there is a division of the left side of the womb.
5.85cd/ For women, there is miscarriage, and the crops in that case are mediocre.
The two anal fissures are located in the southwest and northwest, on the right and left sides respectively.
Pain in the anus indicates little rain; however, if it occurs on both sides, there is the destruction of the queen, or specifically on the left side.
5.87ab/ Having made a hold with the eastern quarter, one should retreat even further toward the east.
5.87cd/ That is called *sañchardana*; it bestows security and abundant crops upon the world.
5.88ab. That [constellation] in which there is first a seizing and afterwards a falling away is called *jaraṇa*.
5.88cd. In that [constellation], people, agitated by the fear of hunger and weapons, seek refuge.
5.89ab/ If the light appears first in the middle, that is called "splitting in the middle" (madhyavidaraṇa).
5.89cd/ It causes internal strife, brings about an abundance of food, but does not cause excessive rain.
5.90ab/ At the borders there is great purity, while in the center there is darkness known as the "cracking of the ends.
5.90cd/ In this [period], there is the destruction of the region called the center and the failure of the autumn harvest.

5.91ab/ All these liberations should also be stated for the Sun; however, in this case, 5.91cd/ just as the eastern direction is assigned to the Moon, so too should the western direction be assigned to the Sun.
5.92ab/ If a fall of dust occurs within seven days after the release [of the comet], it causes the destruction of food supplies.
5.92cd/ Frost portends fear of disease, and an earthquake portends the death of a preeminent king.
5.93ab/ A meteor portends the destruction of the counselor, while clouds of various colors bring incomparable fear.
5.93cd/ Thunder indicates the destruction of the fetus, and lightning brings suffering from the king and fanged beasts.
5.94ab/ A halo portends suffering from disease; a flaming horizon brings fear of the king and danger from fire.
5.94cd/ A harsh and violent wind brings about fear arising from thieves.
A thunderclap, a rainbow, and a celestial staff portend fear of famine and the threat of foreign armies;
likewise, a battle between planets and the appearance of a comet signify war between kings.
5.96ab/ When the falling of rain occurs without alteration for seven days, a period of plenty is to be predicted.
5.96cd/ And whatever inauspiciousness arises from an eclipse, all that goes to destruction.

5.97ab/ If, at the end of the lunar fortnight, an eclipse of the sun should occur once the lunar eclipse has ceased; 5.97cd/ then there will be misfortune for the subjects and mutual enmity between husbands and wives.
5.98ab/ But if an eclipse of the moon is seen after an eclipse of the sun, O brahmins,
5.98cd/ then people become joyful and partakers of the fruit of many sacrifices.
Chapter 6: On the Movements of Mars.
6.01ab. If it forms a retrograde motion from its point of heliacal rising in the ninth, eighth, or seventh asterisms;
6.01cd. then that retrograde at rising causes heat and brings suffering to those who live by fire.
6.02ab/ When Mars is retrograde from the twelfth, tenth, or eleventh lunar mansion, there is a "tearful face" (aśrumukha) yoga.
6.02cd/ It vitiates flavors at its rising and causes diseases as well as drought.
6.03ab/ A serpent [rising] from the thirteenth or fourteenth asterism brings its results at sunset;
it causes distress from fanged beasts, serpents, and wild animals, yet ensures an abundance of food.
6.04ab/ When the face [of the moon] turns from the fifteenth to the sixteenth [tithi], it is called "Red-Faced" (rudhirānana).
6.04cd/ At that time, it brings about facial diseases along with fear, yet also results in an abundance of food.
6.05ab. From the seventeenth or even from the eighteenth [nakṣatra], the Asi-musala comet causes distress to bands of robbers. 6.05cd. It brings about drought accompanied by the fear of weapons.
If Mars, having risen in the asterism of Bhāgya (Pūrvaphalgunī), turns back toward Vaiśvadeva (Uttaraphalgunī),
or if it sets in Prājāpatya (Rohiṇī), it oppresses even the three worlds.
6.07ab/ When Venus, having risen in the asterism Śravaṇā, undergoes retrogression in Puṣya, it causes affliction to those consecrated on the head (anointed kings).
6.07cd/ It destroys the people arrayed in the direction of the asterism in which it rose.
If the Red One (Mars) traverses through the middle of Maghā, then King Pāṇḍya perishes; there is danger from the exertion of weapons and drought.
6.09ab/ If Mars, having pierced Maghā, pierces Viśākhā, he causes famine;
6.09cd/ he causes a terrible epidemic if, having pierced Rohiṇī, he passes through it.
6.10ab. When Mars moves to the south of Rohiṇī, it causes the obstruction of timely rain.
6.10cd. Or, if it smokes or possesses a crest [of flames], it shall destroy those dwelling in the Pāriyātra mountains.
When Mars moves through Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Mūla, the three Uttaras, and Jyeṣṭhā,
it causes the destruction of masses of clouds.
6.12ab/ The rising of the planets is auspicious when occurring in Śravaṇa, Maghā, Āditya (Pūrvaphalgunī), Hasta, and Mūla;
6.12cd/ and for Mars, it is auspicious in Ekapadā (Pūrvabhādrapadā), Aśvinī, Viśākhā, and Prajāpatya (Rohiṇī).

6.13 If the son of the Earth moves along the northern path, possessing a vast and stainless form, the color of the *kiṃśuka* and *aśoka* flowers, with clearly radiant rays, and a luster like that of molten copper;
He brings auspiciousness to the protectors of the earth and wins the hearts of the subjects.
Chapter 7: The Course of Mercury (Budhacārādhyāya) 7.01ab.
Mercury never rises free from portents.
7.01cd. It causes fear of water, fire, and wind, or else brings about the decrease or increase in the price of grain.
7.02ab/ Moving through Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Prajāpatya [U.prājāpatya], Indu, and Vaiśvadeva [K.viśvadaivāni],
7.02cd/ the son of the Moon (Mercury), crushing them, causes drought accompanied by the fear of disease.
7.03ab. When Mercury is situated in the asterisms beginning with Ārdrā and ending with Maghā, there is suffering for the people.
7.03cd. [This occurs] through the falling of weapons, fear of famine, disease, drought, and distress.
7.04ab/ Moving through the six constellations beginning with Hasta and afflicting them is inauspicious for cattle.
7.04cd/ It causes an increase in oil, liquids, and prices, and makes the earth abound in food.
7.05ab/ When Mercury, destroying the asterisms Ārdrā, Kṛttikā, Bhadrapadā-uttarā,
and Mṛgaśiras, 7.05cd/ causes the destruction of the bodily constituents of living beings.
When the son of the Moon (Mercury) transgresses the asterisms Āśvinī, Śatabhiṣaj, Mūla, and Revatī,
he causes injury to merchants, physicians, those who live by boats, aquatic creatures, and horses.
If the son of Indu (Mercury) should afflict even one of the three constellations beginning with Pūrvā,
while moving through the world, he brings fear of hunger, weapons, thieves, and disease.
7.08ab/ Prākṛta, vimiśra, saṃkṣipta, tīkṣṇa, yogānta, ghora, and pāpa—
7.08cd/ these are the seven destinies proclaimed with reference to the lunar mansions in the Parāśara-tantra.
7.09ab/ The Vāyavya, Yāmya, and Paitāmaha [asterisms] are known as Prākṛta, and the Bahulas are also so designated.
7.09cd/ The mixed course is declared to consist of Śaśi, Śiva, Pitṛ, and Bhujaga-daiva.
7.10ab/ In the abridged [list], Puṣya, Punarvasu, and the two Phalgunīs are included.
7.10cd/ Under Tīkṣṇā, there are the two Bhadrapadas, Śakra (Jyeṣṭhā), Aśvayuj (Aśvinī), and Pauṣṇa (Revatī).
The root [verses] state: "The end of Yoga, the two Āṣāḍhas, and the course of the Moon's son."
7.11cd / Ghorā, Śravaṇa, Tvaṣṭra, Vasudeva, and Vāruṇa likewise.
7.12ab/ It is called "Pāpā," as well as Sāvitra, Maitra, and that which has Śakra and Agni as its deities.
7.12cd/ He himself stated that the characteristic of the movement [of the moon] is determined by the days of rising and departure.
These are twenty-two (22), eighteen (18),
and eleven (11).
Of the Prakrits and the others.
In the Prākṛtagati, there is health, abundant rain, the flourishing of crops, and security;
in the Saṃkṣiptā and Miśrā, these effects are mixed; and in the others, they are the opposite.
7.15ab/ According to the opinion of Devala, these [paths] are the straight (ṛju), the very winding (ativakra), the winding (vakrā), and the deficient (vikalā).
7.15cd/ Five, four, two, and one days are assigned to the straight and the others respectively, as they are multiplied by six.
7.16ab/ A straight course is beneficial for living beings, whereas an excessively crooked course leads to ruin.
7.16cd/ A curved course brings fear of weapons, and a deformed one generates fear and disease.

7.17ab/ If Mercury rains during the months of Pauṣa, Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, Vaiśākha, or Māgha, it portends fear for the world; however, if he remains away from those regions, he brings about auspicious results.
If the slender crescent of the moon is seen during the month of Kārttika or Āśvayuja, it then brings about dangers from weapons, thieves, fire, disease, water, and hunger.
When the Moon has set, cities are besieged; when it has risen, those same cities attain liberation.
7.19cd/ Others, however, who are experts in that matter, say that when [the moon] has risen in the west, there is gain for those born in the east.
7.20ab/ Furthermore, Mercury is beneficial when it has the luster of gold, or the color of a parrot, or resembles the *sasyaka* gem;
it should be glossy in form and not light. 7.20cd/ In the opposite case, the son of the Moon (Mercury) does not bring about auspicious results.
Chapter 8: The Course of Jupiter (Bṛhaspati-cārādhyāya) 8.01ab/ That lunar mansion with which the minister of the Lord of Gods (Jupiter) rises,
8.01cd/ the year named after that [mansion] is to be declared according to the sequence of months.
The years beginning with Kārttika are associated with two asterisms starting from Āgneya (Kṛttikā) in successive order;
however, the fifth year, the penultimate year, and the final year each consist of three asterisms.
8.03ab/ There will be damage to carts, fires, those who depend on them, and cattle, as well as the outbreak of disease and weapons.
8.03cd/ However, there will be an abundance of red and yellow flowers during the Kārttika year.
In the Saumya year, there is drought; crops are destroyed by deer, mice, locusts, and birds;
there is fear of disease, and even among friends, enmity arises for kings.
In Pauṣa, the world performs auspicious deeds and kings cease their mutual hostilities;
the price of grain is two or three times [the usual rate], and rites for prosperity meet with success.
In the month of Māgha, there is an increase in the worship of ancestors, affection among all beings,
prosperity consisting of health, rain, grain, and wealth, as well as the acquisition of friends.
In the year of Phālguna, one should know that there will be security, rain, and crops here and there;
yet women will suffer misfortune, thieves will be powerful, and kings will be fierce.
8.08ab/ In Caitra, there is scant rain; food is dear, yet the kings are peaceful and mild.
8.08cd/ There is an increase in the treasury and grain, but there is suffering for those who possess beauty.
In Vaiśākha, the subjects, together with their king, are devoted to dharma, free from fear, and joyful;
there is the commencement of sacrificial rites and the ripening of all crops.

8.10ab/ In Jyeṣṭha, those distinguished by birth, family, wealth, and guilds, as well as kings who know the Dharma, are afflicted. 8.10cd/ And grains are affected, with the exception of *kaṅgu* and the *śamī* species.
In Āṣāḍha, crops ripen in some places while there is drought elsewhere;
security and prosperity are mediocre, and kings become distracted.
8.12ab. In the year of Śrāvaṇa, there is security, and the crops ripen properly.
8.12cd. Those who are minor heretics and those who are devoted to them are afflicted.
8.13ab/ In Bhādrapada, the vine-born [crops] reach maturity, as do the previous grains.
8.13cd/ No other grain will grow; there will be plenty in some places and danger in others.

8.14ab/ If rain falls incessantly in the month of Āśvayuja, the subjects will be joyful and there will be security. 8.14cd/ There will be an increase in the vital breath of all living beings and an abundance of food.
When Jupiter moves through the northern path, it brings about prosperity, health, abundance, and security;
when it moves through the southern path, the opposite occurs; and when it moves through the middle path, it yields middling results.
8.16ab. Moving through two signs in a year, it is auspicious and yields middling results;
8.16cd. if it should ever move for more than that, it destroys the crops.
8.17ab/ There is danger from fire if it is fire-colored; if yellow, disease; if dark, the onset of battle.
8.17cd/ If green, there is affliction from thieves; but if red, there is danger from weapons.
8.18ab. When Jupiter is seen by day with a smoky luster, there is drought and the death of the king.
8.18cd. When it is seen at night, large, spotless, and with bright stars, the subjects are well.
8.19a Rohiṇī and Kṛttikā constitute the body of the year; the two Āṣāḍhās are the navel.
8.19b The asterism of Sārpa (Āśleṣā) and that of the Pitṛs (Maghā) are the heart and the flower; from these, when pure, auspicious results follow.
8.19c If the body [asterisms] are afflicted by malefics, there is danger from fire and wind; if the navel [asterisms] are so afflicted, there is danger caused by hunger.
If [the moon] is in Puṣya, there is a loss of roots and fruits; furthermore, if it is in Hṛdaya, the destruction of the grain is certain.
8.20a Multiply the elapsed years since the time of Śakrendra by four; 8.20b having added [the result] to the Rudras (eleven), one should multiply them by four.
Having performed the addition, [proceed as follows].
Having added the time of Śakra and the kings obtained [from the previous calculation],
and having subtracted sixty regions, one should divide by sixty;
[the result gives] the Yugas beginning with Nārāyaṇa.
The remainders obtained [from the divisions] shall be the years in successive order.

8.22ab. Having added twelve separately for each year multiplied by nine, and having divided by four, one obtains the asterisms beginning with Vasudevatā and the remainder as the portion of the year. 8.22cd. [Thus one determines] the asterism and the remaining degrees constituting the year.

Viṣṇu, Surejya (Bṛhaspati), Balabhit (Indra), Hutāśa (Agni), Tvaṣṭṛ, and the lord of the Uttaraproṣṭhapadās; these are declared to be, in order, the lords of the yugas: Pitṛ, Viśvedeva, Soma, Śakra, Anala, Aśvin, and Bhaga.

8.24ab/ *Saṃvatsara* is Agni; *Parivatsara* is Arka, the one garlanded with cool rays (the Moon) and so forth; 8.24cd/ *Anuvatsara* is Prajāpati, and *Idvatsara* is the Lord of the Daughter of the Mountain (Śiva).
8.25ab/ In the first [month] there is rain at the beginning; in the second, it is said to have abundant water; in the third, it releases water later.
8.25cd/ That which is the fourth yields little water, and the fifth is said to be a year of scanty rain.
8.26ab/ The first four yugas have Viṣṇu, Indra, Jīva, and Anala as their presiding deities;
8.26cd/ one should know that the next four are middling, and the final four are inferior.

When Jupiter rises in the month of Māgha, having entered the first quarter of Dhaniṣṭhā, then that year, which precedes the sixty-year cycle by name, is called Prabhava; it brings welfare to all beings.

8.28ab / In some places there is drought, agitation from wind and fire, calamities, and diseases caused by phlegm; 8.28cd / nevertheless, when this *prabhava* year has begun, the people do not suffer such misery.
Therefore, the second [period] is designated as Vibhava; the third is Śukla, and beyond that is Pramoda.
These years—Prajāpati and so forth—are praised in ascending order, as are their respective fruits.
When the crops of rice, sugarcane, barley, and so forth have been fully ripened, when [the land] is freed from fears, and when hostilities have been pacified;
Then, the kṣatriya rules the earth, which is filled with joyful people and freed from the defects of the Kali age.

In the first age, [the periods] are Ādya, Aṅgiras, Śrīmukha, Bhāvasa, and Yuvan; in the second age, they are Dhātu and so forth. Five years are [assigned] in due order, three of which are recommended here, and two others are equal [in merit].
8.32ab. During the first three years, the goddess rains as much as desired, and the world is free from fear and disease.
8.32cd. Even during the final two years there is good rain; however, in this period, diseases and the onset of war occur.
8.33ab. In the Śākra yuga, the first is called Īśvara; they say the second year is Bahudhānya.
8.33cd. One should know Pramāthin, Vikrama, and then another, Vṛṣa, through the conjunction of Jupiter’s motion.

In an auspicious year, the first and second [planets] produce results that imitate those of the [previous] year for the subjects; however, the malefic Pramāthin and Vṛṣavikrama bestow both abundance and the fear of disease.
8.35ab/ And the first year of the fourth age, which they call Citrabhānu, is excellent; 8.35cd/ but the second, known by the name Subhānu, is middling, bringing disease and causing death.
8.36ab/ Thereafter, the king is a great rain-cloud that brings deliverance, and he is delighted by the increase of his crops.
8.36cd/ They declare the fifth period to be auspicious, characterized by the power of love and filled with festivities.
8.37ab. In the Tvaṣṭra yuga, the first year is said to be Sarvajit, while the other is indeed Sarvadhārī.
8.37cd. From that [Sarvadhārī], Virodhin, Vikṛta, and Khara are praised; here, the second [Virodhin] is for fear, while the remaining ones [are auspicious].
8.38ab/ Then Nandana, Vijaya, Jaya, and likewise Manmatha; after him is Durmukha.
8.38cd/ Among these, the first three pairs are auspicious; Manmatha yields equal results, while the other is inferior.
8.39ab/ In the seventh yuga, there shall be Hemalamba; thereafter Vilambi and Vikārin.
8.39cd/ Following that, Śarvarī is remembered, and then Plava is the fifth year according to the influence of Jupiter.
In the first year, there will be rain accompanied by many calamities and abundant winds;
in the second year, the crops will be meager and not well-watered. In the third and fourth years, there will be great distress, yet plenty of water.
If it is a *plava* [year], there will be famine; therefore, a *śobhana* [year] is excellent, as it brings abundant water.

In the Vaiśva yuga, the first year is called Śobhakṛt (the "Gladdening"), and the second is Śubhakṛt (the "Auspicious"). The third is Krodhī (the "Angry"), followed in sequence by Viśvāvasu and Parābhava.
8.42ab/ The first and the last years are pleasing to the subjects, while the third year brings many evils.
8.42cd/ The final two are equal; however, in the case of defeat, there is fire, suffering from weapons and disease, and danger to the twice-born and cattle.
In the ninth yuga-cycle, the first year is Plavaṅga, the next is Kīlaka, and after that is Saumya;
then Sādhāraṇa and Rodhakṛt—thus, the years named Kīlaka and Saumya are bestowers of auspiciousness.
8.44ab/ A monkey-year is difficult for subjects, characterized by a general scarcity of water and various calamities.
8.44cd/ Then, the fifth year, known as Rodhakṛt (the Obstructer), brings wonderful rain and an abundance of crops therein.

The tenth cycle, which has Indra and Agni as its presiding deities, begins with the first year known as Paridhāvī; following that, there shall be Pramadin and Vikrama, and thereafter the Rākṣasa and Anala years.
8.46ab/ In the *paridhāvin* [year], there is the destruction of the Middle Country, the loss of kings, scanty rain, and outbreaks of fire.
8.46cd/ In the year known as *pramādin*, people become indolent; there is civil unrest and the destruction of red flowers and seeds.
8.47ab. Vikrama, Tatpara, Sakalalokanandana, Rākṣasa, Kṣayakara, and Anala; 8.47cd. Among these, Rākṣasa produces summer grain, while Anala brings about the wrath of fire and pestilence.
In the eleventh [year], Piṅgala, Kālayukta, Siddhārtha, and Raudra indeed appear, as does Durmati.
In the first [year], however, there is heavy rain accompanied by thieves, along with labored breathing and a cough accompanied by trembling of the jaw.
8.49ab/ That which is appropriate for the time [of the year] possesses many virtues, whereas that known as Siddhārtha has many defects.
8.49cd/ Raudra is declared to be extremely fierce and destructive; he who is Durmati produces moderate rainfall.

8.50ab. When the Yuga is in the Bhāgya [asterism], the first [Yuga] known as Dundubhi brings about great abundance of crops. 8.50cd. Following that, the one known as Aṅgāra (or Udgārin) leads to the ruin of kings and brings irregular rainfall.
The third year is said to be Raktākṣa; in it there is danger caused by fanged beasts and diseases.
The fourth is Krodha, which produces great anger and leaves kingdoms empty through conflicts.
8.52a "Decline" refers to the final period of the final age; it causes great destruction.
8.52b It produces fear among the Brahmins, yet brings prosperity to the farmers. 8.52c Likewise, it brings increase to the Vaiśyas and Śūdras, as well as to those who seize the property of others.
8.52d All that was taught during the sixty-year cycle has been recounted here in brief.
8.53ab/ With matted locks of stainless rays, a massive form, and a luster like the white water-lily, the kunda flower, or crystal;
8.53cd/ if he, the teacher of the immortals, were not struck by the planets and remained on the path of truth, he would bring welfare to mankind.

Chapter 9: The Course of Venus. 9.01ab. The paths (vīthīs) beginning with Aśvinī are declared by some, in groups of three asterisms respectively, as being named Nāga, Gaja, Airāvata, Vṛṣabha, Go, Jaradgava, Mṛga, Aja, and Dahana.
In the Nāga [region], however, there are three asterisms—Pavana (Svāti), Yāmya (Bharaṇī), and Anala (Kṛttikā)—from the region of Pitāmaha (Jyeṣṭhā).
In Govīthī, there are Aśvinī, Pauṣṇa (Revatī), and the two Bhadrapadas.
9.03ab/ From the Śravaṇa [nakṣatra] onwards, three asterisms belong to Jāradgava; the three beginning with Anurādhā (Maitra) belong to Mṛga.
9.03cd/ Hasta, Viśākhā, and Citrā (Tvāṣṭra) belong to Aja; the two Aṣāḍhās belong to Dahana.
9.04ab. Three by three of these are situated respectively on the northern, middle, and southern paths.
9.04cd. Of those [nine], one each is situated to the north, middle, and south [of each group].
9.05ab. Others describe the paths of the streets as being situated according to the path of the asterisms (bhamārga).
9.05cd. Likewise, the stars of the constellations are situated to the south, north, and in the middle.

The northern path is said to begin with the asterism of Yāmya (Bharaṇī) and so forth; the middle path begins with Bhāgya (Pūrvaphalgunī) and so forth; and the southern path begins with Āṣāḍhā and so forth—thus have the paths been defined by some.
9.07ab/ Astrology is a scripture based on tradition; it is not for us to engage in dispute regarding it.
9.07cd/ Rather than attempting to judge it for ourselves, I shall state the opinion of the majority.
9.08ab/ When Venus has set or risen while situated in the northern paths (vīthīs), it brings about abundance of food and auspiciousness.
9.08cd/ In the middle paths, it yields middling results; in the southern paths, its results are miserable.
9.09ab/ The results are respectively: most excellent, excellent, middling, inferior, low, and miserable;
9.09cd/ one should declare them to be even more miserable in the *saumya* and other paths, in their respective order.
9.10ab. The first group of four constellations beginning with Bharaṇī produces abundance of food.
9.10cd. [However, it] generates fear in the regions of Vaṅga, Aṅga, Mahiṣa, Bāhlīka, and Kaliṅga.
9.11ab/ If another planet rises here while [the Moon] is still above the horizon, it shall destroy the kings of Bhadrāśva, Śūrasena, Yaudheya, and Koṭivarṣa.
9.11cd/ [It shall destroy] the kings of Bhadrāśva, Śūrasena, Yaudheya, and Koṭivarṣa.
The four lunar mansions beginning with Ārdrā constitute the second group; they lead to the abundance of water and crops, yet they bring misfortune specifically to Brahmins who engage in cruel deeds.

9.13ab/ When it is occupied by another [planet] here, misfortune touches the Mlecchas, forest-dwellers, those who live by dogs, and those possessing cattle; 9.13cd/ as well as the Gonardas, the low-born Śūdras, and the Vaidehas.
9.14ab/ Moving through the five asterisms beginning with Maghā, the risen Venus causes the destruction of crops;
9.14cd/ it generates fear of famine and thieves, and brings about the humiliation of the high-born and the elevation of the low-born.
9.15ab. One who is oppressed by the father’s [side] destroys others, such as the Śabaras and Śūdras;
9.15cd. as well as the Puṇḍras, Aparāntas, Śūlikas, Vanavāsins, Draviḍas, and Sāmudras.
9.16ab/ This fourth mandala, consisting of the three asterisms beginning with Svāti, brings about freedom from fear.
9.16cd/ It leads to the increase of the Brahmins, the Kṣatriyas, and abundance of food, but causes dissension among friends.
9.17ab/ When [the planet] enters this [constellation], death comes upon the lord of the Kirātas, and he crushes the Ikṣvākus,
9.17cd/ as well as the Pratyantas, Avantis, Pulindas, Taṅgaṇas, and Śūrasenas.
The five constellations beginning with Jyeṣṭhā cause hunger, theft, and disease to afflict the people of Kaśmīra, Aśmaka, Matsya, Cārudeṣṇa, and Avanti.
9.19ab. Here one should mount [horses] from Draviḍa, Ābhīra, Ambaṣṭha, Trigarta, and Saurāṣṭra.
9.19cd. Those from Sindhu and Sauvīra cause destruction; this is the slaughter of the Lord of Kāśī.

9.20ab. This auspicious constellation-group of six stars, beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā, forms the sixth mandala. 9.20cd. It is filled with abundant wealth and herds of cattle, possesses no small amount of grain, though in some places it may be accompanied by fear.
9.21ab. In this [year], the Śūlikas, Gāndhāras, and Avantyas suffer oppression. 9.21cd. There is slaughter among the Vaidehas, and an increase in the border Yavanas, Śakas, and Dāsas.
In the western direction, the first group beginning with Svāti and the first group beginning with Jyeṣṭhā also form an auspicious circle.
In the eastern direction, the first group beginning with Maghā (Pitrya) is auspicious; the remaining groups yield results as previously described.
If Venus is seen when the sun has not yet set, it causes fear throughout the entire day;
if it is seen at midday along with the moon, it brings about the destruction of kings, armies, and cities.
9.24ab/ Having split the mountain of Anala, it proceeds with rivers whose currents have overflowed their banks;
9.24cd/ the earth becomes level, with its high and low ground made indistinguishable by those streams.
When the cart of Prajāpati is broken, the earth, as if having committed a sin,
bears the appearance of a skull-bearer's vow, variegated with hair, bones, and fragments.
9.26ab/ Uśanas, when approaching the moon, is declared to cause the destruction of liquids and crops.
9.26cd/ But when he enters Ārdrā, he brings about the ruin of the Kośalas and Kaliṅgas and pours down a mass of water.
9.27ab/ Furthermore, when Venus is situated in Punarvasu, there is great disorder among the Aśmakas and Vaidarbhas.
9.27cd/ Under Puṣya, there is abundant rain and conflict with the Vidyādharas.
