9.28ab/ Moving through Āśleṣā, Venus brings terrible affliction from serpents;
9.28cd/ piercing Maghā, it causes great harm to ministers and brings abundant rain.
9.29ab. When [Jupiter] is in Bhāgya, it brings about the destruction of the Śabaras and Pulindas and causes the release of masses of water.
9.29cd. In Āryamaṇa, it destroys the Kurus, Jāṅgalas, and Pañcālas, and bestows rain.

9.30ab/ When Citrā is situated [therein], there is suffering for the artisans of the Kauravas and the obstruction of water. 9.30cd/ There is suffering for well-diggers and birds; however, the rain is auspicious.
9.31ab. Under Svāti, there is abundant rain, but distress afflicts messengers, merchants, and sailors.
9.31cd. Even under Jyeṣṭhā and Kṛttikā, one should know that there is good rain, yet danger for merchants.

9.32ab. In Maitra (Anurādhā), there is conflict with the Kṣatriyas; in Jyeṣṭhā, distress among the leaders of the Kṣatriyas. 9.32cd. In the Mūla [nakṣatra], there is trouble for the hereditary physicians; and in all three of these, there is drought.
9.33ab. When Āpya (Śatabhiṣaj) is ascendant, there is suffering from water-born [diseases]; when Viśveśa (Uttarā Bhādrapadā), diseases break out.
9.33cd. In Śravaṇa, there is disease of the ears; under Dhaniṣṭhā, there is fear of heretics (pāṣaṇḍins).
In Śatabhiṣaj, there is suffering for vintners; in Ajaikapada, for those who live by gambling.
And in this [asterism], when Venus is present, it also brings water to the Kurus and Pañcālas.
9.35ab/ Under Āhirbudhnya (Śatabhiṣaj), there is the acquisition of fruits and roots; under Revatī, it is for those who travel.
9.35cd/ Under Aśvinī, it is for horse-keepers; but under Yāmya (Bharaṇī), it is for Kirātas and Yavanas.
When the son of Bhṛgu passes into the sight [of the earth] or sets on the fourteenth, fifteenth, or likewise the eighth lunar day of the dark fortnight,
then the earth appears as if composed of water.
9.37 When Jupiter and Venus are situated in the seventh signs from each other at the two opposite solstices (the northern and southern limits),
then the subjects, afflicted by disease, fear, and grief, do not see even the water released by Indra.
9.38ab/ When Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, and Saturn are all situated in the forward course (aprapatha) of Venus,
9.38cd/ then there occur battles between men, elephants, and Vidyādharas, and winds that raise up the ends of the world.
9.39ab/ Friends do not remain steadfast in friendship, nor are the twice-born truly devoted to their duties.
9.39cd/ Nor does Vāsava give even a drop of water; he shatters the heads of the mountains with his thunderbolt.
9.40ab/ When Saturn [is in its period], the Mlecchas, cats, elephants, donkeys, buffaloes, black grains, and pigs;
9.40cd/ as well as the Pulindas and Śūdras of the southern region, go to ruin through the arising of eye diseases and ailments of wind.
9.41ab When Venus is eclipsed by Mars, it destroys the subjects through fire, weapons, famine, drought, and thieves.
9.41cd Then the moving and unmoving world, as well as the northern region, would be afflicted by the quarters [of space], fire, lightning, and dust.
When Venus stands in front of Jupiter, it destroys everything white—the twice-born, cattle, and the abodes of the gods.
Furthermore, the clouds shed rain in the form of hailstones toward the eastern quarter; there will be a multitude of diseases in the throat, and the autumn harvest will be meager.
9.43a When Mercury is situated in front of Venus at its setting or rising, it brings about water.
9.43b It causes diseases born of bile and jaundice, and it nourishes summer ailments.
9.43c It destroys those who have renounced the world, those who maintain the sacred fire, physicians, elephant-keepers, and horses.
[One sees] Vaiśyas, cows together with vehicles, kings, and yellow-colored things in the western direction.

9.44a If [the planet] is not red, there is danger from fire; if it is red, there is an outbreak of weapons. 9.44b If it is as yellow as a streak of gold, there are diseases when the deity is worshipped. 9.44c If its form is greenish-brown, there is an aggravation of asthma and cough.
Water does not fall from the sky when it has the appearance of ash, parched, and dark.
9.45ab/ Bearing the luster of curd, the kumuda lily, and the moon, with clearly blossoming rays, large-bodied,
9.45cd/ moving well, unchanging, endowed with victory, the maker of the form of the Kṛta age, he is named Śveta (the White).
Chapter 10: The Course of Saturn.
If Saturn, the son of the Sun, is situated in Śravaṇā, Svātī, Hasta, Ārdrā, Bharaṇī, or Pūrvaphalgunī (Bhāgya) and is well-aspected, he makes the earth abounding in water.
10.02ab/ When the deities are Ahi, Varuṇa, and Purandara, there is good security, yet not an excess of rain.
10.02cd/ At the root [of each], it causes hunger, weapons, and drought; I shall describe each one individually.
10.03ab/ When Saturn is situated in Aśvinī, there are horses, horse-keepers, poets, physicians, ministers, and thieves.
10.03cd/ In Bharaṇī, there are dancers, musicians, those skilled in song, the lowly, and the deceitful.
10.04ab/ When Saturn is in Bahulā, those who subsist on fire and army commanders are afflicted.
10.04cd/ In Rohiṇī, the people of Kośala, Madra, Kāśī, Pañcāla, and carters suffer.
10.05ab. Under Mṛgaśiras, there are calves, officiating priests, sacrificers, noble people, and the Middle Country.
10.05cd. When Raudra (Ārdrā) is situated [therein], there are those from Pārata, Ramaṭhas, oil-pressers, washermen, and thieves.
10.06ab/ Under Āditya: the Pañcanadas, the borderlands, Surāṣṭra, Sindhu, and Sauvīra.
10.06cd/ Under Puṣya: bell-makers, herdsmen, Yavanas, merchants, gamblers, and flowers.
10.07ab/ Under Āśleṣā, there are aquatic plants and serpents; under Maghā, the Bāhlīkas, Cīnas, and Gāndhāras.
10.07cd/ Under Pūrvaphalgunī, there are spear-bearers, pārata, vaiśyas, storehouses, and merchants.
10.08ab/ In Bhāgya, there are sellers of liquids, prostitutes, young girls, and Mahārāṣṭras.
10.08cd/ In Āryamaṇa, there are kings, jaggery, salt, beggars, water, and Takṣaśilās.
10.09ab/ Under Hasta, barbers, wheelwrights, thieves, physicians, tailors, and elephant-seizers [are afflicted].
10.09cd/ Unchaste women, artisans, and garland-makers suffer.
10.10ab/ When Citrā is situated [as the lunar mansion], there will be women, scribes, experts in painting, and various painted articles.
10.10cd/ In Svātī, there will be bards, spies, messengers, charioteers, boatmen, actors, and the like.
10.11ab/ In the region called Aindrāgna, there is a decline of Traigarta, Cīna, Kaulūta, Kuṅkuma, and lac.
10.11cd/ Furthermore, crops, as well as madder and safflower, go to ruin.
10.12ab/ The Maitras, Kulūtas, Taṅgaṇas, Khaśas, and Kaśmīras, along with their ministers and spies,
/ 10.12cd/ suffer affliction, and the bell-ringers [are affected], as well as dissension among friends.
10.13ab/ Under Jyeṣṭhā, there are kings, royal priests, those honored by the king, hosts of heroes, noble families, and guilds.
10.13cd/ Under Mūla, however, are the people of Kāśī, Kośala, and Pañcāla, as well as fruits, medicinal herbs, and warriors.
10.14ab/ When Venus is in the sign of Cancer, the people of Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kauśala, Girivraja, Magadha, Puṇḍra, and Mithilā suffer distress; 10.14cd/ as do those who dwell in Tāmraliptī.
10.15ab. When Saturn moves in Viśveśvara, it destroys the Daśārṇas and the Yavanas;
10.15cd. as well as Ujjayinī, the Śabaras, the Pāriyātrikas, and the Kuntibhojas.
10.16ab/ Under Śravaṇā, there is victory for royal officials, eminent Brahmins, physicians, domestic priests, and the Kaliṅgas.
10.16cd/ Under Dhaniṣṭhā, there is victory for the Lord of Magadha and prosperity for those in charge of wealth.
10.17ab. Under Ārdrā and Śatabhiṣaj, there is success for physicians, poets, vintners, and those whose livelihood is trade and commerce.
10.17cd. Under Āhirbudhnya, rivers are navigable, and there is gain from women and gold.
10.18ab/ When Saturn moves through Revatī, the royal servants residing in Krauñcadvīpa and the autumnal crops are afflicted, as are the Śabaras and the Yavanas.
10.19 When Jupiter, the minister of Mahendra, and the son of the Sun (Saturn) have both entered the constellation Viśākhā, which belongs to Agni,
then there shall be a most terrible disorder among the subjects and the destruction of cities, as the two planets have reached a single asterism.
10.20ab/ If Saturn is variegated, he causes fear of hunger; if his rays are yellow, he brings about fear of weapons.
10.20cd/ If he is red in color, he causes fear of war; and if he resembles ashes, he creates much enmity.
10.21a Pure as the luster of lapis lazuli, it brings welfare to living beings;
10.21b resembling the color of a reed or an atasī flower, it is auspicious;
10.21c and whatever color it may take on, it brings about results corresponding to that very color.
10.21d "The son of the Sun causes destruction," such is the proclamation of the sages.
Chapter 11: On the Movement of Ketu. 11.01ab:

Having examined the movement of Śikhin according to Gārgya, the Pārāśara system, and that composed by Asita and Devala, 11.01cd: and having observed many other [traditions], this unconfused account of its movement is now composed.
11.02ab/ Neither its appearance nor its disappearance can be known through the methods of calculation, because comets (ketus) are of three kinds: celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial.

11.03ab/ When there is no fire, that which has the form of fire is said to have the very form of its banner (smoke). 11.03cd/ This is after setting aside fireflies, piśācas, dwellings, gems, jewels, and so forth.
11.04ab/ Now, those [comets] that appear in the sky over banners, weapons, temples, trees, horses, elephants, and so forth, are celestial;
those situated among the constellations are divine; otherwise, they are terrestrial comets (śikhin).
11.05ab/ Some say there are one hundred and one comets, while others speak of a thousand.
11.05cd/ The sage Nārada, however, declared that the comet is but a single entity possessing many forms.
11.06ab/ Whether there be one or many [omens], what is the point? The result must be stated in every case.
11.06cd/ By means of its rising, setting, positions, touches, smokiness, and colors;
11.07ab/ for as many days as it is visible, for so many months is the ripening of the fruit.
11.07cd/ One should state the months and years from the first [day] onwards, after three fortnights have passed.
11.08ab/ Short, slender, bright, glossy, straight, not long-standing, white,
11.08cd/ whether risen or having been rained upon [or, according to K., seen], the comet brings abundance of food and happiness.
A comet that has arisen with a form contrary to what was described above does not bring auspicious results;
it is especially so if it resembles a rainbow or possesses two or three crests.
11.10ab/ Twenty-five rays, known as Hāra, Maṇi, and Hema, together with the Śikhā, are visible in the eastern and western directions; those born of the Sun bring about opposition from kings.
11.11ab/ Those sons of Agni who resemble parrots, dahana, bandhujīvaka, lac, and blood,
11.11cd/ when seen in the southeast, they too portend danger from fire.

11.12ab/ Those [comets] with curved crests, born of Death, are rough and black, and they are also that many in number. 11.12cd/ When they are seen in the southern quarter, they announce the death of the people.
The twenty-two sons of the Earth (Mars) are circular in shape like mirrors, possess rays, and resemble water or oil; they bring fear of hunger when situated in the northeast.
The three sons of the Moon, resembling the rays of the moon, silver, frost, and the kumuda and kunda flowers, are seen to the north; they bring about abundance and prosperity.
The son of Brahmā alone, three-crested and composed of the three social classes, brings about the end of the ages;
arising from no fixed direction, he is to be known as the one called Brahmadaṇḍa.
11.16ab/ One hundred [comets] have been mentioned, including this one; excluding this single one from that total, 11.16cd/ I shall describe nine hundred comets with clearly defined characteristics.
11.17ab/ Mercury and Jupiter rise in the northeast; those known as the eighty-four [asterisms] are the sons of Venus.
11.17cd/ They possess large white stars and, being glossy, they yield intense results.
11.18ab/ Smooth, endowed with luster, and having two crests— these sixty hairs growing from Śanaiścara’s body,
11.18cd/ seen everywhere, are known as "Golden" (kanaka) and yield very painful results.
11.19ab/ The "Vikacā" [stars] are the sons of Guru; they consist of one white star and are devoid of crests.
11.19cd/ Sixty-five in number, they are glossy and situated in the southern quarter; they are malefic.
11.20ab/ Not too distinct, subtle, long, white, and appearing in any desired direction; 11.20cd/ those born from Mercury are known as "thieves"; these fifty-one [types] yield evil results.
11.21ab/ Sixty sons of Mars, resembling blood and fire, with three tufts and stars, are known by the name Kauṅkumas; they are malevolent and stationed in the northern quarter.
11.22ab/ Thirty more than those [of Rāhu] are known as the *tāmasakīlakas*. 11.22cd/ When they are situated in the sun or the moon, their results are as stated for the movement of the sun.
11.23ab/ There is another hundred and twenty [fires] known by the name Viśvarūpa;
11.23cd/ [they are] givers of fear through fierce fire, their bodies enveloped in garlands of flames.
11.24ab/ Dark-red, devoid of stars, having the form of chowries, and with scattered rays;
11.24cd/ these seventy-seven harsh [planets] called Aruṇa belong to Vāyu and bring about evil.
11.25ab. The eight Prajāpatis are named Gaṇakas, resembling clusters of stars.
11.25cd. And there are two hundred and four [spheres] that are square, belonging to the lineage of Brahmā.
11.26ab/ Those born of Varuṇa known as Kaṅkas have the appearance of thirty-two clusters of bamboo thickets.
11.26cd/ Endowed with a luster like that of the moon, these comets are said to yield severe results.
11.27ab/ Ninety-six are the sons of Kāla, known as Kabandhas; they have the form of headless trunks (kabandha).
11.27cd/ They bestow fearlessness upon the Puṇḍras [or Caṇḍas], and their stars are deformed; these are the Śikhins.
11.28ab/ Nine comets of the intermediate directions have arisen, white, large, and each having a single star.
11.28cd/ Thus there are a thousand comets; I shall now describe their specific characteristics.
11.29ab/ A large, glossy-bodied Vasāketu rising in the north at sunset causes immediate death; yet it also brings about excellent abundance of food.
11.30ab/ That comet (asthiketu) possessing those characteristics is said to be rough and bringer of fear from famine.
11.30cd/ If such [a comet] is glossy and appears in the east, it is called Śastra and brings about civil strife and pestilence.
11.31ab/ On the new moon day, the Kapālaketu is visible, with a smoky-colored ray and crest. 11.31cd/ Moving across the eastern half of the sky, it causes hunger, pestilence, drought, and disease.
11.32ab. In the east, on the path of Vaiśvānara, there is the comet Śūlāgra, with dark-brown, rough, and copper-colored rays.
11.32cd. Reaching one-third of the sky, it is called Raudra; its fruit is equal to that of Kapāla.
11.33ab/ When the comet has its tail pointing toward the south, rising one finger-breadth in height,
it moves in such a way that its length increases as it proceeds toward the north.
Having touched the seven sages, Dhruva, and Abhijit itself, the moon returns;
having traversed half of the sky, it sets toward the south.
It extends from the banks of Prayāga as far as Avantī and the Puṣkara forest;
it also reaches northward to the Devikā river—this is what is generally called the Madhyadeśa.
In some places and at various times, he strikes down other regions as well with disease and famine;
the ripening of his fruit lasts for ten months, though by some it is said to be eighteen.
Visible before midnight, with its tip pointing south, is the white comet (Śvetaketu) and another;
the one called Ka has the shape of a yoke, while two others appear simultaneously, visible for seven days.

If the two [planets] are glossy, they bring about abundance and prosperity; however, if that which is named Kana (Mercury) appears excessively so, it causes distress for ten years produced by the outbreak of weapons.
11.39ab/ White, matted in appearance, rough, and dark-brown, it moves away having traversed three parts [of the sky].
11.39cd/ It turns back toward the left and leaves only one-third of the subjects remaining.
11.40ab/ When situated in Kṛttikā, Ketu appears with a smoky crest.
11.40cd/ He is to be known as Raśmiketu; he brings forth results similar to those of Śveta.
11.41ab/ Dhruvaketu has an indefinite course, magnitude, color, and form, appearing everywhere.
11.41cd/ Whether celestial, atmospheric, or terrestrial, this [Dhruvaketu] is auspicious when it is glossy, yielding desired results.
11.42ab/ In the case of kings, it appears among the divisions of the army; and in the case of countries, among houses, trees, and mountains.
11.42cd/ In the case of householders, it goes to see the household utensils that are subject to destruction.

11.43ab. One named Kumuda, possessing the luster of a white water-lily, with its crest pointing eastward in the western quarter, when seen for one night, brings incomparable abundance for ten years, so it is said.
11.43cd. He indeed causes a state of great plenty for ten years.
11.44ab. At one time it is invisible for a single watch, while at another it appears as an exceedingly minute star;
its crest-jewel is like a stream of milk flowing from the breast, with a straight, white tuft.
11.45ab/ Rising at this very time, he brings about an abundance of food for four and a half months;
11.45cd/ and he generally causes the appearance of small creatures.
11.46ab/ Furthermore, when Jalaketu appears in the west with a glossy crest rising toward the rear,
11.46cd/ for nine months it brings about abundance of food and peace for the world.
11.47ab/ Bhavaketu is visible for one night in the east as a subtle star, smooth [in appearance].
11.47cd/ It has a crest that curls to the right, resembling the tail of a monkey.
11.48ab/ One should indicate that for as many *muhūrtas* as it remains visible, there will be months of incomparable abundance; 11.48cd/ but if it is parched, there will be life-ending diseases.
11.49ab/ On the following night, Padmaketu shall be white as a lotus stalk;
11.49cd/ for seven years he brings about abundance, filled with great joy.
11.50ab. A whirlpool (āvarta) appearing at midnight with a curl to the left, resembling the color of dawn and glossy on its other side;
11.50cd. For as many moments as it remains visible, for that many months it brings about an abundance of food.
11.51ab/ Afterwards, at the time of twilight, the one named Saṃvarta, with smoke-colored and copper-red crests,
11.51cd/ having pervaded a third part of the sky, stands fierce upon the tip of his trident.
11.52ab/ For as many muhūrtas as it remains visible, for that many years it destroys [the earth].
11.52cd/ It strikes down kings with the falling of weapons and also afflicts the constellation of its rising.
11.53ab/ Having abandoned those [asterisms] that are auspicious, when [a comet] is shaken by its tails or has touched them;
11.53cd/ death occurs for those kings whose [natal] asterism it touches; I shall now declare who they are.
11.54ab. Under Aśvinī, one should destroy the king of Aśmaka; under the Bharaṇīs, the Kirāta monarch; 11.54cd. under Kṛttikā (Bahulā), the lord of Kaliṅga; and under Rohiṇī, the ruler of Śūrasena.
11.55ab/ Likewise, [the planet] destroys the king of the Auśīnaras in Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), and the lord of those who live by water-products in Ārdrā;
11.55cd/ it kills the lord of the Aśmakas in Āditya (Punarvasu), and the sovereign of Magadha in Puṣya.
11.56ab/ One born under Āśleṣā becomes Asikeśa; under Maghā, Aṅga; and under Pūrvaphalgunī, Pāṇḍyanātha.
11.56cd/ Under Uttaraphalgunī, one becomes the ruler of Ujjayinī; under Hastā, the lord of Daṇḍaka.
11.57ab/ One who knows [the signs] should predict the death of the ruler of Kurukṣetra when [Jupiter is in] Citrā.
11.57cd/ The kings of Kāśmīra and Kāmboja do not exist during the Prābhañjana [year].
If [the moon] should be in Viśākhā, Ikṣvāku and the lord of Alakā are slain;
in Anurādhā, the lord of Puṇḍra; and in Jyeṣṭhā, there is the slaughter of a universal monarch.
11.59ab/ Under Mūla, the lords of Andhra and Madra perish; under Jyeṣṭhā, the king of Kāśī meets his death.
11.59cd/ Under Vaiśvadeva (Anurādhā), the Yaudheyakas, the Arjunāyanas, the Śivis, and the Caidyas [perish].

One should destroy the lord of the Kaikeyas, the ruler of the Pañcanada, the king of Siṃhala, and the lord of Aṅga; likewise, the king of Naimiṣa and the Kirāta—these six [are to be destroyed] in sequence starting from Śravaṇā.
A fire with its crest struck by a meteor, or one that is auspicious yet appears excessively so due to heavy rain,
is inauspicious for the Colas, Avagāṇas, Sitahūṇas, and Cīnas.
Whichever direction the crest of his peacock-feather plume bends, whichever direction it points,
or whichever constellation it touches— those regions he shall traverse,
having destroyed [enemies] through his divine power, just as Garuḍa does.
Having gone there, the king enjoys the pleasures of others who indulge in them.
Chapter 12: The Course of Agastya.
By him, the ocean was suddenly made exceedingly beautiful through the drying up of its waters, as its peaks were excavated by the claws of sea-monsters amidst the mountains within.

12.01c Falling with showers of excellent jewel-water mingled with pearls, as if to reproach the gods whose crest-jewels were once [so] limited; 12.01d [as if to reproach] those gods whose crest-jewels were formerly [meager].

And by that [mountain], even as it carried away water, the ocean was made to shine most brilliantly, adorned with coral reefs like mountains containing jewels and corals, and graced by the serpents emerging from them.
The great ocean— with its shimmering whales, crocodiles, and serpents, and its scattered heaps of jewels—
though it had become a vessel for calamities, was made to yield the splendor of the immortals by him who drank its waters.
12.04ab/ Even when its water has been swept away, the lord of rivers, strewn with trembling timi-fish, pearl-oysters, and conchs,
bears a luster like a lake in autumn, filled with waves, white lotuses, and swans.
He who possesses the luster of a cloudless autumn sky made the sky— filled with dark clouds for its water, the stars for its gems, the crystal moon,
and the rays from the jewels on the hoods of serpents for its peacocks— appear like the curved body of the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa).
12.06a It was adorned with flags raised high and fluttering, which, with their moving peaks, seemed intent on blocking the path of the sun’s chariot;

while the kings of beasts, with their heads covered by swarms of bees following the scent of the blood-smeared ichor they had licked from the elephants' temples, wore what appeared to be crests of *bāṇa* flowers.

He stilled the Vindhya mountain—which seemed to scrape the surface of the sky; which was filled with the deep, joyful songs of swarms of intoxicated bees wandering in terror from full-blown trees pulled down by elephants;
which possessed mountain peaks inhabited by hyenas, bears, tigers, and monkeys;

which was embraced in secret by the river Revā as if by a beloved woman devoted to Love; which contained gardens frequented by the gods; and which was attended by Brahmins subsisting on water, roots, and air.
And hear now of its arising.
12.07 When the sage named Agastya rises, the waters— which had been defiled by the impurity of contact with dust— become clear again by their very nature, just like the hearts of the virtuous.
With ruddy geese resting upon both her banks and rows of swans crying out as she nourishes them,
with her front teeth whitened and reddened by betel, the autumn river shines like a smiling woman.
12.09ab/ The autumnal river, adorned with rows of wandering bees and filled with blue and white lotuses near the indīvaras,
shines like a clever woman full of passion, casting side-glances from her creeper-like eyebrows.

In the nights, the night-lotus— with its petals like beautiful eyelashes and its ring of ripples— opens its flower, which is covered by bees, in order to behold the moon’s splendor brought forth by the departure of the clouds.
The pond was like an eye, beautiful with its dark pupil.
With her hand full of ponds filled with various and diverse lotuses, swans, ruddy geese, and ducks,
she seems to offer abundant water for the guest-offering (*argha*) to the one named Agastya, consisting of many jewels, flowers, and fruits.

12.12ab/ That water which was abandoned by the command of the Lord of the Immortals, and whose depths were encircled by serpents with their bodies coiled around it; 12.12cd/ which had been utterly corrupted by the poison-fire emitted from the hoods of those snakes—becomes auspicious through the sight of Agastya.
12.13ab Even by remembering him one dispels sin, how much more so through hymns of praise to the one born from the waters?
12.13cd The method for his worship as prescribed by the sages—I shall describe it exactly thus for the benefit of the king.

12.14ab. Having understood its manifestation according to each region through the prescribed calculation, the knower should indicate it. 12.14cd. And that occurs when [the planet] has reached Ujjayinī at a point equal to the degrees of the true sun called "vowels" (svaras).
12.15ab/ When the nocturnal darkness has been slightly pierced by the networks of the dawn’s rays in the southern quarter;
12.15cd/ and when the divisions of the directions have been announced by the astrologer, the king, being self-restrained, should offer the guest-offering (argha) upon the earth.
With fragrant flowers and fruits produced in their season, with jewels born of the ocean, with gold and garments,
with a cow, a bull, and various foods accompanied by supreme rice-pudding;
With curds, parched grains, fragrant incense, and ointments.

12.17a If a king, placing his trust in this *argha* and bestowing it, 12.17b becomes free from the defects of disease and has conquered the faction of his enemies; 12.17c and if he should give [it] correctly for seven years, [he will attain prosperity].
He attains lordship over the earth, which has the ocean as its girdle.
12.18ab/ A twice-born man, having been offered the guest-offering according to his means, obtains the Vedas, women, and sons;
12.18cd/ a Vaiśya obtains cattle and abundant wealth, and a Śūdra the alleviation of disease—all of them obtain the fruit of dharma.
12.19a A rough [flash] causes diseases, while a tawny one brings drought;
12.19b a smoky one is an ill omen for cattle, and a throbbing one portends fear; 12.19c one resembling the color of madder foretells famine and battles.
And one named Agastya shall perform a siege of the city with minute [missiles].
If [the moon] is seen resembling gold, with the luster of crystal, as if satisfying the earth with the tips of its rays,
then the earth becomes abundant in food and rich in security, freedom from disease, and prosperity for its people.
If struck by a meteor or a comet, it brings about the fear of famine and even pestilence;
for it is said that when the sun has entered the constellation Hasta, it sets as soon as Rohiṇī is reached.
Chapter 13: The Movement of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣicāra).
The northern quarter, graced by those seven sages, shines like a single-stringed necklace adorned with white lotuses; it appears as if smiling and as if possessed of a protector.
13.02ab/ The Uttarās dance as it were through the instructions of the Dhruva-nāyaka, along with those that revolve;
13.02cd/ and I shall declare their course according to the opinion of Vṛddhagarga.
13.03ab/ While King Yudhiṣṭhira was ruling the earth, the sages were in the Maghā constellation;
13.03cd/ and the Śaka era [was calculated] as being diminished by six, two, five, and two years from the time of that king.
13.04ab. They move through each constellation for one hundred years.

13.04cd. Even before sunrise, they lead [the planets] straight from the opening [of the gate], being joined there; these always rise together with the virtuous ones (the lunar mansions) toward the northeast.
In the eastern part stands the blessed Marīci; to his west is Vasiṣṭha.
Next to him is Aṅgiras, then Atri, and close to him is Pulastya.
13.06ab. Pulaha, Kratu, and Bhaga were seated in order starting from the east.
13.06cd. There, the virtuous Arundhatī took refuge with Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages.
13.07ab/ Struck by meteors, thunderbolts, smoke, and the like, discolored, lusterless, and short [comets] destroy their respective classes.
13.07cd/ Those that are broad and glossy lead to the prosperity of those same classes.
13.08ab/ Marīci should be known as the cause of affliction for the Gandharvas, gods, Dānavas, those perfected by mantras and herbs, Yakṣas, and Nāgas; 13.08cd/ and likewise for the Vidyādharas.
When struck, Vasiṣṭha destroys the Śakas, Yavanas, Daradas, Pāradas, Kāmbojas, and forest-dwelling ascetics; yet, when endowed with its full rays, it brings about prosperity.

13.10ab/ Those endowed with knowledge are declared to be the Aṅgirasas, as well as the wise Brāhmaṇas. 13.10cd/ From Atri [proceed] those born in the wilderness, aquatic creatures, the ocean, and rivers.
13.11ab/ Rākṣasas, piśācas, dānavas, daityas, and bhujaṅgas are said to be the progeny of Pulastya.
13.11cd/ Of Pulaha, however, are roots and fruits; of Kratu, sacrifices along with those who maintain the sacrifices.
Chapter 14: On the Constellations and the Tortoise.

14.01ab: Divided into nine parts by the groups of three constellations beginning with Āgneya (Kṛttikā) and so forth, 14.01cd: the regions of Bhāratavarṣa are distributed from the center toward the east and the other directions.
14.02ab/ Bhadra, Arimeda, Māṇḍavya, Śālva, Nīpa, and Ujjihāna are enumerated;
14.02cd/ as well as Maru, Vatsa, Ghoṣa, Yāmuna, Sārasvata, Matsya, and Mādhyamika.
14.03ab/ Māthuraka, Upajyotiṣa, Dharmāraṇya, and Śūrasena;
14.03cd/ Gauragrīva, Uddehika, Pāṇḍu, Guḍa, Aśvattha, and Pāñcāla.
14.04ab/ Sāketa, Kaṅka, Kuru, Kālakoṭi, Kukura, and the Pāriyātra mountain;
14.04cd/ Audumbara, Kāpiṣṭhala, and Gajāhvaya—this is the Middle Country.
14.05ab/ Now, in the east [are] the mountains Añjana, Vṛṣabhadhvaja, Padma, and Mālyavat;
14.05cd/ [and there are the peoples] Vyāghramukha, Suhma, Karvaṭa, Cāndrapura, and Śūrpakarṇa.
14.06ab/ The Khaśas, Magadhas, Śibis, Giri, Mithilas, Samataṭas, Uḍras, Aśvavadaṇas, and Danturakas;
14.06cd/ The Prāgjyotiṣas, Lauhityas, Kṣīrodas, Samudras, and Puruṣādās.
14.07ab/ Udayagiri, Bhadra, Gauḍaka, Pauṇḍra, Utkala, Kāśi, Mekala, and Ambaṣṭha; 14.07cd/ Ekapada, Tāmraliptaka, Kośalaka, and Vardhamāna.
14.08ab/ In the southeastern direction are Kośala, Kaliṅga, Vaṅga, Upavaṅga, Jaṭhara, and Aṅga;
14.08cd/ as well as Śaulika, Vidarbha, Vatsa, Andhra, Cedi, Kāśī, and Ūrdhvakaṇṭha.
14.09ab/ The Vṛṣas, Nālikeras, Carmadvīpas, those dwelling at the edge of the Vindhya mountains, and Tripurī;
14.09cd/ the Śmaśrudharas, Hemakuḍyas, Vyālagrīvas, and Mahāgrīvas.
14.10ab/ Kiṣkindha, Kaṇṭakasthala, the Niṣāda kingdoms, Purika, and the Dāśārṇas;
14.10cd/ together with the Nagna, Parṇa, and Śabara peoples—these are the regions in the triangle beginning with Āśleṣā.
14.11ab/ Now, to the south [are] Laṅkā, Kālāja, Saurikīrṇa, and Tālikaṭa;
14.11cd/ [and] Girinagara, Malaya, Dardura, Mahendra, Mālindya, and Bharukaccha.
14.12ab/ The Kaṅkaṭas, Kaṅkaṇas [or Taṅkaṇas], Vanavāsins, Śibikas, Phaṇikāras, Koṅkaṇas, and Ābhīras; 14.12cd/ The Ākaras, Veṇās, Āvartakas [or Āvantakas], Daśapuras, Gonardas, and Keralas.
14.13ab/ Karṇāṭa, Mahāṭavī, Citrakūṭa, Nāsikya, Kollagiri, and Cola; 14.13cd/ Krauñcadvīpa, Jaṭādhara, Kāverī, and Riṣyamūka.
14.14ab/ Vaidūrya, Śaṅkha, Muktā, Atri, Vāricara, Dharmapaṭṭana, and Dvīpa;
14.14cd/ Gaṇarājya, Kṛṣṇa, Vellūra, Piśika, Śūrpādri, and Kusumanaga.
14.15ab/ Tumbavana, Kārmaṇeyaka, Yāmya, Udadhita, and Tāpasāśrama are the Ṛṣikas;
14.15cd/ Kāñcī, Marucīpaṭṭana, Ceryāryaka, Siṃhala, and Ṛṣabha are the [other regions].
14.16ab/ Baladevapaṭṭana, Daṇḍakāvana, Timiṅgilāśana, Bhadra,
14.16cd/ Kaccha, Kuñjaradarī, and Satāmraparṇī are to be known [as the names of the regions].

14.17ab/ In the southwestern direction (nairṛtyāṃ diśi) are the regions of the Pahlavas, Kāmbojas, Sindhus, and Sauvīras; 14.17cd/ as well as Vaḍavāmukha, Arava, Ambaṣṭha, Kapila, Nārīmukha, and Ānarta.
14.18ab/ The Pheṇagiris, Yavanas, Mārgaras, Karṇaprāveyas, Pāraśavas, and Śūdras;
14.18cd/ the Barbaras, Kirātas, Khaṇḍas, Kravyādas, Ābhīras, and Cañcūkās.
14.19ab/ Hemagiri, Sindhu, Kālaka, Raivataka, Surāṣṭra, Bādara, and Draviḍa;
14.19cd/ these are to be known as [the regions] here, along with Mahārṇava, during the triad of lunar mansions beginning with Svāti.
In the western direction are Maṇimat, Meghavat, Vanaugha, Kṣurārpaṇa, and the Sunset Mountain (Astagiri);
also Aparāntaka, Śāntika, Haihaya, Praśastādri, and Vokkāṇa.
The Pañcanadas, Ramaṭhas, Pāratas, Tārakṣitis, Jṛṅgas, Vaiśyas, Kanakas, and Śakas—
those Mlecchas who dwell in the western direction are devoid of moral restraint.
In the northwestern direction, there are the Māṇḍavyas, Tukhāras (or Tuṣāras), Tālas, Halas, and Madras;
as well as the Aśmakas, Kulūtas, Haḍas, the Kingdom of Women, Nṛsiṃha, Vanakha, and Sthas.
The Veṇumatī, Phalgulukā, Guluhā, Marukuccha, and those called Carmaraṅga;
and likewise the Ekavilocana, Śūlika, Dīrghagrīva, and Āsyakeśa tribes.
To the north are Kailāsa, Himavat, the mountain Vasumān, and Dhanuṣmān;
as well as Krauñca, Meru, the Northern Kurus, and the Kṣudramīnas.
14.25ab/ Kaikaya, Vasāti, Yamunābhoga, Prastha, Arjunāyana, and Agnīdhra;
14.25cd/ Ādarśa, Antardvīpin, Trigarta, Turagānana, and Śvamukha.
14.26ab/ The Keśadharas, Cipiṭanāsikas, Dāserakas, Vāṭadhānas, and Śaradhānas; 14.26cd/ as well as the Takṣaśilas, Puṣkalāvatas, Kailāvatas, and Kaṇṭhadhānas.
14.27ab/ The Ambaras, Madrakas, Mālavas, Pauravas, Kacchāras, Daṇḍas, and Piṅgalakas; 14.27cd/ the Māṇahalas, Hūṇas, Kohalas, Śītakas, Māṇḍavyas, and Bhūtapuras.
The Gāndhāras, Yaśovatīs, Hematalas, Rājanyas, Khacarās, and Gavyas; the Yaudheyas, Dāsameyas, Śyāmākas, and Kṣemadhūrtas.
14.29ab/ In the northeast [are the lands of] Meruka, Anaṣṭarājya, Paśupāla, Kīra, and Kāśmīra;
14.29cd/ [and those of] Abhisāra, Darada, Taṅgaṇa, Kulūta, Sairindhra, and Vanarāṣṭra.
14.30ab/ The Brahmapura, Dārva, Āḍāmara, Vanarājya, Kirāta, Cīna, and Kauṇinda;
14.30cd/ as well as the Bhalla, Paṭolaja, Jaṭāsura, Kunaṭa, Khaṣa, Ghoṣa, and those known as the Kucika.
14.31ab. Those who follow the single-footed [Ekacaraṇas], the inhabitants of Suvarṇabhūmi, the Vasudhanas, and those dwelling in heaven;
14.31cd. The Pauravas, the Cīranivāsins, the Trinetras, the Muñjādrikas, and the Gandharvas.
14.32ab. By means of the groups beginning with Āgneya, when afflicted by malefic planets, the kings in sequence—14.32cd.
the Pāñcāla, the Māgadha, and the Kāliṅga—go to their destruction.
14.33ab. Furthermore, Āvantya, Ānarta, and Sindhusauvīra will meet their death; 14.33cd. as will King Hārahaura, the Lord of Madra, and another, the Kauṇinda.
Chapter 15: The Array of Constellations (Nakṣatravyūhādhyāya) 15.01ab.
In the constellation Āgneya (Kṛttikā), there are those who offer white flowers, those who maintain the sacred fires, those who know mantras, and those who know the Sūtras and Bhāṣyas.
15.01cd. Also, miners, barbers, the twice-born, potters, domestic priests, and astrologers.

15.02ab. Under Rohi�ṇī, those engaged in vows, trade, royalty, wealth, and partnerships, as well as carters, 15.02cd. and those endowed with cattle, bulls, aquatic creatures, farmers, mountains, and sovereignty [prosper].
15.03ab/ Under Mṛgaśiras, there are fragrant garments, lotuses, flowers, fruits, jewels, forest-dwellers, birds, 15.03cd/ deer, Soma-drinkers, Gandharvas, lovers, and messengers with letters.
15.04ab/ Under Raudra, those who delight in killing, binding, lying, adultery, theft, deceit, and sowing dissension;
15.04cd/ and those skilled in the rites of husked grain, sharp mantras, malevolent magic (abhicāra), and the propitiation of vetālas.
15.05ab. Under Āditya, people are endowed with truthfulness, generosity, purity, noble lineage, beauty, intelligence, fame, and wealth.
15.05cd. There is an abundance of the finest grain; merchants are devoted to service, as are the artisans.
15.06ab/ Under Puṣya, there are barley and wheat, forests of rice and sugarcane, ministers, and kings;
15.06cd/ those who live by water, virtuous men, and those devoted to sacrifices and rites.
15.07ab/ When Āhidaiva is [the presiding nakṣatra], there will be artificial bulbs, roots, fruits, insects, snakes, and poisons;
15.07cd/ those devoted to seizing the wealth of others, husked grain, and all physicians [will flourish].

15.08ab/ Under the Pitṛs, men will be rich in wealth and grain, possessing storehouses and taking refuge in mountains; 15.08cd/ they will be devoted to their ancestors, merchants, brave, carnivorous, and haters of women.
15.09ab/ Under the Prākphalgunīs, there are actors, young women, those who are fortunate, musicians, artisans, and commodities for sale;
15.09cd/ as well as cotton, salt, honey, oils, and also children.
15.10ab. Under Āryamaṇ, people are devoted to gentleness, purity, discipline, heretics, giving, and the scriptures;
15.10cd. they are fond of beautiful grains, great wealth, and ritual acts, along with the lords of men.
In Hasta, there are thieves, elephants, chariot-warriors, high officials, artisans, and merchandise;
there are also grain-husks, those endowed with sacred learning, merchants, and those possessed of splendor.

15.12 In the [region of] Tvāṣṭra, there are those skilled in the knowledge of ornaments, gems, dyeing, painting, music, and the preparation of perfumes; those proficient in mathematics and weaving; and physicians who are the pillars of the royal capital.

15.13ab. Under Svāti, there are birds, wild animals, horses, merchants, grains, and things abundant in wind. 15.13cd. [The people are] unstable in friendship, light in character, ascetics, and skilled in trade.
15.14ab. Trees with red flowers, fruits, and branches are dedicated to Indra and Agni; likewise are sesame and mung beans.
15.14cd. Cotton, black gram, and chickpeas are also the portions belonging to Purandara and Hutāśa.
In the Maitra [fortnight], those endowed with heroism, who delight in assemblies of leaders of hosts, in virtuous company, and in vehicles;
those who are righteous in the world, and everything produced in autumn—[these flourish].
15.16ab/ Those born under Paurandara are exceedingly brave, endowed with noble lineage, wealth, and fame, and are takers of others' property.
15.16cd/ They are kings desirous of victory and also leaders of armies.
15.17ab. In Mūla, there are physicians with their medicines, leaders of guilds, and those who subsist on flowers, roots, and fruits.
15.17cd. Those who possess great wealth through seeds, and those who live by means of fruits and roots [will also be found there].
15.18ab/ Under Āpya (the water element), they are gentle, travel by way of water, and are endowed with truthfulness, purity, and wealth.
15.18cd/ They are builders of bridges, those who live by water, and [dealers in] fruits, flowers, and aquatic products.
In Viśveśvara, there are great ministers, wrestlers, elephants, horses, and those devoted to the deities;
there are also stationary warriors who possess enjoyments and are endowed with splendor.
15.20ab/ Skilled in illusion, ever-exerting themselves in their duties, and capable in their tasks;
15.20cd/ energetic, devoted to the Dharma, followers of the Lord (Bhāgavatas), and speakers of truth.

15.21ab/ In an even sign, men are free from pride, impotent, and firm in friendship; they are disliked by women. 15.21cd/ They are devoted to giving, possessed of great wealth, and intent on tranquility.
15.22ab. Under Varuṇa and Īśa are those who live by nets, fish-trapping, and aquatic products; those who live by water-dwellers.
15.22cd. Also included in this group are pig-butchers, washermen, vintners, and fowlers.
15.23 On this day, those men who act like thieves, herdsmen, predators, usurers, the base, and the deceitful;
those who are devoid of religious duties and vows; and those who are skilled in wrestling—[these are the characteristics of this day].

In Āhirbudhnya, there will be learned brahmins endowed with ritual sacrifices, charity, and austerity, possessing great wealth; as well as heretics who follow the stages of life (āśramins), lords of men, and the finest grains.
15.25ab/ Under the asterism of Puṣya, one should deal in aquatic products, fruits, flowers, salt, gems, conch-shells, pearls, and lotuses;
15.25cd/ as well as fragrant flowers, perfumes, merchants, sailors, and ship-captains.
15.26ab. Under Aśvinī are those who seize horses, army commanders, physicians, servants, and horses;
15.26cd. horse-riders, merchants, those endowed with beauty, and horse-guards.
In the southern quarter, there are cruel beings who consume blood and flesh, intent on killing, binding, and beating;
they belong to low-born families and are deficient in strength of character.

The three eastern asterisms together with Kṛttikā are for the elder sons of kings; those beginning with Puṣya and the three Uttaras are for kings; and the asterism of Revatī, Anurādhā, the Pitṛ-daivata (Maghā), and the asterism of Prajāpati (Rohiṇī) are for farmers.
15.29ab/ They declare that Āditya, Hasta, Abhijit, and Āśvinī belong to merchants;
15.29cd/ while Mūla, Trinetra (Ārdrā), Anila (Svātī), and Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj) belong to those of fierce birth who possess great power.
15.30ab/ The asterisms presided over by Soma, Indra, Citrā, and Vasu have come under the sovereignty of those who serve.
15.30cd/ Āśleṣā, Viśākhā, Śravaṇa, and Bharaṇī indicate birth from the Caṇḍāla caste.
15.31ab/ That which has entered the orbit of the Sun or Saturn, is afflicted by the retrograde motion or the conjunction of Mars,
15.31cd/ or is undergoing an eclipse, struck by a meteor, or necessarily oppressed by the Moon.
15.32ab. That [plan] is declared to be "vitiated," or indeed as having reached a state contrary to its own nature (prakṛti-viparyaya-yāta).
15.32cd. When the defects of the aforementioned categories have been stated, that which proceeds by way of their opposites leads to success.
Chapter 16: The Chapter on the Yogas of Planetary Aspects (Grahabhaktiyoga).
To the east [of the Narmadā] are the regions of Ardhaśoṇa, Oḍra, Vaṅga, Suhma, Kaliṅga, and Bāhlīka;
as well as Śaka, Yavana, Magadha, Śabara, Prāgjyotiṣa, Cīna, and Kāmboja.
16.02ab/ The Mekalas, Kirātas, Viṭakas, those born on the outer and inner mountains, and the Pulindas;
16.02cd/ [These are] the eastern half of the Draviḍas and the southern bank of the Yamunā.
16.03ab/ Campā, Udumbara, Kauśāmbī, Cedi, Vindhya forest, and Kaliṅga;
16.03cd/ Puṇḍra, Golāṅgūla, Śrīparvata, and Vardhamāna.
16.04ab/ Then, [the following are auspicious] for sugarcane, thieves, iron, deserts, cowherds, and seeds;
16.04cd/ as well as for husked grain, pungent substances, trees, gold, fire, poison, and those heroic in battle.
The Sun is the lord of physicians, quadrupeds, farmers, kings, those who inflict violence, travelers, thieves, wild beasts, forest-dwellers, the famous, and the fierce.
16.06ab/ Giri-salila-durga, Kośala, Bharukaccha, Samudra-romaka, and Tuṣāra;
16.06cd/ Vanavāsi, Taṅgaṇa, Hala, Strīrājya, and Mahārṇava-dvīpa.
16.07ab/ Of sweet-tasting flowers, fruits, water, salt, gems, conch-shells, pearls, and lotuses;
16.07cd/ Of rice, barley, medicinal herbs, wheat, Soma-drinkers, Ākrandas, and Brahmins.

16.08ab/ The Moon is the lord of white objects, fortunate things, horses, those who cause pleasure, young women, army commanders, food, and garments; 16.08cd/ as well as of horned animals, night-stalkers, farmers, and those who know the sacrificial rites.
16.09ab/ Those situated on the western banks of the Śoṇa, Narmadā, and Bhīmarathī; 16.09cd/ [The rivers] Nirvindhyā, Vetravatī, Siprā, Godāvarī, and Veṇā.
The Mandākinī, Payoṣṇī, Mahānadī, Sindhu, Mālatī, and Pārā rivers;
the northern Pāṇḍyas, the Mahendra mountain, the Vindhya and Malaya mountains; and the Colas.

The Draviḍas, Videhas, Andhras, Aśmakas, Bhāsāpurakas, and Kauṅkaṇas, along with the Mantriṣikas; the Kuntalas, Keralas, Daṇḍakas, and Kantipurakas, as well as the Mlecchas and those of mixed descent.
The regions situated along the Nāsikya, Bhogavardhana, Virāṭa, and the slopes of the Vindhya mountains,
as well as those who drink the waters of the Sutoyā, the Tāpī, and the Gomatī; [therein dwell] the Nāgaras,
agriculturalists, Pāratas, those who live by fire, and those whose livelihood is the use of weapons.
16.12cd / Of forest-dwellers, those from mountain fastnesses, those from market towns, executioners, the cruel, and the arrogant.
16.13ab/ [The sight of] a king, a prince, an elephant, a hypocrite, a child, a blow, or a cowherd;
16.13cd/ [or of things that are] red, fruits, flowers, coral, an army commander, molasses, wine, or pungent substances.
The son of the Earth (Mars) is the lord of treasuries, temples, those who maintain the sacred fire, mines, quarries, Śākyas, monks, thieves, rogues, those with long-standing enmity, and gluttons.
The Lohitya, the Sindhu river, the Sarayū, the Gāmbhīrikā, and the one called Rathā;
the Gaṅgā, Kauśikī, and other rivers; and the peoples of Videha and Kamboja.

Those residing in the eastern half of Mathurā, on the Himavat, Gomanta, and Citrakūṭa mountains, as well as those in Saurāṣṭra, at the Setu, along water routes, in market towns, in caves, and those dwelling in the mountains; 16.16.

16.17ab/ Those who know the construction of wells and water-lifting machines, the art of music, painting, the coloring of gems, and the preparation of perfumes; 16.17cd/ those skilled in drawing, vocal music, arithmetic, personal adornment, longevity, and the various crafts.

16.18ab/ Those who live by means of spies, fraudulent persons, children, poets, rogues, or informers; those devoted to malevolent magic (abhicāra); 16.18cd/ Messengers, eunuchs, those skilled in comedy, and those who know the treatises on spirits and the art of sorcery (indrajāla).
16.19ab/ Guards, actors, dancers, ghee, oil, fats, seeds, and bitter substances; 16.19cd/ Those observing vows, elixirs, experts, and mules belong to the son of the Moon (Mercury).
16.20ab/ The eastern part of the Sindhu river region, the western half of Mathurā, Bharata, and Sauvīra;
16.20cd/ Srughna, the northern regions, the Vipāśā river, the Śatadrū river, Ramaṭha, and Śālva.
16.21ab/ The Traigartas, Pauravas, Ambaṣṭhas, Pārutas, Vāṭadhānas, and Yaudheyas; 16.21cd/ as well as the Sārasvatas, Arjunāyanas, Matsyas, and the half-village kingdoms.

16.22ab/ Those devoted to elephants, horses, royal priests, kings, ministers, auspicious rites, and rituals for prosperity; 16.22cd/ And those endowed with compassion, truthfulness, purity, vows, learning, charity, and righteousness.
16.23ab/ Citizens, wealthy men, those who know the meaning of words, experts in the Vedas, and those skilled in sorcery and policy;
16.23cd/ And the regalia of a lord of men, such as the parasol, the banner, the chowries, and so forth.
16.24ab/ Śaileya, kuṣṭha, māṃsī, tagara, rasan, saindhava, and vallīja;
16.24cd/ madhurarasā, madhūcchiṣṭa, and coraka—these constitute the [ingredients] of jīva.
16.25ab/ Takṣaśilā, Mārtikāvata, Bahugiri, Gāndhāra, and Puṣkalāvataka; 16.25cd/ Prasthala, Mālava, Kaikaya, Dāśārṇa, Uśīnara, and the Śibis.
And those who drink from the Vitastā, the Irāvatī, and the river Candrabhāgā,
become endowed with chariots, silver mines, elephants, horses, mahouts, and wealth.
16.27ab/ Fragrant flowers, ointments, ornaments of jewels and diamonds, beds of lotuses;
16.27cd/ excellent young women, the requisites for passion, and the enjoyment of refined food and sweet wine.
16.28ab/ Gardens, water, lovers, fame, happiness, generosity, and beauty;
16.28cd/ Learned men, ministers, merchants, potters, and various birds—these are the threefold groups.
Silk, fine cloth, woolen blankets, silk-cotton, *rodhra* leaves, cinnamon, nutmeg, eaglewood, *vacā*, long pepper, and sandalwood belong to Bhṛgu.
16.30ab/ Ānarta, Arbuda, Puṣkara, Saurāṣṭra, Ābhīra, Śūdra, and Raivataka;

16.30cd/ that region where the Sarasvatī has disappeared is the western country. 16.31ab/ [The people] born in the land of the Kurus, Prabhāsa, Vidiśā, Vedasmṛti, and those born on the banks of the Mahī.
16.31cd / Those who are wicked, foul, base, oil-pressers, lacking in strength of character, and emasculated;
16.32ab. Prisoners, fowlers, the impure, fishermen, the deformed, the elderly, and pork-sellers;

16.32cd. Those worshipped by the multitude, those who have failed in their vows, Śabaras, Pulindas, and those devoid of wealth; 16.33ab. Those who consume pungent and bitter substances, elixirs, widows, women, serpents, thieves, and buffalo-keepers.
16.33cd/ Donkeys, young camels, chickpeas, *vātala* (or *vātula*) beans, and *niṣpāva* beans belong to the son of the Sun (Saturn).
16.34ab/ The Mleccha tribes, who are Śūdras, dwell upon mountain peaks, in ravines, and in caves;
they are jackal-eaters, Śūlikas, Vokkāṇas, horse-faced, and deformed in limb.
16.35ab/ They are defilers of their families, violent, ungrateful, thieves, devoid of truth and purity, and lacking in charity.
Those who are skilled in fighting with donkeys or wild beasts, who resort to pits of intense anger, and are base, are [of the type described].
16.36ab/ All living beings will be afflicted, deceitful, demonic, and full of sloth;
16.36cd/ and they will be utterly abandoned by righteousness during the reign of the enemy of the sun and moon (Rāhu).
The Giridurgas, Pahlavas, Śvetas, Hūṇas, Colas, Āvagāṇas, Marus, and Cīnas are frontier peoples,
wealthy, possessed of great ambition, perseverance, and valor.
Those who delight in disputes over others' wives, who take pleasure in seeking out the vulnerabilities of others, who are intoxicated with pride,
who are foolish, unrighteous, and desirous of victory— these are declared to be under the influence of Ketu.

If at the time of its rising, that great planet possesses bright rays and remains in its natural state, and has not been struck by thunderbolts, meteors, dust-storms, or the oppression of malefic planets; and if it is situated in its own house, has reached its exaltation, and is aspected by benefic planets—
He becomes auspicious for those by whom he is proclaimed as their lord.
When the characteristics are contrary to those previously described, his dominion comes to ruin;
the people become afflicted by civil strife, fear, and disease, and the kings likewise fall into suffering.

16.41ab/ If kings have no fear caused by enemies, nor certainly by their own sons or by ministers, 16.41cd/ and if there is drought for the countryside, then people go to unprecedented cities, mountains, and rivers.
Chapter 17: On the Conjunction of Planets.
17.01ab: Just as and when a future battle is predicted by those who know the three periods of time, 17.01cd:
the method for that knowledge has been composed by me in this Karaṇa, based upon the Sūryasiddhānta.
17.02ab/ Of the planets moving in the sky, situated one above the other in their own orbits,
17.02cd/ because of the extreme distance, they appear as if they have attained equality within the range of vision.

17.03ab/ Due to the application of the "approaching" (āsanna) and "stepping" (krama) movements, along with piercing (bheda), marking (ullekha), crushing (aṃśumardana), and the leftward (asavya) [movements],
17.03cd/ battle is said by sages such as Parāśara to be of four kinds.
17.04ab/ In the *bheda* [aspect], there is destruction by rain, as well as division among friends and great families.
17.04cd/ In the *ullekha* [aspect], there is danger from weapons, conflict with ministers, and loss of beloved food.
17.05ab/ When there is opposition between the rays [of the planets], there are wars among kings, as well as injuries from weapons, disease, hunger, and oppression.
17.05cd/ And when the rays are counter-clockwise (apasavya) during the conflict, battles break out among the rulers of the earth.
17.06ab. The Sun is the "Cry" (ākranda) when situated in the middle; he is a "Citizen" (paura) when stationed in the east or west, and a "Marcher" (yāyin) otherwise.
17.06cd. Mercury, Jupiter, and Saturn are always "Citizens"; the Moon is the "Cry."

17.07ab/ Ketu, Mars, Rāhu, and Venus—these are the "marchers" (yāyin); when afflicted, they destroy [the native]. 17.07cd/ They bring victory to the "crier" (ākranda), the "marcher," and the citizens; being victorious themselves, they grant victory to their own faction.
When one citizen is killed by another citizen, the citizens strike down other citizens and kings;
likewise, it is the same for the *yāyyākranda* and the *nāgara-yāyi-graha*.
17.09ab/ That which is situated in the southern direction, harsh, trembling, returning without reaching its mark,
minute, 17.09cd/ mounted upon another, deformed, lusterless, and discolored— that is defeated.
One endowed with characteristics opposite to those described [above] is to be designated as having attained victory.
Even one situated in the southern direction is possessed of victory if it is broad, glossy, and radiant.
17.11 Both [planets] become endowed with rays, broad, and glossy at their conjunction;
therein there is mutual affection. If they are the opposite [of these qualities], they destroy their own sides.
17.12ab/ If a battle or a meeting occurs when [the planets] are unmanifest by their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇaiḥ*),
17.12cd/ then for kings on earth as well, the result should likewise be declared as unmanifest.
17.13ab. When Mars is defeated by Jupiter, the Bāhlīkas, the Yāyins, and those who subsist by fire will suffer.
17.13cd. By Mercury, the Śūrasenas, the Kaliṅgas, and the Śālvas are afflicted.
17.14ab/ When the wheel of Saturn is conquered, the citizens triumph and the subjects perish.
17.14cd/ When Venus is conquered, there is distress in the storehouses, among the Mlecchas, and among the Kṣatriyas.
17.15 When Mercury is struck by Mars, the kings of Vṛkṣa, Sarit, Tāpasa, and Aśmaka,
as well as those situated in the northern direction and those initiated for sacrifices, undergo great distress.
When Jupiter is conquered by Mercury, the city-dwellers will be joined with Mlecchas, Śūdras, thieves, and those seeking wealth;
the inhabitants of Traigarta and the mountains will suffer, and the earth will tremble.
17.17 When Mercury is afflicted by Saturn, there is destruction of sailors, warriors, lotuses, wealth, and pregnant women;
when defeated by Venus, there is an outbreak of fire and the ruin of crops, clouds, and travelers.
17.18ab/ When Jupiter is afflicted by Venus, the Kulūtas, Gāndhāras, Kaikayas, and Madras [suffer];
17.18cd/ the Śālvas, Vatsas, Vaṅgas, and cows, as well as the crops, are oppressed [or destroyed].
When Jupiter is struck by Mars, there will be moderate [results]: [the prosperity of] regions, lords of men, and cattle.
And when struck by Saturn, [there is harm to] the Arjunāyanas, Vasātis, Yaudheyas, Śibis, and Brahmins.
When Jupiter is defeated even by Mercury, the Mlecchas, those who profess truth, and those who bear weapons shall prevail;
the Middle Country will go to ruin, as will whatever fruit arises from devotion.
17.21ab/ When Venus is defeated by Jupiter, the invader meets with destruction;
17.21cd/ there is conflict between the Brahmins and the Kshatriyas, and Indra does not withhold rain.
The Kośalas, Kaliṅgas, Vaṅgas, Vatsas, Matsyas, along with those from the Middle Country,
as well as the eunuchs and the Śūrasenas, will undergo great suffering.
17.23ab/ When Mercury is conquered by Mars, there is the slaughter of chief warriors and battles among kings.
17.23cd/ [If] by Mercury, there is the destruction of mountain-dwellers, the ruin of milk products, and scant rainfall.
17.24ab/ When Venus is defeated by Saturn, those chief among the virtuous, those who live by weapons, and the Kṣatriyas [are afflicted].
17.24cd/ Those born of water are also oppressed; otherwise, the fruit of devotion is common [to all].
17.25ab/ When the dark [Jupiter] is struck by the white [Venus], there is an increase in prices and suffering for those who pride themselves on being snakes or birds.
17.25cd/ When struck by Mars, there is affliction for the regions of the Taṅgaṇas, Andhras, Uḍras, Kāśis, and Bāhlīkas.
When Saturn is overcome by Mercury, the limbs, merchants, birds, cattle, and elephants are tormented;
when it is overcome by Jupiter, women, Mahishakas, and Shakas are greatly afflicted.
17.27ab/ This specific distinction has been stated regarding those struck by Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn.
17.27cd/ However, the fruit should be declared as different from the planetary division; for when struck, they destroy their own respective divisions in whatever manner.

Chapter 18: On the Conjunction of the Moon with the Planets If the moon passes to the north of the planets according to their respective positions, that is a clockwise (pradakṣiṇa) movement which brings auspiciousness to kings; if it passes to the south, the moon does not bring prosperity.
18.02ab. If the Moon goes to the north of Mars, there is victory for those powerful mountain tribes;
18.02cd. the Kṣatriyas are delighted and march forth, and the earth abounds in grain and rejoices.
18.03ab/ When the hare-marked moon [Jupiter] is to the north of its own son [Mercury], it brings about prosperity for the citizens and ensures abundance of food.
18.03cd/ It causes an accumulation of grain and increases the treasury of kings, yet it brings distress to the people.
When the Moon is situated north of Jupiter, there is prosperity for citizens, twice-born men, kṣatriyas, and scholars;
likewise, there is growth for righteousness and the middle country, along with abundance of food and joyful subjects.
If the Moon moves north of Venus, it brings an increase in treasuries, elephants, and horses;
there is victory for those who march forth and for archers, and there is also an abundance of excellent crops.
If the Moon should move clockwise around Saturn, there will be victory for the kings of cities;
the Śakas, Bāhlikas, Sindhus, and Pahlavas, together with the Yavanas, shall experience great joy.

18.07ab/ For those lunar mansions and planets toward which the moon moves in the north and is free from affliction, it nourishes their respective goods, people, other devotees, and regions; by moving southward, it destroys them.
18.08a Whatever result is taught for a planet when it is situated to the north of the moon,
18.08b all that becomes exactly the opposite when it is to the south;
18.08c thus have been proclaimed the conjunctions of the lunar mansions and the planets with the moon.
Indeed, there is no battle between the moon and the planets or the lunar mansions.
Chapter 19: The Results of Planetary Years.
19.01a: Everywhere the earth is covered with sparse crops, and forests are, by fate, surrounded by predatory beasts eager to devour.
The rivers do not flow with abundant water,
and medicines, though possessing great potency, are no longer as effective.
The son of Aditi blazes fiercely even in the season of winter;
the mountain-like clouds do not release much water;
and the sky has its host of stars and the moon deprived of their luster.
The communities of ascetics, along with the herds of cattle, are perishing.

19.03a Endowed with unbearable forces consisting of elephants, horses, and infantry, 19.03b they move about, excelling with bows, swords, and clubs; 19.03c kings, together with their royal followers, slaughter [their enemies] and seize lands in battle.
Then, in the year of the Sun, on its day, and furthermore in the month.
The sky was pervaded by clouds resembling moving mountains, possessing the luster of serpents, collyrium,
bees, and buffalo horns, filling the entire earth with their pure waters.
The quarters of the sky resounded with the deep, longing cry of the elephant.

The waters abound with lotuses, water-lilies, and blue lilies; the groves are filled with blossoming trees resounding with the humming of bees; and the cows yield abundant milk and are a delight to the eyes.
19.05d Beautiful women delight beautiful men with uninterrupted amorous play.
19.06a Fields of wheat, rice, barley, various grains, and excellent sugarcane;
19.06b the earth, rich with cities and mines, is protected by kings;
19.06c marked by funeral mounds and resounding with the proclamations of the best of sacrifices.
When the year had fully entered the cold season.
19.07a A fire, violently fanned by the wind, rages on, most fierce, desiring to burn down villages, forests, and cities;
19.07c those struck by the falling hosts of bandits cry out, "Alas! Alas!"
19.07d Deprived of their own property and lacking cattle, the multitudes of mortals on earth [are reduced].
19.08a Even though their forms are gathered together and raised high in the sky,
19.08b the clouds release no abundant water anywhere;
19.08c the crop, though grown within its proper boundaries, undergoes withering.
Others take away even what has been accomplished due to a lack of discipline.
19.09a Kings are not fully intent on the duty of protecting [their subjects];
19.09b there is an abundance of diseases arising from bile and the provocation of serpents;
19.09c thus afflicted by such things, these subjects come to ruin.
In the year of the Son of the Earth, the crops will fail.
19.10 There is an increase in those who practice illusion, sorcery, trickery, and the arts of the city; in music, painting, mathematics, and the knowledge of weapons;
and kings display wonders out of a desire to please.
They give to one another things that produce joy.
In this world, the fourfold means of livelihood (*vārtā*) is unerring and complete, and the triple Veda (*trayī*) functions perfectly,
like the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) under a wise ruler;
yet there are some whose intellects remain deeply attached even to the supreme syllable (*adhyakṣara*).
And those striving for the supreme state through the sciences of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī).

The Moon, born from the one marked with a deer, produces affection in those who know humor, messengers, poets, children, and eunuchs, as well as in those who know logic and dwell by bridges, water, or mountains, during its own year.
Or else, in that month, there will be an abundance of medicinal herbs upon the earth.
19.13a A sound, rising at the sacrifice, traveling to heaven,
19.13b vast, and piercing the minds of those who steal the sacrifice, 19.13c wanders incessantly among the best of the twice-born.
It brings joy to the heart of those who partake in the portions of the sacrifice.

19.14ab/ Then the earth, abounding in excellent crops and enriched by many elephants, infantry, horses, wealth, and vast herds of cattle, shone forth; its people, rivalling the denizens of heaven, flourished under the protection of the kings.

When the year of the preceptor of the king of the gods is auspicious, the earth is covered with various lofty clouds that satiate the ground with water; the land abounds in excellent crops and is endowed with supreme prosperity.
The earth, resembling a mountain, was filled with rice and sugarcane;
its embankments were completely saturated by the water released from the clouds,
and it was strewn with beautiful ponds covered in clusters of lotuses.
She shines like a young woman whose limbs are radiant with fresh ornaments.

The royal power on earth had its vast forces and enemy factions destroyed; its quarters resounded with the proclaimed shouts of manifold victories; and it was a realm where the virtuous were delighted while the wicked were utterly ruined.
The rulers protect the earth, which is enriched with cities and mines.
In the springtime, honey is drunk with beloved women; enchanting songs are sung together with flutes and lutes;
and food is enjoyed in the company of guests, friends, and kinsmen.
In the year of the planet Venus, there shall be a proclamation of victory for Madana.
The kingdoms were agitated by numerous battles with hosts of arrogant bandits, stripped of their many cattle and wealth,
and filled with people wailing for their slaughtered kinsmen.
19.19d Families agitated by the most severe diseases and by hunger.

19.20a The sky was devoid of clouds, though stirred by the wind; 19.20b the surface of the earth had its many branches broken off, and the heavens were shrouded in excessive dust from which the rays of the sun and moon had vanished.
And even the slender rivers, though containing water, were devoid of moisture.
19.21a Some crops that have grown perish for lack of water; 19.21b others, sprinkled with water, reach full maturity;
19.21c thus does the enemy of Vṛtra rain down only sparingly upon the grain.
19.21d When the year of the son of the Sun (Saturn) is always in progress.

19.22a A planet that is minute, lacking rays, situated in its depression, or defeated by others does not bestow its full fruit; one that is otherwise than this bestows nourishment. 19.22c Whatever inauspiciousness occurs in an inauspicious year, there is an increase of that which is produced in the month.
And likewise, even an auspicious result should be treated as palliative when there is mutual conflict.
Chapter 20: On the Constellation-Quadrangles (Grahaśṛṅgāṭaka) 20.01ab.
In whichever direction all the lunar mansions and planets are seen entering the Sun, 20.01cd.
there will be danger in that direction from the fury of weapons, famine, and disease.
20.02ab/ Having the shapes of a wheel, a bow, a rhombus, a staff, a city, a spear, or a thunderbolt;
20.02cd/ they cause hunger or drought in the world, and lead to war among the lords of men.
20.03ab/ In whichever portion of the sky the series of planets is visible when the sun has reached the end of the day,
20.03cd/ there another king arises, and there is great affliction from a foreign army.
20.04ab/ If the planets should meet in that same lunar mansion (*ṛkṣa*), they would destroy the people born there.
20.04cd/ But if their pure rays do not obstruct one another, they bring them prosperity.
20.05ab/ Those known as *graha*, *saṃvarta*, *samāgama*, *sammoha*, *samāja*, and *sannipāta*,
along with the *kośa*— I shall describe their characteristics together with their results.
20.06ab. When four or five [planets] move together with the citizens (the Moon) in a single asterism, it is called Saṃvarta; when joined by Ketu and Rāhu, it is Sammoha.
20.07ab. A citizen joined by other citizens, or a traveler accompanied by other travelers, is called a *samāja* (assembly).
20.07cd. If another person should arrive at the meeting of a *yama* and a *jīva*, then it is a *kośa* (treasury).
20.08ab/ If one [planet] has risen in the west and another in the east, that is called a conjunction (sannipāta).
20.08cd/ Those whose bodies are unaltered, glossy, and broad are auspicious when they meet.
20.09ab/ But the two [yogas] known as Saṃvarta and Samāgama are equal, being the Sammoha and Kośa [respectively], which bring fear to living beings.
20.09cd/ That called Samāja is declared to be very auspicious (susama), whereas in Sannipāta there is indeed the provocation of enmity.
Chapter 21: On the Characteristics of the Womb.
21.01ab: Food is the life-force of the world, and food is dependent upon the rainy season.
21.01cd: Therefore, the rainy season must be examined with great effort.
21.02ab/ Having observed those characteristics which were set down by the sages, this [work] is now composed, based on the treatises written by Garga, Parāśara, Kāśyapa, Vajra, and others.
21.02cd/ [It is composed] based on the works authored by Garga, Parāśara, Kāśyapa, Vajra, and so forth.
The astrologer who, with a focused mind, remains day and night attentive to the characteristics of the fetus—
his speech, like that of a sage, does not prove false when he points out the water [of the birth].

21.04ab / Or what else is superior to this scripture, by knowing which alone, even in a degenerate age, one becomes a seer of the three times? 21.04cd / Even in the Kali age, though time is subject to destruction, one becomes a perceiver of the past, present, and future.
21.05ab. Some say that the days of conception would occur after the end of the bright fortnight of Kārttika.
21.05cd. That is not the opinion of many; I shall now state the view of Garga and others.
21.06ab/ When the moon has entered the asterism Āṣāḍhā, or Pūrvāṣāḍhā, starting from the first day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, 21.06cd/ one should know the characteristics of the embryos.
Whichever lunar mansion the Moon enters when conception occurs,
the birth will take place in that very same mansion ninety-five days later, according to the power of the Moon.

21.08ab/ Those born during the bright fortnight [are strong] in the dark fortnight, and those born during the dark fortnight in the bright; those born by day [are strong] at night, and those born at night by day. 21.08cd/ And those born at the junctions (sandhyā) are strong at the junctions.
21.09ab. Conceptions occurring under Mṛgaśīrṣa and the following asterisms, as well as those born during the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, yield poor results.
21.09cd. One should indicate the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa by means of the dark fortnight of Pauṣa.
21.10ab/ Conceptions occurring in the bright fortnight of Māgha reach delivery in the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa.
21.10cd/ One should indicate that those [conceived] in the dark fortnight of Māgha will deliver in the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada.

Those [asterisms] that arise in the bright fortnight of Phālguna are to be assigned to the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada; however, those that arise in the dark fortnight of that same month belong to the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja.
Clouds born during the dark fortnight of Caitra or the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja hold embryos;
those produced in the dark fortnight of Caitra rain during the bright fortnight of Kārttika.
Clouds that had arisen in the east later appear in the west;
likewise, in the remaining directions as well, there occurs a reversal of both the clouds and the wind.

The wind blows pleasantly, softly, with water-laden drops, and auspiciously from the direction of Indra; the sky is clear, and both the moon and the sun are encircled by glossy, white, and thick halos.

When the sky is broad, vast, glossy, and dense, filled with thick, needle-like, razor-edged, and red clouds; when it has the dark luster of a crow’s egg and the moon and stars are clearly visible; [then rain will fall].
An auspicious twilight is characterized by the deep thundering of Indra’s bow, lightning, and mock suns;
meanwhile, flocks of birds and herds of wild animals remain quiet, with the moon, Śiva, and Śakra stationed in their respective quarters.
The planets are large, moving clockwise, and possessed of lustrous rays, free from portents; likewise, the trees have unimpaired sprouts, and men and quadrupeds are joyful.

21.18ab/ All [these factors] are nourishers of embryos; however, whatever specific [factor] exists here, 21.18cd/ produced by the very nature of its own season, for the growth of the embryo—that I shall now describe.
21.19ab. In the months of Pauṣa and Mārgaśīrṣa, there is a glow at twilight and clouds accompanied by halos.
21.19cd. In Mṛgaśīrṣa it is not excessively cold, but in Pauṣa there is a heavy fall of snow.
In the month of Māgha, the wind is powerful, while the sun and the moon have their radiance obscured by frost;
it is exceedingly cold, and the rising and setting of the sun, even when accompanied by clouds, are auspicious.
In the month of Phālguna, dry and fierce winds and dense clouds are auspicious;
likewise, partial halos and a tawny or copper-colored sun are favorable.
In the month of Caitra, clouds accompanied by wind, rain, and halos are auspicious for conception.
In Vaiśākha, clouds characterized by dense winds, water, lightning, and thunder are likewise for the benefit [of the world].
Resembling pearls and silver, with the luster of tamāla trees, blue lotuses, and collyrium, these clouds—
dense and containing abundant water— take on the forms of aquatic creatures within their depths.
Scorched by the rays of the fierce sun and fanned by gentle breezes,
the clouds release their water in torrents at the time of their ripening, as if they were filled with rage.

21.25ab/ Signs of injury to the fetus include the falling of meteors, thunderbolts, and dust, and the burning of the quarters; 21.25cd/ as well as earthquakes, the appearance of hollows in the earth, spikes, comets, planetary conflicts, and atmospheric explosions.
21.26ab/ An abnormal shower of blood and other such portents, a halo (parigha), rainbows, and the appearance of Rāhu;
21.26cd/ by these three kinds of portents and others, the embryo is destroyed.
21.27ab/ By those general characteristics produced by the nature of the seasons, there is growth of embryos; 21.27cd/ by the opposites of those very same [characteristics], their contrary occurs.
Furthermore, when the moon is in the two Bhadrapadās, Viśvā (Uttarabhādrapadā), Ambu (Śatabhiṣaj), Deva (Pūrvaphalgunī), or Paitāmaha (Uttaraphalgunī),
the embryo increases in all seasons and results in much rain.
A conception occurring in conjunction with Śatabhiṣaj, Āśleṣā, Ārdrā, Svāti, or Maghā is auspicious;
it sustains the fetus for many days, but if struck by threefold portents, it destroys it.
In the months beginning with Mṛgaśīrṣa, there are eight, six, sixteen,
twenty-four, twenty, and then three days [of conjunction] with one lunar mansion out of the five.

By five signs it rains for a hundred yojanas; from that point on, it decreases by half and half again with each subsequent sign. That embryo which possesses only one form [of sign] rains over five [yojanas].

21.32ab [K.21.36ab]: In the case of five omens, the amount is one *droṇa*; in the case of the embryo, three *āḍhakas*; by wind, three; 21.32cd [K.21.36cd]: by lightning, six; by clouds, nine; by thunder, twelve at the time of birth.
21.33ab/ When joined with a malefic planet, the clouds produce hailstones, thunderbolts, and rain of fish.
21.33cd/ But when the Moon or the Sun is conjoined with or aspected by a benefic, they cause abundant rain.
21.34ab. Excessive rain at the time of conception, occurring without any apparent cause, leads to the absence of an embryo.
21.34cd. If more than one-eighth of a *droṇa* of rain has fallen, the embryo becomes miscarried.
If, due to the affliction of planets and other such factors, the embryo does not rain at the time of delivery,
then at the time of its own birth, it bestows water mixed with hailstones.
Just as the milk of a cow held for a long time becomes solid,
so too does water, when its time has passed, attain solidity.
That cloud which is accompanied by wind, water, lightning, thunder,
and rain is possessed of five forms and becomes full of water; if it releases its water excessively during the period of gestation, [it is a sign of abundance].
Having reached the time of birth, he creates a spray of water.
Chapter 22: On Conception.

22.01ab. The four days beginning with the eighth of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha are the days for the retention of the vital breath (vāyu). 22.01cd. They are auspicious when the winds are gentle and favorable, and the sky is covered by glossy clouds.

22.02ab. In that very same manner, when rain falls during the four asterisms beginning with Svāti, the months are to be known in sequence as starting with Śrāvaṇa. 22.02cd. These [rainfalls] are called *parisruta* and *dhāraṇā*. 22.03ab. If these should be of a uniform nature, they are auspicious; however, if they are intermittent, they do not lead to welfare.
22.03cd / And fears of thieves have been declared here, as well as the verses of Vasiṣṭha.
Accompanied by lightning, accompanied by droplets, accompanied by winds that raise dust,
and with the sun and moon obscured— these are the meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās), the auspicious concentrations.
But when auspicious flashes of lightning appear,
then the wise man should declare an increase in all crops.

22.06ab/ Rain accompanied by dust and rain are auspicious, as are playful activities involving children; 22.06cd/ so too are the melodious cries of birds and play in dust, water, and similar elements.
22.07ab/ When halos around the sun and moon are glossy and not excessively marred,
22.07cd/ then rain should be known to occur, which brings about the prosperity of all crops.
22.08ab/ When the clouds are glossy, compact, and move in a clockwise direction, 22.08cd/ then there shall be a great rain for the flourishing of all crops [and the accomplishment of all goals].
Chapter 23: On the Rains.

When the month of Jyeṣṭha has passed and it has begun to rain under the asterism of Pūrvāṣāḍhā, those who know [the signs] should declare the auspicious or inauspicious results, as well as the measure of the water.
23.02ab. With reference to a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍaka) that is one cubit in width, the measurement of the water is specified as follows:
23.02cd. One should measure fifty palas of water fallen [into it] by means of this [measure], which is an āḍhaka.
23.03ab/ By one who has caused the earth to be marked with seals, or by drops [of water] upon the tips of blades of grass;
23.03cd/ by him who has rained, the first measurement of the water must be declared.
23.04ab / Some say that the area rained upon is a circle of ten *yojanas*;
others say it is twelve, according to the opinion of Garga, Vasiṣṭha, and Parāśara, and not more than that.
23.05ab/ And in whichever lunar mansions it has rained heavily, in those very same ones it will generally rain again.
23.05cd/ If, however, no rain has fallen in Āpya and the others, then there will be drought for all.
23.06ab/ In Hasta, Āpya (Śatabhiṣaj), Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Citrā, Pauṣṇa (Revatī), and Dhaniṣṭhā, there are sixteen droṇas;
23.06cd/ in Śatabhiṣaj, Aindra (Jyeṣṭhā), and Svāti, there are four; and in Kṛttikā, ten.
In Śravaṇa, Maghā, Anurādhā, Bharaṇī, and Mūla, there are ten and four [droṇas] respectively;
in Phalgunī, twenty-five; and in Punarvasu, twenty droṇas.
In the asterisms named Aindrāgna and Vaiśva, there are twenty; in Sārpa, ten plus three (thirteen);
in Āhirbudhnya, Āryamaṇa, and Prājāpatya, there are five times five (twenty-five).
Fifteen are proclaimed for Āja and Puṣya, and for Vājibha, there are twelve.
23.09cd. Eighteen droṇas are declared for the Raudra [nakṣatra], provided these are free from portents.

23.10 When a lunar mansion is afflicted by the Sun, Saturn, or Ketu, and struck by the three kinds of portents caused by Mars, there is neither well-being nor rain; however, when it is conjoined with benefics and free from affliction, there is well-being.
Chapter 24: The Chapter on the Rohiṇī Yoga.

In a grove resounding with the humming of bees clinging to flowers on trees growing from crevices in heaps of golden stone, and filled with the deep sounds of the warbling of many birds and the songs of young celestial maidens;
