24.02ab/ That which Bṛhaspati spoke to Nārada upon the peak of the mountain that is the abode of the gods,
and that which Garga, Parāśara, and Kāśyapa [spoke] to their assemblies of disciples;
Having observed those [treatises] as they truly are, intended for the purpose of attaining union with Prajāpati and the Moon,
I am now prepared to speak of them in concise form.

24.04ab/ Having observed that the constellation Prajeśa (Rohiṇī) has been approached by the moon during the dark fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, 24.04cd/ the astrologer, based on the instructions of the treatises, must declare what is auspicious or inauspicious for the world.
24.05ab/ The conjunction (yoga) is to be stated exactly as it will occur in the future; that conjunction of the lunar mansions has been declared by me in the Karaṇa.
24.05cd/ The result is to be proclaimed according to the magnitude, brilliance, color, and path of the moon, as well as by portentous winds.
To the north of the city, or even in front of it, on a raised piece of ground where he has stayed for three days, intent upon the fire-sacrifice,
he should draw the planets together with the hosts of constellations.
One should worship with incense, flowers, and offerings.
Adorned on all four sides with jars containing gems, water, and medicinal herbs— well-honored, covered with young tree shoots, and possessing roots that do not wait for the season.
A twice-born man should dwell upon a sacrificial mound strewn with Kuśa grass.
Having consecrated all the seeds with the mantra of the Great Vow (mahāvrata) and placed them in the jar,
they should be soaked with water containing gold and *darbha* grass.
24.08d A man [should be purified] with the mantras of Marut, Varuṇa, and Soma (or Saumya).
One should fix a smooth black banner,
equal in length to the staff and three times its height;
once the determination of the directions has been made at the outset, the wind [shall blow].
24.09d When the moon has entered that yoga, it is to be grasped by her.
24.10a Therein, half-months are to be calculated by means of the watches (praharas); 24.10b days for the sake of the year-sign (varṣānimitta) are [calculated] by its parts.
24.10c Moving with the left [hand], it always bestows auspiciousness.
24.10d In whom [the world] is established, that is the powerful Vāyu.

24.11a But when the conjunction has occurred, those seeds which have sprouted here, 24.11b which were held within the jar— of those, whatever portion has sprouted, that is its [share]. 24.11c Whatever portion has sprouted, that is its [share].
Among them, only this one attains growth; no other does.

24.12 When the quarters resound with the cries of peaceful birds and deer, the sky is clear, and the wind is blameless—this is praised when the moon has entered Rohiṇī. Hereafter, I shall describe the effects of clouds and winds.
In some places with clouds black and white, in others white, and in others black, like serpents, appearing only on their coiled bellies and backs;
24.13c–d. With their bellies and backs visible only as they were coiled.
24.13d Enveloped by broad flashes of lightning for tongues.
The sky was as if strewn with various clouds, white like the interior of a blooming lotus, their edges tinted by the radiance of the sun’s rays.
24.14d White as honeybees, saffron, and *kiṃśuka* flowers.
Or [the sky] may be completely obscured by dark clouds,
variegated by flickering lightning and divine rainbows,
and agitated by herds of elephants and buffaloes.
The sky was like a forest enveloped by a forest fire.
Or else, the sky was covered by clouds resembling heaps of slabs from the Añjana mountain,
or rather, by clouds possessing the captivating luster of snow, pearls, conch shells, and the rays of the moon.
With lightning for their golden girths, cranes for their prominent teeth,
flowing water for their ichor, and moving ears for their trunks;
and with the beauty of raised banners in the form of various rainbows.
And it was surrounded by clouds and nagas, dark as the tamala groves.
24.18a Of the masses of clouds, dark as blue lotuses, standing in the sky colored by the twilight;
24.18b [They resemble] the multitudes of [the attendants] of him who is clothed in yellow garments.
Or when they steal away the splendor of Hari.
If the deep and clear sounds [of the lutes] are blended with the cries of peacocks, cātaka birds, and frogs, they will fill the sky and hang over the ends of the quarters.
24.19d Water-givers, pouring forth torrents of water upon the earth.
If the sky is thus obstructed for three days, or two days, or even a single day by masses of clouds of the forms previously described, there will be an abundance of food.
And the earth shall have joyful people and abundant water.
24.21a By those who are rough and small, their bodies driven by wind; 24.21b resembling camels, crows, pretas, or monkeys; 24.21c or in the forms of other such contemptible beings.
And with silent clouds, there is neither auspiciousness nor rain.
Just as the sun with its fierce rays produces water in a cloudless sky,
so does he [the Buddha] cause the lake of the Dharma to bloom at night with its abundance of white lotuses.
If the sky is purified by the stars, it portends a good rain.

24.23a From years arising in the eastern direction, there is the production of crops; 24.23b from those born in the south-eastern quarter, there is an outbreak of fire; 24.23c in the southern [quarter], the crop perishes, and in the south-western [quarter], half [is lost].
If the rain-bearing clouds are situated behind, there will be auspicious rainfall.

24.24a When [the smoke] arises from the northwest, there is wind and rain; 24.24b when it arises from the northern quarter, the rain is abundant. 24.24c When it increases in the direction of the north pole (Sthāṇu), the crops will be excellent.
And thus the wind bestows its fruits upon the various quarters.
24.25a The falling of meteors, lightning, and thunderbolts; 24.25b the burning of the quarters, atmospheric crashes, and earthquakes; 24.25c the cries of beasts and of birds—these [are portents].
Just as the clouds are to be grasped, so indeed are they.
With those jars marked with names, beginning with the north and arranged clockwise starting from the month of Śrāvaṇa,
and filled with water, that month becomes a giver of water.
If [the figures] are heard [as they are], there will be no rain; if they are deficient, it should be calculated accordingly.
And with other jars marked with the names of kings, as well as others likewise marked with the names of countries— some broken, some leaking, some with insufficient water, and others completely full.
The fortunes should be declared according to their respective correspondences.
Whether the moon is far away or near,
situated on the southern path in whatever manner,
if it joins with Rohiṇī in every respect, [it portends a great calamity].
One should declare this world to be truly miserable.
When the moon moves northward while touching [the asterism],
then there will be good rain accompanied by many calamities; when it moves northward without touching [it] in conjunction, [there will be no rain].
It brings about abundant rain and auspiciousness.
When the moon is situated in the middle of the cart of Rohiṇī, people, deprived of refuge and having their food begged by infants, wander away to some unknown place.
24.30d They drink water from jars heated by the sun.
If Rohiṇī follows behind the moon when it has first risen, then those afflicted by love will surely experience auspicious fortune.
24.31d Women remain under the sway of desire.
If the moon follows behind like a lover following his beloved woman,
those afflicted by the arrows of the one whose banner bears the sea-monster [Cupid] [will suffer].
At that time, men were under the sway of women.

24.33a If the moon should be in the southeastern quarter (Āgneyī), there will be a great calamity; 24.33b If it is in the southwestern quarter (Nairṛtī), the crops will be beset by misfortunes and go to their destruction.
24.33c When the moon is situated in the northeastern or northwestern quarters (Prājāpatya or Vāyavya), there is a middling abundance of grain.
When [the planet] has gone toward the direction of Sthāṇu (the North), there are very many virtues, such as the increase in the price of grain, rain, and so forth.
If it strikes the junction-star (yogatārakā), or if it covers it with its body,
they declare that in the case of a strike there is terrible danger, while in the case of a covering, O King, there is the death of a ruler caused by a woman.

24.35ab/ At the time of entering the cow-pen, if a bull or even a black animal goes ahead; 24.35cd/ Or if there is much water in a variegated [spot], it is middling; but not so when it is white, for those intent on the perception of water.
If the moon joined with Rohiṇī is not seen in the sky because it is shrouded by clouds, then great danger from disease is imminent; yet the earth shall be endowed with abundant water and crops.
Chapter 25: The Yoga of Svāti.
Whatever fruit results from the conjunction with Rohiṇī, that same fruit occurs when the Moon is conjoined with Svāti and Āṣāḍhā.
All this should be considered during the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha; I shall now declare the specific distinction regarding this.
25.02a When rain falls during the first watch of the night under the asterism Svāti,
all crops reach full growth;
25.02b in the second part [of the night], sesame, mung beans, and black gram [flourish].
In the third [month], there is the summer [rain], but not the autumnal rains.
25.03ab/ If it rains during the first part of the day, there will be good rain; likewise, if it rains during the second part, there will be rain accompanied by insects and snakes.
25.03cd/ If it rains during the middle or the latter part of the day, the rain will be moderate; if it rains throughout both day and night, the rain will be unceasing.
25.04ab/ The star known as Apāṃvatsa is said to be situated level with the north of Citrā. 25.04cd/ When the moon is near it, its conjunction with Svāti brings auspiciousness.

25.05 If, on the seventh lunar day during the conjunction with Svāti in the darkness of the month of Māgha, snow falls, or the wind blows with fierce velocity, or even if the water-laden clouds thunder incessantly;
or if the sky becomes filled with garlands of lightning, with the moon, sun, and stars vanished—
This rainy season is to be known as one in which the countryside is joyful and endowed with all crops.
25.06ab/ Likewise in Phālguna, Caitra, or even in the dark fortnight of Vaiśākha;
25.06cd/ one should recognize the Svāti-yoga, especially in Āṣāḍha.
Chapter 26: The Chapter on the Āṣāḍhī Yoga.
26.01ab: On the day of Āṣāḍhī, seeds that have been weighed and consecrated with mantras increase in weight when measured again on the following day.
If that [weight] increases and what was deficient is no longer produced,
then the mantra is employed for the consecration of the scale.
26.02ab/ Sarasvatī, the Goddess of Truth, is to be praised through the application of mantra.
26.02cd/ For you shall reveal that which is true, O you who are indeed devoted to truth within Truth.
26.03ab/ By that truth by which the moon, the sun, the planets, and likewise the hosts of luminaries, 26.03cd/ arise here in the east and subsequently set in the west;
Whatever truth is in all the Vedas, whatever truth is among those who discourse on Brahman,
and whatever truth is in the three worlds— let that truth be seen here.
"You are the daughter of Brahmā, proclaimed as Ādityā;
by lineage you belong to Kaśyapa, and by name you are renowned as Tulā."
26.06a Her carrying-cloth is made of linen, bound together with four threads; 26.06b it is six finger-breadths wide and has a looped fringe;
26.06c and the length of the threads is ten finger-breadths.
26.06d There are exactly six girth-straps in the middle of both loops.
26.07a Gold should be placed on a sling in the southern [section]; 26.07b the remaining substances and waters likewise in the northern [section].
26.07c With waters from wells, from the Sindhu, and from lakes;
26.07d Rainfall is classified as inferior, middling, and superior.

26.08a Elephants [are indicated] by the teeth; cattle, horses, and so forth, by the hair; 26.08b kings, by gold; the twice-born and others, by beeswax; 26.08c likewise, countries, years, months, and the directions [are indicated].
The remaining substances abide in the form of the self.
26.09ab. A balance made of gold is the best, one of silver is middling; in the absence of these two, it should be made of khadira wood.
26.09cd. Or that arrow with which a man was pierced shall serve as the balance, being one span (vitasti) in measure.
26.10ab/ For that which is deficient there is loss, for that which is excessive there is increase; when weighed on a scale, what is equal is balanced by the equal.
26.10cd/ This secret of the balance and the treasury has been declared; a man should apply it even in the administration of the kingdom.
26.11a In Svāti, the Aṣāḍhās, and Rohiṇī, malefic planets entering into conjunction are not auspicious; 26.11b however, even when two such conjunctions occur, one should fast and accept [the rite].
26.11d When an intercalary month doubles [the duration].
When all three yogas are similar in their results,
then it should be declared without doubt; however,
in the case of the opposite, that which arises from Rohiṇī [is the result].
That very same result is declared to be even greater.
26.13ab/ There is success, or the provocation of fire, and rain that is slight, moderate, or excellent;
26.13cd/ it is abundant with water and wind, nourishing and auspicious, according to the winds from the east and other directions.

If, on the fourth day of the dark fortnight of Āṣāḍha, when the moon is in the asterism Ajaikapāda, the rain-god Parjanya pours down rain, the monsoon is auspicious; if not, it is not so. However, if on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha there is a wind from the northeast (aiśāna), [the monsoon will be excellent].
When the sun of sharp rays sets, there will be an excellent abundance of crops.
Chapter 27.01ab on the Wind-Circle: If, on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, the wind should blow from the northeast (Īśāna), [it portends prosperity].
When the sun of sharp rays sets, there will be an excellent abundance of grain.
When the wind from the sky— tossed by the surging crests of the waves of the eastern ocean and driven by the impact of the massed manes of the sun’s and moon’s rays—
[strikes] the dense canopy of dark clouds that stand immovable and grow thick with the onset of autumn;
27.02d Adorned with the abundant crops of spring, the entire earth shines, [then one should know the land to be prosperous].
27.03 When the wind, its form unbroken [and skilled at striking the peaks of Mount Malaya], blows in the sky toward the fire, and while this yoga is occurring, the blessed sun has departed; then,
[the earth] is eternally illuminated, its surface embraced by the crests of flames.
With the heat of its own limbs and its breaths, the earth vomits forth a mass of ashes.
27.04a Causing the monkeys to dance with trees that have canopies of creepers with palm leaves,
27.04b when this harsh sound of the southern wind blows during this yoga,
27.04c those who are elevated by every effort [in yoga] are struck like elephants with the goads of palm-leaf whips.
Then the clouds release drops of scanty water, like miserly farmers.
When the southwest wind blows incessantly at sunset, tossing about heaps of fine cardamom, lavalī, and cloves upon the ocean,
it bears the weight of a covering carpet made of fragments of human bones covered by hunger and thirst.
Then the earth appeared like a drunken woman or a fierce and fickle female ghost.
27.06 When, at the time of the sun's rays falling [upon the earth], a wind arises from behind, agitated by the tossing of its mane and causing dust-storms to rise;
then the land, abounding in grain, will engage in battle with a multitude of excellent warriors.
The earth, in various places, was incessantly drenched with flesh and blood.

27.07a If, at the time of the Āṣāḍhī festival, when the sun has set, 27.07b a wind from the northwest arises with increased force, possessing a body like a cloud and resembling the upper half of a serpent;
27.07c one should know that the earth is filled with streams of water and resounds with the joyful croaking of frogs who have emerged and are delighted.
The earth, marked solely by the splendor of its crops, was like an army of fortune through its abundance of happiness.
When, at the end of summer, the sun has swallowed the circle of rays upon Mount Meru,
and a northern wind fragrant with the scent of blossoming *kadamba* trees blows,
then the clouds become intoxicated, possessing all the splendor of flickering lightning.
Like madmen, they fill the earth—which has lost the rays of the moon—with their waters.
27.09ab. If, when the month of Āṣāḍha has passed, on the fourth day of the dark fortnight under the asterism Ajapāda (Pūrvabhādrapadā), the cool Īśāna should be attended by the hosts of immortals;

27.09cd. if the rain-god Parjanya pours down rain, the rainy season is auspicious; if not, then it is not [so], nor is there a wind fragrant with Punnāga, Aguru, and Pārijāta, accompanied by a fierce roar.
27.10ab/ If the sky were not devoid of the rays of the moon and sun, nor bereft of stars; [if the earth were in the fullness of its youth with abundant waters and filled with ripened crops];

27.10cd/ I do not consider that to be the auspicious month of Bhādrapada in which the Lord does not send rain. [At that time, righteous kings, having subdued their enemies, protect the social orders.]
Chapter 28: On Immediate Rainfall.

28.01a–b: In a query regarding rain, if the Moon occupies a watery sign and enters the ascendant during the bright fortnight, or if it is situated in a quadrant (kendragah), [rain will fall immediately].
When aspected by benefics, Venus produces abundant water; when aspected by malefics, it yields little water.
During the rainy season, Venus, like the Moon, releases its waters before long.
If he touches a moist substance, or water, or that which is designated as such;
or if he is near water, or intent upon some task involving water—
the querent should be told without doubt that there is water before long.
28.02d Or where the sound "water" is heard at the time of inquiry.
Standing upon the peak of the mountain of sunrise, difficult to behold due to its excessive brilliance, resembling molten gold and possessing the luster of smooth vaidūrya,
the sun makes the waters abundant on that day during the rainy season.
And if, having ascended high into the sky, it blazes exceedingly intensely;
When the water is tasteless and has the luster of a cow’s eye, when the quarters of the sky are as clear as the firmament,
when there is a transformation of salt [in the air], and when the sky takes on the appearance of a crow’s egg;
when the wind ceases and fish leap about as if moving upon dry land— [then these portents occur].
The repeated croaking of frogs is a sign that the arrival of water is imminent.
28.05a Cats are scratching the ground intensely with their claws;
28.05b there is a mass of rust from metals with a rank odor;
28.05c and on the road, embankments have been built by children.
28.05d They announce that water has been obtained before long.
If mountains resemble heaps of powdered collyrium, or if their caves are choked with mist,
and if halos around the moon are like the eyes of a cock, they bring rain.
28.07a Without injury to the ants, 28.07b the transfer of their eggs occurs; 28.07c likewise, the mating of snakes and the climbing of snakes upon trees [take place].
28.07d The omens of rain and the leaping of cows.
28.08a Lizards perched upon the tops of trees, 28.08b casting their gaze toward the expanse of the sky;
28.08c and if cows likewise look upward toward the sun, [it portends rain].
Then water falls before long.
If cattle do not wish to leave their pens and shake their ears and even their hooves,
and dogs behave like cattle, one should predict that water will fall.
28.10a When dogs stand upon the roofs of houses, or 28.10b if they howl with their faces turned toward the vast sky;
28.10c and if there is lightning during the day originating from the direction of the wielder of the Pināka bow (the north-east).
Then patience becomes exactly like water.
When the moon resembles the eyes of a parrot or a pigeon, when it is honey-colored,
and when a second moon shines in the sky;
Then the water falls from the sky before long.
28.12a If there is thunder at night and lightning by day, 28.12b resembling blood and standing like a staff,
28.12c and the wind is cool from the front—
If there were then an arrival of water, it would be so.
28.13a If the young shoots of the creepers, turned upward toward the expanse of the sky, were to bathe in water and dust; 28.13b if birds were to resort to them;
28.13c and if reptiles were to frequent the tips of the grass.
Then the falling of rain is near.
When the clouds at twilight possess colors similar to those of peacocks, parrots, blue jays, and cātakas, and when they steal the luster of the hibiscus flower and the lotus; 28.14b–c.
Resembling water-waves, serpents, crocodiles, tortoises, boars, and fish,
and possessing a great accumulation of hollows, they do not yield water for long.
28.15 White as plaster or the moon at their edges, yet with the dark luster of collyrium or bees in the center; glossy, with many folds, dripping drops of water, and forming breaks in the stairways—
these clouds born from the region of Indra move toward the west, or those arising from the quarter of Varuṇa move toward the east.
28.15d Those rain-clouds which soon abandon their abundant water upon the earth.
If, at the rising or setting of the sun, there appear a rainbow, a meteor-like cross-bar, a mock sun, a red halo, lightning, or a circular halo, one should predict that abundant water will soon fall.
28.17a If the sky resembles the color of a partridge feather, 28.17b and flocks of birds cry out joyfully 28.17c at the rising and setting of the sun, by day or by night, [then there will be rain].
The clouds release their water before long.
If the rays of the thousand-rayed sun are unfailing,
as if uplifted like the hands of the mountain that supports the earth,
and when the cloud thunders level with the ground;
That becomes a great sign of rain.

28.19ab. During the rainy season, the Moon, having entered the seventh house from the son of Bhṛgu (Venus) and being aspected by benefics; 28.19cd. Or [the Moon] situated in the ninth or fifth house from Saturn, or in the seventh house, leads to the arrival of water.
Generally, at the time of the rising and setting of the planets, during their conjunctions, and when they transit through the zodiacal signs;
at the end of a fortnight, at the solstices, and when the sun has entered Ārdrā—rain falls with certainty.
28.21 When Mercury and Venus meet, or Mercury and Jupiter, or Jupiter and Venus meet, rain falls.
However, when Mars and Saturn meet, there is danger arising from wind and fire, provided they are not visible to one another and are not conjoined with benefic planets.
When the planets are situated either in front of or behind the sun,
they then make the earth appear as if it were a single vast ocean.
If a firefly enters near the clouds during the nights,
then the god of rain will soon pour down an abundance of water that fills the fields.
28.24ab/ Even when it is raining, if a jackal howls at the time of dusk, 28.24cd/ then there will be bad weather for seven days; of this there is no doubt.
Chapter 29: On Flowers and Creepers.
29.01. Observing the abundant growth of fruits and flowers upon the trees, one should know that commodities will be easily obtained and there will also be a successful harvest of crops.
29.02ab/ By means of the *śāla* tree, *kalama* rice is indicated; by the red *aśoka*, *raktaśāli* rice;
29.02cd/ by the *kṣīrikā* tree, *pāṇḍūka* rice; and by the blue *aśoka*, *sūkaraka* rice.

If the *nyagrodha* tree grows as large as a barley grain, there will be a harvest of *ṣaṣṭika* rice; by the growth of the *tinduka*, the same applies. By the growth of the *aśvattha* tree, the ripening of all crops is to be known.
29.04ab/ When the *jambū* trees [bear fruit], sesame and beans [thrive]; by the growth of the *śirīṣa*, there is the ripening of *kaṅgu* grain.
29.04cd/ Wheat [thrives] with the *madhūka* trees, and barley grows when the *saptaparṇa* [is in bloom].
29.05ab/ One should predict cotton from the *atimuktaka* and *kunda* flowers, and mustard seeds from the *aśana*.
29.05cd/ From the *badarī* fruits one should indicate horse-gram (*kulattha*), and from the *cirabilva* one should point to mung beans (*mudga*).
From the flowers of the linseed plant (*atasī*) and the reed (*vetasa*), as well as the blossoms of the *palāśa*, kodrava grain is to be known;
from the *tilaka* tree, conch shells, pearls, and silver; and from the *iṅguda* tree, hemp (*śaṇa*).
Elephants are to be predicted from *hastikarṇa* flowers, and horses from *aśvakarṇa*;
cows are indicated by *pāṭala* flowers, and goats and sheep by *kadalī*.
29.08ab/ Gold is [indicated] by campaka flowers; the perfection of coral by bandhujīva; 29.08cd/ diamond by the growth of kuravaka; and cat's-eye by nandikāvarta flowers.
29.09ab. One should know that pearls [are indicated] by the sindhuvāra flower, and saffron by the kusumbha;
29.09cd. a king is indicated by the red lotus, and a minister by the blue lotus.
29.10ab / A merchant [attains success] with golden flowers, Brahmins and domestic priests with lotuses, and a commander of forces with white water-lilies (kumuda).
29.10cd / A master of an army [attains it] with fragrant water-lilies (saugandhika), and an increase of gold with the arka flower.
29.11ab/ Through mango trees there is security; through *bhallātaka* trees, danger; and likewise through *pīlu* trees, good health.
29.11cd/ Through *khadira* and *śamī* trees, famine; through *arjuna* trees, auspicious rain.

29.12ab/ There will be abundance of food when [the moon is eclipsed] by Picumanda and Nāgakusuma; likewise by Kapittha. 29.12cd/ By Nicula there is fear of drought, and by Kuṭaja there is fear of disease.

29.13ab Through dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, and flowers, as well as sugarcane and fire, [there is success]; and with the kovidāra flower, 29.13cd through the growth of the śyāmā creeper, unchaste women attain prosperity.
29.14a At whatever time and place trees, shrubs, and creepers are seen with glossy, gapless leaves, 29.14b–c at that time a beautiful rain is predicted.
29.14d It is taught that water is scanty when [the clouds] are rough and full of gaps.
Chapter 30: On the Characteristics of the Twilight (Sandhyā).

From the time the sun has half-set until it has half-risen, as long as the sky remains indistinct in its stellar appearance, that duration is the period of twilight; and the results [of omens] during this time are according to these following signs.
30.02ab/ By means of [omens such as] deer, birds, wind, halos, enclosures, crossbars, cloud-trees, and rainbows;
30.02cd/ And by means of celestial cities, sunbeams, staffs, dust, and oily colors.
A deer repeatedly crying out loudly and fearfully portends the destruction of a village;
if it is blazing in the sun and making a great sound to the south, it causes the slaughter of an army.
30.04ab/ If [the wind] is on the right, there is a battle; if it is calm on the left, there is a meeting of armies.
30.04cd/ During twilight, if the wind is mixed [in direction] within the circle of animals, there will be rain.

30.05ab. A morning twilight resounding with the cries of blazing beasts and birds portends the destruction of the country. 30.05cd. If they cry out from the southern direction with blazing mouths, it foretells the siege of the city.

When there is the shaking of houses, trees, and gateways, accompanied by heaps of dust and clods of earth, when the wind is violent, when there is a terrifying roar, and when birds fly about harshly, the twilight is inauspicious.
When the trees have their leaves stirred and shaken by a gentle breeze, or when there is no wind at all;
when the birds and beasts utter sweet and peaceful cries—such a twilight is honored.
30.08ab/ At the time of twilight, glossy rainbows, lightning, fish-shaped halos, and circular halos; 30.08cd/ as well as Indra’s bow, Airāvata, and the rays of the sun, quickly bring about rain.
30.09ab/ Interrupted, uneven, shattered, distorted, crooked, turned to the left, or revolving;
30.09cd/ And thin, short, defective, or turbid—such rays portend war and drought.
30.10ab/ Radiant, clear, straight, long, and turning to the right; 30.10cd/ these rays of the sun in a cloudless sky bring welfare to the world.
The rays of the sun, which extend from the beginning, middle, and end of the day, are white, glossy, unbroken, and straight; these bring rain and are known as "unfailing" (amogha).
30.12ab/ Those that are speckled, brown, tawny, variegated, madder-red, green, or brindled;
30.12cd/ these, when associated with the third lunar mansion (Tridiva), portend drought, though they cause little fear for seven days.
30.13ab/ If copper-colored, it portends the death of the commander-in-chief; if resembling yellowish-red, it forebodes his misfortune.
30.13cd/ If green, it indicates the destruction of cattle and crops; if smoke-colored, the loss of cattle.
30.14ab/ Those with a madder-red luster portend a panic caused by weapons and fire; those that are brown portend wind and rain.
30.14cd/ Those resembling ashes portend drought, while those that are variegated and speckled portend a thinning of the population.
When the evening dust, resembling the powder of *bandhūka* flowers or collyrium, approaches the sun,
then the worlds are oppressed by hundreds of diseases.
The white passion leads to the peaceful increase of the world.
30.16ab/ A conglomeration of the sun’s rays, clouds, and winds standing like a staff is called a *daṇḍa*.
30.16cd/ Situated in the intermediate directions, it is inauspicious for kings; situated in the cardinal directions, it is inauspicious for the twice-born and other classes.

30.17ab/ When seen at the beginning, middle, or junctions of the day, it causes fear and affliction from weapons. 30.17cd/ A comet appearing white and facing the east destroys the Brahmins and the other castes in that direction.

A cloud situated in the middle of the sky, blue at its tip like curd and obscuring the sun, brings heavy rain; likewise, clouds that are yellow-speckled and rooted in dense masses cause abundant showers.

30.19ab/ When the cloud-tree (abhravṛkṣa) is in its favorable phase and has subsided, there is death for the marching king. 30.19cd/ If it resembles a young tree, there is the death of the crown prince and the minister.
30.20ab/ Having the luster of blue water-lilies, beryl, and lotus filaments, and released by the wind;
30.20cd/ the twilight, illuminated by the rays of the sun, immediately brings rain.
30.21ab/ If it is joined with an inauspicious form, thick clouds, a city of gandharvas, mist, smoke, or dust;
30.21cd/ during the rainy season it causes drought, and at other times it brings about the fury of weapons.

30.22ab/ In the seasons beginning with winter, the colors [of the twilight]—resembling crimson, yellow, white, variegated lotus, and blood—are natural; they are auspicious when occurring at twilight during their own season, while any other is a portentous anomaly.
A sword-bearing figure in human form, like a scattered cloud, moving toward the sun portends fear from an enemy.
When the white city (Sita-khapura) is overtaken by the sun, there is the acquisition of a city; if it is split, there is destruction.
If a cloud with white edges and a dark center appears to the left of the sun, it brings rain;
and so too if there are clouds resembling clumps of vīraṇa grass.
30.24d [He was] with those arising from the quarters that were not yet illuminated by the sun.

A white Parigha comet at the time of the sun's rising causes the ruin of kings; one with a body resembling blood brings about the provocation of armies; while one bearing the form of gold increases the strength [of the king].
On both sides of the sun were two enclosures (paridhis), possessing abundant water and endowed with physical forms;
then [there appeared] those who traverse all the quarters of the sky.
There are no enclosures, nor even a drop of water.
Clouds appearing at the two twilights that take the forms of banners, umbrellas, mountains, elephants, and horses portend victory; those resembling blood portend battle.
Clouds resembling heaps of smoke from straw increase the strength of kings, provided their forms are not parched and they remain stationary.
30.29ab/ Clouds that are slow-moving, resembling trees, and shining with a pale-red hue; 30.29cd/ such dense clouds at both twilights are like cities and bring about auspiciousness.
If the sky is filled with the cries of blazing birds, jackals, and beasts, and is accompanied by the appearance of a staff, dust, a crossbar, and the like,
or if it is daily affected by solar anomalies, it portends the destruction of the country, its king, and its food supply.

If the eastern quarter [is affected] at that very moment at night, or the western twilight, the fruit [of the omen] occurs within three days; whereas halos, dust, and parigha-meteors produce results immediately, unless otherwise [stated]. The same applies to the sun’s rays, Indra’s bow (rainbow), lightning, mock-suns, clouds, and winds.
On that very same day, moreover, birds [portend death] in eight days, and wild animals in seven days.
30.32a Twilight shines for one *yojana* with its radiance;
30.32b lightning illuminates six [yojanas] with its flash; 30.32c the sound of thunder travels for five years.
30.32d There is no limit [to the number of deaths] during the falling of meteors.
30.33a But its halo is known as Pratyarka; 30.33b it has the appearance of three yojanas, while that of the parigha is five.
30.33c The circle of the halo is visible at six, five, or ten [yojanas].
The bow of the Lord of the Ten Immortals shines forth.
Chapter 31: On the Characteristics of the Burning of the Quarters (Digdāha).
A burning of the quarters that is yellow portends fear for the king; one with the color of fire portends the destruction of the country.
Furthermore, that which is reddish-brown and accompanied by a counter-clockwise wind, when observed, brings about the destruction of the crops.
31.02a He who, by his excessive brilliance, creates illumination;
31.02b he who, like the sun, even reveals shadows;
31.02c he portends great danger to the king.
The provocation of weapons is indicated by symptoms corresponding to blood.
31.03a In the east, there is suffering for the Kṣatriyas and the lords of men; 31.03b in the southeast, suffering for artisans and youths;
31.03c in the south, there is suffering for Vaiśyas along with fierce men.
31.03d Messengers and women who have remarried are in the corner.

31.04a But afterwards, the Śūdras and those who live by agriculture [suffer]; 31.04b the thieves, along with those who possess horses, when [the planet] is situated in the quarter of Vāyu (the northwest); 31.04c and the Brahmins suffer affliction in the north.
And heretics and merchants [prosper] under Śārvarī.
The sky is clear, the stars are stainless,
and the wind blows favorably;
and the burning of the quarters is as bright as gold.
For the welfare of the world, including its kings.
Chapter 32: On the Characteristics of Earthquakes.
32.01ab: Some say that an earthquake is caused by creatures dwelling deep within the waters; others say it arises from the rest of the world-elephants who are exhausted by the burden of the earth.
32.02ab. Some say that when the wind is struck by the wind, it falls to the ground making a sound; 32.02cd.
however, other teachers declare that this is caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa).

32.03ab/ In ancient times, when mountains possessed of wings were falling down and springing up, the Earth, trembling, spoke with bashfulness to the Grandfather (Brahmā) in the assembly of the immortals: 32.03cd/ [She spoke] in the assembly of the gods.

32.04ab/ "O Blessed One, this name 'Acala' (the Immovable) which has been given to me by you is not [true], for it is applied to those who are immovable while others are moving. I am not capable of enduring this hardship."
Beholding her face— with its voice somewhat faltering, its lower lip slightly quivering,
slightly downcast, and its eyes filled with tears— the Grandfather spoke.
"O Indra, withdraw your wrath; cast down your thunderbolt for the shattering of the mountain's wings!
Having said, "It is done," Śakra told the Earth, "Do not fear."
However, for the sake of understanding the good and evil results, the deities Anila (Wind), Dahana (Fire), Surapati (Indra),
and Varuṇa will cause tremors in the first, second, third, and fourth quarters of day and night respectively.
The four [asterisms] beginning with Āryamaṇ—namely Āditya, Mṛgaśiras, and Aśvayuj—constitute this Vāyavya maṇḍala; its forms appear within seven days.
When the sky is filled with smoke and the wind stirs up dust from the earth,
the sun moves about scorching the trees, its rays appearing dim and feeble.
32.10ab/ When there is an earthquake in the northwest (Vāyavya), the destruction of crops, water, forests, and medicinal herbs is declared.
32.10cd/ There occurs swelling, asthma, insanity, fever, and cough, as well as suffering for merchants.
32.11 When [Saturn] is in the second house, those who possess beauty, those who bear weapons, physicians, women, poets, musicians, merchants,
and artisans are afflicted, as are the people of Saurāṣṭra, Kuru, Magadha, Daśārṇa, and Matsya.

32.12ab/ Puṣya, Āgneya (Kṛttikā), Viśākhā, Bharaṇī, Pitrya (Maghā), Aja (Pūrvaphalgunī), and that which is called Bhāgya (Uttaraphalgunī); 32.12cd/ this is the group of the Fire-eater (Agni), and it produces these forms:
The sky, covered by falling stars and meteors, appears as if ablaze with a conflagration spreading in all directions;
accompanied by the wind, the seven-flamed fire wanders for a period of seven days.
32.14ab/ In the southeast, there is the destruction of clouds, the depletion of reservoirs of water, enmity with kings,
32.14cd/ and ringworm, scabies, fever, erysipelas, and jaundice.
32.15ab/ Those of blazing energy and fierce nature—the Aśmakas, Aṅgas, and Bāhlīkas—are oppressed;
32.15cd/ as are the Taṅgaṇas, Kaliṅgas, Vaṅgas, Draviḍas [or Draviṇas], and various kinds of Śabaras.
32.16ab/ Abhijit, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Rohiṇī, Jyeṣṭhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Anurādhā;
32.16cd/ this is the mandala of the Lord of the Gods, and these also constitute its forms.
32.17ab/ With bodies both moving and motionless, thundering deeply and flashing with lightning,
32.17cd/ the clouds, resembling buffalo-horns, black bees, and serpents, pour down rain.
The [Aindra] hymn destroys those renowned for their lineage, birth, and family, as well as kings and hosts of Gaṇapas;
it is the remedy for dysentery, throat-obstruction, diseases of the mouth, and difficult vomiting.
32.19ab/ Kāśi, Yugandhara, Paurava, Kirāta, Kīra, Abhisāra, Hala, and Madra;
32.19cd/ Arbuda, Surāṣṭra, Suvāstu, Mālava, and Pīḍākara—[these regions] will receive desirable rain.
32.20ab/ Those belonging to the deities Pūṣan, Āpa, Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, Mūla, Ahirbudhnya, and Varuṇa;
32.20cd/ this is the Varuṇa circle, and its characteristic signs are as follows.
32.21ab/ The clouds are abundant, possessing the luster of blue lotuses, bees, and crushed collyrium, and uttering sweet sounds;
32.21cd/ their bodies are illuminated by lightning as they pour down showers like rain-torrents or goads.
The Vāruṇa [wind] destroys those dwelling by the ocean and rivers, brings excessive rain, and removes enmity;
it strikes down the Gonardas, Cedis, Kukuras, Kirātas, and Vaidehakas.
32.23ab/ An earthquake occurs after six months, and a thunderclap reaches its fruition after two.
32.23cd/ Others have declared that other portents as well [reach fruition] by means of these [other] circles.

A meteor, a lion, the city of Candra, and dust; thunderclaps, earthquakes, and conflagrations of the quarters; an exceedingly fierce wind, the eclipsing of the sun and moon, and portents among the constellations and clusters of stars.
Rain in a cloudless sky is a portent; so too is rain accompanied by wind, smoke without fire, or sparks and flames [without a source].
Or a wild animal may enter the middle of a village, or the bow of Indra (a rainbow) may be seen at night.

Auras halos, fragmented halos, rivers flowing upstream, the sound of trumpets in the sky, and whatever else occurs contrary to nature—the results of these should be declared by the planetary spheres themselves.
An [unfavorable] planet belonging to Indra overcomes one belonging to Vāyu, and Vāyu likewise overcomes one belonging to Indra; thus they overcome each other.
32.24cd/ Even tremors occurring at the ocean, the sacrificial fire, the horizons, or the lunar mansions [portend calamity].
In the fire and wind mandalas, there are the calamities of death for renowned lords of men;
moreover, the people are tormented by hunger, fear, pestilence, and drought.
32.26ab/ When Venus and Jupiter are in the sectors of Varuṇa and Indra, there is abundance of food, auspicious rain, and joy in the world;
32.26cd/ cows yield abundant milk, and kings have ceased their enmities.
32.27ab/ Wind [yields results] in four fortnights, fire in three, and the King of the Gods (Indra) within seven days;
32.27cd/ Varuṇa bears fruit immediately; and in these portents, no specific time limit has been prescribed.
The wind moves two hundred [yojanas], fire one hundred and ten yojanas,
the lord of waters eighty, and the wielder of the thunderbolt more than sixty.
If an earthquake occurs on the third, fourth, or seventh day, or likewise on the first day of a month, a fortnight, or a three-fortnight period, it brings about the destruction of the sovereign king.
Chapter 33: On the Characteristics of Meteors (Ulka-lakṣaṇādhyāya).
Meteors (ulkās) are the forms of those celestial bodies that fall after having exhausted their auspicious fruits in the sky.
They are divided into five types: the Dhiṣṇya, the Ulkā, the Aśani, the Vidyut, and the Tārā.
33.02ab/ A meteor (ulkā) yields its fruit in a fortnight; likewise, a firebrand from the constellations (dhiṣṇya) and a thunderbolt (aśani) do so in three fortnights.
33.02cd/ Lightning does so in six days; likewise, a star (tārā) brings it to fruition.
33.03ab. The star Tārā is proclaimed to yield one-quarter of its fruit, while the lunar mansion (dhiṣṇya) yields half its fruit.
33.03cd. The three—lightning, meteors, and thunderbolts—yield their full fruit.

33.04ab/ A thunderbolt, with a great roar, falls upon men, elephants, horses, wild animals, stones, houses, trees, and cattle; 33.04cd/ tearing asunder the surface of the earth, it has the shape of a discus.

33.05ab/ Suddenly, the lightning, producing terror among living beings with its *taṭataṭa* sound, falls blazing upon the heaps of fuel that are living beings. 33.05cd/ Crooked and vast, it descends, ignited amidst the masses of sentient beings who serve as its kindling.
33.06ab. The *dhiṣṇyā* is lean with a small tail; ten *dhanus* are seen as its height, plus a little more.
33.06cd. Resembling glowing coals, it is two *hastas* in measure.

33.07ab/ Long, white, and resembling the fibers of a copper-colored lotus, the star moves obliquely, downwards, or upwards, as if being carried through the sky. 33.07cd/ It travels across the firmament as though it were being borne along.
33.08ab/ A large meteor with a slender tail falls, increasing in size as it reaches the head [of the planet].
33.08cd/ And it becomes long; there are many varieties of this [lineage].
33.09ab/ Those resembling a ghost, a weapon, a donkey, a camel, a crocodile, a monkey, a tusked beast, a plough, or a deer;
33.09cd/ those having the form of an iguana, a snake, or smoke, as well as that which has heads on both ends—these are inauspicious.
33.10ab/ Having the luster of a banner, a fish, a mountain, an elephant, a lotus, the moon, a horse, refined silver, and a swan;
33.10cd/ And having the forms of the śrīvṛkṣa, a thunderbolt, a conch, and a svastika— these bring auspiciousness and abundance.
33.11ab/ Falling in great numbers from the middle of the sky, they portend the destruction of the king and the kingdom.
33.11cd/ Whirling above the heavens, it announces confusion for the world.
When it touches the moon and the sun, or when it is emitted from them along with an earthquake,
it generates fear of the arrival of a foreign army, danger to the king, famine, and drought.
33.13ab/ A meteor that moves counter-clockwise around the sun and the moon portends the destruction of the citizens and the enemy.
33.13cd/ A meteor emerging from the front of the sun brings good fortune to the traveler.
A white, red, yellow, or black meteor (ulkā) destroys the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa;
situated respectively at the head, the chest, the flanks, or the tail, these meteors shall destroy them in that order.
33.15ab/ A [line] falling toward the northern direction and so forth is harsh and brings misfortune to Brahmins and the other castes.
33.15cd/ One that is straight, smooth, unbroken, and directed downward leads to their prosperity.
33.16ab/ Dark-brown, reddish, blue, blood-colored, fire-colored, black, or resembling ashes, and rough;
33.16cd/ A twilight that occurs during the day, being crooked and torn asunder, portends fear of an enemy invasion.
33.17ab / The destruction of those who are devoted to that [constellation] is ordained by the affliction of the lunar mansions and planets.
33.17cd / Striking the Sun and Moon at their rising or setting causes the death of citizens and others respectively.
33.18ab/ When an ulkā strikes Bhāgya, Āditya, Dhaniṣṭhā, or Mūla, young women suffer.
33.18cd/ When it strikes Puṣya, Anila, or Viṣṇudeva, there is affliction for Brahmins and Kṣatriyas.
33.19ab/ When the fixed (dhruva) and gentle (saumya) planets are struck, there is suffering for kings; when the fierce (ugra) and cruel (sadāruṇa) ones, for thieves.
33.19cd/ When the swift (kṣipra) ones are struck, there is suffering for those skilled in the arts; and when a common (sādhāraṇa) planet is struck, [there is suffering] for all.
33.20ab/ If these [omens] occur upon images of the gods, they cause fear for the king and the kingdom.
33.20cd/ If they occur upon Śakra, there is suffering for kings in their palaces and for their masters.
When a meteor falls upon a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), it causes suffering to those residing in that region who are devoted to agriculture and are afflicted by the seizure of their hopes.
33.22ab/ If [the bolt] falls at the city gate, there will be the destruction of the city; if on the threshold (indrakīla), the destruction of the people is declared.
33.22cd/ If it falls in a Brahmanical sanctuary, it shall slay the Brahmins; if in a cow-pen, the cattle-owners.
When the sounds of shouting, the slapping of arms, musical instruments, singing, and loud cheers occur at the time of a falling meteor,
they portend danger for the kingdom along with its king.
If a comet remains for a long time in the sky with a staff-like appearance, it portends danger to the king; and that which stays in the sky as if suspended by a thread likewise forebodes ill.
Or she whose form is equal to the banner of Mahendra.
Moving against [the direction of] a merchant, it portends misfortune; moving crosswise, it harms the wives of kings;
moving downward, it kills kings; and moving upward, it destroys Brahmins.
Having the form of a peacock's tail, she brings about the destruction of the world;
creeping like a serpent, she bestows misfortune upon women.
A maṇḍala situated like a parasol destroys the city and the priest;
situated like a bamboo thicket, it causes harm to the kingdom.
Resembling a predatory beast or a boar, garlanded with sparks, or else broken into fragments and accompanied by a shrieking sound, such a lightning bolt brings misfortune.
Resembling the bow of the Lord of the Gods, it destroys clouds in the sky when it pertains to sovereignty;
however, if it moves crookedly against the wind, or turns back, it is not auspicious.
From whatever direction an army approaches to overwhelm the city, from that very direction the king experiences fear;
yet, by departing toward whichever blazing quarter [the fire] falls, he shall soon conquer his enemies.
Chapter 34: On the Characteristics of Halos The rays of the sun and the moon, becoming condensed by the wind and forming into circles,
appear as halos (pariveṣas) in the sky with various colors and shapes amidst thin clouds.
34.02ab/ They are red, blue, pale-white, pigeon-grey, cloud-colored, variegated, green, and white;
34.02cd/ they are presided over by Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Nirṛti, Vāyu, Īśa, Pitāmaha, and Agni.
Dhanada produces the *mecaka* (cloud) through the mutual support of their qualities, while others [the clouds] repeatedly dissolve;
that too, produced by the wind, yields little fruit.
A halo appearing like the color of a blue jay, a peacock, silver, oil, milk, or water; produced at its proper time, complete in its form, and glossy, brings about welfare and abundance.
Moving across the entire sky, possessing many hues, resembling blood, and rough;
appearing incomplete, shaped like a cart, a bow, or a crossroads—such a comet is malefic.
34.06ab/ If it is as dark as a peacock's throat, excessively black, or multicolored, there is the death of a king; if it is smoky, there is fear.
34.06cd/ If it resembles a rainbow or has the luster of an aśoka flower, there will be battles.
When it is abundant in a single color, glossy, and filled with razor-like clouds, it brings immediate rain during its own season; and when it is yellow and blazing like the sun, it does so as well.
34.08ab/ A great, turbid sound arising from the three twilights, accompanied by the cries of blazing beasts and birds, brings fear;
when struck by lightning, meteors, and the like, it kills the king with a weapon.
34.09ab/ When the Sun and the Moon are red day and night, there is the death of a king every day.
34.09cd/ The same occurs when they are frequently eclipsed or situated at the ascendant or in the setting point of the sky.

A double halo causes fear to the commander-in-chief but does not provoke excessive anger toward weapons; a triple or greater number [of halos] causes the provocation of weapons, fear for the crown prince, and the siege of a city.
34.11ab/ When the planets and the moon are obstructed by a lunar mansion, there will be rain in three days or conflict in a month.
34.11cd/ If an inauspicious planet occupies the hour (horā), the lord of the birth, or the birth asterism, it portends ill for the king.
34.12ab When Saturn enters the halo-circle, it causes the destruction of minor grains. 34.12cd It produces wind and rain, and is the destroyer of stationary crops and those who practice agriculture.
34.13ab. When Mars is surrounded by a halo, there is a rout of princes, army commanders, and troops, along with fear of fire and weapons.
34.13cd. When Jupiter is surrounded by a halo, there is suffering for the domestic priest, ministers, and the king.
34.14ab. When Mercury is [the ruler], there is an increase in ministers, stationary property, scribes, and abundant rain.
34.14cd. When Venus is [the ruler], there is suffering for travelers, kṣatriyas, and queens, but food is dear.
34.15ab/ When Ketu is eclipsed, there arises fear from hunger, fire, death, kings, and weapons;
34.15cd/ when Rāhu is eclipsed, there is danger to the fetus, as well as disease and fear of the king.

34.16ab/ One should recognize wars when two planets appear within a halo around either the sun or the moon. 34.16cd/ When three such planets are present, it is declared that there will be fear of famine and drought.
34.17ab/ A king, together with his ministers and domestic priest, falls under the power of death when [the planets] are in the four [houses].
34.17cd/ Know that it is like the dissolution of the world when [the planets] are situated in the five houses beginning with the fifth (the mandala).
34.18ab/ One should predict the slaughter of the king specifically from the rising of a lunar mansion planet (tārāgraha),
or else from the rising of a comet (ketu) among the lunar mansions.
34.19ab. One who kills a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra occurs respectively on the first lunar day (pratipad) and the following days.
34.19cd. One who performs inauspicious deeds against guilds, cities, or the treasury occurs on the fifth lunar day and the subsequent days.
34.20ab/ If it occurs on the eighth lunar day, it is harmful to the crown prince; thereafter, for three [days], it is harmful to the king.
34.20cd/ A siege of the city occurs on the twelfth day; a disturbance of the army on the thirteenth.
A halo appearing on the fourteenth day causes suffering to the king's wife,
but on the fifteenth day it brings suffering to the lord of men himself.
The central line of the halo is to be known as the boundary between those situated within the city-dwellers and those traveling outside, while the core of the *ākranda* is its innermost part.
34.23ab/ Those whose [omens] are red, dark, and dry shall suffer defeat;
34.23cd/ those whose portion is glossy, white, and radiant shall achieve victory.
Chapter 35: On the Characteristics of Indra’s Bow.
The rays of the sun, struck by the wind in a cloudless sky, assume various colors;
those which appear in the atmosphere in the shape of a bow are known as Indra’s bow (the rainbow).
35.02ab Some teachers say that it arises from the breaths of the serpents of infinite lineages.
35.02cd For kings who advance toward it, this brings about defeat.
Water that is unbroken, deep-set in the earth, radiant, glossy, dense, and of various colors; that which rises twice and flows in a downward direction is praised, as it yields abundant water.
35.04ab/ A halo appearing in the intermediate directions portends the destruction of the rulers of those directions; one devoid of clouds causes a great mortality.
35.04cd/ When it is pale-red, yellow, or blue, evils arise from weapons, fire, and famine.
35.05ab/ If it stands in the midst of water, there will be drought; if on the ground, the destruction of crops; if on a tree, disease.
35.05cd/ If on an anthill, there is fear of weapons at night; if it is an Indra-bow (rainbow), it portends the death of a minister.
35.06ab/ It brings rain during a drought and stops rain during a rainy season; it belongs to Indra.
35.06cd/ It always indicates rain from behind, and it is called the bow of the wielder of the thunderbolt.
When the bow of Indra appears at night in the direction of Ākhaṇḍalā (the northeast), it portends suffering for the king; however, it destroys calamities arising from the south, the west,
and the north.
35.07d [He should consult] the commander-in-chief, the leader, and the minister.
35.08ab/ At night, a rainbow appearing white in color and so forth causes suffering for the twice-born and others.
35.08cd/ And in whichever direction it appears, it shall soon destroy the foremost ruler of that region.
Chapter 36: Characteristics of the City of Gandharvas (Gandharvanagara-lakṣaṇādhyāya).
A city of clouds appearing in the north and other directions portends harm to the domestic priest, the king, the commander-in-chief, and the crown prince, respectively.
A city of clouds that is white, red, yellow, or black portends the destruction of the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes.

36.02ab/ A [halo] situated in the northern direction brings victory to the king of the city and destroys discoloration. 36.02cd/ When seen in the peaceful quarter (the west) with a gateway, it leads to the victory of the king.
36.03ab/ Arising from all directions and persisting continuously, it portends fear for kings and their kingdoms.
36.03cd/ Resembling smoke, fire, or a rainbow, it destroys thieves and forest-dwellers.

36.04ab/ A pale city of Gandharvas that has arisen, causing lightning strikes and wind; 36.04cd/ If it appears on the right, there is death for the king; if on the left, fear of enemies; if on the left [of the observer], victory.
When a city of many colors and forms, complete with banners, flags, and arches, appears in the sky,
then the earth drinks the abundant blood of elephants, men, and horses in battle.

Chapter 37: On the Characteristics of the Counter-Sun (Pratisūrya) A counter-sun is auspicious when it possesses the color and luster of the sun's rays for that particular season, is glossy, resembles beryl, is transparent, and is white; such a sign portends security and an abundance of food.
If yellow, it produces disease; if appearing like the Aśoka flower, it leads to the outbreak of weapons.
A garland of sun-like halos portends fear from bandits, calamity, and the death of the king.
The sun-like comet (pratisūrya) produced by day causes rain; situated to the north it causes wind, while situated to the south it causes wind as well.
When situated on both sides, it brings fear of water; when above, it destroys the king; when below, it kills the people.
They say that the slaying of the king is signaled by dust resembling a dense mass of thick darkness;
with mountains, cities, and trees no longer distinguishable, all directions are shrouded.
In whichever direction a mass of smoke first arises or in whichever it vanishes, fear will come from that very direction within seven days; of this there is no doubt.
When the mass of dust is white, there will be suffering for the ministers and the people;
before long, weapons will fall into a state of great agitation, and success will be extremely difficult to achieve.
If it yawns at sunrise for one day or even two days,
as if covering the expanse of the sky, it portends most terrible danger.
It brought about an uninterrupted accumulation of merit for one night for the slayer of the preeminent king,
and it served for the security of the remaining wise rulers of men.
In whatever kingdom a thick mass of dust spreads for two nights,
one should recognize that the arrival of a foreign army is imminent there as well.
If it falls for three nights, there will be a fourfold destruction of the flavor of food;
if it occurs for five nights amidst dust, there will be an upheaval of the kings' armies.
When dust arises, freed from the rising of comets and other such portents, it brings intense fear;
the teachers say that in seasons other than winter, its fruit is unfailing.
[Chapter 38: On the Characteristics of Thunderclaps]
When the wind, struck by another wind, falls from the sky onto the earth, then a *nirghāta* occurs; it is inauspicious, accompanied by the cries of blazing birds.
38.02ab. At sunrise, the magistrate, the king, the wealthy man, the warrior, the woman, the merchant, and the courtesan [should be attacked]; 38.02cd.
During the second watch, one should strike the goats and sheep, as well as the Śūdras and the citizens.
In the third watch, he afflicts those who serve the king and Brāhmaṇas;
in the fourth watch, however, he afflicts Vaiśyas, water-carriers, and thieves.
When the sun has set, it destroys lowly crops during the first watch;
during the second watch of the night, it afflicts hosts of piśācas.
38.05ab/ One should destroy horses and elephants in the third [watch], and marching troops in the fourth.
38.05cd/ In whichever direction it proceeds with a terrifying and shattered sound, that direction it destroys.
Chapter 39: On Crops.
39.01ab/ Those auspicious and inauspicious configurations for the crops of summer and autumn, which were declared by Bādarāyaṇa regarding the sun's entry into Scorpio and Taurus, are here set forth.
39.02ab/ When the Sun enters Leo, if the angles from that position are occupied by benefic planets,
or are aspected by strong benefics, there is an increase in summer crops.
39.03ab/ When the Sun has entered the eighth sign, and Jupiter and the Moon are situated in Aquarius and Leo,
or situated in Leo and Aquarius, there is the production of summer crops.
39.04ab/ When Venus or Mercury is situated in the second house from the Sun, or both are so situated simultaneously;
39.04cd/ or likewise when they are both in the twelfth house—the accomplishment [of the undertaking] occurs through the exceedingly favorable aspect of Jupiter.
39.05ab. When the Sun is in the middle of the auspicious *ali* and Jupiter and the Moon are in the seventh house, there is supreme prosperity.
39.05cd. When the Sun is situated at the beginning of *ali* and Jupiter is in the second house, there is partial accomplishment.
39.06ab. When Venus, the Moon, and Mercury are conjoined with the eleventh, fourth, and second houses from the Sun in Aries, there is an abundant harvest.
39.06cd. If Jupiter is in the tenth house, there is an excellent yield of cattle.
39.07ab. When Jupiter is in Aquarius, the Moon in Taurus, the Sun in Leo, Mars and Saturn in Capricorn;
39.07cd. there is great success, followed later by fear of a foreign army and disease.
39.08ab/ When the Sun is between two malefic planets and is situated in Libra, it destroys the grain.
39.08cd/ A malefic planet in the seventh house destroys every child as soon as it is born.

39.09ab. A malefic planet situated in the house of wealth (the second house), not aspected by benefics, destroys the crop already grown. 39.09cd. It clearly causes the production of that which is sown later.

39.10ab/ When two malefic planets are situated in the seventh or a quadrant from the Sun located in Scorpio, they cause the destruction of crops; however, this does not happen everywhere if they are aspected by benefics.
39.11 When two malefic planets are situated in the seventh and sixth houses from the Sun located in Scorpio,
there is then the production of crops, but a decline in their price.
39.12ab/ By this very same rule, when the Sun enters Taurus,
those who know [the science] should recognize it as leading either to the destruction or the prosperity of the autumnal crops.
When the Sun, moving through the three signs beginning with Aries, is conjoined with or aspected by Mercury,
it makes summer grain inexpensive, abundant, and fit for consumption without fear.

39.14ab. Likewise, when the Sun is situated in a bow, a deer, or a jar, it is like the autumnal crop. 39.14cd. This should be understood as occurring during the period of accumulation; however, the opposite occurs through conjunction with a malefic aspect.
Chapter 40: Determination of Substances.

40.01ab: Those zodiac signs which have been declared by the sages to be the lords of various substances for the purpose of determining their auspicious or inauspicious nature—those I shall now explain according to tradition.
40.02ab/ For garments, wool, and baskets; for lentils, wheat, rālaka, and barley; 40.02cd/ for land-growing herbs and for gold, the ram is proclaimed [as the sacrificial animal].
In Taurus, there will be cattle, clothing, flowers, wheat, rice, barley, buffaloes, and daughters of Surabhi (cows).
In Gemini as well, there will be grain, autumnal crops, creepers, lotus roots, and cotton.
In Cancer, there are kodrava grain, plantain, dūrvā grass, fruits, tubers, leaves, and cinnamon;
in Leo, there are husked grains, juices, and the skins of lions and other such animals mixed with jaggery.
In the sixth [sign], there are linseed, peas, horse-gram, wheat, mung beans, and flat beans;
in the seventh sign, there are black gram, barley, wheat, and mustard seeds.
In the eighth house, there is sugarcane, along with salt, metals, and goats and sheep;
but in the ninth, there are horses, salt, clothing, weapons, sesame, grain, and roots.
In Capricorn, there are trees, shrubs, and the like, as well as salt, sugarcane, gold, and black iron.
In Aquarius, there are water-born products, fruits, flowers, gems, and various types of ornaments.
In Pisces, there are gems produced from shells, water-born diamonds, various kinds of oils, and the multitude of fish species have been described.
Jupiter situated in the fourth, seventh, second, ninth, or fifth house from the lord of the sign brings about prosperity;
and Mercury situated in the second, eleventh, tenth, fifth, or eighth house likewise causes increase.

Venus causes loss when situated in the sixth or seventh house, but causes gain in the remaining houses. Malefics situated in the houses of increase (upacaya) bestow auspicious results, while in the remaining houses they cause loss.
40.11ab/ When malefic planets, being strong, are situated in the places of affliction (pīḍāsthāna) of a sign,
40.11cd/ there occurs high prices and scarcity of the goods associated with that sign as previously described.
40.12ab/ For those signs whose benefics are strong in their favorable positions,
40.12cd/ there shall be an increase in those substances, as well as high value and popularity [or, according to another reading, power and rarity].
Even when there is affliction of its domain, a sign does not cause affliction if it is aspected by strong benefic planets; likewise, there is a reversal of this effect when the aspectors are malefic.
Chapter 41:

On the Valuation of Commodities. Having observed excessive rain, meteors, falling rods, halos, eclipses, and circular rings, as well as other portents occurring on the new moon day or the full moon day;
41.02ab. One should declare the specific prices for the zodiac signs in sequence, month by month, according to the Sun's position.
41.02cd. Whatever portents occur on other lunar days, they bring about tumultuous distress for kings.
41.03ab. When the Sun has entered Aries, one should collect the summer grains;
41.03cd. when it is in Taurus, one should collect forest roots and fruits; in the fourth month, there will be profit from those two.
41.04ab/ When [Jupiter] is situated in Gemini, one should collect all kinds of liquids and grains;
41.04cd/ by selling them in the sixth month, the seller shall obtain a vast profit.

41.05ab. When the sun is in Cancer, having placed honey, fragrant substances, oil, ghee, and molasses [in the vessel], 41.05cd. the profit in the second month is twofold; if it is less or more than that, there is a forfeiture.

41.06ab/ In the month of Siṃha, there is the acquisition of gold, gems, skins, armor, weapons, pearls, and silver. 41.06cd/ In the fifth month, there is gain; otherwise, for the seller, there is loss.
41.07ab/ When the sun has entered Virgo, one who purchases chowries, camels, young elephants, and horses,
41.07cd/ obtains a twofold profit by selling them in the sixth month.
41.08ab. Under Libra, one should take woven goods, gems, woolen blankets, glass, and yellow flowers;
41.08cd. as well as grains; after six months, the profit shall have doubled.
41.09ab/ When the sun is situated in Scorpio, fruits, tubers, roots, and various gems,
41.09cd/ having been stored for two years, yield double their profit.
When the clouds have passed, one should collect saffron, conch shells, coral, glass, and pearls; these then become double their value within half a year.
When the sun is situated in the signs of Capricorn or Aquarius, one should collect iron vessels and grain;
by keeping them for a month and then giving them away, one who seeks profit obtains a twofold return.
When the sun has entered Capricorn, one who stores roots, fruits, tubers, vessels,
and gems for half a year obtains the desired profit.
In whichever sign the Moon or the Sun is conjoined with or aspected by its own or a friendly planet, there that [sign] is declared to be a source of gain.
41.14a When the full moon is conjoined with or aspected by benefics along with the Sun,
41.14b the cool-rayed one is said to immediately cause an increase in the price of goods;
41.14c however, if it is conjoined with or aspected by malefics, the Sun destroys it.
Having understood the states present in the house of reception, one should declare the results, both good and bad.
Chapter 42: The Perfection of Indra’s Banner.
The immortals said to Brahmā: "O Blessed One, we are not able to fight back against the Asuras in battle;
therefore, we have come to you for refuge, as you are the protector of those seeking shelter."
The Blessed Keśava spoke to the gods:
"That banner which he shall give you—upon seeing it in battle, the Daityas will not stand against you."
42.03ab. Having obtained their boons, those gods, together with Indra, went to the Ocean of Milk and praised him.
42.03cd. [They praised him] who bears the Śrīvatsa mark and whose chest is illuminated by the radiance of the Kaustubha jewel.
42.04ab/ [One should meditate upon] the Lord of Śrī, the inconceivable, the peerless, who is equal toward all embodied beings from every side, the subtle;
42.04cd/ the Supreme Self, Viṣṇu, who is without beginning and whose end is unknown.
Praised by them, that god Nārāyaṇa was pleased and granted them a banner,
which was like a sharp-rayed sun to the frost-like lotus-forests of the faces of the wives of both Asuras and Suras.
Having reached that banner, which was produced from the splendor of Viṣṇu, stationed upon a radiant chariot adorned with eight wheels and variegated with jewels,
and which blazed like the sun in autumn, Śakra rejoiced.
Adorned with a network of small bells, equipped with garlands, umbrellas, bells, and baskets,
and bearing the raised banner of the King of the Gods, he brought the enemy army to destruction in battle.
The lord of the gods gave a bamboo staff to Vasu, the king of Cedi, who was a follower of Uparicara;
that lord of men worshipped it according to the prescribed rites.

42.09ab/ Delighted by the festival, Maghavat spoke thus: "Those kings who shall act in this manner, 42.09cd/ they shall become like Vasu, possessed of wealth, and their commands shall be effective upon the earth."
42.10ab/ And their subjects will be joyful, free from fear and disease, and provided with abundant food.
42.10cd/ And he shall proclaim the truth and falsehood in the world through signs, like a banner.
42.11ab. Just as in former times, worship was offered to him by kings seeking the increase of their forces and victory;
42.11cd. that worship, performed at the command of Śakra, I shall explain according to the traditional scripture.
42.12ab. Its construction should be undertaken on an auspicious lunar day, asterism, and at a propitious moment (muhūrta).
42.12cd. The astrologer and the master builder should proceed to the forest for the purpose of selecting timber.
42.13ab/ Those growing in gardens, temples, cemeteries, anthills, on roads, or on funeral pyres;
42.13cd/ And those that are humpbacked, upright, withered, thorny, or covered with creepers and *vandāka* moss.
Those trees that are abodes for many birds, hollows, or those afflicted by wind and fire,
as well as those designated with feminine names— these are not auspicious for the purpose of Indra’s banner.
42.15ab. Arjuna, ajakarṇa, priyaka, dhava, and udumbara—these five are the best. 42.15cd. One should select any one of these as the most excellent, or else another tree.

42.16ab. Having first worshipped, according to the prescribed rule, [the image] produced from white or black clay, the twice-born man, having approached it in a secluded place at night and touched it, should recite this mantra:
42.17ab/ To those beings who dwell here in this tree, may there be well-being; let there be homage to you!
42.17cd/ Having accepted this offering, please change your residence.
42.18ab. A king chooses you; may it be well with you, O best of trees!
42.18cd. For the sake of the banner of the King of the Gods, please accept this worship.
42.19ab. One should cut down the tree at the time of dawn, having positioned oneself facing either north or east.
42.19cd. A crackling sound from the axe is not auspicious; a smooth and solid sound is beneficial.
42.20ab/ One should avoid a fall that does not grant victory to the king, one that is not extended forward, or one where the front part is not bent.
42.20cd/ One should also avoid a fall that is not stuck [to the opponent's body], or one where either side is reversed; otherwise, one should abandon such a fallen position.
Having cut the staff four finger-breadths from the top and eight from the base, one should cast it into the water;
then, having lifted it out, one should carry it to the city gate by means of a cart or by men.
42.22ab. When the *arabhaṅga* breaks, one should know there is a breakdown of strength; when the rim (*nemi*) breaks, the destruction of the force is to be understood.
42.22cd. When the axle (*akṣa*) breaks, there is loss of wealth; likewise, when the linchpin (*aṇi*) breaks, there is misfortune for the carpenter.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada, the king,
surrounded by the citizens and led by astrologers, ministers, chamberlains, and brahmins, all wearing fine attire, [should proceed].
42.24ab/ Wrapped in new, unwashed garments, the citizens should bring the staff of Indra into the city;
42.24cd/ Adorned with garlands, perfumes, and incense, they should usher it in amidst the sounds of conchs and trumpets.
Adorned with beautiful banners, arches, and forest-garlands, the city was filled with joyful people;
its streets were swept and honored, and crowded with well-dressed courtesans.
The city had its marketplaces and houses well-adorned, resounded with the abundant chanting of the Vedas on auspicious days, and its crossroads were crowded with actors, dancers, and singers.
42.27ab. In that regard, white banners bring victory; yellow ones bestow disease. 42.27cd. Those of variegated form grant victory, while red ones lead to the outbreak of weapons.
If elephants and other animals fall while being made to enter a pillar, it portends fear; likewise, when children clap their hands, it forebodes either battle or a conflict of beings.
42.29ab. Having planed it again according to rule, the carpenter should mount the staff upon the frame.
42.29cd. On this eleventh day, the lord of men should cause a vigil to be held.
Wearing white garments and a turban, the domestic priest shall offer oblations into the fire with mantras dedicated to Indra and Viṣṇu; the astrologer shall observe the omens.

42.31ab/ A fire that has the appearance of a desired object, fragrant, oily, dense, and radiant with flames; 42.31cd/ such a fire brings about auspiciousness, while one contrary to this is inauspicious; the details regarding [such fires] during a journey have been explained at length.
At the conclusion of the *svāhā* offering, the sacrificial fire of the king blazed forth spontaneously with bright flames; its luster was gentle and its crest turned to the right,
resembling the Ganges whose beautiful necklace is the water of the Yamunā, the daughter of the Sun.
He brings the earth, girdled by the ocean, under his control.
In that fire, which resembled gold, the *aśoka*, the *kuraṇṭaka*, the lotus, the *vaidūrya*, and the blue lotus,
there was no darkness nor any space within the palace.
It renders the king's [splendor] eclipsed by the rays of jewels.
42.34a For those whose multitude of chariots, oceans, clouds, and elephants / 42.34b produce a sound equal to fire or even a drum;
/ 42.34c by them, [the earth] was struck by the friction of herds of elephants blinded by rut.
In that vehicle, the quarters of the sky become like darkness.
When the standards, jars, horses, elephants, and kings fall under the control of [the enemy] kings in accordance with their respective types,
then the earth— with its rising and setting mountains as its lower lip and the Himavat and Vindhya ranges as its breasts— comes under their subjection.
When the fire is fragrant with the ichor of elephants, earth-lotuses, parched grain, clarified butter, and honey,
the ground before the king appears as if strewn with the luster from the crest-jewels of prostrate monarchs.
Whatever has been stated regarding the auspicious and inauspicious [effects] that arise when the banner of Indra (the rainbow) appears in the forms of the seven rays—
that should be considered during times of birth, sacrifice, pacification of the planets, journeys, and marriages as well.
Having honored the Brahmins with jaggery, cakes, milk-rice, and other offerings, as well as with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā),
[the king] should be awakened on the twelfth day under the asterism Śravaṇa, or otherwise at any time apart from Śravaṇa.
42.39ab. Manu stated that seven or five Śakra-kumāris should be made by those who know the rules; 42.39cd.
those named Nanda and Upananda should be one-quarter and one-half [respectively] less than the height of the banner-pole.
42.40ab/ When [the shadow] exceeds sixteen parts, there are two, Jaya and Vijaya, and the other two, Vasu and Dhara;
42.40cd/ Śakrājanitrī is greater than these by one-eighth in the middle.

42.41ab/ One should gradually present those variously shaped ornaments, which were fashioned long ago by the delighted gods for the one whose banner is the celestial elephant. 42.41cd/ These should be given as jewel-encrusted trappings in their proper order.
42.42ab/ Resembling a red Aśoka flower and square-shaped, it was first fashioned by Viśvakarman;
42.42cd/ the girdle was given by Svayambhū and by Śaṅkara, bearing many colors.
42.43ab. A third ornament, eight-sided and blue-red, was given by Indra. 42.43cd. Yama gave a fourth, a black and radiant *masūraka* gem.
42.44ab/ Varuṇa is the color of madder; that fifth [face] has six corners and resembles a wave of water.
42.44cd/ Mayūra and Keyūra are the sixth; Vāyu is the color of a rain cloud.
42.45ab. Skandha gave his own armlet, the seventh, which was highly variegated, for the banner.
42.45cd. The eighth was given by the Fire-god, resembling the flame of a fire and having the circular form of a sacrificial oblation.
Indra gave a ninth neck-ornament resembling lapis lazuli;
Tvaṣṭṛ, the Sun, gave a tenth, which was radiant and resembled the wheel of a chariot.
The eleventh is Udvaṃśa, resembling a lotus and presided over by the Viśvedevas; the twelfth is Niveśa (or Nivaṃśa), which has the luster of a blue lotus and is presided over by the sages (munis).
42.48ab. A thirteenth [limb] of Ketu is fashioned somewhat below and above, broad at the top.
42.48cd. Jupiter and Venus, resembling the juice of lac, bestow it upon his head.
42.49 Whatever ornament has been fashioned for the sake of the banner by whichever immortal,
that should be understood by the wise as belonging to that respective deity.
The circumference of the first bowl (piṭaka) is one-third of the height of the banner-pole;
from that first one onwards, each subsequent bowl is diminished by one-eighth of its own height.
On the fourth day, the one learned in the scriptures should perform the consecration of the banner of Indra;
and, being self-restrained, he should recite these mantras sung by Manu in the traditional scriptures.

42.52ab/ By Hara, Arka, Vaivasvata, Śakra, and Soma; by Dhaneśa, Vaiśvānara, and the Holder of the Noose (Varuṇa); 42.52cd/ by the hosts of great ṛṣis together with the quarters and the apsarases; and by Śukra, Aṅgiras, Skanda, and the Marut-gaṇas.
42.53 Just as you have been honored with noble ornaments that are uniform in providing vigor, so too, O God, with a joyful heart, accept those auspicious ornaments here at this sacrifice.
