42.54ab/ Viṣṇu, the unborn, the imperishable, the eternal, the one of uniform nature, the Boar, the Puruṣa, the ancient;
42.54cd/ you are the Ender, the destroyer of all, the fire, the thousand-headed one, the hundred-fold willed, the praiseworthy.
I invoke the poet, the seven-tongued one, the protector Indra, our own savior, the lord of the gods;
I call upon Śakra, the slayer of Vṛtra, the leader of the host. May our heroes be victorious.
42.56 When filling [the vessel], raising it up, entering [the temple], bathing, as well as during the arrangement and offering of garlands,
the king, while fasting, should recite these auspicious mantras of Indra’s banner.
It is adorned with umbrellas, banners, mirrors, fruit, half-moons, variegated garlands, plantain trees, and stalks of sugarcane;
it is decorated with lattice windows featuring lions and serpents, and by the guardians of the world (lokapālas) in the various directions.
One should raise up the mark of the Thousand-eyed One, which has unsevered cords, a foundation of solid timber, and well-fitted mechanisms, bolts, bases,
and arches.
It was provided with young shoots from trees of solid heartwood that had been broken off.
42.59a Amidst the unceasing clamor of the people with auspicious benedictions and prostrations,
42.59b with the sharp sounds of *paṭaha* drums, *mṛdaṅga* drums, conchs, kettledrums, and the like,
42.59c and with the Brahmins reciting words prescribed by the Vedas.
And one should raise a banner that is free from inauspicious sounds.
Surrounded by the citizens, who held fruits, curd, ghee, parched grain, honey, and flowers in their outstretched hands, and who bowed their heads while offering praises,
the Lord of Creatures [approached] the banner of the Lord of the Unblinking Ones (Viṣṇu).
One should cause a city with its foremost gate bent toward the enemy to be built for the destruction of foes.
42.61a Not too fast and not too slow, without trembling;
42.61b with flower garlands, baskets, and other ornaments intact;
42.61c such rising is desired; what is otherwise would be inauspicious.
The domestic priest should pacify that [calamity] for the king with rites of propitiation.
When carnivorous beasts, owls, pigeons, crows,
and herons are stationed upon a banner, they portend great danger for the king;
and by the presence of a blue jay, they declare fear for the crown prince.
The hawk, swooping down, causes terror to the eyes.

42.63a If the royal parasol breaks or falls, there is death for the king; 42.63b honey [produced] by bees hidden therein portends thieves; 42.63c and furthermore, a meteor destroys the domestic priest.
And the thunderbolt struck the queen of the king.
A fallen banner portends the destruction of the queen; the falling of a cluster of stars (piṭaka) causes drought; and the breaking of a comet at its middle, tip, or base likewise brings calamity.
It destroys the ministers, the king, and the citizens.
When [the city] is shrouded in smoke, there is danger from fire; when in darkness, there is delusion; and when it is filled with snakes that have been broken or fallen, the ministers do not survive.
Furthermore, beginning with the water-dwellers, the twice-born and the other classes gradually waste away.
But in the event of a breakage, the death of the harlot and of the maiden has been declared.
42.66a In the case of cutting a rope or tearing a lap-cloth, there is suffering for the child; 42.66b there is affliction for the king’s mother and for the mother’s lineage.
42.66c Whatever the wandering minstrels (*cāraṇas*) or children should do...
42.66d That very thing will become such, whether evil or auspicious.
Having worshipped the risen [image] for four days and honored it thoroughly, on the fifth day, the king,
together with his ministers, should dismiss the auspicious mark.
42.67d For the further increase of his own strength, like that of the wielder of the thunderbolt.
"This ritual, initiated by Uparicara Vasu and continued in succession by kings as well, has been performed;
by following this rule, a monarch shall not incur fear caused by enemies."

Chapter 43: On the Nīrājana Rite O Blessed One, whose eyelashes are the clouds, whose eyes are the moon and the sun, and whose navel is the lotus— when [the sun] has risen, one should perform the lustration (*nīrājana*) of the horses, elephants, and men.
On the twelfth, the eighth, or the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
or in the month of Āśvayuja, one should perform the propitiatory rite known as Nīrājana.
In the northeast direction of the city, on auspicious ground,
an archway (toraṇa) made of excellent timber should be constructed, sixteen cubits in height and ten cubits in width.
43.04ab. The hall for propitiatory rites (śāntisadma) shall consist of branches of the *sarja*, *udumbara*, and *kakubha* trees, and be abundant with *kuśa* grass.
43.04cd. Its doors shall be adorned with fish, banners, and wheels fashioned from bamboo.
43.05ab/ For the sake of the prosperity of horses staying in the peace-chamber, one should tie around their necks *pratisarā* made of *bhallātaka*, *śālī*, *kuṣṭha*, and *siddhārtha*.
43.06ab/ With mantras dedicated to the Sun, Varuṇa, the Viśvedevas, Prajāpati, Indra, and Viṣṇu,
43.06cd/ one should perform the propitiatory rite for the horses in the sanctuary of peace for seven days.
43.07ab. Having been honored, they must not be addressed with harsh words, nor should they be struck.
43.07cd. Freed from fear by the sounds of the "auspicious day" proclamation, conchs, trumpets, and songs, [they should proceed].
43.08ab/ On the arrival of the eighth day, one should prepare a hermitage facing north, to the south of the archway,
covered with kuśa grass and bark garments, with the fire in front of it and on the altar.
43.09ab/ Sandalwood, kuṣṭha, samaṅgā, yellow orpiment, realgar, priyaṅgu, vacā; 43.09cd/ Dantī, amṛtā, añjana, turmeric, suvarṇapuṣpī, and agnimantha.
43.10ab/ White [gudūcī], along with pūrṇakośā, kaṭambharā, trāyamāṇā, and sahadevī; 43.10cd/ nāgakusuma, svaguptā, śatāvarī, and somarājī.
43.11ab/ Having prepared these [substances] in the jars, one should properly offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) along with the ritual requisites.
43.11cd/ With various kinds of foods, abundant in honey, milk-rice, and barley-gruel.
43.12ab/ Fuel-sticks made of khadira, palāśa, udumbara, kāśmarya, or aśvattha wood;
43.12cd/ The sacrificial ladle (sruk) should be made of gold or silver by one desiring prosperity.
43.13ab. The illustrious king, facing the east and standing upon a tiger skin, should remain near the fire, accompanied by the horse-physician and the astrologer.

43.14ab/ Whatever has been stated regarding the march [of an army], in the ritual for the sacrifice to the planets, and concerning the banner of Mahendra; 43.14cd/ the characteristics of the altar, the domestic priest, and the fire should be understood in this [context] as well.
Having honored a horse endowed with the auspicious marks and an excellent elephant— both consecrated and bathed,
and having adorned them with unwashed white garments, perfumes, garlands, and incense—
he should lead them slowly to the base of the hermitage archway, consoling them with gentle words.
The quarters of the sky were filled with the sounds of musical instruments, conchs, and the proclamation of "an auspicious day."
43.17ab/ If, having been brought forward, the horse should stand with its right foreleg raised;
43.17cd/ then that lord of men conquers his enemies before long, without effort.
43.18ab/ One who is terrified by the king should not desire the remaining activities of elephants and horses.
43.18cd/ That which was explained regarding the expedition (yātrā) should be considered here according to the proper method.

43.19ab. Having consecrated the food-ball (piṇḍa), the domestic priest should give it to the horse; if the horse should smell it, or eat it, he brings victory. Otherwise, it is declared to be the reverse.
Having dipped a branch of the *udumbara* tree into the waters of the jars, he should touch the horses;
likewise, he should touch the army, along with the king and the elephants, with mantras for pacification and nourishment.
Having performed a propitiatory rite for the prosperity of the kingdom,
the Brahmin should further pierce an image of the enemy made of clay in the region of the heart with a trident, using mantras intended for malevolent rites.
43.22ab. Then the domestic priest, having consecrated it with mantras, should give the bit to the horse;
thereafter the king, having mounted, should proceed toward the north, consecrated by the *nīrājana* rite, together with his army.
The breeze was fragrant with the scent of rut flowing from elephants delighted by the sound of drums and conchs;
and with the mass of light flickering from the tips of their crest-jewels, he blazed like the sun at the end of the rainy season.
43.24ab/ With rows of swans flying here and there, the king of mountains appeared as if with white chowries.

43.24cd–25ab. With beautiful garlands and garments being wafted by breezes carrying the scent of refined perfumes, he was adorned with crowns, earrings, and armlets set with many-colored gems and diamonds;
colored by the radiance of abundant jewels, he bore the splendor of Indra’s bow.
Surrounded by horses that seemed to leap into the sky and by elephants that seemed to tear asunder the earth,
the king should march like Śakra, encircled by men who resemble the gods who have conquered their enemies.
Alternatively, adorned with a vajra and pearls, wearing white garlands, a turban, ointments, and garments,
with a parasol held over him, the son of Bhrigu rests upon the back of an elephant like the moon atop a cloud.
He whose army—filled with joyful men, horses, and elephants; radiant with the luster of spotless weapons; and unshakable yet terrifying to the enemy faction—shall soon conquer the earth.
Chapter 44: The Chapter on the Characteristics of the Khañjanaka Bird.
Regarding this bird named the khañjanaka, I shall now declare those fruits which have been proclaimed by the sages upon its first appearance.
44.02ab/ A bull that is stout, with an elevated throat and a black neck, is a "Bhadra" (auspicious) type and brings about prosperity.
44.02cd/ One that is black from the mouth down to the throat is a "Sampūrṇa" (complete) type, which fulfills one's hopes.
44.03ab/ A crow with a black spot on its throat and white at the tips of its cheeks brings emptiness; if it is empty itself, it makes one destitute.
44.03cd/ One that is yellow or pale-yellow is called a *gopīta*; such a *khañjana* seen [in these colors] causes affliction.
44.04ab/ Then, upon trees bearing sweet and fragrant fruits and flowers, in sacred reservoirs of water,
44.04cd/ on the heads of elephants, horses, and serpents, and in palaces, gardens, and mansions—
44.05ab/ Near cows, a cow-pen, a gathering of the virtuous, a sacrifice, a festival, a king, or a brahmin;
44.05cd/ Or near an elephant stable, a horse stable, an umbrella, a banner, a fly-whisk, and so forth.
44.06ab/ In places smeared with gold, white garments, lotuses, and water-lilies, or near offerings;
44.06cd/ and upon vessels of curd or heaps of grain, the wagtail brings good fortune.
44.07ab/ If it falls into mud, there is the acquisition of sweet food; if it falls onto cow dung, there is an abundance of milk products.
44.07cd/ If it falls on a grassy plot, there is the acquisition of clothing; if it stands upon a cart, there is displacement from one's country.
44.08ab/ In the house-section (gṛhapatale), there is loss of wealth when [the asterism] is in Vadhra; in Aśuci, there is imprisonment and disease.
44.08cd/ But in Pṛṣṭha, it quickly brings about union with beloved ones for goats and sheep.
44.09ab/ Situated upon the bones of a buffalo, camel, or donkey, in a cremation ground, at the corner of a house, on gravel, or on a mountain;
44.09cd/ and [situated] upon a wall, ashes, or hair, it is inauspicious, portending death, disease, and fear.
Flapping its wings, the Khañjana bird is not auspicious; however, drinking water while perched on a riverbank at sunrise, it is praised and brings desired results, whereas at sunset it is not so.
When the *nīrājana* ceremony has concluded, in whichever direction the king sees a wagtail (*khañjana*) flying away, his enemy who has gone in that direction quickly comes under his control.
44.12a Wherever he engages in sexual intercourse, there a treasure is found;
44.12b but wherever he vomits, beneath that spot there is glass (kāca).
44.12c They also teach that there is charcoal in his excrement.
To dispel that curiosity, one should dig into the earth.
A bird that is dead, mutilated, split, or diseased bestows fruits corresponding to its own condition;
however, one that is settling in the sky brings wealth and the meeting with kinsmen.

The king, having observed an auspicious bird on the ground in an auspicious location, should perform an offering (*argha*) accompanied by fragrant flowers and incense; thus, being well-received with joy, it attains prosperity.
Even upon seeing an inauspicious Khañjana bird, a king who is devoted to the worship of Brahmins, teachers, virtuous men,
and gods shall not incur misfortune, provided he does not eat meat for seven days.
44.16ab. The result [of the first appearance] until the end of the rainy season is determined daily according to the remainder of the day.
44.16cd. It should also be inferred from the direction, location, form, ascendant, asterism, and whether [the planet] is pacified, combust, and so forth.
Chapter 45: On Portents I shall now declare those portents which Garga proclaimed to Atri;
this is their summary: a portent is any deviation from the natural state.
45.02ab. Through the misconduct of men, a calamity arises from the accumulation of evil.
45.02cd. Those portents—celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial—indicate this.

45.03ab/ When the deities become displeased due to the misconduct of men, they create these calamities; 45.03cd/ therefore, to counteract them, the king should perform propitiatory rites within the kingdom.
45.04ab/ Celestial [omens] consist of abnormalities of the planets and constellations, meteors, thunderclaps, winds, and halos;
45.04cd/ as well as cities of Gandharvas, rainbows, and so forth—these are what is atmospheric.
45.05ab/ Terrestrial [portents], arising from both moving and stationary sources, attain pacification when struck by the corresponding propitiatory rites.
45.05cd/ Those originating in the sky attain softness, but some say that celestial [portents] do not subside.
Even divine affliction comes to an end through the gifts of abundant gold, food, cattle, and land,
as well as by standing on the ground in a temple of Rudra for the duration of a cow’s milk-yielding time and performing ten million oblations (koṭihoma).
45.07ab/ For the king himself, his sons, his treasury, his vehicles, his city, his wives, and his domestic priest, as well as for the world;
45.07cd/ destiny, when prepared, ripens in these eight ways for the monarch.
45.08ab/ The occurrence of causeless breaking, shaking, sweating, shedding tears, or talking by [images of] deities,
shrines, and temples portends the destruction of kings and their countries.

45.09ab/ The breaking, falling, overturning, sinking, or getting stuck of a deity’s carriage, a cart-axle, a wheel, a yoke, or a banner; 45.09cd/ as well as their displacement, collapse, or entanglement, do not bring auspiciousness to the country or the king.
45.10ab/ That which arises from the sages, dharma, the ancestors, and Brahmā is the transformation of the twice-born;
45.10cd/ that which arises from Rudra and the world-protectors is the ill fortune of cattle.

45.11ab/ That arising from Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn pertains to domestic priests; that born of Viṣṇu pertains to the people at large; 45.11cd/ and that arising from Skanda and Viśākha pertains to regional rulers and sovereign kings.
When there is a portentous anomaly involving Vedavyāsa as the minister, Vināyaka as the commander-in-chief,
and Viśvakarman as the creator, it is ordained for the destruction of the worlds.
Whatever abnormality may occur among the gods, princes, princesses, women, or servants,
it pertains to the king’s sons, daughters, wives, and attendants.
45.14ab/ For Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Guhyakas, and Nāgas, this very same [rule] is prescribed.
45.14cd/ And for all of them, the ripening of the fruit occurs within eight months.
45.15ab. Having perceived the divine manifestation, the pure domestic priest, having fasted for three days and bathed, 45.15cd.
shall worship the image with baths, flowers, ointments, and garments.
45.16ab. The domestic priest should attend according to rule with the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), edible foods, and abundant offerings.
45.16cd. He should offer the cooked oblation (*sthālīpāka*) according to rule with mantras bearing the appropriate characteristics.

45.17a Thus, for the pacification of disturbances caused by the gods, for seven nights, 45.17b worship of the twice-born and the hosts of deities, as well as festivals of song and dance, 45.17c should be performed according to the rules by kings; for those [kings] by whom these are practiced, [no misfortune shall arise].
The ripening of evil deeds occurs, yet it is obstructed by sacrificial gifts.
45.18ab/ In whose kingdom fire blazes without being ignited, and blazes even when it possesses fuel,
45.18cd/ the suffering of that lord of men and of his kingdom is to be known.
45.19ab. When water, meat, or something wet appears in a fire, there is the death of a king; when it appears among weapons, there is a fierce battle.
45.19cd. It portends the destruction of armies, villages, and cities, and causes fear from fire.
45.20ab/ When palaces, mansions, gateways, banners, and so forth are consumed by fire,
or struck by lightning, the arrival of a foreign army will certainly occur within six months.
Smoke arising without fire, dust, and darkness appearing during the day—these portend great danger.
The disappearance of stars at night when the sky is cloudless, or their appearance during the day, likewise brings about calamity.

45.22ab. They say that a fire [seen] with smoke, flames, and sparks, appearing upon beds, clothes, or hair, brings fear to cities, quadrupeds, birds, and humans. 45.22cd. [If it appears] on beds, garments, or hair, it portends death.
If weapons exhibit portents such as flaming, slithering, or sound, or if they emerge from their scabbards and tremble,
or if there are other such abnormalities regarding the weapons, one should predict a swift and tumultuous, fierce battle.
45.24a With *Āgneya* mantras, using fuel-sticks from a milk-tree,
45.24b the fire should be offered oblations with mustard seeds and clarified butter;
45.24c thus, when there is a transformation of the fire and other elements, pacification is achieved.
And gold should be given to the Brahmins on this occasion.
45.25ab/ If there is the sudden breaking of branches of trees, one should predict preparations for war.
45.25cd/ If they laugh, there will be exile from one's country; and if they weep, there will be an abundance of diseases.
If it rains out of season, there will be dissension within the kingdom; if it rains when the flowers have fully blossomed, there will be the slaughter of children.
If milk flows from a tree, there will be the destruction of all wealth.
45.27ab/ In the case of wine, there is the loss of mounts; in blood, battle; in honey, disease.
45.27cd/ In the case of oil, there is fear of famine; in the case of flowing water, great fear.
45.28ab. When dry plants sprout, there is a depletion of vitality and food; and when withered trees blossom, there is danger from diseases.
45.28cd. When fallen objects rise up on their own, there is fear arising from divine (supernatural) causes.
45.29ab. For when flowers or fruit appear out of season on a tree that has been worshipped, O King, it is indicated as a sign of the king’s death.
45.29cd. If there should be smoke or even a flame upon it, that too leads surely to the king’s death.
45.30ab/ When trees move, or even when they speak, the destruction of people is predicted. 45.30cd/ When there is a deformity of trees, the fruition of the result occurs after ten months.

45.31ab. Having placed an umbrella over the tree that has been honored with garlands, perfumes, incense, and garments, 45.31cd. one should perform the recitation of the Rudra-mantra for the sake of auspiciousness; here, there are exactly six oblations [consisting of the six-limbed oblation] to the Rudras.
The king should feed the Brahmins with milk-rice mixed with honey and ghee.
In this case of an unnatural portent caused by trees, those seeking welfare declare that the gift to be given is the earth itself.

45.33ab. When two or three stalks of lotuses, barley, and so forth arise from a single root, it portends the death of their respective owners. 45.33cd. Likewise, if flowers or fruits grow in pairs, it indicates the same for those who preside over them.
If there is excessive growth of crops and the production of various fruits and flowers on trees,
it will certainly result in the arrival of a foreign army.
When oil from sesame seeds becomes half [in quantity], or when the sesame seeds themselves become oilless, and when food loses its flavor, then one should recognize that there is very great danger.
A flower or fruit that has been deformed should be placed outside the village or the city;
for the sake of pacification, a *caru* oblation dedicated to Soma should be prepared here, or an animal should be offered as a sacrifice.

45.37a And having observed a deformity in the crops, that very field should first be given to the twice-born; 45.37b in the midst of that very [field], one should offer a sacrificial pap (caru) here to Bhauma.
Having performed [it], one does not incur the fault arising from that.
45.38ab. In the case of drought or excessive rain, there will be famine, the fear of hunger, and the threat of foreign armies.
45.38cd. Indeed, when [rain falls] out of season, there is disease; when it arises from a cloudless sky, there is the death of the king.
45.39ab/ When the cold and heat are inverted even though the seasons have set in correctly,
45.39cd/ within six months there will be danger to the kingdom, danger from disease, and that produced by divine [forces].

45.40ab/ If it rains continuously for seven days out of season, there will be the death of a preeminent king. 45.40cd/ If it rains blood, there will be the mobilization of weapons; if it rains flesh, bone, fat, and so forth, there will be a great pestilence.
45.41ab. One should recognize fear from rains of grain, gold, bark, fruit, flowers, and the like.
45.41cd. From a rain of charcoal and dust, that city goes to destruction.
45.42ab/ When stones fall without clouds, or when living beings are rained upon;
45.42cd/ Or when there is a breach during excessive rain, it causes a plague for the crops.
In the case of a rain of milk, ghee, honey, curd, blood, or hot water,
the destruction of the country is to be known; and in the case of a rain of blood, there shall also be war among kings.
45.43ab/ If, when the sun is free from blemish, its shadow is not seen or appears contrary [to its direction], 45.43cd/ then a very great danger has arrived for the country; this should be predicted.
45.44ab/ When a rainbow is seen in a cloudless sky during the day, or even at night,
45.44cd/ whether in the east or in the west, then there will be a very great danger of famine.
45.45ab/ A sacrifice (yāga) to the Sun, the Moon, Parjanya, and Vāyu is prescribed during times of disturbances in the rain.
45.45cd/ Gifts of grain, food, cattle, gold, and dakṣiṇā should then be given; thus the evil is pacified.
45.46ab/ The diversion of rivers causes a city to become desolate before long.
45.46cd/ Likewise, the drying up of those things that should not dry up, or of other bodies of water such as lakes and the like, [portends the same].
45.47ab/ When rivers carrying oil, blood, and flesh become turbid and agitated, and even flow in the opposite direction, 45.47cd/ they announce the arrival of a foreign army within six months.
45.48ab/ Flames, smoke, boiling, weeping, and crying out from wells; 45.48cd/ And singing and chatter [therein] are taught as portents of a plague among the people.

45.49. When water appears where there is no excavation, or when there is a reversal of the smell and taste of waters, or when there is a transformation of reservoirs of water, there is great danger; for this [remedy], one should perform this pacification.
In the event of a transformation of water, one should perform worship of Varuṇa with mantras dedicated to Varuṇa;
by means of those very same [mantras], one should perform recitation and fire-oblations, and thus the evil comes to rest.

45.51ab/ When there is a disorder in the birth of women, or when they give birth to two, three, four, or more [at once]; 45.51cd/ And when [birth occurs] at an insufficient or excessive time, there is the destruction of the region and the family.

45.52ab. If twins are born from a mare, a camel, a buffalo, a cow, or an elephant, their death occurs in battle. 45.52cd. The result of the birth is realized after six months; there are two verses by Garga regarding the pacification [of these omens].
A man who desires his own welfare must abandon the wives of others within his domain; he should satisfy the twice-born with their desired objects and likewise perform rites for peace in this matter.
45.54ab/ Quadrupeds should be released from their own herds into foreign lands;
45.54cd/ otherwise, they might destroy the city, the master, or the herd itself.
45.55ab/ It is improper for animals to mate with those of another species, or for cows to do so;
45.55cd/ or for bulls to drink from one another, or for a dog to drink from the offspring of a cow.

Within three months, one should know that the arrival of the enemy will occur there without doubt. To counteract that, these two verses were pointed out by Garga: 45.56ab/ Within three months, one should know that the arrival of the enemy will occur there without doubt. 45.56cd/ To counteract that, these two verses were pointed out by Garga.
45.57ab/ Abandonment, banishment, or giving—whichever of these he performs quickly, that shall become auspicious for him.
45.57cd/ In this case, he should satisfy the Brahmins and cause the recitation of mantras and burnt offerings to be performed.
The domestic priest shall worship Dhātṛ with an offering of cooked rice (sthālīpāka) and Paśu with an animal sacrifice,
using the Prājāpatya mantra, accompanied by abundant food and sacrificial fees.

If a vehicle should move when separated from its draft animal, or fail to move when joined with one, there will then be danger to the kingdom; likewise, if the wheels sink or break, the same result follows.
When the sounds of singing and musical instruments are heard in the sky, or when there is a displacement of moving and stationary objects, then death, disease, or the defeat by an enemy shall occur.
If the sound of musical instruments is not struck, or if there is no sound when they are struck,
or if there is a failure in their production, or if another person enters [the instrument], it portends the death of the king.

When there is contact between a cow and a plow, or when there is a transformation of household utensils such as a ladle or a winnowing basket, and likewise when there is the howling of a jackal, there is fear of weapons; such is the word of the Sage.

45.63ab. Among these rites dedicated to Vāyu, the king should worship Vāyu with parched grain flour (saktu). 45.63cd. The five verses beginning with "āvāyoḥ" should be recited by the self-restrained twice-born.
45.64ab/ One should satisfy the Brahmins with the finest food and with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
45.64cd/ And oblations accompanied by abundant food and sacrificial fees should be performed with great effort.
45.65ab/ If forest-dwelling birds that frequent the wilds enter the city without fear; 45.65cd/ Or if those that roam by day wander at night, or those that roam by night wander during the day.
45.66ab/ Deer or birds that form circles during both twilights,
or that cry out in a flock while facing a blazing quarter of the sky, portend danger.
Hawks [or dogs] seem to wail at the gate, and blazing jackals howl;
or if a dove or an owl should enter the palace of the lord of men.
The crowing of cocks at nightfall and the warbling of cuckoos at the beginning of the winter season,
as well as hawks and other birds moving in a counter-clockwise circle in the sky, portend danger.
45.69ab/ A flock of birds gathering on the household shrines, gateways, and doors;
45.69cd/ And the appearance of honey, anthills, or lotuses [in these places] also portend destruction.
45.70ab. If dogs enter houses with bones, corpses, or body parts, it portends a plague.
45.70cd. If animals or weapons utter cries, it signifies the death of the king; such is the word of the Sage.
45.71ab. In the case of abnormalities among wild animals and birds, the wise man should perform rites accompanied by sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*).
45.71cd. And the mantra "The gods are the pigeons" (*devāḥ kapotāḥ*) should be recited by five twice-born men.
With one [verse], "O Sudevā," cows together with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given;
or he should mutter the *Śākunasūkta* and the "Heads of the Vedas" (*Vedaśiras*).
45.73ab/ In the case of the collapse or breaking of Śakra’s banner, Indra’s pillar, a column, a door, or a water-shed;
45.73cd/ likewise, from the [collapse or breaking] of doors, arches, or standards, there is the death of the king.
45.74ab/ The blazing of both twilights and the appearance of smoke in the forest without fire;
45.74cd/ and the cracking and trembling of the earth, even in the absence of fissures, cause great fear.
Devoted to heretics and nihilists, he abandons virtuous conduct, is prone to anger,
envious, cruel, and his mind is intent on conflict.
In whatever [constellation] the king [is situated], there is the destruction of that country.
"Strike! Seize! Cut! Break!"—thus do children, with weapons, sticks, and stones in their hands, shout as they strike; even there, fear arises quickly.
45.77ab/ That house in which there is a depiction of deformed spirits using charcoal, red ochre, and other such materials,
45.77cd/ or which is decorated with the image of a leader (nāyaka), goes to ruin before long.

A house that is variegated with cobwebs, rags, and limbs; one that is not honored during the two twilights; one that is beset by quarrels; and one where women are constantly left in a state of impurity—such a house goes to ruin.
45.79ab. When *yātudhānas* are seen, one should declare that death has swiftly arrived.
45.79cd. For their counteraction, Garga performed this propitiatory rite (*śānti*).
Then one should perform great propitiatory rites (*mahāśānti*), offerings (*bali*), and provide abundant foods; and one should worship Mahendra with the *Māhendrī* hymns.

45.81ab. When there is the destruction of the king’s country, or at the rising of Ketu, or during an eclipse of the sun or moon; 45.81cd. the occurrence of portents at their own proper seasons does not lead to harm.

45.82ab. Furthermore, those portents which do not produce calamities because they are produced by the very nature of the season—one should recognize them through these verses composed by the son of a seer, which are stated in brief.
45.83ab/ The sounds of thunderbolts, lightning, earthquakes, twilight, and atmospheric portents;
45.83cd/ Halos, dust, smoke, and the sun rising or setting with a reddish hue.
45.84ab. From trees there arises an abundance of sap, oil, flowers, and fruits; 45.84cd. And an increase in cattle, birds, and honey occurs for the welfare of the month of Madhava (Vaiśākha).
45.85ab/ Turbid with the falling of stars and meteors, with the orbs of the sun and moon turned tawny;
45.85cd/ Struck by fireless conflagrations, explosions, smoke, dust, and wind.
If one observes the twilight sky to be as red as a lotus and resembling an agitated ocean,
and sees the drying up of the waters of rivers during the summer, one should predict auspiciousness.
45.87ab/ The appearance of Indra’s weapon (a halo), a halo around the sun or moon, lightning, and the sprouting of withered trees;
45.87cd/ as well as earthquakes characterized by trembling, upheaval, deformity, rumbling, and splitting of the earth.
In the rainy season, the swelling of lakes, rivers, and wells, the overflowing of water, and the floating of objects; as well as the sliding of mountains and houses—these do not bring about fear.
45.89ab/ There is the wonderful sight of celestial women, bhūtas, gandharvas, and aerial chariots;
45.89cd/ and the sight of planets, lunar mansions, and stars in the sky during the day.
The sounds of singing and musical instruments are heard upon the forested mountain ridges;
the growth of crops and the decrease of water are recorded as the characteristics of the sinless autumn.
45.91ab. Cold winds and frost, the crying out of wild animals and birds; 45.91cd. Or the sight of beings such as Rākṣasas and Yakṣas, and speech that is non-human.

In the winter season, it is recorded that the quarters of the sky shrouded in the darkness of smoke, along with the heavens, forests, and mountains, as well as the high rising and setting of the sun, are considered auspicious.
Falls of snow, violent winds, and portents; the sight of deformed and wondrous things; a sky with the luster of black collyrium, variegated by the falling of stars and meteors.
45.94ab/ The production of variegated offspring among women, cows, goats, horses, deer, and birds,
45.94cd/ as well as the transformations of leaves, sprouts, and creepers, are auspicious signs in the cold season.

45.95ab/ For these [omens], being born of the very nature of the seasons, are seen to bestow auspicious results when occurring in their own season. 45.95cd/ But when they appear outside of their season, they are seen as portents that are exceedingly terrible.
Whatever verses are uttered by the insane, whatever is spoken by children,
and whatever women speak— there is no deviation from that [truth].
First she moves among the gods, and afterwards she moves among humans;
for this Sarasvatī, being true, does not speak unless impelled.
Even one who is unversed in calculation, by perceiving portents, becomes renowned and a favorite of the king;
this secret teaching of the Sage has thus been declared.
45.98d By knowing which, a man becomes a seer of the three times.

Chapter 46: On the Portents of Peacocks and Painted Partridges First, I have described in detail the auspicious and inauspicious results based on celestial and atmospheric phenomena occurring during planetary movements, conjunctions, battles, journeys, and so forth.
46.02a Furthermore, it is not proper for Varāhamihira to commit this error of being an abridger; 46.02b that is his fault.
46.02c This should not be said by those who know [the subject], for it is a verse following the results already stated.
46.02d That which is celebrated as the "Varhicitraka" is the excellent limb.
46.03ab. That very nature of his is what has been proclaimed and restated.
46.03cd. Even if I do not speak this myself, nevertheless, I am subject to censure in this matter.

46.04ab/ Those situated in the northern path are radiant; all of them bring security, abundance, and auspiciousness. 46.04cd/ Those situated on the southern course are devoid of luster; they cause the fear of famine, thieves, and death.
When the son of Bhṛgu (Venus) is situated in the treasury house (the second house) and the Lord of Speech (Jupiter) is in Puṣya,
the kings will be free from enmity and enjoy happiness, while the people will be joyful and free from disease.
If the other planets afflict Kṛttikā, Maghā, Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa,
or Indrā (Jyeṣṭhā) while leaving the Sun alone, then the western quarter is afflicted by misfortune.

46.07a If [the comet] stands like a banner in the east at the end of the day, 46.07b there will indeed be conflict among the kings of the eastern regions; 46.07c if it occurs in the middle, there will indeed be suffering for the central lands.
46.07d But not with those [rays] that are harsh, though they possess brilliance like [the light of] rays.
46.08ab/ But when they resort to the southern quarter, there is a destruction of the clouds of the South;
46.08cd/ and with those that are small, rough, and thin, there is conflict, whereas with those endowed with large bodies and rays, there is prosperity.
46.09ab/ Those with clear rays on the northern path bring peace; they belong to kings.
46.09cd/ Those with short bodies and the color of ashes cause harm to the kings of the land.
If the stars, along with the planets, are accompanied by smoke, flames, and sparks; or if they do not appear at all, even though there is no apparent cause for such an occurrence.
The entire world, together with its kings, goes to destruction.

When the pair of cool-rayed moons shines in the sky, then there is an exceedingly auspicious increase of the twice-born; immediately thereafter, there is conflict among those of the intermediate caste when the pair of suns appears.
The dissolution of the world occurs after three or four [yugas], and so forth.
46.12a When the comet Śikhin touches the Munis, Abhijit, Dhruva, and the asterism of Maghavat, it brings about the destruction of clouds and causes grief by destroying auspicious deeds.
46.12c If it should then touch Bhujaṅgama, there will certainly be a cessation of rain.
And the countryside, crowded with children, flees in terror and goes to ruin.
Moving through the asterisms at the eastern gates, the son of the Sun (Saturn) performs a retrograde motion;
he causes severe famine, terrible fear, hostility among friends, and drought.
46.14ab/ If the son of the Sun (Saturn), or Rahu, or Ketu pierces the cart of Rohiṇī;
46.14cd/ What can I say? For the entire world enters into total destruction in an ocean of misfortune.
When the sun constantly rises and the entire circle of the stars revolves,
then the world, with all its moving and unmoving beings, experiences the fruit of its previously committed unwholesome deeds.
46.16a Stationed in the bow [house], rough and resembling blood, it causes fear of hunger;
46.16b The Moon (Candra) indicates military exertion and victory from whichever side its string is drawn.
46.16c Having downward-pointing horns, it destroys cattle and brings about the destruction of crops as well.
If it blazes or emits smoke, it portends nothing but the death of the king.
Lustrous, full-bodied, with even horns, broad and lofty, moving northward along the Nāgavīthī, the Moon— when seen free from malefic planets and joined by benefics— brings exceeding joy to the world.
46.18ab. When the moon enters the asterisms of Pitrya, Maitra, Puruhūta, Viśākhā, or Tvāṣṭra, it forms a conjunction.
46.18cd. It is not auspicious when it moves to the south; however, it would be a bringer of welfare and auspiciousness if it moves toward the north or remains in the middle.
46.19ab. A *parigha* is a line of clouds appearing obliquely at the rising or setting of the sun. 46.19cd. A *paridhi*, however, is a secondary sun; a *daṇḍa* is straight and resembles a rainbow.
46.20ab/ Those rays of the sun which are long and unfailing at either sunrise or sunset; 46.20cd/ [They form] the straight fragment of Indra’s bow that is red, and the long Airāvata [rainbow].
The twilight lasts from half-way until sunset, as long as the stars have not yet become visible;
it also lasts from the time the sun’s light begins to fade until half-way until sunrise.

46.22ab. At that time of twilight, the auspicious or inauspicious results should be declared by means of these signs. 46.22cd. If all these are glossy, rain occurs immediately; if they are rough, there is danger.
The iron bar [of the halo] is unbroken, the sky is stainless, and the rays of the sun are dark-blue;
the beams are glossy, the rainbow is faint, and the lightning flashes toward the northeast.
Or, when the tree-like cloud is embraced by the rays of the sun, it appears glossy.
46.23d There would be rain, or else at the time of sunset a great cloud would cover the sun.
46.24ab. A planet that is broken, crooked, black, short, or pierced by the marks of crows and the like;
46.24cd. in whatever region the sun is harsh, there generally occurs the ruin of the king.
46.25ab/ A flock of flesh-eating birds approaches from behind the army of one who desires to fight.
46.25cd/ For that person, there will be a great rout of the forces, while victory belongs to those with birds at their front.
If, at the rising or the setting of the sun, a banner-like cloud resembling a city of the Gandharvas obstructs the solar disc,
then one should declare that a perilous battle has befallen the king.
A twilight that is praised when hushed by the sounds of birds and deer, gentle, and accompanied by soft breezes, is auspicious;
however, one that is covered in dust, harsh, or resembling the color of blood portends the destruction of the people.
46.28a Whatever has been explained at length by the sages, all that has been recounted by me here, avoiding redundancy;
46.28b even after hearing the song of the cuckoo, the crow still caws.
That which was produced by his own nature could not be overcome by the cuckoo.
Chapter 47: On the Bathing Ceremony under Puṣya.
The king is the root of the progenitor of subjects; because the world’s misfortune and fortune arise from the injury or the honoring [of him], therefore there is concern for the king.
47.02ab/ That pacification which was explained by the Self-Existent One for the sake of Mahendra, the preceptor of the gods;
47.02cd/ having obtained it, Vṛddhagarga spoke thus—listen to it as [explained] to Bhāguri.
47.03ab/ The Puṣya-bath for the king must be performed by an astrologer and the domestic priest.
47.03cd/ There is nothing more purifying than this, nor anything that puts an end to all portents.
47.04ab/ Devoid of *śleṣmātaka*, *akṣa*, thorny, pungent, bitter, and foul-smelling trees;
47.04cd/ abandoned by undesirable birds such as owls, vultures, and the like.
In a forest region filled with young trees, shrubs, creepers, and spreading vines,
abounding mostly in charming and sweet-smelling trees whose leaves and shoots are uninjured;

47.06ab/ By means of the cock, the jīvañjīvaka, the parrot, the peacock, the woodpecker, the blue jay, and the harīta; 47.06cd/ And by the krakara, the cakora, the kapiñjala, the vañjula, the pigeon, and the śrīka.
47.07ab/ And when it resounds near the forest with bees intoxicated by drinking the nectar of flowers, with male cuckoos and others; 47.07cd/ Or else in a clean field-dwelling.

47.08ab/ On the delightful sand-banks of rivers, which sport with playful women and are scarred by the claws of water-birds; 47.08cd/ One should perform [the rite] upon those hips of the sandy shores that generate delight for both the eyes and the mind.

In that lake, where white swans soar like umbrellas, where ducks, ospreys, and cranes raise their songs, where the blue lotuses are in full bloom like eyes, and which possesses the splendor of the In that place dwell the playful women of the lotus-ponds, whose faces are like full-blown lotuses, whose voices possess the sweet resonance of the kalahamsa swan, and whose breasts are like lofty, budding buds.
One should perform [the rite] in a cow-pen where the ground is covered with the foam from a cow's rumination, fragments of dung, and the marks of hoof-wounds,
and which is filled with the festival of calves lowing and frolicking immediately after birth.

Or else, on the shore of the ocean, crowded with ships laden with jewels that have safely arrived, its edges variegated by water-dwelling creatures and white birds nestled among thickets of *nicula* trees.
In those hermitages where anger is conquered by forbearance as a lion is subdued by a doe, or rather, where the young of birds and deer have been granted safety;
47.13cd. Or else, in those hermitages where the young of birds and deer have been granted safety.
In that glorious house, there were fawn-eyed women whose steps were impeded by the weight of their hips, adorned with girdles and anklets, and who possessed the sweet speech of cuckoos.
47.15ab/ In sacred shrines, at holy fords, and in delightful places such as gardens;
47.15cd/ On ground sloping toward the east or north, and where water flows from left to right.

47.16ab/ That which is abandoned by ashes, charcoal, bones, saline soil, husks, hair, pits, and the dwellings of crabs; 47.16cd/ and that which is devoid of holes made by porcupines and mice, as well as anthills.
47.17ab/ The *dhātrī* tree—dense, fragrant, glossy, sweet, and symmetrical—is for victory.
47.17cd/ Even in the military camp, it should be employed in this same manner according to the requirements.
Having departed from the city at night, the astrologer, minister,
and officiating priest should offer an oblation in the eastern direction, or in the northern, or in the direction presided over by the Lord of the North (Īśāna).
47.19ab. With parched grain, unbroken rice, curd, and flowers, the self-restrained domestic priest, bowing low, should perform the invocation.
47.19cd. Then the mantra for that occasion was proclaimed by the sages.
47.20ab. Let all the gods come here, those who desire worship;
47.20cd. as well as the Nāgas from every direction, the twice-born, and whoever else is entitled to a share of the offerings.
47.21ab. Having thus invoked them all, the domestic priest should then speak as follows:
47.21cd. "Having received worship tomorrow, they shall depart after bestowing peace upon the lord of the earth."

47.22ab. Having performed worship for those who have been invited, they should dwell there for that night. 47.22cd. The ritual for dreams regarding auspicious and inauspicious omens during a journey has thus been described.
On another day at dawn, one should bring together the ritual materials possessing the qualities as previously described;
having gone to the site on the ground, there are also verses sung here by the Sage.
47.24ab. Having drawn a mandala upon that [surface], one should fashion the earth there;
47.24cd. [a world] possessing various mines of jewels and diverse locations.
The domestic priest should assign the Nāgas, Yakṣas, gods, and ancestors to their respective places,
as well as the Gandharvas, Apsarases, sages, and Siddhas.
47.26ab/ And the planets together with all the constellations, the Rudras together with the Mothers;
47.26cd/ Skanda, Viṣṇu, and Viśākha, as well as the world-protectors and the celestial women.
Having prepared distinct pigments that are pleasing to the heart and endowed with excellent fragrances,
the wise man should worship [the deities] with perfumes, garlands, and ointments, each according to its own [prescribed] manner.
47.28ab/ With various kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten, as well as fruits, roots, and meat;
47.28cd/ And with various delightful drinks, such as wine, milk, and fermented liquors.
47.29ab/ Hereafter, I shall describe the worship of those [deities] as they are depicted here.
47.29cd/ That ritual for the planets which has been prescribed in the *grahayajña* (sacrifice to the planets) must be performed.
47.30ab/ Piśācas, sons of the Asuras, and Dānavas are to be worshipped with meat, rice, and wine.
47.30cd/ The ancestors (Pitṛs) [are to be worshipped] with ointments, collyrium, sesame seeds, and also with meat and rice.

The sages, however, should worship the Nāgas with Sāman and Yajus verses, with Ṛg-verses, and with perfumes, incense, and garlands; they should honor them with unguents of the color of aloe-wood and with the three sweets.
47.32ab/ One should honor the gods with incense, clarified butter offerings, garlands, jewels, hymns of praise, and prostrations;
47.32cd/ and the gandharvas and apsaras with fragrant perfumes and most sweet-smelling garlands.
47.33ab. One should perform the worship of all the remaining [deities] with offerings appropriate for all castes (sārvavarṇika).
47.33cd. These include protective cords (pratisara), garments, banners, ornaments, and sacred threads (yajñopavīta).
47.34ab. Having established the fire in the western part of the mandala, or alternatively on the altar to the south;
47.34cd. one should take up the ritual materials: long darbha grass that is free from seeds.
47.35ab/ Fried grain, clarified butter, unbroken rice, curd, honey, white mustard, perfumes, flowers, incense, 47.35cd/ Gorocanā, collyrium, sesame seeds, and fruits that are naturally sweet.

47.36ab. With those same materials, one should perform the worship of the bath upon the western altar using bowls of milk-rice mixed with ghee. 47.36cd. That altar is for the purpose of the bath [for one who has already bathed].
Having placed firm jars in its corners, their necks wrapped with white thread and their openings covered with sprouts and fruits from milk-exuding trees;
47.38ab. One should take the substances for the Puṣya-bath, which are mixed with water filled [in jars] along with gems;
47.38cd. one should take those substances for the Puṣya-bath that were sung by Garga.
Jyotiṣmatī, trāyamāṇā, abhayā, aparājitā, jīvā, viśveśvarī, pāṭhā, samaṅgā, and likewise vijayā.
One should place the *sahā*, *sahadevī*, *pūrṇakośā*, *śatāvarī*,
*ariṣṭikā*, *śivā*, and *bhadrā* into those jars.
The *brāhmī*, the *kṣemā*, the *ajā*, all kinds of seeds, gold,
auspicious objects as they may be obtained, as well as all medicinal herbs and juices.
47.42ab. Jewels, all kinds of fragrances, bilva, and vikaṅkata;
47.42cd. medicinal herbs with auspicious names, gold, and auspicious objects.

47.43ab. At the outset, one whose life has been shortened by old age should spread out the hide of an ox endowed with auspicious marks, with its neck pointing toward the east. 47.43cd. [He should spread it] so that the hair is turned upward.
47.44ab/ Then there should be the unblemished hide of a bull, a warrior, and a red deer; 47.44cd/ then the third should be that of a lion, and after that, that of a tiger.
47.45ab/ One should spread these four skins upon that sacrificial altar;
47.45cd/ when an auspicious moment has arrived and the moon is conjoined with the Puṣya asterism.
A throne (bhadrāsana) made of gold, silver, or copper by one [artisan],
or fashioned from the wood of a milk-exuding tree, should be placed upon hides.
Its height is of three kinds: one cubit, one and a quarter cubits, and one and a half cubits;
it bestows auspicious results for those seeking the status of a local ruler, a conqueror of neighboring territories, or universal sovereignty, respectively.
47.48ab. Having placed gold beneath him, the lord of men should sit there with a serene mind.
47.48cd. He should be surrounded by ministers, trusted friends, the domestic priest, astrologers, and citizens bearing auspicious names.
47.49ab/ With the sounds of the Vedas proclaiming "Auspicious Day" (Puṇyāha) resounded by bards, citizens, and Brahmins;
47.49cd/ And with the auspicious sounds of drums, conchs, and trumpets, all misfortune was dispelled.
47.50ab/ The domestic priest, having covered [the king] who is dressed in unwashed linen with a woolen blanket,
47.50cd/ and having performed the offerings and worship, should consecrate him with jars filled with clarified butter.

47.51ab/ The measure of the water-jars is eight, twenty-eight, or even one hundred and eight. 47.51cd/ With each increase [in number], the merit increases; and this mantra, sung by the Sage, is to be used here.
Clarified butter (ājya) is declared to be splendor; clarified butter is the supreme remover of sin.
Clarified butter is the food of the gods; in clarified butter all the worlds are established.
Whatever impurity has come upon you— whether terrestrial, atmospheric, or celestial—
may it all go to destruction through contact with this clarified butter.
47.54ab/ Having removed the blanket, the domestic priest should then consecrate the lord of men with the waters for the Puṣya-bath, together with fruits and flowers, using this mantra:
47.54cd/ [The priest] should consecrate the king with this mantra.
May the gods consecrate you, as well as those who are the ancient Siddhas—
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the Sādhyas, and the hosts of Maruts.
The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the two Aśvins, the best of physicians;
Aditi, the mother of the gods, as well as Svāhā, Siddhi, and Sarasvatī.
47.57ab Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Śrī, as well as Sinīvālī and Kuhū; 47.57cd Danu, Surasā, Vinatā, and Kadrū.
May all the wives of the gods who have not been mentioned, as well as the mothers of the gods,
and the divine hosts of Apsarases, consecrate you.

May the constellations, the auspicious moments (muhūrta), the junctions of the fortnights, days, and nights, the years, the lords of the days, and the divisions of time— the *kalās*, *kāṣṭhās*, *kṣaṇas*, and *lavas*—
all these auspicious components of Time consecrate you.
These and other sages were devoted to the Vedic vows.
Let those ascetics, together with their wives and disciples, consecrate you;
as well as the hosts of gods in their celestial chariots, the Manus, and the oceans.
And the highly blessed rivers, as well as the nāgas and kimpuruṣas;
the highly blessed vaikhānasa brahmins and those who are sky-dwellers.
The Seven Sages together with their wives, as well as the fixed positions [of the stars],
are Marīci, Atri, Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu, and Aṅgiras.
Bhṛgu, Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, then Sanandana,
Sanātana, Dakṣa, Jaigīṣavya, and Bhagandara.
Ekata, Dvita, Trita, Jābāli, Kaśyapa, Durvāsas, Durvinīta, Kaṇva, and likewise Kātyāyana.
Mārkaṇḍeya, Dīrghatapas, Śunaḥśepha, Vidūratha, Ūrdhva, Saṃvartaka, Cyavana, Atri, and Parāśara.
Dvaipāyana, Yavakrīta, and Devarāja with his younger brothers;
mountains, trees, creepers, and sacred shrines.
Prajāpati and Diti, the cows who are the mothers of the universe,
the divine vehicles, and all the worlds, both moving and unmoving.
The fires, the ancestors, the stars, the clouds, the sky, the directions, and the waters—
these and many others are of auspicious renown and are pure.
47.70ab. May they consecrate you with waters that destroy all portents, 47.70cd.
just as Maghavan was consecrated by them with joyful minds; may they bring you prosperity, long life, and health.
Thus, with these and others prescribed in the *Atharvavedakalpa*, together with the hosts of Rudras,
and with the *Kauṣmāṇḍa*, *Mahārauhiṇa*, and *Kuberahṛdaya* mantras, as well as with the *Samṛddhi* mantra;
Having recited the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā* and the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*,
the lord of men, once bathed, shall wear a pair of garments made of cotton.
Having sipped water for purification amidst the sounds of conchs announcing an auspicious day, and having worshipped the gods, the preceptor, and the brahmins,
he should then offer his own worship to the parasol, the banner, and the weapons.
With these verses beginning with "rāyaspoṣa," which bestow long life and luster,
one should consecrate a new ornament that brings victory.
Having gone to the second altar, the king should sit down upon the skins;
and these skins are to be offered one above the other in this manner.
47.76ab/ Of the bull, the wild cat, the ruru deer, and the spotted antelope; 47.76cd/ Above those [are the signs] of the lion and the tiger, and after that [the others].
47.77ab. The domestic priest should offer oblations into the fire at the principal location with fuel-sticks, sesame seeds, clarified butter, and other materials.
47.77cd. [He should do so] with the verses dedicated to the Three-eyed One (Śiva), Śakra, Bṛhaspati, Nārāyaṇa, and Nityagati.
The astrologer should declare the omens regarding fire as indicated by the banner of Indra;
then, having brought the rite to its complete conclusion, the domestic priest, with palms joined in reverence, should speak.
May all the hosts of gods depart, taking with them the worship from the king,
after having granted abundant success (*siddhi*) for their return once more.
Therefore, the king should honor the astrologer and the domestic priest with abundant wealth,
as well as other persons worthy of sacrificial gifts, such as those learned in the Vedas, according to their merit.
Having granted security to his subjects and released animals from places of slaughter,
he should effect the release of prisoners, with the exception of those who have committed internal crimes.
47.82ab. When this is employed under each constellation, it brings about happiness, fame, and the increase of wealth.
47.82cd. It has been declared that the *pauṣī* full moon, even without the conjunction with Puṣya, bestows half the fruit; it is [otherwise] said to be supreme for rites of pacification (*śānti*).
During national calamities and portents, at the appearance of Rāhu and Ketu,
and during the oppression by the planets, one should perform the Puṣya-bath.
47.84ab/ There is no calamity in the world that is not pacified by him; 47.84cd/ nor is there any other auspicious rite that surpasses this one.
For a king desiring supreme sovereignty and longing for the birth of a son,
this procedure is recommended prior to his consecration.
For the sake of Mahendra, Bṛhaspati of great renown spoke this [treatise],
which is the supreme means for performing ablutions that bring about longevity, the increase of progeny, and good fortune.
47.87ab. By this very same procedure, one should then cause an elephant or a horse to be bathed. 47.87cd. One who does so shall attain supreme perfection, being liberated from all disease.
Chapter 48: On the Characteristics of Silk Fabrics (Paṭṭa-lakṣaṇādhyāya).
The characteristics of silk fabrics have been described in detail by the teachers;
here, I shall provide a concise summary that encompasses all their essential points.
48.02ab/ A turban that is eight finger-breadths wide in the middle bestows auspiciousness upon kings.
48.02cd/ Seven [finger-breadths] are prescribed for the queen of a lord of men, and six for the crown prince.
48.03ab. The headband of the commander-in-chief has a width of four aṅgulas at its center.
48.03cd. And there are two [others] for the palace; these five are proclaimed as the types of headbands.
48.04ab/ All of them are twice as long as they are wide at the center, and half as broad on the sides.
48.04cd/ And all are fashioned from pure gold for the increase of prosperity.
O Lord of the Earth, one with five tufts [of hair] belongs to the crown prince; one with three tufts belongs to the king and the queen;
one with a single tuft belongs to the commander of the army; and a ribbon of favor is worn without a tuft of hair.
If the cloth being woven extends easily to its full width,
there will be prosperity and victory for the lord of the earth, as well as happiness and abundance for his subjects.
A wound that has arisen in the middle causes the destruction of life and kingdom;
one that has burst open in the middle should be abandoned, as it creates obstacles, whereas one that has burst open on the sides is auspicious.
48.08ab/ When an inauspicious omen arises, one who knows the scriptures should prescribe a propitiatory rite for the king.
48.08cd/ A turban [consecrated] with auspicious omens leads to the increase of both the king and the kingdom.
Chapter 49: On the Characteristics of the Sword.
The best sword measures fifty fingers (aṅgulas) in length; it may be less by twenty-five.
A wound [or mark] should be known from its measurement in fingers; one situated on an uneven joint is inauspicious.
49.02ab/ Wounds resembling a śrīvṛkṣa, a vardhamāna, an umbrella, a śivaliṅga, an earring, or a lotus; 49.02cd/ as well as those resembling a banner, a weapon, or a svastika, are praised.
Wounds on a rhinoceros that have the shapes of a chameleon, a crow, a heron, a carnivorous beast,
a headless torso, or a scorpion, as well as those that follow the lines of its hide or are numerous, do not bring good fortune.

49.04ab/ One that is cracked, short, blunt, or broken like a bamboo, which is not pleasing to the eye or the mind; 49.04cd/ and one that makes no sound—these are declared undesirable; the opposite of what has been stated yields desirable results.

49.05ab/ A ringing sound is said to portend death, while its emerging from the scabbard indicates defeat. 49.05cd/ If it emerges of its own accord, there will be battle; if it blazes, victory is attained with the sword.
One should not open it without a reason, nor should one pry it apart; one should not look at its interior, nor speak of its price;
one should not disclose its provenance, nor should one offer to appraise it.
49.06d A king who has not purified himself must never even touch his sword.
49.07ab/ Those shaped like a cow’s tongue, resembling the blue lotus or the leaf of a bamboo,
and those with tips like the leaf of a *karavīra*, or with points like a spearhead or a circle, are praised.
49.08ab/ Once completed, it must not be cut; it should be tested by touchstones and made to conform to the prescribed measurements.
49.08cd/ If it is cut at the base, the owner dies; if it is cut at the top, his mother dies.

49.09ab/ In whichever part of the hilt there may be a scar, that very same [mark] on the sword [is to be noted]. 49.09cd/ Just as a mole on women is described by seeing it on their private parts, so it is here; one must speak of it after observing it on the face [of the blade].
Alternatively, when the questioner touches a limb while holding a sword,
the physician, having understood this treatise, should determine that there is a wound on the part of the body held within the scabbard.
49.11ab/ When the head is touched at the first finger-breadth, at the second there is contact with the forehead;
49.11cd/ and at the third, [contact] between the eyebrows; and at the fourth, when the eyes are touched.
The first five [ripenings] are located in the nose, lips, cheeks, jaw, ears, neck, and shoulders;
the twelfth is situated in the chest, and the thirteenth is to be known as being in the two armpits.
49.13ab/ On the breasts, heart, abdomen, flanks, and navel, fourteen and so forth are to be known.
49.13cd/ At the base of the navel, on the hips, and in the private parts, they begin from nineteen.
In the twenty-second [digit], there would be a wound on the thighs; in the twenty-third, in the middle of the thighs;
in the twenty-fourth, on the knee; and in the twenty-fifth, on the shank.
49.15ab/ In the middle of the shanks, at the ankles, on the heels, in the feet, and also in the toes;
49.15cd/ according to the opinion of Garga, [the measurements] range from twenty-six to thirty [aṅgulas].
49.16ab/ The death of a son, the acquisition of wealth, the loss of wealth, prosperity, and imprisonment—
49.16cd/ one should indicate these results in sequence by means of wounds located on the fingers starting from the first.

49.17ab/ The acquisition of a son, quarrels, the gain of elephants, the death of a son, and the acquisition of wealth; 49.17cd/ Then, in sequence, destruction, the attainment of a wife, and mental anguish—from the sixth [year] onwards.
49.18ab/ Gain, loss, acquisition of a woman, killing, increase, death, and satisfaction;
49.18cd/ these are to be known as occurring in the [houses] beginning with the fourth, and loss of wealth occurs in the twenty-first.
49.19ab. Acquisition of wealth, non-extinction, arrival of riches, death, prosperity, and lack of ownership;
49.19cd. Sovereignty, death, and kingship—these are the results in sequence up to the thirtieth [year].
Beyond that, there is no further specific result; however, those situated in the uneven or even houses yield results of evil or merit respectively.
By some authorities, they are declared to be fruitless beyond thirty degrees, up to the limit of the apex (agra).
49.21ab/ A fragrance like that of oleander, blue lotus, elephant ichor, ghee, saffron, jasmine, and campaka brings auspiciousness;
49.21cd/ whereas a smell resembling cow urine, mud, or fat is inauspicious.
49.22ab/ A scent resembling the fat of a tortoise, blood, or alkaline ash brings fear and suffering.
49.22cd/ One with the luster of beryl, gold, or lightning brings victory, health, and prosperity.
49.23 This is the weapon-drink of Uśanas, by which one who desires blazing prosperity drinks blood, and one who longs for excellent offspring offers oblations.
And for one who desires inexhaustible wealth, [it is attained] through water.
If one seeks the accomplishment of a goal through evil means, it is like drinking the milk of a mare, a camel, or a female elephant;
or [seeking it] with the bile of a fish, or the milk of a deer, a horse, or a goat.
49.24d For the severing of an elephant's trunk, [use arrows] with a *satāla* core.
Milk of the *arka* plant mixed with soot from a rhinoceros horn, combined with the dung of a pigeon and a rat, constitutes a medicinal paste; then,
one should drink oil that has been churned from this [mixture].
49.25d After being sharpened, there shall be no blunting upon stone surfaces.
An iron [vessel] that has been soaked for a day in an alkaline solution of *kadalī* mixed with churned buttermilk,
and then thoroughly cooled upon a stone, does not undergo fracture.
And he experiences no dullness even when dealing with other metals.
Chapter 50: On the Science of Limbs (Aṅgavidyā) An astrologer,
observing the auspicious and inauspicious [signs] brought forth by the direction, the rising sign, and the position,
and having mentally examined the configuration of his own limbs and those of others belonging to the querent, should declare [the outcome].
For he is omniscient and all-seeing, being the pervasive Lord whose nature encompasses both the moving and the unmoving;
through their gestures and speech, he reveals to seekers the fruits of their actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious.

A site that is level, covered with very glossy tree-bark and foliage, bearing abundant flowers, fragrant grasses, and many fruits; sheltered by the shade of trees known for their auspicious names from which unworthy birds have departed;
and which is the abode of gods, sages, brahmins, virtuous men, and perfected beings (siddhas), and is sprinkled with excellent flowers and grain—[such a place is recommended].
And [the forest] was delightful, produced by the purity of the sweet, clear water, and possessed lush green grass.
50.03ab/ Not with trees that are cut, split, infested by worms, gnawed by rats, thorny, scorched, rough, or crooked;

nor with those having malefic nodes (saṃkrāntis), associated with cruel birds, or bearing contemptible names; nor with those that are dry, withered, covered in many leaves, or [like] skins (or armor).
A cemetery, a deserted dwelling, a crossroads, as well as that which is unpleasant, uneven, or perpetually saline,
and [places] filled with refuse, charcoal, potsherds, and ashes—
But a heap covered with husks or dry grass is not auspicious.
50.05ab. It is not auspicious when joined with those who have renounced the world, the naked, barbers, enemies, prisoners, butchers, and likewise dog-cookers; 50.05cd.
nor when joined with gamblers, ascetics, those who are oppressed, or sellers of weapons and *mādhvīka* wine.
The east, north, and northeast directions are praised for an inquirer, but not the northwest, south, southeast, southwest, or west; there is auspiciousness during the forenoon, but not at night.
50.06d For one who asks a question during the two twilights or in the afternoon.
Whatever auspicious or inauspicious omen has been declared regarding the rules for a journey should also be mentioned here;
whether it was seen before one’s eyes or brought by the people.
50.07d Then [the answer] stands upon the palm of the questioner's hand or on his garment.
50.08a Now, the limbs [of a man]: the thighs, lips, breasts, testicles, feet, and teeth;
50.08b the arms, hands, cheeks, hair, neck, nails, and also the thumbs;
50.08c together with the temples, armpits, shoulders, ears, anus, and joints—these are [the parts] in a man.
In a woman, the eyebrows, nose, buttocks, folds of skin, hips, and the collection of lines on the fingers [are auspicious].
The tongue, the neck, the two insteps, the pair of heels, the shanks, the navel, the earlobes, the nape of the neck,
the face, the back, the collarbones, the knees, and the ribs.
The heart, the palate, the eyes, the urinary organ, the chest, and the sacrum.
50.10ab/ Success may occur quickly with those called "neuter" (napuṃsaka), such as the head or the forehead, but with others designated by different names, it occurs after a long time.
50.10cd/ Success might occasionally arise through neuters, but never through those that are rough, wounded, broken, or emaciated among the aforementioned types.
50.11ab/ If the big toe is touched or even moved, there will be pain in the eyes;
50.11cd/ if it is the finger, there is grief for a daughter; if the head is struck, there is fear of the king.

50.12ab/ Separation [from one's own body] occurs when a rag is torn from one's chest; the taking away of a rag brings misfortune. 50.12cd/ The attainment of a beloved occurs for one who, having grasped a rag, asks while placing his feet upon [the other's] feet.
50.13ab. If she scratches the ground with her big toe while thinking of a field, 50.13cd.
or if she scratches her feet with her hand, she will have female slaves.

Upon seeing a palm leaf, birch bark, or a cloth, one should contemplate a garment; upon seeing hair, chaff, bone, or ashes, one should contemplate [impurity]. Upon observing a rope, a net, or a bark-garment, disease takes hold as a binding.

One should prescribe [a remedy] with long pepper (pippalī), black pepper (marica), dry ginger (śuṇṭhī), and water-lilies (vārida); with lodh tree (rodhra), costus (kuṣṭha), cloth (vasana), water-lilies (ambuja), and cumin (jīraka).
One should speak of it with spikenard (gandhamāṃsī) and dill (śatapuṣpā); for one who asks, one should consider it with tagara.

50.16ab/ When the [specified] signs are observed, there is the destruction of women, men, those afflicted by defects, all objects, the paths, sons, wealth, grain, and offspring; 50.16cd/ as well as the destruction of bipeds, quadrupeds, and the earth.
50.17ab/ By means of *nyagrodha*, *madhuka*, *tinduka*, *jambu*, *plakṣa*, mango, *badara*, and *jātīphala* fruits;
50.17cd/ And by means of wealth, gold, a man, iron, silk, silver, and *udumbara* wood, one also attains [the desired object].
A vessel filled with grain and a full water-jar bring about the increase of one's family;
however, the dung of elephants, cows, and dogs causes the destruction of wealth, young women, and friends.
50.19ab. One shall obtain cattle, elephants, buffaloes, lotuses, silver, and tigers when these are seen together.
50.19cd. One obtains a collection of sheep, wealth, clothing, sandalwood, silk garments, and ornaments.
50.20ab. Questions are posed by men upon seeing an elder, a śrāvaka, or a wandering mendicant.
50.20cd. [Questions] arise regarding friends, gambling, wealth, courtesans, kings, childbirth, and business matters.
50.21ab/ By Śākyas, preceptors, Arhats, Nirgranthas, those skilled in signs, merchants, and fishermen;
50.21cd/ And by thieves, army commanders, traders, female slaves, warriors, shopkeepers, and those condemned to death.
If an ascetic or a vintner is seen, the cattle-herding that was undertaken during one's absence will be lost;
if a hunter is seen, it will remain in the heart of the questioner; and if a gleaner is seen, there will be failure in the livelihood.

Anxiety arising from social associations, family life, and exertion, as well as from the pursuit of gain and power.
When she said, "Point it out," Jayādhvagā replied:
"Having examined my thought, speak;
[tell me] quickly that which is present in the midst of all people."
And the daughter of Bandhucora said, "Let it be seen."

50.25 When [the breath] is situated in an internal limb, one's own kin arise; when in an external limb, outsiders [arise]. By the movement [of the breath] in the big toe and the other toes, there will be male and female servants. In the shanks, there is a servant; from the navel, a sister; and in the heart, one's own wife.
"O son and daughter, when the touch is made by the collection of the thumb and fingers of the hand."
Having touched his mother on the belly, his teacher on the head, his arms on the right and left [to represent] his brother and his brother’s wife, one should thus identify the thief.
Furthermore, [one should avoid] from excessive bending of the limbs or from crushing them; or likewise, having observed a thief carrying away an empty vessel held by people;
or [anything that is] stolen, fallen, wounded, forgotten, ruined, broken, or gone.
One does not obtain what has been stolen from one who utters undesirable sounds such as "unmuṣita" and "mṛta."
All that which has been described— namely husks, bones, poison, and so forth—
causes death when taken together with clay by those afflicted by pain, along with tears and wounds.
Even upon touching a single part, the wind situated within would forcibly carry it away.
Having eaten an excessive amount of food at that time, one who remains satiated would say:
50.30ab/ From touching the forehead, [one sees] śūka; from seeing [the grain], śāli-rice.
50.30cd/ From touching the chest, food called ṣaṣṭika; and from touching the neck, barley-gruel (yāvaka).
50.31ab/ When touching the sides of the abdomen, the breasts, the belly, or the knees, [the signs are] mung beans, milk, and sesame gruel.
50.31cd/ Furthermore, when one tastes the lips or licks them, it should be known as the sweet taste.
When [the tongue is touched by] salt, it becomes parched; when by sour, the tongue throbs and the mouth contorts;
furthermore, when by pungent, astringent, or bitter-hot substances, one hiccups and spits.
50.33a If one hears something dry or bitter upon the discharge of phlegm, or sees it mixed with meat;
50.33b or if there is a sensation of touching the eyebrows, cheeks, or lips, that is an omen concerning birds (śākuna).
"It has been eaten by him"—this is what was said as the reason for this.
Having touched the head, throat, hair, jaw, temples, ears, shanks, and bladder,
one has eaten the flesh of an elephant, buffalo, ram, boar, cow, hare, deer, or rhinoceros.
50.35ab. Even when an inauspicious omen is seen or heard, one should say that lizard and fish meat has been eaten.
50.35cd. In such a manner should one determine the miscarriage of a fetus in a query.
When a male, female, or neuter [sign] is seen, inferred, situated before one, touched, or when there is the sight of drink, food, flowers, or fruit, birth occurs; and this is auspicious.
50.37a If, having touched the eyebrow, the belly, or a finger with the thumb, one asks about pregnancy, then there shall be such a thought regarding the fetus.
50.37b [If one touches] with honey, clarified butter, and the like, or with gold, gems, and coral...
Or [he may be defeated] by those standing at the front, or by his mother, his nurse, and his own sons.
If [the planet] is in the Karaga yoga in the seventh house, there will be a fetus in the womb; due to the influence of evil omens, that [fetus] may be miscarried.
If Pīṭha [is there], it draws out that womb.
50.38d And even when there is pressure or a wound on the hand.

50.39ab/ When the right nostril is touched, one should predict [the result] after one month; when the left, after two years. 50.39cd/ Similarly, when the ear is touched, it is after two months; and when the breast, after four months.
50.40a At the base of the braid, three sons and two daughters;
50.40b five sons in the ear and three in the hand;
50.40c and five in succession at the tip of the thumb.
On the big toe of the foot and on both heels, one obtains a daughter.
50.41ab/ When the touch occurs on the left or right thigh, two children—a daughter and a son—are born.
50.41cd/ When the middle of the forehead is touched, there will be four or three sons.
The head, forehead, eyebrows, ears, cheeks, jaw, teeth, throat,
the left and right shoulders, the two hands, the chin, and the neck.
The chest, the right breast and likewise the left, the heart, the sides, the belly, and the hips;
the buttocks, the anal junction, the pair of thighs, and the knees.
50.43d Then the calves and the feet [are assigned] to Kṛttikā and the following [nakṣatras].
Thus has been declared this clear mark of bodily contact for the attainment of one's desired goal, having thoroughly examined the treatises;
he who possesses vast intellect and noble mind understands all of this.
He is always honored by the people of the king's realm.
Chapter 51: On the Characteristics of Pustules (Piṭaka-lakṣaṇādhyāya) 51.01ab/ Those pustules which are white, red, yellow, and black, appearing respectively for the Brāhmaṇas and the other [castes],
51.01cd/ yield, in their respective order, the results as declared for those castes, but not for those born outside the [four] primary lineages.
51.02a Those lines on the head that are very glossy, distinct, and beautiful bring a mass of wealth; those arising from the forehead bring good fortune.
51.02b Those arising from the pair of eyebrows bring misfortune, while those arising from the space between them quickly bring union with beloved people and ill character.
51.02c Those arising from the middle of the brows bring sorrow, and those situated within the sockets of the eyes bring the sight of desired objects.
In the region of Śaṅkha, those who have gone forth into homelessness fall into tears at the places where they once stood; they dwell in anxiety, even in excessive anxiety.
51.03a Marks on the nose and cheeks bring clothing and sons; on the two lips, they grant the acquisition of food.

51.03b Likewise, those situated on the surface of the chin grant abundant wealth; on the forehead, 51.03c and similarly on the jaws, marks produce ornaments; on the throat, they produce food and drink.
In the ear, even the collection of the six elements is knowledge whose nature is the self.

51.04a If [the mark] is located on the head, the joints, the neck, the heart, the breasts, the sides, or the chest, it brings about death by iron weapons or death itself; 51.04b [if on other parts], there is the gain of sons and daughters, or even grief;
51.04c [if on the shoulder], there is the attainment of beloved ones, or else wandering repeatedly for the sake of alms.
51.04d Fires arising from dry grass bring about the destruction of wealth in many ways.
Those born on the back and the pair of upper arms bring about the destruction of the mass of suffering and enemies;
those born on the wrists bring about self-restraint; and those arising from the pair of forearms bring about ornaments and the like.
51.06a Those [lines] located on the fingers and the belly bring the acquisition of wealth, good fortune, and even grief;

51.06b On the navel, excellent drinks and food; below that, the seizure of wealth by thieves in this world; 51.06c Wealth and grain on the bladder; then a young woman on the penis; and sons and daughters [on the testicles].
Those born in the anus or the scrotum bestow wealth or good fortune.
51.07ab/ Through the thighs, there is the acquisition of vehicles and women; through the knees, injury from enemies.
51.07cd/ Through the shanks, there is injury by a weapon; through the ankles, they bestow the distress of travel and bondage.
