51.08ab/ Those born in the hips, the heels, or the feet [indicate] loss of wealth, sexual intercourse with forbidden women, and travel on the road.
51.08cd/ There is imprisonment in the collection of fingers and on the thumb, and honor from the circle of kinsmen.
51.09ab/ Eruptions, boils, and pustules on the right side, but injuries on the left, are auspicious for men; the reverse is true for women.
51.10 Thus has this classification of the [various] parts of the body been declared from head to foot;
the classification of wounds and moles (tilakas) should also be conceived in exactly the same way. The appearance of freckles, marks, and whirls (āvartas) occurs in that same manner.
It produces the results proclaimed for living beings while residing within their bodies.
52. On the Science of Architecture (Vāstuvidyā).

52.01ab: Now, therefore, this knowledge of architecture—which has come down through a succession of sages from the Lotus-born Brahmā—is being set forth by me for the pleasure of skilled astrologers. 52.01cd.
52.02ab. There was indeed some being that had come into existence, obstructing the two worlds (heaven and earth) with its body;
52.02cd. having been suddenly seized by the host of gods, it was cast down face downwards.
And wherever a deity was seized by whom, he remained presiding right there;
thus the Creator fashioned that "Man of the Site" (Vāstunara) consisting of immortal beings.
52.04ab/ The king’s palace should be one hundred and eight cubits in width;
52.04cd/ likewise, it should be five and a quarter cubits less than that in length.
52.05ab/ Sixty-four [units] for the quarters of the army commanders, each reduced by six;
52.05cd/ thus, five houses [in total], with the length increased by one-sixth [of the width].
52.06ab. Sixty minus four is the number of houses for the minister; five [houses].
52.06cd. The length for the king’s queens is that [number] increased by one-eighth of itself, or half of that.
52.07ab/ Thus, sixty-six [yojanas] each are allotted to the crown prince; eighty [yojanas] are for his younger siblings.
52.07cd/ And for those born after them, it is three-fifths [of that], five [yojanas], and half of that again.
52.08ab/ For feudatories, eminent men, and royal servants, [the conduct] is equal to that toward the king and his ministers.
52.08cd/ There is a distinction for the king and the crown prince, as well as for chamberlains, courtesans, and those skilled in the arts.
52.09ab/ For all superintendents and officials, [the punishment] is equal to that for misappropriating the treasury.
52.09cd/ For the crown prince, ministers, the superintendent of works, and envoys, it is half [of that].
52.10ab/ Forty decreased by four, four, and four, up to five;
52.10cd/ increased by one-sixth is the height for the astrologer, the domestic priest, and the physician.
52.11ab/ Whatever the width of the site, that indeed is the auspicious determination for the height. 52.11cd/ In houses consisting of a single hall, the length is twice the width.
The expansion for the four castes consists of thirty-two [verses], decreasing by four each time;
up to sixteen [years of age] is the limit, as those below that are exceedingly inferior.
52.13ab/ For Brahmins, the length [of the staff] is with a tenth part added; for Kṣatriyas, it is joined with an eighth part.
52.13cd/ For Vaiśyas, it is joined with a sixth part; for Śūdras, it is joined with a quarter.
52.14ab/ The treasury and the pleasure-palace should be situated at a distance equal to that between the king’s residence and the commander-in-chief’s quarters.
52.14cd/ The residences of the royal officers should be located at intervals corresponding to the difference in rank among the four classes of the army.
52.15ab. Now, for the Pāraśava and other [mixed-caste] classes, the house should be equal to half the sum of their own measurement and that of their father.
52.15cd. For all [classes], a dwelling that is smaller or larger than their own measurement brings inauspiciousness.
52.16ab/ For those in the animal stage of life, for grain, weapons, fire, pleasure, and houses, [the distance] is immeasurable.
52.16cd/ The authors of the treatises do not desire [a limit] beyond one hundred cubits.
When the total width of the commander-in-chief and the king is divided by seventy and then halved,
the hall is obtained by dividing by fourteen, and the portico by dividing by thirty-five.
52.18ab/ In [halls] beginning with thirty-two cubits, the halls increase by four, four, three, and three [cubits] respectively.
52.18cd/ They are increased by seventeen, twenty-three, fifteen, and thirteen finger-breadths [of the respective cubit].
52.19ab/ Three, three, two, two, and two finger-breadths [are the widths] of these [fingers] in order of their decrease;
52.19cd/ [the lengths are] nineteen, twenty, eighteen, and three [finger-breadths].
52.20ab/ A pathway equal to one-third of the hall should be made outside the building.
52.20cd/ If it is located in front [of the building], that site-plan is named Soṣṇīṣa.
52.21ab. "Supported by the side" means with a firm base, while "standing on the flank" refers to being situated at the side.
52.21cd. "Well-established" means [the posture] honored on all sides by those learned in the treatises; thus, all [of these] are esteemed.
The height of the house should be one-sixteenth of its width plus four cubits;
for all [stories], the height of each successive floor is reduced by one-twelfth.

52.23ab/ The wall of all dwellings shall be one-sixteenth part of the total width. 52.23cd/ This applies to those constructed with baked bricks; however, for those made of wood, there is no such fixed rule.
The width for both the king's gate and the gate of the army commander is seventy-one parts plus one-eleventh;
the height is equal to the number of finger-breadths [of the width], and the thickness is half that of the door.
52.25ab/ For the Brahmins and the other castes, one-fifth of the width [of the door] is eighteen finger-breadths;
52.25cd/ the width of the door is increased by one-eighth, and its height is three times that width.

The thickness [of the two arms] should be measured in finger-breadths (aṅgula) according to the number of cubits (ucchrāya-hasta) [of the image]. That same measurement, increased by one and a half, should be applied to both the two branches (śākhā) as well as to the two udumbara posts.
52.27ab/ The width of these [pillars] is one-eightieth of their height multiplied by seven. 52.27cd/ For a pillar, the width at the top is one-ninety-sixth of its height, diminished by one-tenth.
52.28ab. The *rucaka* is a regular square; the *vajra* has eight corners and is double [the size]; 52.28cd.
but with thirty-two [corners] merged into the middle, it is circular—thus it is called the *vṛtta*.
Having divided the pillar into nine parts, one part shall be the shaft (vahana), another part its capital (ghaṭa),
and one part each for the lotus (padma) and the upper lip (uttaroṣṭha).
The thickness of these scales, one above the other, is equal to their height;
for those scales that are not equal [in height], it is less by one-quarter for each successive scale.
52.31ab/ A site where the veranda is not obstructed on all sides is called *sarvatobhadra*.
52.31cd/ It should be constructed with four doors for kings and assemblies of gods.
52.32ab/ The Nandyāvarta [layout] consists of side-entrances (alinda) that run clockwise from the wall of the main hall (śālā).
52.32cd/ In this case, leaving aside the western door, the remaining [doors] should be constructed.
52.33ab/ The porch at the entrance, then another on the right, and then another auspicious one;
52.33cd/ and in that case of the *vardhamāna* [type], the door must not be made on the right.
Another [type of svastika] has its outer corner at the lintel (alinda), while the two others arise from the front corners;
another is held open up to that point with the entrance facing east— this [svastika] is auspicious.
The two side-wings (avalinda) at the front and rear are situated at the ends, with the remaining two fixed as the limit;
a door in the *rucaka* [corner] facing north is not auspicious, while other directions are praised.
The *nandyāvarta* is the best among all, as is that known as the *vardhamāna*;
the *svastika* and *rucaka* are middling, while the remaining types bring auspiciousness to kings and others.
A three-winged house (triśālaka) lacking the northern wing but having a golden center is auspicious;
a site devoid of the eastern wing is an excellent field that brings prosperity.

52.38ab. A three-hall house (triśālaka) lacking the southern wing is a cullī; it causes the destruction of wealth. 52.38cd. One lacking the western wing is a pakṣaghna; it causes the ruin of sons and engenders enmity.
52.39ab/ Siddhārtha is in the western half of the north-western corner; Yamasūrya is in the north-western corner of the western hall.
52.39cd/ That which is called Daṇḍa is in the north-eastern corner; that which is called Vāta is in the south-eastern corner.
52.40ab. If the *śālā* is in the east and the *gṛhacullī* in the west, and the *kāca* is in the south and the north;
52.40cd. there is the attainment of wealth when it is in the *siddhārtha* configuration, but the death of the householder occurs in the *yamasūrya* configuration.
In the Daṇḍa house, there is the infliction of punishment; in the one called Daṇḍākhya, there is always strife and agitation caused by wind.
In the Cullī house, there is loss of wealth; in Kāca, conflict with kinsmen is recorded.
52.42ab. In the division into eighty-one parts, there are ten lines each extending east-west and north-south.
52.42cd. At the center are thirteen gods, while thirty-two reside in the outer squares.
52.43ab/ Śikhin, Parjanya, Jayanta, Indra, Sūrya, Satya, Bhṛśa, and Antarikṣa;
52.43cd/ [These are] in order starting from the northeast (Aiśānī), with Anila in the southeast corner.
52.44ab/ Pūṣan, Vitatha, Bṛhatkṣatra, Yama, the one called Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛga;
52.44cd/ Pitṛ, Dauvārika, Sugrīva, Kusumadanta, Ambupati, and Asura.
52.45ab. Then Śoṣa, Pāpayakṣman, and the disease (Roga) are in the corner; then Ahi and Mukhya. 52.45cd. Then Bhallāṭa, Soma, and Bhujaga; then Aditi and Diti follow in order.
In the center, Brahmā is the lord of the nine squares; Aryaman is situated in the east.
From him, at every other square, proceeding clockwise, are Savitṛ and Vivasvat.
52.47ab/ Therefore, Vibudhādhipati, Mitra, and the other [named] Rājayaṣman; 52.47cd/ as well as Pṛthivīdhara and Apavatsa—these are at the periphery of Brahmā’s [altar].
52.48ab/ Āpa is in the northeast corner, and Sāvitra is in the southeast;
52.48cd/ Jaya is in the southwest, and Rudra is in the northwest, within the inner squares.
52.49ab/ Likewise, the Waters, Apavatsa, Parjanya, Agni, and Diti—this is one group.
52.49cd/ Thus, in each corner, there should be five deities occupying one square each.
The remaining external two-footed ones are declared to be twenty in number;
the other four remaining ones, beginning with Aryaman, are three-footed and are situated in the cardinal directions.
This Puruṣa has his head toward the northeast; he is face-downward, and on his head is the Fire-god.
Water is in his mouth, Āryaman is in his breast, and Apavatsa is in his chest.
52.52ab/ The external deities beginning with Parjanya are located on the eyes, ears, chest, and shoulders.
52.52cd/ The five beginning with Satya are on the arms, and Savitṛ and Sāvitra are on the hand.
Vitatha is joined with Bṛhatkṣatra at the sides; Vivasvat is situated in the belly;
and the thighs, knees, shanks, and buttocks are presided over by Yama and the others respectively.
These [deities] are situated on the right side in these very positions, and those on the left side are as follows:
Śakra and Jayanta are in the penis; Brahmā is in the heart; and the Father (Pitṛ) is located in the feet.
Alternatively, having laid out eight groups of eight squares and drawing diagonal lines across the corners,
Brahmā occupies four squares in this [mandala], while those situated in the corners of Brahmā occupy half a square each.

And there are eight half-padas in the outer corners; those situated on both sides of them are with a half [a quarter]. Those which remain from what has been mentioned are twenty, and they consist of two padas each.
52.57ab/ One should know that the junctions of the bamboo-segments and those parts of the feet which are level in the middle are the vital points; a wise man should not cause them pain.
52.58ab/ When these [planets] are afflicted by impure vessels, stakes, pillars, and so forth, as well as by thorns;
52.58cd/ they cause pain in a corresponding limb of the householder.

52.59ab/ If the master of the house scratches a limb while the offering to the immortals is being made, 52.59cd/ that omen will be inauspicious; or if there is a distortion of the fire, it is accompanied by a thorn (or danger).
52.60ab. In an image made of wood, there is loss of wealth; in one made of bone, injury to cattle and fears of disease.
[Two verses inserted by K.: 53.60cd. In one made of iron, there is fear of weapons; in those made of skulls or hair, there shall be death.]
If charcoal appears, one should predict fear of thieves; if ashes, one should always indicate fear of fire.
Indeed, a thorn situated in a vital spot is extremely inauspicious, unless it consists of gold or silver.
Whether it strikes a vital point or not, a mass of chaff obstructs the arrival of wealth;
even a peg, if situated in a vital spot, causes harm.
From Rogā one obtains Vāyu; from Pitṛ, Hutāśana; also from Vitatha, Śoṣasūtra;
from Mukhya, Bhṛśa; from Jayanta, Bhṛṅga; and from Aditi, Sugrīva.

52.62ab/ Those nine points where they converge are declared to be the "exceedingly vital" (atimarma) spots. 52.62cd/ And that which is one-eighth of a square (pada) is said to be the measurement of a vital point (marma).
The bamboo is as many finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in width as the number of feet and hands [of the image];
the measurement of the vein is specified as being one and a half times the width of the bamboo.

52.64ab/ Desiring happiness, a householder should diligently protect his *brahman* situated within the home. 52.64cd/ Because of defilements such as being touched by food-leavings, the master of the house suffers on account of that [inner *brahman*].
52.65ab. If the Vāstunara is deficient in the right arm, there is loss of wealth and faults regarding women.
52.65cd. If it is deficient in the left, there is loss of wealth and grain; if it is deficient in the head, he is deprived of all virtues.

52.66ab/ For those with defective feet, there are the faults of women, the death of sons, and even servitude; 52.66cd/ but for those dwelling in a man who is free from defects, there are happinesses endowed with honor and wealth.

52.67ab. In houses, cities, and villages, the gods are established everywhere in this manner. 52.67cd. And among them, the castes, beginning with the Brahmins, should dwell according to their respective suitability.
52.68ab. One should know that the dwelling-houses for the Brahmins and the others are situated toward the north and so forth.
And as they enter their abode, those very same [omens] appear on the right side.
52.69ab/ Divided by ninefold threads, or else by eightfold [threads], there are sixty-four gates; 52.69cd/ for those gates, beginning with Anala, this is the presentation of the results.
Fear of fire, birth of daughters, possession of abundant wealth, and being favored by the king;
furthermore, there is a tendency toward anger, untruthfulness, cruelty, and theft due to the influence of the eastern quarter.
52.71ab/ Few sons, servitude, low status, and an abundance of food, drink, and offspring;
52.71cd/ A fierce nature, ingratitude, poverty, and the destruction of one's son's virility result from the south.
52.72ab. Suffering for one's children, increase of enemies, and no acquisition of children or wealth; yet there is the attainment of the fruits of children and wealth.
52.72cd. Abundance of wealth, fear of the king, loss of wealth, and disease—so say others.
52.73ab. Death or imprisonment, the increase of enemies, the gain of children and wealth, and the perfection of all virtues;
52.73cd. the acquisition of sons and wealth, enmity with one's own son, faults regarding a wife, and destitution.

A door that is obstructed by a path, a tree, a corner, a well, a pillar, or a whirlpool brings inauspicious results. However, if one leaves behind ground measuring twice the height of the door, there is no fault.
A door that is struck by a carriage leads to ruin; one with a defect on the side of a young tree brings harm to children.
A door with mud on it portends grief, while one that leaks water is said to cause loss.
If struck by a deity, epilepsy occurs and there is destruction;
with a pillar, women's faults arise and the lineage is destroyed if it faces a Brāhmaṇa.
52.77ab/ If [the aperture] opens by itself, there is madness; if it is closed by itself, there is the destruction of the family.
52.77cd/ If it is too high, there is fear of the king; if it is too low, there is fear of bandits or indeed misfortune.
52.78ab/ That which is above the door of a door does not lead to welfare; that which is narrow brings fear of hunger.
52.78cd/ A door that is gaping leads to the destruction of the family, while one that is crooked brings about the ruin of the lineage.
52.79ab/ If it is excessively pressed down so as to cause pain, it will lead to ruin; if it is bent inward, there will be loss.
52.79cd/ If it is bent outward, there will be exile; if it is confused in its directions, there will be affliction by bandits.
52.80ab/ One should not connect the main entrance with other doors by means of architectural ornamentation (rūpa-ṛddhi).
52.80cd/ And one should adorn it with auspicious objects such as jars, fruits, leaves, and *pramatha* [deities].
52.81ab/ These are situated outside the house in the corners beginning with the northeast (aiśānī).
52.81cd/ They are Carakī, the one named Vidārī, Pūtanā, and the Rākṣasī.

52.82ab/ The defects of those who dwell in the corners of cities, houses, and villages [are as follows]: 52.82cd/ Outcastes such as dog-cookers and others of the lowest castes increase in number precisely in those places.

Trees born in the southern and other directions yield inauspicious results; however, these—namely the *plakṣa*, *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, and *aśvattha*—are praised when situated in the northern and other directions in a clockwise order.
52.84ab/ Thorny trees growing nearby portend danger from enemies; milky trees lead to the destruction of wealth.
52.84cd/ Fruit-bearing trees cause the decline of progeny; one should avoid even the wood of these [trees].
If he does not cut down those trees, he should plant others in their place that are worthy of honor:
the *punnāga*, *aśoka*, *ariṣṭa*, *bakula*, *panasa*, *śamī*, and *śāla*.
The earth, abounding with excellent medicinal herbs, trees, and creepers, sweet, fragrant, smooth, level, and free from hollows,
provides relief from fatigue even for men who have reached it while traveling on a road.
It bestows splendor; how much more so, then, in eternal dwellings?

52.87ab/ If it is in the house of a minister, there is loss of wealth; if near the house of a rogue, there is the death of a son. 52.87cd/ If it is in a temple, there is agitation; and if at a crossroads, there is infamy.
52.88ab/ In a place resembling a shrine (caitya), there is fear caused by planetary spirits; in one crowded with anthills and pits, there are calamities.
52.88cd/ In a depression (gartā), however, there is thirst; in a place shaped like a tortoise, there is the loss of wealth.
52.89ab/ For Brahmins and the other castes, a boat is desired to move from north to east by way of circumambulation.
52.89cd/ A Brahmin may reside anywhere; for the others, however, it is desired [to follow] according to their respective castes.

52.90ab/ Having dug a pit one cubit deep in the middle of the house and filled it back up again; 52.90cd/ if the pit is deficient, that is inauspicious; if level, it is neutral; if there is an excess, it is auspicious.

52.91ab/ Or, if after walking a hundred paces through a pit filled with water, one returns without having lost any [of the water], 52.91cd/ that is auspicious; and whatever sixty-four *āḍhakas* of water there may be [is likewise a sign].
52.92ab/ Or, when a lamp-wick is placed in an unbaked clay vessel set in a pit, it burns most intensely;
52.92cd/ whichever direction that flame points toward, that ground is auspicious for that particular caste.
A flower that does not wither even when left in a pit, remaining consistent with its own color, brings good fortune to him for whom it is intended;
and whatever [flower] delights the mind of a person, that becomes auspicious for him.
52.94ab/ White, red, yellow, and black ground is praised for the Brahmins and the other [castes].
52.94cd/ And its scent is like that of ghee, blood, food, or wine.
The earth, covered in sequence by kuśa grass, abundant śara reeds, dūrvā grass, and kāśa grass, increases prosperity according to the respective castes; it is sweet, astringent, sour, and pungent.

Having gone at the time prescribed by the astrologer to land that has been ploughed, where seeds have sprouted, which has been inhabited by cattle, and which is praised by Brahmins, the householder [should perform the rite].

Having performed the worship of the deities with various kinds of edible offerings, along with curd, unbroken grains, fragrant flowers, and incense, and having honored both the architects and the Brahmins;
52.98 A Brahmin, having touched his head and chest; a Kṣatriya, his thighs; and a Vaiśya, his shanks;
a Śūdra, having touched his feet, should draw a line at the commencement of building a house.
One should perform [the rite] with the thumb, or else with the middle finger or the index finger;
it is auspicious when performed with gold, gems, silver, pearls, or with fruits, flowers, and unbroken grains that yield superior results.
52.100ab/ By [the appearance of] a weapon, death by a weapon; by iron, imprisonment; by ashes, danger from fire;
52.100cd/ by grass, danger from thieves; and by a scratch with wood, danger from the king.

52.101ab/ A footprint that is crooked, drawn with the sole of the foot, deformed, or made with leather, charcoal, or bone brings fear of enemies and suffering. 52.101cd/ One made with a tooth portends misfortune for the husband [or the maker].
52.102ab/ Enmity is indicated by writing in a counter-clockwise direction; prosperity is to be declared by writing in a clockwise direction.
52.102cd/ Harsh speech, spitting, and sneezing are said to be inauspicious.
52.103ab/ When entering a house that has been half-built or completed, the architect should observe the omens;
the householder, standing there, should observe where [the builder] touches and which limb he touches.
52.104ab/ If, when the sun is blazing, a bird at that time cries out with a harsh sound,
52.104cd/ a bone corresponding to the touched limb should be indicated in that place.
Furthermore, at the time of the omen, other animals such as elephants, horses, and dogs may howl;
the bone produced then must be understood as originating from that very limb [of the animal] from which the sound arose.

52.106ab/ When the cord is being stretched out, a braying like that of a donkey indicates a splinter of bone. 52.106cd/ Or, if the cord is leaped over by a dog or a jackal, a splinter is to be indicated.
When a bird utters a sweet cry in a peaceful direction, then it should be declared that there is wealth in that place,
or in the body part presided over by the lord of the house.
52.108ab/ If the measuring cord is severed, death occurs; if the peg is turned downward, a great illness [occurs].
52.108cd/ If the traditional rules regarding the master of the house and the architect are forgotten, death is to be predicted.

52.109ab/ When [the water] falls from the shoulder, there is a headache; when the jar is discarded, there is a calamity for the family. 52.109cd/ If it is broken, there is the death of a worker; if it falls from the hand, there is the death of the householder.
52.110ab/ Having performed worship in the southeast corner, one should first set down the stone. 52.110cd/ The remaining stones and the pillars should likewise be raised in a clockwise direction.
Adorned with an umbrella, garlands, and garments, and having been treated with incense and ointments, it should be raised up;
likewise, a pillar should be erected at the gateway with great effort.
52.112ab/ Likewise, when birds and other creatures are crouching, trembling, falling, or remaining ill-at-ease, [the result is as follows].
52.112cd/ That very same result is declared to be similar to Indra’s banner; and in that case, it is auspicious.
52.113ab/ If [the wind] rises from the northeast, there is loss of wealth and sons, and the death of a son; if it is foul-smelling, there is destruction of kinsmen.
52.113cd/ If it is crooked, there is the ruin of relatives; and if the wind is obscured by the day, there are no pregnancies.
If one desires the expansion of the house, one should then cause it to increase equally on all sides;
otherwise, there will be a defect in one particular direction, so one should instead build first toward the east or the north.
52.115ab/ If [the omen occurs] in the east, there is enmity with friends; if in the south, fear of death, or perhaps prosperity.
52.115cd/ In the west, there is loss of wealth; in the north, increase or mental anguish.
52.116ab/ A temple should be in the northeast, and the kitchen should be in the southeast if it is to be built.
52.116cd/ Utensils and equipment should be in the southwest, and wealth and grain in the northwest.

52.117ab/ When the water [element] is situated in the east and other directions, there is loss of sons, fear of fire, and fear of enemies; 52.117cd/ [respectively], quarrels with women, female wickedness, poverty, and the increase of wealth and offspring.

One should cut down trees that are situated in bird nests, on ruined sites, in dried-up places, in burnt-out temples, or in cremation grounds; and one should avoid cutting those that are milk-exuding trees, *dhava*, *vibhītaka*, *nimba*, or *araṇi* trees.

Having performed offerings and worship at night, one should fell the tree during the day while circumambulating it clockwise. A tree that falls toward the north or the east is auspicious; one that falls in any other direction must not be accepted.
52.120ab/ If the cut is without change, then that wood is auspicious for use in a house.
52.120cd/ But if the circle is yellow, one should indicate a lizard residing within the tree.
52.121ab/ A frog appears when it has the luster of madder; a snake when it is blue; and likewise a chameleon when it is reddish.
52.121cd/ A stone appears when it has the luster of a mung bean; a mouse when it is tawny; and water when it has the luster of a rhinoceros horn.

52.122ab/ One desiring prosperity should not sleep upon grain, cattle, a teacher, fire, or images of the gods, nor along the length of a beam. 52.122cd/ Nor should one sleep with the head toward the north or west, nor naked, nor indeed with wet feet.

He should enter his home, which is strewn with abundant flowers, adorned with archways, beautified by water-filled jars, where the gods are worshipped with incense, perfumes, and offerings, and which resounds with the chanting of Brahmins.
Chapter 53: On the Water-Barrier (Dakārgala) 53.01ab. Therefore, I shall now describe the "Water-Barrier" (dakārgala), which is righteous and conducive to fame, by means of which water is obtained.
53.01cd. Just as there are veins (śirās) within the limbs of men, so too are they situated upon the earth, both elevated and depressed.
53.02ab/ Water fallen from the sky, though originally uniform in color and taste, acquires various tastes and many colors due to its contact with the specific qualities of the earth.
53.02cd/ Having observed that it has thus attained a state of diverse flavors and manifold hues, it should be examined as being exactly like the earth.
53.03ab/ Puruhūta, Anala, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Pavana, Indu, and Śaṅkara are the gods;
53.03cd/ they are to be known as the lords of the directions, starting from the East, in their respective order.
The ninth vein in the center is known as the Lord of the Directions (Dikpati) and is named Mahāśirā;
from these, hundreds of others have issued forth, renowned by their various names.
53.05ab/ Those veins which rise upward from the netherworld (pātāla) and those situated in the four cardinal directions are auspicious;
those arising from the intermediate directions are not auspicious. Therefore, I shall describe the signs of the veins.
53.06ab/ Or, if there is a reed (vetasa) tree in a place devoid of water at a distance of three cubits [from the bank],
then at a depth of one and a half men (puruṣa) behind it, a western vein carries water there.
53.07ab/ Furthermore, at a distance of half a man's height, there is a pale frog as a sign, and then yellow earth.
53.07cd/ And in that place there is a "split-bowl" stone, and water lies beneath it.
53.08ab/ To the north of the Jambu tree, at a depth of three cubits, there is a vein in two directions toward the east;
it smells of earth and iron, is pale in color, and here, within a man's length, is a frog.
53.09ab/ If an anthill should be situated nearby to the east of a Jambū tree,
53.09cd/ then there is sweet water at a distance of two *puruṣas* on its southern side.
53.10ab/ And there is a fish half the size of a man, as well as a stone resembling a pigeon;
53.10cd/ and the earth here becomes blue, and for a long time there is abundant water.
53.11ab. Behind the Udumbara tree, at a distance of exactly three cubits from two men and a half;
53.11cd. there, in a man’s length, is a white snake resembling black collyrium, with its head downward, which yields excellent water.
53.12ab/ If an anthill is visible to the north of an Arjuna tree, then from that Arjuna tree,
at a distance of three and a half *puruṣas* measured in cubits, there is water to the west.
53.13ab/ White earth indicates a lizard; greyish-brown earth, a half-human being; then black earth;
53.13cd/ yellow, white, and sandy earth follow; thereafter, one should predict immeasurable water.

53.14ab/ To the south of a Nirguṇḍī tree that has been covered by an anthill, at a distance of two and a quarter puruṣas, there is sweet water that will not dry up, as indicated by the hands. 53.14cd/ [As indicated] by the hands. At a distance of two and a quarter *puruṣas* to the south of a *nirguṇḍī* tree that has been built up by an anthill, there is sweet water that does not dry up, as indicated by the hands.
53.15ab/ Then there is the Rohita fish, then half-human, then dead earth, then tawny, and beyond that pale;
53.15cd/ then sand with gravel, and further on in sequence, the water appears.
If an anthill is seen to the east of a Badarī tree, there will be water to the west;
it should be indicated by three men at a distance of half a man's height [from the base], where a white house-lizard is present.

53.17ab/ If there is a *badarī* tree with leaves in the western direction, then water is present. 53.17cd/ At a distance of three and one-quarter *puruṣas*, and at a further *puruṣa* from there, the *duṇḍubha* [frog] is the sign.

53.18ab. Leaving three cubits to the south of the junction of the Vilva and Udumbara [rivers], there is water at a distance of three men’s lengths. 53.18cd. At half a man’s length further, it is black, and at that point there is a frog.
53.19ab/ If an anthill is seen at a *kākodumbarikā* tree, there is a water vein there.
53.19cd/ It flows toward the western direction at a distance of three and a quarter men's lengths.
53.20ab. The earth becomes pale-yellow, and the stone takes on the color of cow's milk.
53.20cd. Within half a man’s height, a mouse resembling a water-lily comes into the range of vision.
When a *kampillaka* tree is visible in a region devoid of water,
a vein flows three cubits toward the east, first heading south.
In that [region], the earth appears the color of a blue lotus or pigeon-grey;
there is the ajagandhaka fish in the hand, and the milk is scanty and alkaline.
53.23ab. To the north-west of the Śoṇāka tree, crossing two cubits, there is a vein named Kumudā. 53.23cd. That vein carries water for three men.
53.24ab/ If an anthill is situated on the right side of a Vibhītaka tree,
53.24cd/ then a water vein should be known to exist at a distance of one and a half man-lengths in the eastern direction from it.
If there is an anthill at a distance of one cubit to the west of that very [spot],
there a vein flows toward the north at a depth of four and a half *puruṣas*.

In the first year, the stone is white and called Viśvambharaka; however, in the second year, it becomes the color of saffron. And in the third year having passed, the vein in the western direction disappears.
53.27ab. Where there is a white ant-hill with *sakuśa* grass to the northeast of a *kovidāra* tree; 53.27cd.
in the middle between those two, at a distance of four and a half *nara*s, is water that cannot be disturbed.
In the first [type of] person, there is a snake resembling the interior of a lotus and red earth;
a kuruvinda stone—these are the marks to be described.
53.29ab/ If there is a saptaparṇa tree covered by an anthill, water is to be declared to the north of it. 53.29cd/ This too must be stated by five men, and here also there are signs.
53.30ab. At Puruṣārtha, there is a green frog and the earth resembles yellow orpiment (haritāla).
53.30cd. The stone resembles a cloud, and the vein is gentle, carrying auspicious water.
When a frog is visible standing beneath all the trees,
from that point the water is at a depth of four and a half *puruṣas*.
In the *puruṣa* [stone], however, there occurs a *nakula* [stone], a blue one, then a yellowish earth-like one, and then a white one;
furthermore, a stone resembling a frog is seen therein.
53.33ab/ If a snake’s lair is seen situated to the south of a *karañja* tree;
53.33cd/ then at two cubits to the south, there is a vein at a depth of three and a half men.
53.34ab. In the eastern half of the tortoise, the first vein that emerges is the Pūrvā;
53.34cd. another is Udak, yielding sweet water; and below the Harita stone, there is water.
To the north of the Madhūka tree is the abode of a snake, and to the west of the tree is water;
having avoided five cubits [and] seven and a half fathoms from the first [tree].
In this region, the Ahirāja is the man; the Dhātrī is smoky-colored, and the stone is the color of kuluttha (horse-gram).
The Māhendrī vein always carries water together with foam.
If there is a moist anthill to the south of a *tilaka* tree, accompanied by *kuśa* grass and *dūrvā*, water is found with five men in the western direction; the vein flows toward the east.
53.38ab/ When there is a serpent’s abode behind the Kadamba tree, with water to the south; 53.38cd/ at a distance of three cubits from there, measured by six men minus a quarter.
53.39ab/ And here the Kauberī vein flows with water that has the smell of iron and is unshakeable.
53.39cd/ A frog resembling gold is found there, and the earth is yellow, reaching the height of a man.
If a palm tree or a coconut tree is covered by an anthill,
then six cubits to the west and four cubits to the north of it, there is a southern water vein.
53.41ab. If there is a serpent’s lair to the south of a wood-apple tree, water is to be predicted to the north.
53.41cd. Having bypassed seven cubits and dug down five men-deep, one finds water.
53.42ab. A variegated snake, a black corpse, and even a stone that splits a city;
53.42cd. White earth to the west, and from there the vein proceeds to the north.
53.43ab/ To the left of an *aśmantaka* tree, either a jujube tree (*badarī*) or the dwelling of a snake is seen.
53.43cd/ At a distance of six cubits from it and at a depth of three and a half men, there is water.
53.44ab/ In the first man’s depth, there is a tortoise; [in the second] a grey stone; and [in the third] sandy earth.
53.44cd/ First, the vein is in the south, and the second is in the northeast.
53.45ab/ If there is an anthill to the left of a turmeric tree, there will be water to the east; [K: if it is there, then there is water].
53.45cd/ It occurs at a distance of five and one-third cubits measured by men.
53.46ab/ The earth is dark blue with serpents, and the stone is yellow like an emerald;
53.46cd/ the ground is black, and first there is a Vāruṇī vein, while another is to the south.
53.47ab/ If signs of marshy ground are seen in a region devoid of water;
53.47cd/ where there is vīraṇa grass, dūrvā grass, and soft soil—in that place there is water at a man’s depth.
Bhārṅgī, trivṛtā, dantī, sūkarapādī, and lakṣmaṇā, as well as navamālikā; [these grow] at a distance of two cubits in the north and three men's lengths in the south from the water.
53.49ab/ Trees that are glossy with drooping branches, though they may be stunted or deformed, indicate nearby water.
53.49cd/ Those that are hollow, have withered leaves, and are rough are devoid of water.
53.50ab/ Tilaka, āmrātaka, varuṇaka, bhallātaka, bilva, tinduka, and aṅkola; 53.50cd/ piṇḍāra, śirīṣa, añjana, parūṣaka, vañjula, and atibalā.
53.51ab/ If these [signs] are very glossy and surrounded by anthills, then there is water / 53.51cd/ three cubits to the north, at a depth of four and a half men [or fathoms].
53.52ab/ Where the earth is grassy where it should be grassless, and grassless where it should be grassy; 53.52cd/ there a vein is indicated, or else one must declare that there is treasure therein.
53.53ab/ When there is a reversal between thorny and non-thorny [trees], water is three cubits behind;
53.53cd/ having dug down three men’s depth plus one-third, there will be wealth.
53.54ab/ When the earth, struck by his foot, resounds deeply, there is water in that place.
53.54cd/ At a distance of three and a half *manuṣya*s from there, there will be a northern vein (*śirā*).
53.55ab/ If a single branch of a tree is bent downward or becomes pale, 53.55cd/ it should be understood that there is water beneath that branch at a depth of three *puruṣas* after digging.
53.56ab/ Where there is a transformation of fruit and flower, at that [point] three cubits above are veins;
53.56cd/ with four men [measuring down], there is stone, and below that, yellow earth.
53.57ab/ If the Kaṇṭakārikā is seen without thorns but with white flowers, 53.57cd/ water is to be predicted beneath it at a depth of three men and half a man.
53.58ab/ Where there may be a double-headed date-palm tree in a region devoid of water,
53.58cd/ one should indicate that water is to be found at its western side, at a distance of three men's [lengths].
53.59ab. If there should be a *karṇikāra* tree with white flowers, or a *palāśa* tree; 53.59cd. then water is found at two *puruṣas* to the left, or at three *puruṣas*.
53.60ab/ Wherever there is heat or smoke in the soil, there water is found at a depth of two men’s height.
53.60cd/ And a vein should be indicated by a great flow of water.
In whatever region of a field the grain that has grown goes to destruction—
whether it be overly glossy or excessively pale— a great river exists there in that pair of human [signs].
Just as veins exist in the Maru desert, so shall I hereafter describe them;
the veins situated within the earth-like body of elephants proceed like those in the necks of young camels.
If there is an anthill to the northeast of a *pīlu* tree, water will be found to the west;
the vein should be known to flow northward at a depth of five men's height.

53.64ab. At first there is the sign of a frog; after that, from the brown earth (mṛtkapilā), there shall be yellowish soil (dharitā). 53.64cd. And below the man [in the diagram], there is a stone; beneath that, water (ambhas) is to be indicated.
53.65ab. To the east of that very *pīlu* tree, there is an anthill;
from there, at a distance of four and a half cubits, water is to be declared in the southern direction at a depth of seven men.
In the first man, the snake is white and black, its form being the size of a cubit;
on the right side, it carries a large quantity of alkaline water.
To the north of the *karīra* tree, there is a snake’s lair; to the south of it, there is sweet water.
It should be known to be ten *puruṣas* away, and a frog is found here when one has drunk at this spot.
53.68ab/ If there is a dwelling of snakes behind the Rohītaka tree at a distance of three cubits to the south;
53.68cd/ having dug twelve men’s depths, there is a vein containing salt to the west.
53.69ab/ To the east of the Indra tree, an anthill is visible; to the west, a vein at the distance of one cubit.
53.69cd/ Having dug fourteen men [deep], a tawny-colored lizard is found in the first man.
Or, if there should be a house for serpents to the left of the tree named Suvarṇa,
then at a distance of two cubits to the south, at the end of fifteen men, there is water.
53.71ab/ Here, the soil is alkaline, there is a mongoose, and at half-man's height, there is a stone resembling copper.
53.71cd/ The earth becomes red, and a vein flows there toward the south.
If a jujube tree and a *rohitaka* tree grow joined together even without an anthill,
there will be water at a distance of three cubits behind them, at a depth of sixteen *manus*.
In the first case, the water is flavorful and flows from the right side; in the other, it flows from the left when the vessel is turned face up.
The stone resembles flour, the earth is white, and there is a scorpion with half a human body.
If there is a jujube tree (*badarī*) with its trunk at three cubits from the west, there is water there;
and in the northeast, at a distance of eighteen men, there is a vein of abundant water.
In the eastern direction, at a distance of three cubits, there is a jujube tree accompanied by a pilu tree.
53.75cd/ Here, the water is alkaline and cannot be exhausted even by twenty men.
Where a *kakubha* and a *karīra* are joined together in one place, or a *kakubha* and a *vilva*,
if water is reached by men after twenty-five cubits, [it indicates a treasure].
When there is dūrvā grass and pale kuśa grass upon the top of an anthill, a well should be dug in the center; water will be found here at a depth of twenty-one men.

53.78ab/ Where earth is seen joined with *kadambaka* plants and where *dūrvā* grass appears upon an anthill; 53.78cd/ at two cubits (*hasta*) to the south of that, water is found by men at a depth of twenty-five [cubits].
When there is a Rohītaka tree in the midst of three anthills,
accompanied by various other trees, water should be declared to be there.
53.80ab/ From the center of the four cubits, sixteen finger-breadths to the north is water.
53.80cd/ Having dug forty men’s lengths, a stone is found below, and beneath that, a vein [of water].
53.81ab/ Where there is a śamī tree abounding in knots to the north of an anthill,
53.81cd/ at a distance of five cubits to the west, water is found by men numbering fifty.
When five anthills are situated in one place and the middle one is white,
a vein is indicated there at a depth of fifty-five men's heights.
Where there is a *śamī* tree with its leaves intact on the western side, at a distance of sixty human paces there is water;
at half that distance there is a snake, first sand, and beyond that yellow earth.
Wherever there may be a white Rohītaka tree surrounded by an anthill,
at a distance of one cubit to the east, there is water at a depth of seventy human hands.
Where there is a white *śamī* tree abounding in thorns to the south, there is water;
[the depth is indicated] by seventy [units] plus five men, and the snake is at half a man's height.
53.86ab/ Wherever there is a sign in the Maru region that is not found in the Jāṅgala region, by those [signs] water is to be indicated.
53.86cd/ Those men who are preceded by the Jambu and Vetasa trees are twice as many in the Maru desert.
53.87ab/ Jambū, trivṛtā, maurvī, śiśumārī, sārivā, śivā, and śyāmā;
53.87cd/ these are the creepers (vīrudha), along with vārāhī, jyotiṣmatī, and garuḍavegā.
If, at the abode of a snake, there are *sūkarikā*, *māṣaparṇī*, and *vyāghrapadā* plants,
then three cubits to the north of the anthill, water is found at a depth of three men's height.
53.89ab. This [calculation] should be stated for marshy lands; however, in a desert region (*jāṅgalabhūmi*), it should be stated by means of five men.
53.89cd. By these very same signs, one should declare it in a desert (*marudeśa*) by means of seven.
53.90ab/ Where the earth appears uniform, being devoid of grass, trees, anthills, and shrubs;
53.90cd/ where a change occurs in that ground, there is water there.
Where the ground is smooth, low-lying, sandy, and resonant,
there the water is at a depth of four and a half *mānas*, or perhaps five *mānas*.
53.92ab. In the south, there is abundant water with four men who are very affectionate.
53.92cd. For even in a dense thicket of trees, one should speak in the same way regarding anyone who is deformed.
Where the earth inclines toward a man together with his half [of the field], it is watered by both irrigated (jāṅgala) and marshy (anūpa) waters;
or where there are many insects even without a dwelling, there too is water.
The earth may be hot or cold, or it may have cold and hot water; [these signs appear] at three and a half cubits [from the sun].
A rainbow, a fish, or an anthill [is seen] at four cubits.
If, in a line of anthills, one is particularly elevated, there is a water vein beneath it;
and where the crops wither or fail to grow, there too is water.
53.96ab/ When the three—nyagrodha, palāśa, and udumbara—are found together, there is water beneath them.
53.96cd/ Likewise, when vaṭa and pippala are in conjunction, one should declare that a vein of water is present.
53.97ab/ If there should be a well in the south-eastern corner of a village or a city, 53.97cd/ it constantly causes fear and, for the most part, brings about fire accompanied by human affliction.
In the southwest corner there is the destruction of children, and in the northwest there is danger to women;
having avoided these three directions, wells situated in the remaining directions bring about auspiciousness.
Having observed that *Dakārgala* which was composed by the sage Sārasvata,
I shall now set forth the *Mānavaka*, composed in Āryā verses as well as in other meters.
53.100 Since the trees, shrubs, and creepers are glossy and their leaves are without gaps, there is water nearby;
there are lotuses, kṣura-grass, uśīra, and guṇḍrā growing in clusters.
53.100d Whether they be kāśa or kuśa grasses, or nalikā or nala reeds.
There may be date palms, rose-apples, arjunas, and reeds;
or trees, shrubs, and creepers laden with milky sap; or parasol trees, elephants, nagas, lotuses, and nipa trees.
And there should be *naktamāla* trees together with *sinduvāra*.
53.102a Either the *vibhītaka* or the *madayantikā* [is present];
in that place where these three persons are, there is water.
53.102c If there is another mountain upon a mountain, [there too is water].
Even there, at the root, water is found at a depth of three men.
Where the earth is mixed with muñja-grass fibers, kāśa, and kuśa grass, and is dark blue, soft, and gravelly,
there the water is abundant and of excellent taste.
53.103d Or where the earth is black or red.
When the earth is copper-colored and contains grit, it produces astringent and alkaline soil;
when it is tawny, it produces salt;
and when it is pale white, salt is likewise indicated.
Pure milk [is obtained] from the blue earth.
The *śāka*, *aśvakarṇa*, *arjuna*, *bilva*, and *sarja* trees;
the *śrīparṇī*, *ariṣṭa*, *dhava*, and *śiṃśapā* trees;
and trees, shrubs, and creepers with perforated leaves.
And those that are rough indicate water to be far away.
53.106a That earth which has the color of the sun, fire, ashes, camels, or donkeys is declared to be waterless.
53.106b Red sprouts accompanied by milky sap [indicate] Karīra trees.
If the earth is red, there will be water beneath the stones.
53.107a Having the luster of lapis lazuli, mung beans, or a dark cloud;
53.107b or resembling a ripe udumbara fruit; 53.107c or having the hue of a bumblebee or collyrium, or which is tawny.
The stone should be known as one whose water is near to it in abundance.
53.108a That which resembles a pigeon, honey, or ghee;
53.108b which has a color equal to that of linen cloth;
53.108c and which is identical in form to the Soma creeper—
And she too quickly makes the water inexhaustible.
53.109a Endowed with copper-colored spots that are variegated,
53.109b resembling pale ash, camels, or donkeys;
53.109c or having a thumb-like mark or a flower-like mark resembling a bumblebee.
And the stone that has the color of the sun or fire is without water.
Those which have the appearance of moonlight, crystal, pearl, or gold; those with the luster of sapphire, vermilion, or collyrium;
and those that resemble the rays of the rising sun or yellow orpiment—these are the [omens].
53.110d These are auspicious, for this is the conduct of sages in this matter.
For these rocks are indeed indivisible and auspicious, always frequented by yakṣas and nāgas;
and in the kingdoms of those kings where they are found—
For them, there shall never be a lack of rain.
When a stone does not break, then,
having kindled a fire with *palāśa* wood and *tinduka* wood until it becomes the color of fire, [one should proceed].
Sprinkled with ambrosial water, it undergoes blossoming.
Water boiled with the ashes of the *mokṣaka* tree,
or that which has been sprinkled seven times over,
should be used together with the alkali of reeds for the treatment of a stone.
53.113d Blowing [on it] after it has been heated by fire.
Buttermilk,
sour gruel, and liquor, along with horse gram and jujube fruits, having been placed together in that [vessel] and heated for seven nights, [are ready].
For they indeed split a stone with sprinklings of water.
53.115a Neem leaves and bark, the stalks of sesame, along with apāmārga, tinduka, and guḍūcī— 53.115c an alkali prepared from these by boiling them in cow’s urine [is used].
53.115d Thus, when heated six times, the stone is split.
Milk of the *arka* plant mixed with the soot from a rhinoceros horn, combined with the dung of a pigeon and a rat, constitutes a medicinal paste; then,
one should drink oil churned from this [paste] using a chisel.
53.116d Thereafter, there shall be no obstruction for one sharpened upon stones.
An iron object that has been soaked for a day in an alkaline solution of plantain mixed with churned buttermilk, and then thoroughly quenched in water,
does not break when struck against a stone.
And even among other metals, there is no dullness for it.
53.118 A bank extending from east to west retains its water for a very long time,
whereas one extending from south to north generally suffers a breach due to waves driven by the wind.
If one desires to protect that [latter bank] from the impact of the waters, one should do so with strong timber.
Or it may be crushed by elephants, horses, and the like, or even by stones and other such things, as they pile up.
Its banks were covered with *kakubha*, *vaṭa*, mango, *plakṣa*, and *kadamba* trees, along with *nicula*, rose-apple, cane, and *nīpa*;
it was further adorned with *kurabaka*, palm, *aśoka*, and *madhūka* trees, interspersed with *bakula*.
And an exit gate should be constructed in one part, with a water channel lined with stone;
its door should be set within a treasury-chamber, fitted without any gaps.
Having done that, he should then cover it over with dust.
53.121ab/ A formulation consisting of añjana, mustā, uśīra, along with the powders of rājakośātakī and āmalaka, 53.121cd/ combined with the fruit of the kataka, should be placed into the well.
If water should become turbid, pungent, salty, or tasteless, or even if it should have an unpleasant odor,
it becomes pure and delicious through this [practice].
It is very fragrant and endowed with other excellent qualities.
53.123ab/ Hasta, Maghā, Anurādhā, Puṣya, Dhaniṣṭhā, the Uttarās, Rohiṇī,
and Śatabhiṣaj— this group of lunar mansions is recommended for the commencement of wells.
Having offered an oblation to Varuṇa, one should place a peg made of *vaṭa* or *vetasa* wood at the location of the vein;
after worshipping it with flowers, perfumes, and incense, one should install it first.
[Having observed the opinions of Baladeva and others, which go beyond Jyotiṣmatī, I have first proclaimed this Meghodbhava;
and this second [work], the Bhaumadaśārgala, has been correctly expounded by Varāhamihira through the grace of the Sage.
54. Chapter on the Ayurveda of Trees.
54.01ab/ Water reservoirs that are devoid of shade at their edges are not pleasing;
therefore, one should establish groves along the edges of the water.
54.02ab/ Soft soil is beneficial for all trees; one should sow sesame seeds therein.
54.02cd/ When they have flowered, one should crush them; this is the first rite regarding the earth.
54.03ab/ Ariṣṭa, aśoka, punnāga, śirīṣa, and priyaṅgu—
these auspicious trees should first be planted in a grove or within the houses.
54.04ab/ The jackfruit, the *aśoka*, the plantain, the rose-apple, the *lakuca*, and the pomegranate; 54.04cd/ as well as the grape, the *pālīvata*, the citron, and the *atimuktaka*.

54.05ab/ These trees, having been smeared with cow dung, are to be planted from the trunk (kāṇḍa). 54.05cd/ Alternatively, they may be planted at the root or at the stem, provided one exerts great effort thereafter.

One should plant those that have not yet sprouted during the cool season (śiśira), those that have already sprouted at the onset of winter, and those with well-formed trunks at the arrival of the rains, each according to its proper direction.
54.07ab/ By means of ghee, uśīra, sesame, honey, viḍaṅga, milk, and cow dung,
54.07cd/ [trees] smeared from the roots to the trunk undergo the healing of transference and the curing of sores.
Having become pure and having performed worship of the tree with baths and ointments, one should plant it; and once planted, it grows by means of those very same leaves.

54.09ab/ At evening and at dawn during the hot season [or at the end of summer], and every other day during the cold season; 54.09cd/ and during the rainy season when the earth is dry, trees that have been planted should be watered.
54.10ab/ Jambu, vetasa, vānīra, kadamba, udumbara, and arjuna;
54.10cd/ Bījapūraka, mṛdvīkā, lakuca, and pomegranates [grow there].
The *vañjula*, *naktamāla*, *tilaka*, *panasa*,
as well as the *timira* and *āmra-taka*— these sixteen are recorded as belonging to the marshy (*anūpa*) region.
The best [distance] is twenty cubits, the middling sixteen;
the distance from one spot to another for trees should be at least twelve [cubits].
54.13ab/ Trees that have grown through mutual contact and touch one another,
54.13cd/ do not yield fruit properly when they are oppressed by their intertwined roots.
54.14ab/ From cold, wind, and heat, disease arises, and the leaves turn pale;
54.14cd/ there is no growth of new shoots, the branches wither, and the sap flows away.
54.15ab. Now, the medical treatment for these begins with purification by means of a surgical instrument.
54.15cd. One should sprinkle them with milk-water mixed with a paste of *viḍaṅga* and clarified butter.

54.16ab/ When there is a failure of fruit, one should sprinkle with water boiled and then cooled with *kulattha*, *māṣa*, *mudga*, sesame, and barley; this leads to an abundance of fruits and flowers.
54.17ab/ Two āḍhakas of the powder of the dung of sheep and goats, one āḍhaka of sesame seeds;
54.17cd/ One prastha of parched grain flour, one droṇa of water, together with a tulā of beef.

54.18ab/ After these have been kept for seven nights, a sprinkling should be performed upon the great tree; 54.18cd/ as well as upon anthills, shrubs, and creepers, always for the sake of fruit and flowers.
The seed, soaked in milk for ten days,
joined with clarified butter in the hand,
and repeatedly dried by means of cow-dung;
And it was perfumed with the flesh of krauñca birds, deer, and peacocks.
When applied to prepared ground and combined with meat, fish,
and hog’s fat, and then sprinkled with water mixed with milk, that [ground] indeed becomes covered with flowers.
54.21ab. Even with the powder and groats of rice, mung beans, and sesame, she makes a vine of tamarind;
54.21cd. and when sprinkled with putrid meat and constantly fumigated with turmeric, it becomes [a source of] delight.
54.22a For the purpose of preparing a *kapittha* creeper, the roots of *āsphota*, *dhātrī*, *dhava*, and *vāsikā* [are used]; 54.22c as well as those of *palāśinī*, *vetasa*, and *sūryaballī*.
Together with *śyāmā*, *atimuktā*, and *aṣṭamūlī*.
When the milk has been boiled and well-cooled,
one hundred *tāla* stalks and a *kapittha* seed should be placed [in it]; these should be dried day by day by the rays of the sun.
This is the rule for one month; after that, it should be increased.
Having dug a pit two cubits long and twice as deep, and having filled it with the prescribed water,
one should dry it out and burn it with honey and clarified butter.
One should apply a plaster mixed with ashes.
One should fill [the vessel] with powdered mung beans, sesame seeds, and barley, using clay placed inside;
and one should destroy [the enemy] with fish, meat, and water.
54.25d Until that [substance] has attained the state of density.
When the seed is sown four finger-breadths deep and sprinkled with fish-water and meat-water,
it quickly becomes a creeper with auspicious sprouts.
54.26d Astonishing, she covers the pavilion.
54.27ab/ This seed should be infused a hundred times with a paste made from the fruit of *aṅkola*,
or with oil, or with the fruit of *ślaiṣmātaka*.
When sown in soil mixed with water from a ritual pitcher, it produces fruit in that very moment; what wonder is there in this, that a branch becomes laden with a weight of fruit?
The wise man, having removed the husks from the seeds of the *śleṣmātaka*,
should soak them seven times in this manner with water from the *aṅkola* and *vijjalā* plants in the shade.
Having rubbed these [seeds] with buffalo dung and cow-dung and having placed them in dried cow manure,
when combined with hail-water and clay, they yield fruit within a single day once sown.
54.31ab/ Dhruva, Mṛdu, Mūla, Viśākhā, Guru-bha (Jyeṣṭhā), Śravaṇa, as well as Aśvinī and Hasta; 54.31cd/ these asterisms have been declared by those with divine vision for the planting of trees.
Chapter 55: On the Characteristics of Palaces.
Having provided abundant water and established gardens, one should construct a temple for the deities for the sake of increasing fame and merit.
55.02ab. Those worlds which are attained through sacrifices and works of public utility—by one desiring to prosper in them, 55.02cd.
a dwelling for the gods should be constructed; for both [results] are seen here.
In these places— whether they are provided with water and gardens or not—
the deities come to dwell.
In the lakes, where the sun’s rays were warded off by the canopies of lotuses,
and where the waters were rendered pure by rows of white water-lilies tossed upon the shoulders of swans;
55.05ab/ Resounding with the cries of swans, kāraṇḍavas, cranes, and ruddy geese;
55.05cd/ Where water-fowl rested in the shade of the nicula trees growing on the banks.

Where the girdles are the rows of *krauñca* birds, the sweet voices are the melodious calls of the *kalahaṃsa* swans, the garments are the waters of the rivers, and the waist-bands are the shimmering *śapharī* fish.
55.07ab/ The rivers have blossoming trees as their head-ornaments, confluences as their rounded hips, sandbanks as their elevated breasts, and swans as their smiles.
55.08ab/ Deities always take delight in the regions at the edges of forests, along rivers, on mountains, and near waterfalls; 55.08cd/ as well as in cities provided with gardens.
55.09ab/ Those very plots of ground (bhūmi) which have been prescribed for Brāhmaṇas and the other castes in the matter of building construction (vāstukarman),
55.09cd/ those same ones are recommended for them even in the case of temples (devatāyatanas).
55.10ab/ A temple for the deity should always be constructed with sixty-four squares. 55.10cd/ And the central door therein is recommended when it is situated on a cardinal axis.
Whatever the width may be, its height should be twice that;
the hip is said to be equal to one-third of that height.
The inner sanctum (garbha) shall be half the width [of the temple], and the other walls shall surround it on all sides. The door shall be one-fourth the width of the sanctum and twice as high.
The branch of the udumbara tree is one-quarter of its height in width;
likewise, the thickness of the two branches is recorded as being equal to one-quarter of their span.
55.14ab/ It is praised when it has three, five, seven, or nine branches.
55.14cd/ One should place two door-keepers at the lower fourth part of the branches.
The remainder [of the area] should be adorned with auspicious birds, śrīvṛkṣa trees, svastikas, jars,
pairs of lovers, leafy creepers, and pramathas.
The image together with its pedestal (piṇḍikā) should be one-eighth less than the measurement of the door;
therein, two parts shall be for the image and the third part for the pedestal.
55.17ab/ Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Vimānacchanda, and Nandana;
55.17cd/ Samudga, Padma, Garuḍa, Nandivardhana, and Kuñjara.
The Cave-King (guhārāja), the Bull, the Swan, the Sarvatobhadra, and the Jar;
likewise the Lion, the Circle, the Quadrangle, the sixteen-sided, and the eight-sided [mandalas].
55.19ab/ Thus these twenty temples have been declared by me according to their names;
55.19cd/ I shall now describe their characteristics in the very order previously stated.
Therein, Mount Meru is hexagonal, consisting of twelve levels and possessing various caverns;
it is provided with four gates and is thirty-two cubits in width.
55.21ab/ Mandara, thirty cubits in height and possessing ten stories, is endowed with a peak.
55.21cd/ Kailāsa also has a peak; it is twenty-eight [cubits] and has eight stories.

55.22ab/ Fitted with latticed windows and known as a *vimāna*, it is twenty-one units in length. 55.22cd/ Named Nandana, it has six stories, thirty-two [sections], and is provided with sixteen *aṇḍas*.
The lotus named Samudga is circular; it has eight petals shaped like lotuses, and its base consists of a single tier with a single prong.
The Garuḍa-shaped [temple] is called Garuḍa and Nandī; it is four times six [units] in extent, should be made seven stories high, and adorned with twenty eggs (aṇḍas).
The *kuñjara* is sixteen cubits on all sides from its base; it has an elephant-back roof.
The *guhārāja* is sixteen [cubits], and its *valabhī* (pinnacle) should have three moon-chambers.
55.26ab/ The bull has one horn, twelve cubits in height, and is circular all around.
55.26cd/ The swan is shaped like a swan; the jar is eight cubits in height and has the form of a pitcher.
55.27ab/ Endowed with four gates and many pinnacles, it is the Sarvatobhadra;
55.27cd/ With very beautiful moon-chambers (candraśālās), it has twenty-six [pinnacles] and five stories.
The lion [mandala] is occupied by a lion, has twelve corners, and is eight cubits in extent;
it is square, with four [sides] resembling collyrium and provided with five eggs.

55.29ab/ According to the measurement of the *bhūmikā* finger-breadth, Maya’s [measurement] is one hundred and eight; 55.29cd/ and three and a half cubits (*hasta*) was indeed declared by Viśvakarman.
55.30ab. And here, the wise architects declare one opinion: 55.30cd. Those [buildings] which are deficient when provided with a pigeon-cot (kapotapāli) attain equality [with the full measure].
55.31a This definition of palaces has been stated in brief;
55.31b everything that was composed by Garga is present here.
55.31c Those extensive [treatises] which were composed by Manu and others—
55.31d Having touched upon that [topic], I have here undertaken this exposition.
Chapter 56: On the Characteristics of Vajralepa (Diamond-like Adhesive) Raw *tinduka* fruit, raw *kapittha* fruit, and the flower of the *śālmali*;
the seeds of the *śallakī*, the bark of the *dhanvana*, and *vacā*.

56.02ab/ One droṇa of water should be boiled with these [ingredients] until it is reduced to one-eighth. 56.02cd/ Having removed it from the heat, its paste (kalka) should then be combined with these other substances.

56.03ab/ This paste, consisting of the juices of *śrīvāsaka* and *guggulu*, *bhallātaka*, *kundurūka*, and *sarjarasa*, along with *atasī* and *bilva*, is known as the "adamantine plaster" (*vajralepa*).
56.04ab/ Upon palaces, mansions, roof-terraces, lingas, images, walls, and wells, 56.04cd/ one who is heated [by the sun] should offer [libations]; he shall remain for ten thousand years.
Lac, kunduru, guggulu, soot from a house, the pulp of kapittha and bilva,
nāgaphala, nimba (or balāphala), tinduka, madana fruit, madhūka, and mañjiṣṭhā.

56.06ab. This second paste, consisting of resin of the *sarja* tree, sugar, and *āmalaka*, is called "Vajra. 56.06cd. It possesses the same primary qualities as the former and is to be used for those very same purposes.

56.07ab/ Another paste named Vajratala consists of the horns of a cow, a buffalo, and a goat, the hair of a donkey, and the hides of a buffalo and a cow; 56.07cd/ together with the juices of nimba and kapittha.
56.08ab/ Eight parts of lead and two parts of brass, with one part of bell-metal; 56.08cd/ this formulation described by Maya should be known as the "diamond-compound" (vajrasaṅghāta).
Chapter 57: On the Characteristics of the Image.
57.01ab: When the sun is within a lattice, that most minute particle of dust which comes into view;
57.01cd: one should know that to be the atom (paramāṇu), for it is indeed the first of all measurements.

57.02ab/ An atom (paramāṇu), the tip of a hair (vālāgra), a nit (likṣā), a louse (yūka), a barleycorn (yava), and a finger-breadth (aṅgula)— 57.02cd/ these increase eightfold in succession; such is the measure for one finger-breadth.
57.03ab/ That which is the third part of the temple door, diminished by one-eighth;
57.03cd/ that is the measurement of the pedestal (piṇḍikā), and the image is twice that measurement.
57.04ab/ The mouth is twelve [parts] in width and length according to its own finger-measures;
57.04cd/ but by Nagnajit, the Drāviḍa style is said to be fourteen in length.
57.05ab/ The nose, forehead, chin, and neck are each four finger-breadths [in height]; likewise, the two ears [are four finger-breadths].
57.05cd/ The two jaws are two finger-breadths [in height], and the chin is two finger-breadths in width.
The forehead is eight finger-breadths in width, and beyond that, the two temples are two finger-breadths [in height].
The two temples are four finger-breadths [in length], while the two ears are two finger-breadths in breadth.
57.07ab/ The edge of the ear should be made at the half-fifth [unit] by means of a thread level with the eyebrows;
57.07cd/ and the ear-canal and the *sukumāraka* [hair-whorl] should be level with the junction of the eye.
57.08ab/ Vasiṣṭha declares that the distance between the corners of the eyes and the ears is four finger-breadths (catur-aṅgula).
57.08cd/ The lower lip is one finger-breadth in measure, and the upper lip is half of that.
The *goccha* should be half a finger-breadth [in height], and its mouth should be made four finger-breadths long;
it should be one and a half finger-breadths wide when closed, and three finger-breadths wide when open.
The two nostrils are equal to two finger-breadths (aṅgulas), and the tip of the nose should be known [to be at that distance].
The height [of the nose] should be two finger-breadths, and the distance between the eyes should be four finger-breadths.
The eye-socket measures two finger-breadths; the two eyes together are three parts of that [measure], and the pupil is one-third of that.
The visible portion of the pupil is one-fifth [of the eye], and the expansion of the eye is one finger-breadth.
From one end to the other, the space between the two eyebrows is ten half-finger-breadths (five finger-breadths); the line of each eyebrow is half a finger-breadth;
the distance between the eyebrows is two finger-breadths; and the length of each eyebrow is four finger-breadths.
The hairline should be made with a width of one and a half finger-breadths, equal to the distance between the eyebrows;
at the ends of the eyes, one should apply a *karavīraka* mark measuring one finger-breadth.
57.14ab/ The head is thirty-two finger-breadths in circumference and fourteen in length.
57.14cd/ However, in the case of artistic representation, twelve are seen and twenty are unseen.
The face, including the mass of hair, was declared by Nagnajit to be sixteen units in length;
the neck is ten units wide and twenty-one units in circumference.
57.16ab/ From the throat to the heart is twelve [finger-breadths], and from the heart to the navel it is of that same measure.
57.16cd/ It is stated that the distance from the middle of the navel to the penis is exactly equal to that.
The thighs are twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in measure, and likewise the shanks are twenty;
the knee-caps are four finger-breadths, and the feet are equal to that.
The two feet are twelve units long and six in breadth;
the big toes are three units long, while the index fingers (of the feet) have a circumference of five units and are three units long.
The remaining fingers should be made in sequence, each reduced by one-eighth of an eighth [of the previous].
The height of the thumb is said to be one finger-breadth plus one-fourth of a finger-breadth.
57.20ab/ The nail of the thumb is said by those who know [the science] to be one finger-breadth less a fourth part.
57.20cd/ For the remaining nails, it is half a finger-breadth, or slightly less, in successive order.
57.21ab. At the upper part of the shank, the circumference is said to be fourteen [units], while the width is five.
57.21cd. In the middle, however, it is seven units wide; the circumference is three times seven.
The width across the knees is eight [units], while the circumference is three times eight;
the thighs are fourteen [units] in width, and their circumference at the middle is double that.
The hips are eighteen finger-breadths in width and forty-four in circumference;
the navel is one finger-breadth in depth and likewise in its proportional measurement.
The circumference at the middle of the navel is forty-two [finger-breadths].
The distance between the two breasts is sixteen, and from there upward to the girth-line (kakṣya) it is six finger-breadths.
The shoulders should be eight [units], and the upper arms (bāhu) as well as the forearms (prabāhu) should each be twelve;
the lower arms (pratibāhu) should be six units wide, while the wrists (aṅgulī) should be four finger-breadths.
The sixteen arms have a circumference of twelve units at the base and twelve at the tips of the hands;
the palm is six finger-breadths in width and seven in length.
The middle finger is five finger-breadths long; the index finger is shorter by half a joint;
the ring finger is equal to this [index finger]; but the little finger is shorter by one joint.
The thumb should have two joints; the remaining fingers should each be made with three joints.
The measurement for the nails of all [the fingers] should be half of a joint.
An image should be fashioned with a form adorned with ornaments, dress, and decorations appropriate to its region;
when endowed with the correct characteristics and properly installed, it bestows prosperity.

Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, and Bali, the son of Virocana, were each twenty-one hundred [yojanas] in height; the remaining kings were twelve days' journey less, being of proportions slightly inferior to those foremost ones.
The Lord Viṣṇu should be fashioned with eight arms, four arms, or even two arms;
his chest is marked with the Śrīvatsa and his breast is adorned with the Kaustubha jewel.
Dark as the flax flower, clad in yellow garments, with a serene countenance;
wearing earrings and a crown, with a full neck, chest, shoulders, and arms.
Holding a sword, a mace, and an arrow in his [right] hands, his fourth hand on the right bestows peace;
and in his left hands are a bow, a shield, a discus, and a conch shell.
57.34ab/ Furthermore, one [form] desires four arms: one bestowing peace and another holding a mace;
57.34cd/ on the right side there is thus a conch, and on the left a discus.
For the two-armed [Viṣṇu], the right hand brings peace and the other holds a conch shell;
thus should the image of Viṣṇu be fashioned by those desiring prosperity.
Baladeva should be depicted with a plow in his hand and eyes rolling with intoxication;
he wears a single earring, and his body is as fair as a conch shell, the moon, or a lotus stalk.
The goddess Ekānaṃśā should be depicted between Baladeva and Kṛṣṇa;
her left hand rests upon her hip, while with the other she holds a lotus.
She should be depicted with four arms; with her two left hands she holds a lotus together with a book, and with the two [hands] on the right side she bestows boons and a rosary upon supplicants.
57.39ab. Furthermore, in the left hands of the eight-armed [goddess], there are a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), a bow, a lotus, and a scripture; 57.39cd.
the right hands are joined with a boon-granting gesture (vara), an arrow, and a mirror, and they also hold a rosary (akṣasūtra).
Śāmba, with mace in hand, Pradyumna, bearing a bow, and Surūpa;
and for these two, two women should be depicted holding shields and swords.
Brahmā has a water-pot in his hand, four faces, and sits upon a lotus throne;
Skanda has the form of a youth, holds a spear, and has a peacock as his emblem.
The white four-tusked elephant is the mark of Mahendra; the third eye, situated on the forehead and slanting across it, is the mark of Vajrapāṇi.
On the head of Śambhu is the crescent moon; he has the bull as his emblem, a third eye, and one that is upward-facing.
On his left side are the trident, the bow, and the Pināka; or else, half of him is the Daughter of the Mountain.
With hands and feet marked by lotuses, a serene form, and very fine hair, the Buddha,
seated in the lotus posture, becomes like a father to the world.
The deity of the Arhats should be depicted with arms reaching down to his knees, marked with the Śrīvatsa, and of tranquil form; he is clothed in the directions (naked), youthful, and handsome.
The nose, forehead, shanks, thighs, cheeks, and chest of Ravi (the Sun) are prominent;
he should adopt a northern dress, with his body well-concealed from the feet up to the chest.
Bearing two lotuses upon his own hands with both arms, wearing a crown,
his face adorned with earrings, with a long necklace, and enveloped by celestial beings.
With a face possessing the luster of the interior of a lotus, protected by a tunic, with a countenance brightened by a smile,
and surrounded by a halo of brilliant light from jewels— the Sun, when thus situated, brings auspiciousness to the maker.

An auspicious image that is one cubit in measure bestows wealth; one that is two cubits high brings about security and abundance; and that which measures three or four cubits shall likewise result in the same.
57.50ab. If the woman has an extra limb, there is fear of the king; if she has a missing limb, the performer suffers ill health.
57.50cd. If she has a protruding belly, there is fear of hunger; if her limbs are emaciated, there is loss of wealth.
57.51ab. One should declare death for the perpetrator [of the offense] if there is a wound caused by the falling of a weapon upon her.
57.51cd. A wife who is bent to the left destroys her husband; one who is bent to the right destroys his lifespan.
57.52ab. An upward gaze causes blindness, while a downward-looking gaze brings about anxiety.
57.52cd. Thus, for all images, the auspicious and inauspicious results are the same as those declared by Bhāskara.
57.53ab. Having marked the circumference of the base of the *liṅga* with a cord according to its length, one should divide that into three parts.
57.53cd. At the base it should be square, in the middle eight-sided, and from there [upward] circular.
In a square pit dug into the ground, a pedestal (piṇḍikā) should be constructed in the center;
this pedestal should be level with the visible height of the pit on all sides.
57.55ab. A [halo] that is thin and long portends the destruction of the country; one devoid of sides indicates the ruin of the city.
57.55cd. That halo which has a wound on its head is a sign of total destruction.
57.56ab/ A group of Mothers (mātṛgaṇa) should be fashioned, bearing emblems corresponding to their own names and deities.
57.56cd/ Revanta, mounted on a horse, should be depicted with a retinue engaged in hunting, sporting, and other such activities.
57.57ab/ Yama, holding a staff, rides upon a buffalo; Varuṇa, bearing a noose, is mounted on a swan.
57.57cd/ Kubera has a man as his vehicle, wears a crown on the left side, and has a large belly.
The Lord of the Pramathas, elephant-faced, with a pendulous belly and holding an axe, should be depicted with a single tusk, carrying a radish and a bulbous root with deep blue leaves.
(58) Chapter 58: On Entering the Forest.

On an auspicious day favorable to the performer, as determined by the astrologer, and under favorable omens, his entry into the forest should take place, accompanied by auspicious signs and portents of departure.
58.02ab/ Those born in cremation grounds, on paths, in temples, anthills, gardens, or hermitages of ascetics;
58.02cd/ those originating at sacred shrines (caityas) or confluences of rivers, and those sprinkled with water from a jar.
58.03ab/ Those [trees] that are crushed by creepers growing over hunchbacks, struck by thunderbolts or violent winds,
58.03cd/ Or crushed by elephants that have fallen on their own, dried up, scorched by fire, or whose honey-combs have been destroyed;
58.04ab/ Trees that bestow auspiciousness—those with glossy leaves, flowers, and fruit—should be avoided [if they are inauspicious];
however, having approached a tree that is desired, one should perform worship accompanied by offerings and flowers.
58.05ab/ The *suradāru*, *candana*, *śamī*, and *madhūka* trees are auspicious for the twice-born (*dvijāti*).
58.05cd/ For the *kṣatriya*, the *ariṣṭa*, *aśvattha*, *khadira*, and *bilva* trees bring about prosperity.
58.06ab/ For Vaiśyas, the Jīvaka, Khadira, Sindhu, and Syandana trees grant auspicious fruits.
58.06cd/ And for Śūdras, the Tinduka, Kesara, Sarja, Arjuna, Āmra, and Śāla trees [grant auspicious fruits].
58.07ab/ A linga or an image should be installed according to the direction, as if it were a tree;
therefore, the directions must be marked on the tree, either above or below.
58.08ab/ [This is done] with various foods such as *paramānna*, sweetmeats (*modaka*), boiled rice (*odana*), curd (*dadhi*), sesame paste (*palala*), and *ullopikā*.
Having worshipped the tree with liquors, flowers, incenses, and perfumes.
Having performed worship at night for the hosts of gods, ancestors, piśācas, rākṣasas, serpents, asuras, vināyakas, and others, and having touched the tree, one should speak:
