58.10ab/ You have been designated for the sake of the image of such-and-such a deity.
58.10cd/ Homage to you, O tree; let this worship be accepted according to the prescribed rite.
Whatever beings dwell here,
having accepted this offering presented according to the rules,
may they arrange their residence elsewhere.
May they forgive me today; let there be homage to them.
Having watered the tree at dawn and having cut it down toward the northeast direction with a small axe smeared with honey and clarified butter, [one should proceed].
58.12d One should then strike the remainder in a clockwise direction.
If it falls to the east, or to the northeast, or then to the north,
it shall bring about prosperity;
from the southeast corner, there will be fire and burning in due order.
Pains, fevers, minor ailments, diseases, and the wasting away of horses.
58.14a Those [faults] which were not mentioned regarding this entry into the forest—
namely, those within trees that have fallen, been broken, or are hollow; 58.14b and those prescribed for the Indra-banner and for the site— are [hereby explained].
58.14d In this regard, those [cases] previously mentioned by me should be applied in exactly the same way.
Chapter 59: On the Consecration of Images 59.01ab. A wise man should construct the consecration pavilion (adhivāsana-maṇḍapa) in the southern or northern direction, or in the east.
59.01cd. It should be provided with four arches (toraṇa) and covered with the shoots of auspicious trees.
59.02ab/ On the eastern side of the pavilion, variegated garlands and banners are prescribed.
59.02cd/ In the south-eastern direction they should be red; in the southern and south-western directions they should be black.
59.03ab/ White in the western direction, and pale-white in the north-western;
59.03cd/ Variegated on the northern side, and yellow in the north-eastern corner.
An image made of wood or clay bestows longevity, prosperity, strength, and victory;
likewise, one made of jewels or gold brings benefit to the world and grants nourishment.
An image made of silver brings fame; one made of copper brings an increase of progeny;
but an image or a linga made of stone brings great acquisition of land.
59.06ab/ An image damaged by a conch-shell destroys the chief person and the family.
59.06cd/ One damaged by a hole causes diseases, calamities, and [inexhaustible] decay.

59.07ab/ Having smeared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the center of the pavilion and then strewn it with sand and kuśa grass, one should place the image upon it, with its head and pillow resting on a bhadrāsana seat.
59.07cd/ One should set down the image so that its head and pillow rest upon the bhadrāsana seat.
59.08ab/ With decoctions of water from the *plakṣa*, *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *śirīṣa*, and *vaṭa* trees;
59.08cd/ And with all auspicious medicinal herbs, such as *kuśa* grass and others.
59.09ab/ On islands, on mountains, on anthills raised by elephants and bulls, at the confluences of rivers, and on their banks;
59.09cd/ And with earth from lotus-ponds, along with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and with water from sacred fords (tīrtha).

59.10ab/ Having bathed with water scented with fragrances and containing gold and jewels, while facing the east, she should be honored with the sounds of various musical instruments, auspicious proclamations, and the chanting of the Vedas.
59.11ab. In the eastern direction, the mantras bearing the marks of Indra [are to be recited], and in the southeast, those bearing the marks of Agni.
59.11cd. They should be recited by the foremost of the twice-born and honored with sacrificial fees.
59.12ab/ The twice-born should offer oblations into the fire with the mantras of whichever deity is to be installed.
59.12cd/ The signs pertaining to the fire have been declared by me for the raising of Indra’s banner.
59.13ab / Smoke-filled, moving counter-clockwise, and repeatedly emitting sparks—the fire is not auspicious.
59.13cd / Or, the loss of the officiant's mindfulness and his stumbling about are declared to be inauspicious.
59.14ab/ Having bathed, wearing unwashed garments, well-adorned, and honored with flowers and perfumes, the consecrator should place the image upon a bed well-spread with coverings.
59.14cd/ The consecrator should perform [this] on a bed that has been properly strewn.
Having thus properly consecrated [the image] while it is asleep through songs, dances, and wakeful rituals,
one should perform the formal installation at the time prescribed by the astrologer.
59.16ab/ Having honored [the deity] with flowers, garments, and ointments, accompanied by the sounds of conchs and trumpets,
59.16cd/ one should lead [the image] around the sanctuary with great care, keeping it to the right.
Having offered abundant oblations and having honored the Brahmins, the members of the assembly, and the architects,
and having given pieces of gold, one should cast them into the pit for the pedestal.
Having especially honored the installer, the astrologer, the twice-born, the members of the assembly, and the master builder.
59.18cd/ One becomes a partaker of auspicious things both in this world and in the next, and attains heaven.
59.19a They know the Bhāgavatas as belonging to Viṣṇu, the Magas to Sūrya, and the twice-born smeared with ashes to Śambhu;

59.19b they know the Brahmins who know the sequence of the Mātṛ-maṇḍala to belong to Brahmā; 59.19c they know the Śākyas, whose minds are peaceful, to belong to the Benefactor of All, and the naked ones to the Jinas.
59.19d Whichever deity they have taken refuge in according to their own rule, by them the ritual for that deity must be performed.

During the northern solstice, in the bright fortnight, and when the sun is in the constellation of Śiśira (Punarvasu), with Jupiter situated in its own division; when the ascendant is a fixed sign with a fixed navāṃśa, and the benefic planets occupy the tenth, ninth, or the quadrants (kendras).

59.21ab/ When malefic planets are situated in their houses of accumulation (upacaya), and on a day free from Mars, under the asterisms Dhruva, Mṛdu, Hari, Tiṣya, Vāyu, and Deva; 59.21cd/ And when the day is favorable, the installation of the gods is recommended.

59.22ab. This general [treatise], which bestows benefit upon the worlds, has been composed by me in brief. 59.22cd. [The sections on] consecration and the layout of the Sāvitra [fire-altar] have already been explained separately in detail.
Chapter 60: On the Characteristics of Cows.
60.01a Parāśara spoke this to Bṛhadratha; 60.01b therefore, this [treatise] on the characteristics of cows is now composed.
60.01c I have summarized those [women] who possess auspicious marks;
60.01d nevertheless, I shall describe them all according to the traditional scriptures (āgama).
Cows whose eyes are tearful, turbid, and rough, or which resemble the eyes of a mouse, do not bring good fortune;
nor do those with trembling or flattened horns, or those whose color resembles that of a donkey.
60.03ab/ Those with ten, seven, or four tusks, with pendulous or shaven faces, and with sunken backs;
60.03cd/ those with short or thick necks, a waist like a barley grain, and split hooves.

Those with dark-brown or excessively long tongues, with ankles that are too thin or too large, with overly prominent humps, with emaciated bodies, or with deficient or redundant limbs, are not desired.
Likewise, a bull with excessively large and pendulous testicles,
a chest covered with prominent veins, cheeks thickly set with large veins, and one who urinates in three places [is also to be avoided].
60.06ab/ One with eyes like a cat’s, tawny, or with a black mouth, does not bring good fortune to a twice-born man; indeed, such a one is desired by him.
60.06cd/ One with black lips, palate, and tongue, and who pants excessively, is a destroyer of the herd.
A bull that has thick dung and horns like jewels, a white belly, and the color of a black antelope— even if born in the household— must be abandoned, for it brings about the destruction of the herd.

60.08ab/ A bull whose body is covered with *śyāmaka* flowers, who resembles ash in hue, and has eyes like a cat, brings no good fortune even when accepted by Brahmins. 60.08cd/ Even if it is taken as a domestic animal, such a bull does not produce auspicious results for the twice-born.
And those who, with thin necks and timid eyes, withdraw their feet like emaciated oxen yoked from the mud, being deficient in strength, are unable to bear the burden from behind.

60.10ab/ Those with lips that are soft, firm, and copper-colored; with slender buttocks and copper-colored palates and tongues; 60.10cd/ with short, slender, and high-set ears; with beautiful flanks and well-defined shanks.
60.11ab/ Those with hooves that are copper-colored and firm, broad-chested, and endowed with large humps;
60.11cd/ whose skin and hair are glossy, smooth, and thin, and whose horns are copper-colored and slender.
60.12ab/ Those whose tails touch their bodies and earth, whose eyes have red corners, who breathe heavily,
60.12cd/ whose shoulders are like those of a lion, and whose dewlaps are thin and small, are honored and easy to manage.
Oxen that have counter-clockwise curls on their left side and clockwise curls on their right flank bring good fortune,
as do those whose shanks resemble those of the eṇaka antelope.
Those with eyes like beryl, jasmine flowers, or bubbles, and those with large eyelashes, are praised;
likewise, all those whose heels are not cracked are capable of bearing heavy loads.
60.15ab/ One with a wrinkled nose at the tip of the snout, a cat-like face, and white on the right side;
60.15cd/ having the luster of a lotus, a blue water-lily, or lac, with a beautiful tail and speed equal to that of a horse.

One with pendulous testicles, a belly like that of a ram, and narrow groins and chest is to be known as capable of bearing loads and enduring long journeys; such a horse, equal in speed to a thoroughbred, yields auspicious results.
White in color, with reddish-brown eyes, copper-colored horns and eyes, and a large face—he is named Haṃsa; he is declared to be of auspicious fruit and the increaser of the herd.
One whose tail touches the ground, whose horns are copper-colored [or whose flanks are so], whose eyes are red, and who possesses a hump,
as well as one that is brindled, makes its master the lord of fortune before long.

60.19ab/ Or one with a single white foot, and whatever its color may be, that too produces auspicious results. 60.19cd/ Even one of mixed results is to be accepted, provided it is not exclusively inauspicious.
Chapter 61: On the Characteristics of Dogs A dog with five toes on its feet, three toes on its forefeet, and six nails on its right forefoot;
one with copper-colored lips and a prominent nose, possessing the gait of the lord of beasts (the lion), and which moves about while sniffing the ground; [such a dog brings prosperity].
A dog that has a tail with bristles, eyes resembling those of a bear, and long, soft ears—
if such a dog should be in one's house, it brings abundant prosperity to its master before long.
She whose five toes on each foot have six nails, who has eyes like jasmine,
a curved tail, and long, tawny ears— she is the Mallikākṣī.
She who, as a dog, protects the kingdom, is the nourisher [of the ruler].
Chapter 62: On the Characteristics of the Rooster A rooster with straight feathers and toes, a copper-colored beak, nails, and crest, and white in color,
who crows with a melodious voice at the end of the night— that one brings prosperity to kings, kingdoms, and horses.
A bird that has a neck like barley, or one whose body resembles the jujube fruit,
or one with a large head and many beautiful colors,
is praised in battle; likewise, one the color of honey or a bee brings victory.
62.02d One who is other than this—thin-bodied, weak-voiced, or lame-footed—is not recommended.
A female cock that speaks softly and charmingly, with a glossy body and a beautiful, longing gaze,
bestows upon kings for a very long time the perfections of prosperity, fame, victory, and valor.
Chapter 63: On the Characteristics of the Tortoise.
A tortoise that has the color of crystal or silver, variegated with blue streaks, a body resembling a water-jar, and beautiful ridges is auspicious.
Or if it has a body like the color of dawn, variegated with the shape of mustard seeds,
it bestows the greatness of all kings while remaining in the temple.
63.02ab/ One whose body is dark like collyrium or a bhr̥ṅga-insect, variegated with spots, and possessed of a flawless body;
63.02cd/ or one who has a serpent-like head or a thick neck—he too leads to the increase of the kingdom of kings.
A bamboo pole that has the luster of lapis lazuli, a thick neck, is triangular,
possesses hidden nodes, and is beautiful in its joints is auspicious;
it should be placed in a pleasure pond or in a vessel filled with water.
A tortoise should be fashioned for the sake of auspiciousness by the lords of men.
Chapter 64: The Characteristics of Goats.

I shall now describe the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of goats. Those with nine, ten, or eight teeth are blessed; they should be kept in the house, while those with seven teeth are to be abandoned.
64.02ab/ On the right side, a black circle within a white one brings auspicious results.
64.02cd/ Among those resembling a rishi, or black, or red in color, the white is exceedingly auspicious.
64.03ab/ That jewel which hangs from the necks of goats like a breast is to be known as the "Single-Jewel" (ekamaṇi). It brings auspicious results; those with two or three jewels are most fortunate.

64.04ab/ All those with shaven heads are auspicious; all those entirely white and all those with entirely black bodies are likewise. 64.04cd/ Those that are half-black and half-white, as well as those half-tawny and half-black, bring prosperity.
That goat which wanders at the head of the herd and is the first to plunge into the water is auspicious;
it is either white-headed, or one whose head is marked with the asterism Kṛttikā.
64.06ab/ One with speckled throat and head, resembling ground sesame, and with copper-colored eyes, is praised;
64.06cd/ as is one who has black feet and is white, or one who is black and has white feet.
64.07ab/ That goat which has a black scrotum, is white in the middle, and has a black stripe; 64.07cd/ or that which moves slowly while making a sound—that goat is auspicious.

64.08ab/ That goat whose hair and feet are like those of a rishi, which is pale white in the front and blue at the rear, brings auspiciousness; and there is also a verse on this matter spoken by Garga: 64.08cd/ sa bhavati śubhakṛc chāgaḥ ślokaś ca^apy atra garga^uktaḥ//
64.09ab/ The hunchback, the crooked one, the matted-hair ascetic, and likewise the dwarf—these four are the sons of Śrī; they do not dwell with Alakṣmī.
Furthermore, those that are inauspicious are those whose cries are like the braying of a donkey, whose tails are ablaze, who have deformed claws,
who are discolored, whose ears are cut off, and who have the heads of elephants.
And those whose palates, tongues, and lips are dark-colored.
Adorned with highly praised colors and gems, those who are shaven-headed and have copper-colored eyes— when worshipped in the houses of men, they bring prosperity.
They produce happiness, fame, and prosperity.
Chapter 65: On the Characteristics of Horses One with a long neck, prominent eye-sockets, and broad shoulders, heart, and chest; with a copper-colored palate, lips, and tongue;
with fine skin, hair, and tail-hair; with beautiful hooves, gait, and face; and short ears, lips, and tail—[such a horse is auspicious].
With shanks, knees, and thighs well-rounded, with teeth that are even and white, and possessing a beautiful form,
the horse— pure in all its limbs— constantly brings about the destruction of the enemies of the lord of men.
65.02ab/ [Marks] on the tear-ducts, the jaw, the cheeks, the heart, the throat, the nostrils, the temples, the hips, the bladder, and the knees;
65.02cd/ as well as on the testicles, the navel, the hump, the anus, the left flank, and the legs—these are auspicious.
65.03a Those situated on the throat, the ears, and the neck;
65.03b those situated on the middle of the back and above the eyes;
65.03c those located on the lips, the thighs, the arms, the belly, and the sides.
65.03d Those, together with the forehead, are very beautiful.
Among them, there is one *prapāṇa* mark on the forehead and hair;
two curls (*āvarta*) are recorded for each of the following locations: the ear-cavities, the upper cavities, the head, and the chest.

A young foal has six white teeth; when those become yellowish-brown at two years of age, it is a three-year-old horse if the middle and back pairs have fallen out and grown back again. By counting the dark spots (kālikā) in groups of three according to their sequence from the front pair, they are yellow and white.
Know that from this [poison] there follows the appearance of glass-like opacities, flies, conch-shells, and cavities, as well as the falling out of the teeth.
Chapter 66: On the Characteristics of Elephants.
Those with teeth the color of honey, well-proportioned bodies, who are neither stained nor emaciated, and who are patient, [are auspicious].
Those with symmetrical limbs and even shoulders are auspicious, as are those whose hips resemble those of a boar.
Furthermore, his chest, armpits, and bracelets are flaccid;
he has a protruding belly, thick skin, and a large neck;
and his abdomen, along with the navel, is stout.
And the gaze of the dull-witted elephant is like that of a lioness.
66.03a But deer have short lips, tails, and penises; 66.03b thin legs, necks, teeth, trunks, and ears; 66.03c and large eyes—by these aforementioned characteristics [they are identified].
66.03d Those with mixed elephants have variegated markings.
The height of the Mṛga [elephant] is five cubits, its length is seven,
and its girth measurement is eight cubits;
then, for the Manda and Bhadra types, these dimensions increase by one and two [respectively].
66.04d A mixed-natured elephant has no fixed size.
66.05a The color of the Bhadra is green and its rut is [green]; 66.05b that of the Manda resembles the color of turmeric; 66.05c and the rut of the Mṛga is said to be black.
The rut of a mixed-natured elephant is blended.
Those with copper-colored lips, palate, and faces, with eyes like those of the *kalaviṅka* bird,
with glossy and prominent upper teeth, and broad, long faces; and those whose spinal columns are arched, elevated, long, well-concealed, and deeply set— [these are the marks of a great man].
Their frontal globes are covered with fine, single hairs and resemble tortoises.
66.07a Those with broad ears, jaws, navels, foreheads, and private parts;
66.07b those with nails numbering two, nine, and twenty, and with [soles] raised like a tortoise;
66.07c those with hands marked by three lines, well-rounded, and thick, and possessing beautiful hair—[these are the marks].
And they are blessed, inhaling the fragrant breezes from the lotuses in full bloom.
66.08ab/ Elephants with long fingers, red trunks, and a roar like that of a water-laden cloud;
66.08cd/ with large, long, and rounded necks—such elephants are considered auspicious for a lord of the earth.
66.09a Those with missing, excessive, or deformed nails and limbs;
66.09b those who are hunchbacked, dwarfish, or have horns like rams; 66.09c those whose testicles, fruits, or lotuses are visible or deficient.
66.09d With palates that are dark-brown, blue-black, variegated, or black.

A king who possesses elephants with very small tusks, male bugs, and eunuchs, as well as a female elephant endowed with the characteristics of a male elephant and one that is pregnant, shall go to a foreign land.
They would bring about fruits that are exceedingly distorted.
Chapter 67: On the Characteristics of Men First, [one should examine] stature, measure, gait, compactness, essence, complexion, oiliness, voice, constitution, mental disposition, and ancestry.

67.01c Having carefully examined the field and its purification according to rule, 67.01d the expert knower of the marks of men (sāmudravida) declares whether [the bride] has already been taken or is yet to come.
His feet are free from perspiration, with soft soles that resemble the interior of a lotus;
his toes are closely joined, with beautiful copper-colored nails and well-formed heels;
they are warm, devoid of visible veins, and have well-concealed ankles.
And the feet of the lord of men are elevated like the back of a tortoise.
Feet that are shaped like winnowing baskets, rough, pale-nailed, crooked, covered with prominent veins,
withered, and having sparse toes, bring the suffering of poverty.
Feet that are high-arched and resemble astringent wood (kaṣāya) portend the destruction of one's lineage.
67.03d Two killers of a Brahmin have palms with the luster of well-baked clay; two who have had sexual intercourse with women forbidden to them are yellow.
67.04a With sparse, fine hair on their rounded calves, 67.04b and with excellent thighs resembling the trunks of elephants, 67.04c and with well-developed, symmetrical knees— such are the kings.
Devoid of wealth, their shanks are like those of dogs and jackals.
67.05a In each single pore of kings, there is one hair; 67.05b in those who are wise and learned in the Vedas, two hairs are to be known [in each pore].
67.05c Those men who possess three or fewer [hairs] are destitute and partakers of suffering.
67.05d And likewise, hair is both censured and honored.
67.06a One with fleshless knees dies while away from home; 67.06b those who are deformed and small are unfortunate and poor;
67.06c and they are likewise conquered by women if their [knees] are sunken.
Through large quantities of meat, one obtains a kingdom and long life.

67.07a If the penis is small, one possesses wealth but is childless; if it is thick, one is devoid of riches. 67.07b If the glans is bent downward, one is destitute of sons and wealth; if it is curved, one has sons; otherwise, the opposite. 67.07c If it is bent downward, there is poverty; if it is covered with prominent veins, one has few children.
One with a large knot [in the penis] is happy, yet he brings about an end through urinary disorders and other ailments.
67.08ab/ Kings have penises that are concealed in a sheath; those who are long and broken are devoid of wealth.
67.08cd/ Those with straight and well-formed penises, as well as those whose phalli have few visible veins, are wealthy.
67.09ab/ Death by water occurs when there is one testicle; with uneven [testicles], one is fickle toward women; with even [testicles], one is a king.
67.09cd/ With upturned [testicles], there is a short life; for one with pendulous testicles, the lifespan is one hundred years.
Those with red jewels are wealthy, while those with pale or dirty ones are destitute; those whose urine is accompanied by sound are happy, whereas those whose stream is silent are indigent.
Those whose urine flows in two, three, or four streams, winding to the right as it issues forth, are to be known as lords of the earth; whereas those whose urine is scattered are destitute of wealth.
67.12ab If the stream of urine is single, curved, and prominent in form, it bestows sons but not daughters.
67.12cd Those with smooth, elevated, and even jewels [on the glans] enjoy wealth, women, and gems.
67.13ab And those with jewels that are depressed in the middle become fathers of daughters and are destitute.
Those with moderately prominent [teeth] become possessors of many cattle, and those with teeth that are not excessively large become wealthy.
Those whose seminal vesicles are withered should be known as destitute and unfortunate;
those whose semen has a fragrance like that of flowers are to be recognized as rulers of the earth.

67.15ab/ One with the scent of honey possesses great wealth; one with the scent of fish has many offspring. 67.15cd/ One with a thin semen begets daughters; one with the scent of meat enjoys great luxury.
67.16ab/ If the semen has the scent of wine, one becomes a performer of sacrifices; if it has the scent of alkaline matter, one is poor.
67.16cd/ One who engages in sexual intercourse quickly becomes long-lived; otherwise, he is short-lived.
67.17ab/ One with excessively thick buttocks is destitute, while one with fleshy, even buttocks is endowed with happiness.
67.17cd/ One with buttocks like a tiger's end is wealthy, and one with buttocks like a frog becomes a lord of men.
A king of men with hips like a lion’s possesses wealth; one with hips like those of a monkey or a camel is abandoned by riches.
Those with level bellies are endowed with enjoyments, while those with bellies resembling a jar or a cooking pot are destitute.

67.19ab/ Those with even sides are wealthy; those with depressed and crooked [sides] are deprived of enjoyments. 67.19cd/ Those with level bellies are rich in enjoyments; those with depressed [bellies] are devoid of enjoyments.
67.20ab/ Kings have elevated bellies; men with crooked bellies are dishonest.
67.20cd/ Those with serpent-like bellies become poor, as do those who eat excessively.
67.21ab/ Those with navels that are circular, elevated, and broad are happy;
67.21cd/ But a navel that is very small, invisible, or depressed brings about suffering.
67.22ab/ Situated in the middle of a fold, being uneven, it causes pain from colic and poverty.
67.22cd/ Curving to the left, it produces deceit; curving to the right, it bestows intelligence.
A navel that is broad at the sides indicates long life; one that is elevated above indicates sovereignty; one that is depressed below indicates wealth in cattle;
and a navel with the luster of the pericarp of a lotus makes one a lord of men.

67.24ab. One should know that a king who possesses one, two, three, or four folds [on his belly] is, respectively, one whose end is by the sword, one who enjoys women, one who has many sons, or one who is without folds.
67.24cd. However, one who is without folds should be known as a king.
67.25ab/ Those with uneven lines on their palms become sinful men who approach women who should not be approached.
67.25cd/ Those with straight lines enjoy happiness and are indeed averse to the wives of others.

Those with flanks that are fleshy and soft, and whose body hairs curl to the right, are kings; those with the opposite characteristics are destitute of wealth, deprived of happiness, and servants to others.
67.27ab/ Those whose nipples are not protruding become fortunate; those with nipples that are uneven and long are poor.
67.27cd/ Those with nipples that are full, well-developed, and slightly sunken become lords of the earth and happy.
The heart of kings is elevated, broad, non-trembling, and fleshy;
for those who are poor, it is the opposite—covered with coarse hair and veiny.
67.29ab. Those with even chests are wealthy; indeed, the brave have broad chests, while those with narrow chests possess nothing.
67.29cd. Those whose chests are uneven are destitute and meet their end by the sword.

67.30ab/ One with uneven collarbones that are separated by joints and devoid of flesh is destitute of wealth; 67.30cd/ one with prominent collarbones is a possessor of enjoyments, while one with depressed ones is poor, and one with thick ones is wealthy.
67.31ab/ One with a flattened neck is destitute; or he whose neck is withered and veiny [is likewise].
67.31cd/ One with a buffalo-like neck is a hero who ends by the sword; one with a neck like that of a bull is equal to a bull.
A king with a neck like a conch shell is long-necked and becomes a devourer [of others]. A back that is unbent and hairless brings wealth; otherwise, it brings misfortune.

67.33ab/ The armpits that are free from perspiration, full, elevated, fragrant, and covered with even hair belong to the wealthy; 67.33cd/ those that are otherwise are to be known as belonging to those devoid of wealth.
The shoulders of a poor man are fleshless, covered with hair, broken, and small;
those of the fortunate and the powerful are broad, continuous, and well-knit.
The arms of lords of the earth are round like the trunks of elephants, reaching down to the knees, and symmetrical and fleshy; whereas those of the poor are hairy and short.
67.36ab/ The fingers of those who are long-lived are long; those of the fortunate are curved.
67.36cd/ Those of the intelligent are slender, while those of those devoted to the work of others are flat.
67.37ab/ Those with thick fingers are devoid of wealth; those with fingers bent outward will die by weapons.
67.37cd/ Those with hands resembling monkeys are wealthy, while those with palms like tigers are wicked.
67.38ab/ Kings [attain their status] through hidden, firm, and well-knit joints at the wrist-bands;
67.38cd/ through those that are deficient, they suffer the cutting off of hands, and through those that are loose or noisy, they become destitute.
Men whose palms are depressed are deprived of paternal wealth; those with palms that are level and slightly depressed are wealthy, while those with upturned palms are givers.
67.40ab/ Those with uneven palms are themselves uneven and destitute, while those with palms the color of lac are lords.
67.40cd/ Those with yellow palms approach women who should not be approached; those with parched palms are impoverished.
Those with nails resembling husks are eunuchs; those with flattened or cracked nails are abandoned by wealth.
Those with deformed, discolored nails are seekers of others' faults, while those with copper-colored nails are army commanders.

67.42ab. Those with barley-corns on the thumbs possess wealth; those with barley-corns at the base of the thumbs possess sons. 67.42cd. Those with long finger-joints are fortunate and indeed long-lived.
67.43ab/ Smooth and deep lines belong to the wealthy; by the opposite of that, the poor possess them.
67.43cd/ Those with widely spaced fingers are destitute; those with closely set fingers are accumulators of wealth.
Three lines rising from the wrist and extending to the palm belong to a king;
one whose hands are marked with a pair of fish always bestows gifts through perpetual charity.
67.45ab/ The lines of those possessing wealth and learning are shaped like a thunderbolt; those resembling the tail of a fish belong to the same.
67.45cd/ Those resembling a conch shell, a parasol, a palanquin, an elephant, a horse, or a lotus belong to a king.
67.46ab/ Those with marks resembling a water-pot, a lotus stalk, a banner, or a goad become guardians of treasures.
67.46cd/ Those with marks resembling a rope become wealthy, and those with the form of a svastika attain sovereignty.
Lines resembling a discus, sword, axe, javelin, spear, bow, or lance make one the commander of an army;
those shaped like a mortar make one a performer of sacrifices.
Those endowed with great wealth resemble the storehouse of the one whose banner is the sea-monster (Kāmadeva),
and through the Brahmatīrtha, they are like the sacrificial altars of those who maintain the sacred fire.
67.49ab/ And they perform meritorious deeds through the construction of ponds, temples, and the like, as indicated by the lines forming a triangle.
67.49cd/ The lines at the base of the thumb represent sons; those that are fine represent daughters.

67.50ab/ Lines reaching the forefinger indicate a lifespan of a hundred years; with fewer lines, it should be calculated accordingly. 67.50cd/ With broken lines, there is falling from a tree; those with many lines or no lines at all are destitute.
67.51ab/ Those with chins that are excessively thin and long will be destitute; those with fleshy chins will be endowed with wealth.
67.51cd/ Those with lower lips resembling the bimba fruit and free from crookedness will be kings; those with thin lips will be without wealth.
67.52ab/ Those with lips that are cracked, split, discolored, and rough are deprived of wealth.
67.52cd/ Teeth that are glossy, dense, with very sharp canines, and even are auspicious.
67.53ab. A tongue that is red, long, smooth, and even should be known as belonging to those who enjoy pleasures (bhogin).
67.53cd. Likewise, a palate that is white, black, or rough belongs to those devoid of wealth.

67.54ab/ The face of kings is gentle, well-covered, stainless, smooth, and even; 67.54cd/ that which is the opposite belongs to those who experience suffering, and a large mouth belongs to the unfortunate.

67.55ab/ The face of a woman should be recognized as belonging to those who are childless; a circle [of marks] belongs to the deceitful. 67.55cd/ A long [face] belongs to those devoid of wealth; those with fearful faces are doers of evil deeds.
67.56ab/ Quadrangular for rogues, depressed and crooked for those bereft of sons; 67.56cd/ Excessively short for misers, full and lovely for those who enjoy pleasures.
67.57ab/ A beard that is unbroken at the tips, glossy, auspicious, soft, and well-sloped is favorable.
67.57cd/ Those with beards that are red, rough, and sparse are to be known as thieves.

67.58ab/ Those with fleshless ears meet a sinful death; those with broad, flat ears enjoy great wealth. 67.58cd/ Those with short ears are miserly, while those with ears like spikes become army commanders [or kings].
Those with hairy ears are long-lived, while those with broad ears possess great wealth; those whose ears are covered with visible veins are cruel, whereas those with long, fleshy ears are happy.
One with full, fleshy cheeks is an enjoyer of pleasures and a counselor; one whose cheeks are sunken is not so.
One with a nose like that of a parrot partakes in happiness, while one with a dry nose lives for a long time.

67.61ab/ If the nose is cut off at its base, she goes to those who should not be approached; if it is long, there is good fortune. 67.61cd/ If it is crooked, she is a thief; if the nose is flat, there will be the death of her wife.
67.62ab. Those with prominent, curved, and crooked noses are wealthy; those with noses bent to the right are eaters of meat and cruel.
67.62cd. A nose that is straight, has few openings, and possesses well-formed nostrils belongs to those who are fortunate.
The sneeze of the wealthy is heard once, twice, or thrice in a cluster; it is pleasant and resonant.
That of long-lived persons should be known as being emitted forcefully and with a compact sound.
Those with eyes like lotus petals and red corners of the eyes are wealthy and possessors of fortune;
those with honey-colored eyes like those of a cat are of great wealth, while those with such eyes are sinful.
67.65ab/ Those with deer-like eyes and those with round eyes are thieves; those with squinting eyes are cruel.
67.65cd/ Those with squint-eyed (kekara) eyes are cruel, while those with eyes resembling an elephant's are army commanders—or rather, kings.
Those with eyes as deep as the luster of blue lotuses possess sovereignty; however, for those whose pupils are excessively black, the extraction of their eyes occurs.
Ministership belongs to those with dull vision, while good fortune belongs to those with dark eyes.
A wretched look belongs to the destitute, whereas a moist look belongs to those possessing abundant wealth and enjoyments.
Those with raised eyebrows have short lives; those with broad and elevated eyebrows are exceedingly happy.
Those with uneven eyebrows are poor; those with eyebrows curved like the crescent moon possess wealth.

Those with long, unattached, and thick eyebrows are wealthy; those with eyebrows that are broken or drooping in the middle are devoid of wealth; and those whose eyebrows are curved in the middle are attached to women who should not be approached.

Those with prominent and broad temples are wealthy; those with sunken ones are deprived of children and wealth. Those with uneven foreheads are destitute, while those with a forehead like a half-moon are rich.
67.71ab/ Those with broad shells [on the ankles] become teachers; those with veins spreading over them are devoted to unrighteousness.
67.71cd/ Those with prominent veins become wealthy, as do those whose veins are arranged like a svastika.
Those with sunken foreheads are destined for execution or imprisonment and are devoted to cruel deeds;
those with prominent foreheads become army commanders or kings, while those with narrow foreheads are miserly.
67.73ab/ Weeping that is not dejected, tearless, and affectionate brings auspiciousness to men; 67.73cd/ But that which is harsh, dejected, and full of tears does not bestow good fortune upon men.
A smile that is auspicious is steady, whereas that of a sinner is with eyes closed;
the laughter of the wicked is frequent, and that of the insane is frequent at the end.
If three lines extending across the forehead are present, they belong to those who live for a hundred years;
if there are four, one becomes a lord of the earth and lives for ninety-five years.
Those who go to forbidden women have ninety years of life if the lines are broken;
those with lines reaching to the edge of the hair have a lifespan of eighty years.
67.77ab. With five lines, the lifespan is seventy years; with those standing in a single straight line, it is sixty.
67.77cd. With many lines, it is fifty years; and with crooked lines, it is forty.

67.78ab. One who has thirty [lines] touching the eyebrows lives for twenty years; likewise, one with lines curved to the left [lives for less]. 67.78cd. With small lines, one has a short life; and when they are deficient, the lifespan should be calculated accordingly in between.
67.79ab/ Those with heads that are perfectly round are rich in cattle; those with heads shaped like umbrellas become lords of the earth.
67.79cd/ Those with flattened heads are killers of their fathers and mothers; for those with skull-like heads, death comes after a long time.
67.80ab/ One with a pot-shaped head, a fondness for travel, two heads, or who commits evil deeds is abandoned by wealth.
67.80cd/ However, a large, sunken head belongs to great men; one that is deeply sunken brings misfortune.
With hair that grows one by one, glossy, black, curled, with unbroken tips, soft, and not too abundant, a king or one who partakes in happiness [is endowed].
67.82ab/ The hair of those devoid of wealth is abundant at the roots, uneven, and tawny; it is coarse, short, with thick and split ends. 67.82cd/ It is also excessively curved and very dense.
67.83ab/ Whatever limb is dry, devoid of flesh, or covered with hair is declared undesirable; the opposite of this is entirely auspicious.
67.84ab. He is broad and deep in three [places], elevated in those same three, and short in four;
67.84cd. he is red in seven [places], and long and subtle in five.
The navel, the voice, and the disposition— this triad is declared to be praiseworthy when it is deep in men; likewise, the chest, the forehead, and the face of men [should be broad].
This triad, when expanded, is praised.
67.86a–c. Furthermore, the chest, the armpits, the nails, the nose, the mouth, and the nape of the neck—these six are elevated.
And four are short: the male organ, the back, [the shanks, and the feet].
The neck and the shanks are also conducive to health.
The corners of the eyes, the feet, the hands, the palate, the lower lip, the tongue, and the nails— these seven, when red, truly bring happiness;
while the five— teeth, finger-joints, and hair— should be fine.
But for those who are suffering, it does not grow together with the skin and the nails.
The jaw, the eyes, the arms, the nose, and the space between the breasts— this pentad of long features does not belong at all to men who are not kings.
67.89a Shadow, announcing auspicious and inauspicious results,
67.89b is to be observed among humans, animals, and birds by those who know the characteristics [of signs].
67.89c It manifests the qualities of vital energy even externally.
It was like the radiance of a lamp reflected within a vessel made of crystal gem.
67.90a When the teeth, skin, nails, body hair, and hair are glossy,
67.90b and the earth-born shadow is fragrant,
it brings about contentment, the acquisition of wealth, and prosperity.
And the daily practice of dharma.
67.91a Lustrous, white, clear, and green, it is pleasing to the eye;
67.91b it brings about good fortune, gentleness, happiness, and prosperity.
67.91c Like a mother, it generates the accomplishment of all aims and provides nourishment.
The shadow bestows auspicious fruit upon embodied beings.
Fierce and unassailable, with the color of a lotus, gold, or fire, and endowed with energy, prowess, and majesty—
such a woman is of the nature of Agni and brings victory to living beings.
It bestows the swift attainment of one's desired goal.
67.93a When the wind that has arisen is soiled, harsh, black, and foul-smelling, it brings about death, imprisonment, disease, misfortune, and the loss of wealth.
67.93c But when it has a form like crystal, it is endowed with fortune and is exceedingly noble.
Like a treasure arisen from the sky, she was of pure complexion and possessed of all excellences.
Some say that there are ten shadows arising respectively from water, earth, fire, wind, and space, corresponding in order to the Sun,
the Lotus-navelled One (Viṣṇu), Indra, Yama, and the Moon.
"But they are equal in terms of their characteristics and results"—this is the summary thereof.
67.95ab/ Kings whose voices have the resonance of elephants, bulls, chariot-thunder, kettledrums, clay drums, lions, or clouds;
67.95cd/ but those with voices as harsh and worn-out as a donkey’s are bereft of wealth and happiness.
There are seven essential constituents (sāra): fat, marrow, skin, bone, semen, blood, and flesh; this is the summary of the results for living beings.
67.97ab/ By means of the palate, lips, gums, tongue, corners of the eyes, anus, hands, and feet;
67.97cd/ if these are red, those with red *sāra* possess great happiness, women, wealth, and sons.

Those with glossy skin are wealthy; those with soft [skin] are fortunate; those with thin [skin] are discerning; and those whose essence lies in marrow and fat possess excellent bodies and are endowed with sons and wealth.
Those with thick bones, firm bones, and bone as their primary essence are strong, reach the end of knowledge, and are handsome;
those with abundant semen and gurus are fortunate, learned, and well-formed.
67.100ab/ One whose body is well-nourished, who is learned, wealthy, and handsome, and whose essence is flesh;
67.100cd/ and one whose joints are well-knit, known as "compact" (saṅghāta), should be understood as a partaker of happiness.

67.101ab/ Oiliness (sneha) is to be observed in five [parts]: situated in the voice, tongue, teeth, eyes, and nails. 67.101cd/ Those with these [parts] being oily are endowed with children, wealth, and good fortune; those with them being dry are destitute.
67.102ab/ Radiant and glossy in color, it belongs to kings who possess sons;
67.102cd/ Rough, it belongs to those devoid of wealth; pure, it bestows auspiciousness, but not when mixed.
67.103ab/ Those with faces like a bull, a tiger, a lion, or a garuḍa have the *anūka* as their *sādhya*.
67.103cd/ They possess irresistible majesty, have conquered their enemies, and are lords among men.
Those with faces resembling monkeys, buffaloes, boars, or goats enjoy learning, wealth, and happiness;
those with faces and bodies resembling donkeys or young camels are devoid of wealth and happiness.
67.105ab/ Eight hundred, ninety-six, and eighty-four is the measurement for men;
67.105cd/ these are the counts of finger-breadths according to their own proportions for those who are superior, middling, and inferior.
67.106ab/ One whose body weighs half a *bhāra* experiences happiness; one who is lighter than that becomes a partaker of suffering.
67.106cd/ For those who are exceedingly wealthy, even one and a half *bhāras* is a burden for the lord of all the earth.
A woman of twenty years and a man of twenty-five years may indeed receive the standard measurement of honor and stature,
or at the fourth stage of their life.
67.108ab/ Through the quality of *sattva*, one becomes a man among those of earth, water, fire, wind, ether, gods, humans, *rākṣasas*, *piśācas*, and animals; this is their characteristic.
67.108cd/ Through the quality of *sattva*, one becomes a man; this is their characteristic.
One who has the nature of earth possesses the fragrance of auspicious flowers;
he is endowed with enjoyment, breathes well, and is stable. One who has the nature of water drinks much water.
He is pleasant in speech and a vessel for aesthetic flavor.
67.110 One who is fickle by the very nature of fire is exceedingly sharp, fierce, hungry, and a great eater;
by the nature of wind, one is restless and thin.
And he quickly falls under the sway of anger.
One whose nature is like space (ether), who is skillful, whose mouth is open, who is proficient in the movement of sounds, whose head and limbs are well-formed,
a man endowed with generosity and mild anger; [such a person is a speaker].
And one who is devoted to affection is of divine nature.
67.112ab/ A mortal being endowed with the nature of a sattva is fond of song and ornaments; 67.112cd/ such a man is always characterized by a disposition toward sharing.
67.113a He has a fierce temperament and acts like a rogue; 67.113b he is sinful by nature among the night-stalkers (niśācara).
67.113c A piśāca-natured man is fickle and smeared with impurity.
He talks excessively and his limbs are swollen.
67.114a He who is timid, hungry, and a glutton should be known as a man of the nature of animals;
67.114b thus is the nature of men declared.
That which those who know the characteristics proclaim as the true nature of beings.
67.115 Kings become equal in their gait to the tiger, the swan, the rutting elephant, the bull, and the peacock;
and those whose movement is silent and steady [attain this].
Even those lords, their gait quick and leaping, become impoverished.
For one who is weary, a vehicle; for one who is hungry, food;
for one overcome by thirst, a drink; and protection in times of fear—whatever man possesses these at the proper time, [he is truly blessed].
Those who know the marks of men truly declare him to be fortunate.
Having surveyed the opinions of the sages, I have here briefly described these characteristics of a man.
By studying this, a person becomes esteemed by kings and beloved by all people.
Chapter 68: The Classification of the Five Types of Men.

68.01ab/ When the planets and stars are endowed with strength, situated in their own signs or their exaltations, and occupying the four angular houses (catuṣṭaya), five types of excellent men are born; I shall describe them.
68.02ab/ With Jupiter one becomes a haṃsa; with Saturn, a śaśa; and with Mars, a rucaka. 68.02cd/ With powerful Mercury, one is a bhadra; with Venus, the worshipful deity, a mālavya.
68.03ab/ A man possesses physical vigor from the strength of the Sun and mental vigor from the strength of the Moon;
whatever signs these two occupy, a person will possess the characteristics of those signs.

68.04ab/ Men are characterized by a mixture of those [qualities]—the elements, the primary constituents, natural disposition, luster, complexion, vitality, form, and so forth—[which are] weaker than the sun and the moon.

68.04cd/ Men are characterized by a mixture of those [qualities]—the elements, the primary constituents, natural disposition, luster, complexion, vitality, form, and so forth—[which are] weaker than the sun and the moon.
68.05ab/ From Mars comes strength, from Mercury heaviness, from Jupiter tone of voice, and from Venus oiliness.
68.05cd/ From Saturn comes complexion; the goodness or badness of these [qualities] depends on their respective merits and defects.

68.06ab/ Those kings whose [planets] are mixed in their periods do not become possessors of happiness; 68.06cd/ there are distinctions [of condition] based on [the planets being] in an enemy's house, debilitation, exaltation, fallen, or aspected by benefics or malefics.
The span and the length of the *haṃsa* [type of bow] are ninety-six finger-breadths;
those known as the *śaśa*, *rucaka*, *bhadra*, and *mālavya* increase by three finger-breadths each.
68.08a He who is characterized by *sattva* possesses compassion, steadfastness, 68.08b purity of being, straightforwardness, and devotion to Brahmins and gods;
68.08c one in whom *rajas* predominates [is devoted to] poetry, the arts, sacrifices, and women.
A man whose mind is fully absorbed [in his task] is exceedingly heroic.
One in whom *tamas* predominates is a deceiver of others,
foolish, lazy, prone to anger, and excessively sleepy;
one characterized by a mixture of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* possesses a combination of these traits.
But those seven, together with their subdivisions, are mixed.
68.10 His nose is like that of an elephant; his pair of arms is equal [in length]; his hands reach his knees.
His joints and limbs are full of flesh; his body is even and beautiful, yet slender at the waist.
His face is sixteen finger-breadths in height, and the opening of his ear is three finger-breadths less in width.
With blazing eyes, well-formed cheeks, even white teeth, and lips that were not overly fleshy.
That king, having acquired wealth through his valor, protects the Mālavas, Bharukacchas, Surāṣṭras, and the regions of Lāṭa, Sindhu, and others.
Having made up his mind, he took up residence on Mount Pāriyātra.
68.12ab/ This Mālavya, seventy years old, will completely cast off his life-breaths at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
68.12cd/ This characteristic has been correctly described; henceforth I shall speak of the remaining men.
68.13 His arms are well-developed, symmetrical, and long; his height is equal to the span of his two outstretched arms;
and his cheeks are covered with hair that is soft, fine, and dense.
Indeed, by such a mark, a man becomes truly auspicious.
68.14a With skin as his essence and bright semen, broad and full-chested; 68.14b preeminent in courage, tiger-faced, and steadfast;
68.14c endowed with patience, devoted to dharma, and grateful.
68.14d Walking with the gait of a lordly elephant, he is a knower of many scriptures.
68.15a Wise, handsome, with a beautiful forehead and the mark of a conch;
68.15b skilled in the arts, steadfast, and having a fine belly; 68.15c his hands and feet possess the luster of the interior of a lotus.
The yogi has a well-formed nose and eyebrows that are even and closely joined.
68.16a The fragrance of his body is like that of saffron on leaves moistened by fresh rain, or like the ichor of a lordly elephant mixed with aloe-wood;
68.16b and his hair consists of single-strands, black and curled.
68.16d The state of having the secret parts concealed like those of a horse or an elephant.
68.17 His hands and feet are marked with the plow, club, mace, sword, conch, and discus, as well as the elephant, crocodile, lotus, chariot, and fish;
thus people enjoy his abundant prosperity.
For one whose mind is independent cannot endure their own kin.
68.18a Ninety-six finger-breadths in height, and likewise in weight;
68.18b if he is well-nourished, he shall be the king of the Middle Country.
68.18d Tryādayaḥ [are his]; he is the lord of the entire earth.
Having properly enjoyed the earth acquired through valor for eighty years,
the auspicious one, having cast off his life-breaths at a sacred ford, goes to the abode of the gods.

One with slightly protruding teeth, thin teeth and nails, eyes like the interior of a sheath, and swift movement, is devoted to learning, minerals, trade, and crafts; he has full cheeks, is deceitful,
a military commander, fond of sexual intercourse, his mind attached to the wives of others, and fickle.
The hare is brave, devoted to its mother, and remains hidden in the difficult terrains of forests, mountains, and rivers.
He is eight fingers short of one hundred in height;
his movements are cautious, and he is skilled in detecting the vulnerabilities of others. His marrow is his vital essence, and his conduct is secretive.
For the hare-marked moon is therefore declared not to be very heavy.
68.22a Thin in the middle, with lines resembling a shield, a sword, and a lute;
68.22b Corresponding to a couch, a garland, and a drum; 68.22c And lines rising upwards like a trident.
Or like the footprints of a hare appearing upon the moon.
Whether he be a border-dweller or a regional ruler,
his body is afflicted by the pain of a ruptured scrotum;
such is this hare, seventy years of age.
He goes to the abode of Vaivasvata.
68.24a His face is red with full cheeks and a prominent nose, resembling gold;
68.24b his head is round, his eyes are like honey, and all his nails are red.
68.24c [He is marked] with garlands, a goad, a conch, a pair of fish, the sacrificial fire-wood (kratu-aṅga), a water-pot, and a lotus.
68.24d Marked by these signs, with a voice like a swan’s cry, possessing beautiful feet, he is a swan with serene faculties.
Its taste is like water, its essence is that of semen, it possesses double the [usual] qualities, and its weight is measured by eight hundred *palas*.
Furthermore, its specific dimension is proclaimed by the wise to be ninety-six [units].
The Haṃsa king enjoys sovereignty over the Khaśas and Śūrasenas, in the region between the Gāndhāra and the Gaṅgā-Yamunā rivers;
having ruled for ninety-nine autumns, he meets his death at the edge of the forest.
68.27ab/ One with beautiful eyebrows and hair, reddish-dark in complexion, with a neck like a conch-shell and a very long face;
68.27cd/ he is brave, fierce, excellent, a counselor, a master of thieves, and one who exerts himself in physical exercise.
68.28a As long as the mouth of the rucaka is wide, 68.28b so is its squareness in the middle region; 68.28c it has a delicate luster and is composed of the essence of blood and flesh.
The slayer of enemies, who has accomplished his task through sheer prowess.
68.29 His hands and feet are marked with the skull-topped staff, the lute, the bull, the bow, the thunderbolt, the spear, and the trident;
he is devoted to his teachers, Brahmins, and deities.
It should be one hundred finger-breadths in length and a thousand in measure by weight.
Skilled in the practice of mantras and sorcery, with thin knees and shanks,
having enjoyed the Vindhya mountains along with Mount Sahya and Ujjayinī,
King Rucaka reached [his end] after seventy years.
He meets death by the sword, or else by fire.
68.31a Another five are the Vāmanaka, the Jaghanya, 68.31b the Kubja, the Maṇḍalaka, and the Sācī;
68.31c these are the attendants of the kings previously mentioned.
Listen now to the characteristics of those known as the mixed types.
With all his limbs complete yet being a dwarf with a broken back,
and somewhat [emaciated] in the region between his thighs and armpits—
he is indeed known as the dear attendant of kings.
68.32d The prosperous king was a devotee of Vāsudeva.
One who frequents garlands is named the lowest;
he has ears like a crescent moon and well-knit joints. With semen as his essence, he is a slanderer and a poet.
68.33d He has a rough complexion and thick hands and fingers.
68.34a Cruel, wealthy, and of dull intellect, he is well-known;
68.34b he will have a copper-colored complexion and a disposition for joking. 68.34c On his chest, feet, and hands, there will be marks of swords, spears, and nooses—
68.34d He who bears the mark of a battle-axe is named Jaghanya.
68.35a He who is called Kubja is indeed pure below; 68.35b he is somewhat emaciated and bent in the upper body. 68.35c A frequenter of swans, an atheist, yet endowed with wealth.
A wise man should be brave and grateful.
68.36a Skilled in the arts and fond of quarreling,
68.36b possessing many servants yet conquered by women;
68.36c having honored the world, he suddenly abandons it.
68.36d This man is called "the hunchback," and he is always industrious.
68.37ab. Therefore, one who knows the characteristics of the maṇḍala, a follower of the Rucaka [tradition], and an expert in the practice of sorcery (abhicāra);
68.37cd. One who is devoted to rites such as those involving Kṛtyās and Vetālas, and to the [esoteric] sciences (vidyā).
One with an aged appearance and coarse, rough hair on the head is skilled in destroying enemies;
one whose mind is devoted to the twice-born, the gods, sacrifices, and yoga is wise, yet is conquered by women.

68.39a He who is called Sāmī has an exceedingly deformed body; 68.39b he is indeed a follower of the hare and is unfortunate. 68.39c Yet he is a donor who completes his undertakings with great effort.
In its qualities, it would be equal to the hare itself.
68.40 This definition of a man has been declared by me in brief, having examined the doctrines of the sages;
having studied this, a man will be honored by kings.
And he becomes beloved by all people.
Chapter 69: On the Characteristics of Maidens.
A maiden’s feet should have smooth, elevated, slender, and copper-colored nails; they should be even, well-fleshed, beautiful, and have concealed ankles.
If one desires sovereignty over the earth, one should marry her whose palms have joined fingers and the luster of a lotus.

Feet marked with the signs of a fish, a goad, a lotus, a barley grain, a thunderbolt, a plough, and a sword, and having soles that are warm to the touch and soft, are praised; likewise, the shanks should be hairless, free of veins, and well-rounded.
The two knees are even, with joints that are not prominent.
69.03a Her thighs are firm, hairless, and resemble the trunks of elephants;
69.03b her private parts are broad and like the leaf of the *aśvattha* tree; 69.03c her hips and forehead are broad, and her navel is as prominent as the shell of a tortoise.
And a hidden jewel bestows abundant prosperity.
69.04a Her hips are broad and well-fleshed; 69.04b heavy, they support a multitude of girdles. 69.04c The navel is deep for those of expansive limbs.
And one that moves in a clockwise direction is praised.

69.05a The waist of a woman should be graced by three folds and free from hair; 69.05b the breasts should be rounded, firm, symmetrical, and hard. 69.05c The chest of women should be hairless and soft.
And a neck marked with three folds like a conch shell bestows wealth and happiness.
His lower lip is fleshy, resembling the bandhujīva flower and possessing the beautiful form of a bimba fruit;
his teeth are even and resemble the buds of the kunda jasmine.
They bestow upon women the happiness of a husband and the gift of immeasurable wealth.
69.07a His speech is endowed with courtesy, free from deceit, as sweet as that of the cuckoo or the swan, 69.07b eloquent, undepressed, and bringing abundant happiness;
69.07c his nose is straight, with symmetrical nostrils, beautiful and praiseworthy.
And her gaze was captivating, possessing the luster of the petals of a blue water-lily.
Eyebrows that are not joined, not too broad, not drooping, curved like the young crescent moon, and auspicious are praised;
likewise, a forehead that is shaped like a half-moon, hairless, and neither sunken nor protruding is praised.
A pair of ears that are fleshy, soft, well-proportioned, and symmetrical is praised.
Hairs that are glossy, dark blue, soft, and curled, growing as single strands, bring happiness, as does a symmetrical head.
69.10 With water-pots, seats, horses, elephants, chariots, śrīvṛkṣa trees, sacrificial posts, and arrows;
with garlands, earrings, chowries, goads, and barley-corns; with mountains, banners, and archways;
and with fish, svastikas, altars, fans, conchs, parasols, and lotuses—
Or else, young women go upon the foot, or even upon the palm of the hand, to the state of a queen.
The hands of the king’s wife have concealed wrists and resemble the interior of a young lotus; their fingers have joints that are slender and well-spaced,
and the palms are neither sunken nor overly high, being endowed with auspicious lines.
He makes her not a widow for long, enjoying the happiness of sons and wealth.
69.12a That line which rises from the wrist at the middle finger of a woman, 69.12b and extends across the palm of her hand,
69.12c or likewise that which stands upright on the sole of her foot—
Or else, for a man, it may lead to the happiness of sovereignty.
The line that originates at the base of the little finger and extends into the space between the forefinger and the middle finger indicates a supreme lifespan.
But if it is less than that measure, the lifespan is correspondingly diminished.

69.14a At the base of the thumb, the lines of procreation indicate: 69.14b Sons are shown by broad lines, while daughters are indicated by thin ones; 69.14c Those that are unbroken in the middle [and long] belong to those of great longevity.
For those of very short lifespan, the dimensions are small and easily broken.
69.15a Thus has this been stated as auspicious for women; 69.15b that which is contrary to this is stated to be undesirable.
69.15c Those [signs] which bear especially undesirable fruits—
69.15d I shall enumerate them briefly.
If the earth does not touch either the little toe or the one next to it of a woman,
or if it passes beyond her big toe, she would be [unlucky].
69.16d That ring finger [of hers] belongs to a wanton woman who is exceedingly wicked.
With swollen calves,
prominent veins, withered shanks, and excessive hair or flesh; with a small, shallow, and leftward-spiraling private part.
And the belly of those who are suffering is shaped like a water-pot.
69.18ab/ With a short neck there is extreme poverty; with a long one, the destruction of the family.
69.18cd/ With a neck that is broad and prominent, a woman possesses a fierce temperament.
She whose eyes are squinting or tawny is ill-behaved, as is she whose eyes are dark-brown and flickering; and she who has depressions on her cheeks when she smiles [is likewise ill-fated].
69.19d They say that woman is undoubtedly an unchaste woman.

A woman with a protruding forehead destroys her brother-in-law; one with a protruding belly destroys her father-in-law; and one with a protruding buttocks destroys her husband. One whose upper lip is covered with an excessive growth of hair [is likewise inauspicious].
69.20d Nor is she auspicious for her husband who is excessively tall.
69.21 Her breasts are hairy and covered with filth; her ears are uneven and cause distress;
and her teeth are large, jagged, and irregular.
And those with black flesh lead to affliction and to theft.
With hands resembling flesh-eating creatures such as wolves, crows, and herons, marked like reptiles and owls, and with hands that are withered, veiny, and uneven.
Women become devoid of happiness and wealth.
She who has an elevated upper lip and coarse-tipped hair is fond of quarreling;
generally, such defects are found among those who are ill-favored.
Where there is form, there qualities abide.
69.24ab/ First, the two feet together with the ankles are prescribed; second, the two shanks together with the knees and the circles [of the thighs];
69.24cd/ then third, the penis, the thighs, and the scrotum; and they say that the navel and the hips constitute the fourth.
69.25ab. They say the belly is the fifth; the heart is the sixth, followed by that which is endowed with breasts.
69.25cd. Then they say the shoulders and collarbones are the seventh, and the lips and throat are the eighth.
The ninth [portion] is the eyes together with the eyebrows; the tenth is likewise the head together with the forehead.
In the case of inauspicious [portions], the result of the period (daśā) is inauspicious; in the case of auspicious [portions] beginning with the feet, it is auspicious.
Chapter 70: On the Characteristics of Cutting Cloth.
Aśvinī bestows abundant cloth; Bharaṇī, on the other hand, is a thief.
Under the deity of Fire (Kṛttikā), one is consumed by fire; under Prajeśvara (Rohiṇī), there is the accomplishment of wealth.
In Mṛgaśiras there is danger from mice; in Ārdrā, there is even the loss of life. In Punarvasu there is the arrival of good fortune, and in its first quarter (Pūrvaphalgunī), union with wealth.
If [the moon] is eclipsed in the Bhujanga asterism (Aśleṣā), there is ruin; if in Maghā, one should predict death.
In the asterism called Bhaga (Pūrvaphalgunī), there is fear of the king, while Uttarāphalgunī leads to the acquisition of wealth.
Through the Kara yoga, there is success in one's undertakings; through Citrā, the acquisition of auspicious things;
through Svāti, auspicious food; and through Viśākhā, one becomes beloved by the people.
In the asterism of Mitra (Anurādhā), there is pleasant splendor; in its head-quarter asterism (Jyeṣṭhā), there is the destruction of clothing.
In the Nairṛta (Mūla) asterism, there is immersion in water; and in the asterism presided over by the Lord of Waters (Pūrvāṣāḍhā), there is illness.

If the Vaiśvadeva deity is in the Viṣṇu asterism, even sweet food leads to eye disease. If it is in the Vāsava (Dhātṛ) asterism, they know there will be the acquisition of grain; however, if it is in the Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj) asterism, there is great danger from poison.
In Bhadrapadā, there is danger arising from water; thereafter, there will be the acquisition of a son. And they say that in Pauṣṇa, there is the luster of jewels.
He who desires to enjoy fresh clothing.
Whether it be what was bestowed by a king due to a lapse in judgment, or what was obtained during the rites of marriage—
even if these garments lack good qualities, wearing new cloth shall yield desirable results.
It is auspicious to wear new clothing even under a lunar mansion that is devoid of favorable attributes.
70.08cd / At a wedding, at a royal honor, and at a gathering esteemed by Brahmins.
70.09ab [K.71.1ab] Devas and humans dwell in the corners of the garment, and at the ends of the cords and the middle of the fringes;
70.09cd [K.71.1cd] the remaining three, who are portions of the night-stalkers (niśācara), likewise reside in the bed, the seat, and the sandals.
One should know that [the omen is] spoiled if the cloth is smeared with ink, cow-dung, mud, and the like, or if it is torn, burnt, or cracked;
however, if the cloth is new, the evil is slight or very slight when eaten, while the auspicious result is greater in the upper garment.
70.11ab If death occurs in the portions belonging to the Rākṣasas, there is disease; however, in the human portion, there is birth in a noble family and splendor.
70.11cd In the portion of the immortals (gods), there is an increase in enjoyments; in all the border regions, they say that what is undesirable occurs.
If a sacrificial portion takes the form of a cut-off fragment resembling a heron, a water-fowl, an owl, a dove, a crow, a carnivorous beast, a jackal, a donkey, a camel, or a snake,
it brings to men a danger equal to death.

70.13ab Even if it has the shape of a fracture and is located in the south-western quarter, a line adorned with an umbrella, banner, svastika, vardhamāna, śrīvṛkṣa, jar, lotus, archway, and so forth, bestows prosperity upon men before long.
Chapter 71: On the Characteristics of the Yak-tail (Cāmara).
It is said that the yak-tails were created by the gods in the caves of the snowy mountains for the sake of their hair.
Their colors become yellowish-green,
black, and white, according to the nature of their tails.
71.02a Oiliness, softness, and an abundance of hair; 71.02b clarity and the state of having few bone-joints;
71.02c and whiteness—these are said to be the perfection of their qualities.
Those that are pierced, small, or missing are not auspicious.
71.03a His staff is measured at one and a half cubits, or else one cubit, or again another equal to an aratni;
71.03c it is made of auspicious wood, or encased in gold or silver.
And with all kinds of jewels, for the benefit of kings.
71.04ab/ For the staffs of the scepter, the parasol, the goad, the cane, the bow, the canopy, the spear, the banner, and the chowrie;
71.04cd/ those that are yellowish, reddish-brown, honey-colored, and black are beneficial according to their respective order of colors.
71.05a Bringing about the destruction of mother, land, wealth, and family;
71.05b and causing disease, death, and birth through the [planetary] nodes (parvas);
71.05c by means of two and so forth, increasing by two in sequence.
The fruit is equal for those who have ceased [from unwholesome conduct] at the twelve points.
Success in journeys, the destruction of enemies,
abundant gains, the acquisition of land,
an increase in livestock, and the attainment of one's desires.
71.06d In the first three [groups] of odd-numbered [verses], those are the lords.
Chapter 72: On the Characteristics of the Parasol (Chhatra-lakṣaṇādhyāya).
It should be well-strewn with the feathers of swans, or those of cocks, peacocks, and cranes; it should be covered all over with new silk cloth and be white in color.
72.02ab/ It is adorned with pearls, covered with hanging garlands, and has a crystal base.
72.02cd/ It consists of six cubits of pure gold, with a single staff of nine-jointed bamboo.
72.03ab/ That [umbrella] is half a *daṇḍa* in width, well-enclosed, adorned with jewels, and exalted;
72.03cd/ that umbrella of the king brings supreme auspiciousness and bestows victory.
72.04ab/ For the crown prince, the king’s wives, the commander-in-chief, and the chief of the army,
72.04cd/ the staff shall be four and a half cubits long, with a width made equal to one-fifth [of its length].
For others, however, a peacock-feather umbrella should be made— one that wards off heat, adorned with bands of clear silk on its rim, and featuring a hanging garland of jewels.
But for other men, [the umbrella] that wards off cold and heat should be square;
however, for Brahmins, the umbrella should be made perfectly circular and provided with a straight handle.
Chapter 73: Praise of Women.
In the conquest of the earth, the city alone is the essence;
in the city, the house; and in the house, a single room.
Even there, on the couch, a most excellent woman,
radiant with jewels, is the very essence of the happiness of sovereignty.
73.02ab/ Jewels adorn women, yet women are not adorned by the luster of jewels; 73.02cd/ Bending the mind, they captivate; it is not jewels that do so, but [the touch] of the limbs of women.

73.03a Concealing their outward appearance as they rise up to conquer the enemy force, 73.03b They contemplate statecraft, which is entangled with hundreds of branches of activity— both those performed and those yet to be done; 73.03c They follow the counsel uttered by their ministers.
For kings who serve [the wicked], who are apprehensive on all sides,
and who dwell in an ocean of the waters of suffering, the mere fragment of happiness is the embrace of their beloved.
73.04a Heard, seen, touched, or even remembered, it produces joy for men;
73.04b no jewel other than women has ever been created anywhere by the Lord of the World. 73.04c For their sake are dharma and wealth, as well as the happiness derived from sons and objects of sense.
In the home, women are always to be honored with wealth, respect, and dignity.
73.05a Those who, abandoning virtues, proclaim the faults of women by way of the path of detachment— 73.05b they are wicked people; such is my thought.
Those words of theirs do not express the state of reality.
"Speak the truth: what fault is there in women that has not been committed by men?
Out of audacity, women have been cast aside by men."
They are superior in virtue; this has been stated here by Manu.
73.07ab/ Soma gave them purity; Gandharva [Gandharvas] taught them speech; and Agni gave them the power to consume all things. Therefore, women are equal to [the gods of] the *niṣka* ornament.
73.08ab/ Brāhmaṇas are pure at their feet; cows are pure at their backs;
73.08cd/ goats and horses are pure at their mouths; women are pure in every part.
73.09ab/ Women are an incomparable means of purification; they are never defiled.
73.09cd/ For month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their misdeeds.
Those households which female relatives curse when they have not been honored perish on all sides, as if struck by a malevolent spell (kṛtyā).
Whether it be a wife or a mother, women are the source of men's very existence.
O ungrateful ones, how can there be any well-being for you who revile them both?
73.12ab/ In the scriptures, it is established that when husband and wife transgress [the rules], the fault is equal for both.
73.12cd/ Men do not observe this; therefore, in this matter, women are superior.
But for one who has violated his wife, he is purified by being bound outside with a donkey skin, its hair facing outward, for six months, while saying, "Give me alms."
Even after a hundred years, the underlying disposition toward passion does not depart;
in that regard, men turn back through lack of capacity, while women do so through fortitude.
73.15ab/ "Oh, what audacity on the part of the wicked who revile blameless women! 73.15cd/ Like thieves who are actually stealing, they cry out, 'Stop, thief! while they themselves are the thieves."
A man does not later regret those amorous acts which he performs in secret with passionate women.
Out of gratitude for his past kindness,
the woman embraces the lifeless bodies and enters the seven-tongued fire.
73.17a That man who possesses the enjoyment of a jewel among women, 73.17b even if he is currently penniless, is a lord of the earth in my eyes.
The essence of sovereignty consists of food and women;
everything else is merely firewood that fans the flames of the fire of craving.
The pleasure that comes from embracing a passionate woman endowed with the bloom of her first youth, whose soft voice is gently and sweetly cooed, and whose breasts press against one’s chest.
Therefore, it is not my intention that she should remain in the abode of Dhātṛ.

73.19a There, because of honoring those who are honored, serving those who are to be served by gods, sages, and *siddhas*, and by *cāraṇas*; 73.19b tell me, is there any happiness in the abode of Dhātṛ?
73.19d That which is practiced in secret, not with a woman.
73.20a From Brahmā down to a mere insect, this entire world is bound together by the union of male and female;
73.20b what shame is there in this, where even the Four-faced One [Brahmā] exists?
Even a lord was led astray by a young woman through greed.
Chapter 74: On the Means of Attaining Good Fortune 74.01a For one who possesses good fortune, every pleasure born of the mind is entirely real;
74.01b for another, it is merely a semblance, due to the dissociation of the mind from its object.
Even if she has traveled far away, a woman who conceives through the power of the mind bears a fetus that resembles that man.
Just as a stalk of a tree, having been broken and sown upon the earth, or a seed sown therein, does not become something else,
even so the self is born again in women.
74.02d There is some distinction in that case due to the application of the field.

The self moves together with the mind; the mind [moves] with the sense organ, and the sense organ with its own object—this is the rapid sequence. This very process is the union of the mind; what, then, is there that is unattainable for it?
Wherever the mind goes, there this self has gone.
This Self, residing within the self, is exceedingly subtle in the heart;
it is to be grasped by an unwavering mind through constant application.
Whatever one contemplates, that one attains identity with.
74.04d Therefore, young women have indeed gone to that which is most auspicious.
74.05ab/ Kindness alone is the cause of good fortune; conduct contrary to that leads to enmity.
74.05cd/ Through the employment of spells, herbs, and other fraudulent practices, many evils arise, not peace.
74.06ab/ Abandoning pride, one attains favor; pride brings about misfortune.
74.06cd/ One who is full of pride accomplishes his tasks only with great difficulty, whereas one who speaks pleasant words achieves them without effort.

74.07ab/ That is not true brilliance which consists in impulsive violence, nor is that speech which is unpleasant and uttered by the wicked. 74.07cd/ Those who, having brought their task to completion, remain free from arrogance— they are the truly brilliant, not those who boast.
74.08ab/ He who desires universal popularity and good fortune should speak of everyone’s virtues in their absence.
74.08cd/ He who speaks of another’s faults incurs many evils, even if they are non-existent.
74.09ab/ For the man who follows the practice of helping all, the world follows the practice of helping him all.
74.09cd/ That fame which one gains by providing aid to enemies in their misfortunes cannot be achieved by even a small amount of merit.
Just as fire increases all the more even when covered by grass, so too does a quality reach full growth;
yet he who desires to destroy another's virtues attains only the state of a wicked person.
Chapter 75: On the Science of Procreation (Kāndarpika).
If the blood is in excess, a female is born; if the semen is in excess, a male; but if the blood and semen are equal, a neuter is born.
Therefore, one should employ rejuvenative therapies (rasāyana) that promote the increase of semen.
The roof of the palace, the rays of the moon, honey with its blue lotuses, a beloved languid with intoxication,
the lute, amorous talk, and secret garlands— this collection is the snare of Love.
He who would eat equal parts of copper ore, honey, mercury, iron powder, *pathyā*, bitumen (*śilājatu*),
and ghee for twenty-one days, even if possessed by old age, [would become free from it].
Even at eighty years of age, he delights a woman as if he were a youth.
He who drinks boiled milk with the roots of *kapikacchū* does not suffer from wasting due to sexual indulgence;
nor does he who eats *māṣa* beans cooked in milk and clarified butter.
And six mouthfuls [of food], with milk as the after-drink.
75.05ab/ One who has many wives should drink the powder of vidārī, which has been repeatedly saturated and dried with its own juice; 75.05cd/ this should be taken with boiled milk mixed with sugar.
Having well-impregnated a powder with the fresh juice of *dhātrī* fruits, one should lick it mixed with honey, sugar, and clarified butter,
and subsequently drink milk according to one's digestive capacity.
A person may indulge in sensual pleasure to their heart's content and to their full satisfaction.
If a man desiring [success] repeatedly soaks sesame seeds with boiled goat's milk mixed with [the juice of] goat testicles,
eats them after they have been thoroughly dried, and drinks milk, [he will achieve his desire].
Furthermore, what does the sparrow do before him?
Those men who eat *ṣaṣṭika* rice with ghee mixed with black-gram soup,
and who drink milk afterwards during those nights, do not lie down with passion.
A preparation of ground *vidārī* and *ṣaṣṭika* rice, mixed with the roots of sesame, *aśvagandhā*, and *kapikacchu*,
When cooked, it becomes a *śaṣkulikā*, which is highly aphrodisiac.
If he consumes milk with *gokṣuraka*,
or eats the tubers of *vidārī*,
he will not suffer decline provided that it is digested by him.
If there is a sluggish digestive fire, this powder is for that purpose.
75.11ab/ Harītakī with ajamoda, salt, śṛṅgavera, and pippalī;
75.11cd/ taken as a powder with wine, buttermilk, tarala, or warm water, kindles the digestive fire of the abdomen.
He who eats food that is excessively sour, bitter, salty, or pungent, and who consumes meals consisting largely of alkaline substances and leafy greens,
