becomes deprived of sight, semen, and virility, and brings about many [ailments].
Just as an old man, even when he has obtained a young woman, resorts to various pretexts.
Chapter 76: On the Application of Perfumes.
Garlands, perfumes, incense, garments, ornaments, and the like do not grace one whose hair is white;
therefore, one should employ dyes for the hair just as one does with collyrium and ornaments.
In an iron vessel, having finely ground white cooked *kodrava* grains together with iron powder,
one should apply it to the head where the hair is white and sour.
Having applied [the paste], one should remain after wrapping it with fresh *arka* leaves.
When the second watch has passed,
having removed [the previous application], one should apply a paste of *āmalaka* to the head;
after covering it with leaves, in two watches [of time, it should be washed].
When washed, the head regains its blackness.
Afterwards, having removed the metallic and sour odor from his head with fragrant oils for bathing the head,
[he was honored] with various heart-pleasing perfumes and diverse incenses.
In the inner apartments, he should enjoy the pleasures of sovereignty.
76.05ab/ With equal parts of cinnamon, kuṣṭha, reṇu, nalikā, spṛkkā, rāsa, tagara, and bālaka,
mixed with keśara and patra, this is a head-bath suitable for a king.
76.06ab/ A powder consisting of mañjiṣṭhā, vyāghranakha, conch-shell, tvac, kuṣṭha, and juice,
when combined with oil and heated by the rays of the sun, produces that Campaka-scented oil (campakagandhitaila).
76.07a A fragrance made from equal parts of *patra*, *turuṣka*, *bāla*, and *tagara* kindles the god of love.
76.07b This same *bakula* [fragrance], when combined with *vyāma*, *kaṭukā*, and *ahiṅgu* incense, [is likewise effective].
76.07c With *kuṣṭha*, it acquires the scent of a blue lotus; when combined with *malaya*, the former becomes *campaka*.
It should be known that this consists of jasmine bark combined with atimuktaka and kustumburu.
76.08ab/ One part each of śatapuṣpā and kunduruka, half a part each of nakha and turuṣka;
76.08cd/ two parts of malaya and priyaṅgu—this is the fragrant incense to be burned with jaggery and nakha.
76.09ab/ Guggulu, bālaka, lākṣā, mustā, nakha, and śarkarā constitute an incense in due order.
76.09cd/ Another is a ball-incense (piṇḍadhūpa) made of māṃsī, bālaka, turuṣka, nakha, and candana.
With *harītakī*, conch-shell, *ghana*, and liquid, with jaggery and *utpala*, combined with *śailaka* and *mustaka*,
[the preparation] is increased sequentially starting from the first quarter-verse at the beginning of the new [chapter].
There are many enchanting incenses.

76.11a Four parts each of white mountain [rock] (*śvetaśaila*), *śaileya*, and *mustā*; 76.11b two parts of *śrīsarja*, as well as *nakha* and *guggulu*; 76.11c camphor and *bodha*, mixed with honey—this [is the incense].
This incense for kings is named *kopacchada*.

76.12ab. This powder, consisting of equal parts of cinnamon, uśīra, and patra, combined with half a part of sūkṣmailā, is the most excellent puṭavāsa (scented cloth) when awakened by musk and camphor.
76.13ab/ Ghanasāra, bālaka, śaileyaka, karpūra, uśīra, and nāgapuṣpa;
76.13cd/ vyāghranakha, spṛkkā, aguru, damanaka, nakha, tagara, and dhānya.
76.14ab/ From these four—karpūra, cola, and malaya—arranged according to one’s own desire;
76.14cd/ by means of one, two, three, or four parts, it becomes the "Ocean of Fragrance" (gandhārṇava).

Because of its extremely intense fragrance, one part of camphor must always be used with grains; less than that is not sufficient, and these two should not be given in proportions of two, three, or more.
76.16ab/ They should be fumigated in sequence with *śrī*, resin (*sarja*), jaggery (*guḍa*), and *nakha*, but not with the *piṇḍa* substances.
76.16cd/ Awakening (*bodha*) should be offered with musk (*kastūrikā*) combined with camphor (*karpūra*).
76.17ab/ Herein, there are four thousand and seventy thousand [verses].
76.17cd/ There are one hundred and twenty-seven thousand [verses] concerning perfumes.
76.18ab/ Each single part [of the ingredients] is joined with substances consisting of two, three, or four parts.
76.18cd/ In the same way, one prepares the "six-fragrance" (ṣaḍgandha) by using [ingredients] in two, three, or four parts.

76.19ab/ Just as there are twenty-four types of odor due to the combination of four substances for one [odor], 76.19cd/ so it is for the remaining ones as well; thus, the total sum here is ninety-six.
76.20ab/ When the group of sixteen substances is divided according to fourfold alternatives,
76.20cd/ there arise eighteen hundred and twenty combined.
Since the group is divided into ninety-six varieties and possesses four alternatives, therefore it should be multiplied by ninety-six; that is the number of fragrances.
They declare that the number of places, excluding the last, is obtained by adding each preceding term to the one before it,
having sequentially multiplied them according to the desired variations.
When one policy has been implemented, its withdrawal is another policy.
Aguru, patra, turuṣka, and śaileya consist of two, three, one, and eight parts respectively;
likewise, priyaṅgu, mustā, rasā, and keśa consist of five, eight, two, and three parts respectively.
76.24ab. One part each of spṛkkā, tvak, tagara, and māṃsī;
and seven, four, six, and one parts respectively of malaya, nakha, śrīka, and kunduru.
76.25ab/ Just as in the sixteen-fold tortoise-mixture (*kacchapuṭa*), so too when the four substances are combined;
76.25cd/ those eighteen parts which are here [constitute] the formulations beginning with fragrance (*gandha*) in this [mixture].

76.26ab. Perfumes mixed with *nakha*, *tagara*, and *turuṣka*, and awakened by *jātī*, camphor, and musk; 76.26cd. these perfumes, when fumigated with molasses and *nakha*, should be prepared as "all-auspicious" (*sarvatobhadra*).
In this place, there are many *pārijāta* trees, awakened by nutmeg, musk, and camphor, and sprinkled with honey from mango blossoms;
they are surrounded on four sides by those [trees] chosen at will.

76.28ab. With all incenses (or all formulations) here that are combined with *sarjarasa* and *śrīvāsaka*; 76.28cd. With those [incenses] devoid of *śrī* and *sarjarasa*, along with *bālaka* and cinnamon (*tvak*), there are the bath-pastes.
76.29ab/ Lodhra, uśīra, nata, aguru, mustā, patra, priyaṅgu, vanapathyā;
76.29cd/ having extracted three substances from the nine compartments by means of the kacchapuṭa method.
76.30ab/ Two parts of sandalwood and turuṣka, half a śukti of śatapuppā, and one-quarter part each of kaṭuka, hiṅgu, and jaggery for fumigation; these are the eighty-four kesara fragrances.
Having soaked tooth-sticks for seven days in cow urine mixed with powdered *harītakī*, one should then place them again in scented water.

76.32ab/ With cardamom, cinnamon, leaf-fragrance (*patra*), collyrium, honey, black pepper, nagakeśara, and kuṣṭha, scented water (*gandhāmbhas*) should be prepared. 76.32cd/ Having remained in this for some time, [it is ready].
76.33ab/ With nutmeg, cinnamon leaf, cardamom, and camphor, in proportions of one, four, one, and one part respectively;
76.33cd/ these should be powdered and dried by the rays of the sun.
The clarity of complexion on the face, radiance, purity of the mouth, its sweet fragrance,
and speech that is pleasant to the ear for one who serves [him].
They repeatedly fashion the pieces of wood that are our successive existences.
It kindles desire, reveals beauty, brings about good fortune and fragrance to the mouth;
it provides vigor and destroys diseases born of phlegm.
In this way, betel leaf produces these and other qualities.
When combined with betel nut in excess, the powder produces passion;
when the betel nut is excessive, it causes the destruction of passion; and when the powder is excessive, it causes a foul odor in the mouth.
It renders the fragrance even more excellent than the vessel itself.
76.37a That which is beneficial at night with an excess of betel leaves is likewise fruitful by day; 76.37b otherwise, the failure to perform what has been prescribed is merely a mockery.
76.37c [This is achieved] with *kakkola*, betel nuts, *lavalī* fruit, and *pārijāta*.
It makes the world fragrant with the joy of intoxication and filled with delight.
Chapter 77: On the Union of Man and Woman 77.01ab / With a concealed sword hidden within her braid, her own queen struck down Vidūratha.
77.01cd / And it is said that the queen, having become estranged, killed the King of Kāśī with an anklet smeared with poison.
77.02a Thus, those who are dispassionate produce faults; 77.02b what need is there for others to proclaim those things that take away life?
77.02c Therefore, men are either attached or detached by necessity.
Women must be scrutinized with great effort.
77.03a Their gestures reveal the affection born of love;
77.03b not the mere sight of their navels, arms, breasts, or ornaments;
77.03c nor the tucking up of garments or the loosening of hair.
77.03d Glances with side-long looks, accompanied by the knitting and trembling of the eyebrows.
77.04a Spitting loudly, boisterous laughter, leaping up from one's bed or seat; 77.04b Slapping the limbs, yawning, and requesting only a small amount of easily obtained things;
77.04c Embracing and kissing a child, and looking intently at her friend when she is facing her.
A sidelong glance when she has turned her face away, and scratching the ear while speaking of her virtues.
77.05a And one should recognize this woman by her affectionate gestures;
77.05b she speaks pleasant words and gives her own wealth;
77.05c upon seeing him, she rejoices, her anger having vanished.
One wipes away faults by proclaiming virtues.
77.06a Honoring that friend, being an enemy to his enemies, 77.06b mindfulness of what has been done, and freedom from dejection when away from home;
77.06c Sucking at the breasts and lips, and embracing.
77.06d Then, perspiration and kissing constitute the first application.
77.07a An absence of affectionate gestures, a frowning face, 77.07b turning away, and feigned forgetfulness; 77.07c lack of agitation, and being difficult to satisfy.
77.07d Hostility toward those [who are dear], lack of loving-kindness, and harsh speech.
Having touched or even merely looked [at him], she shakes her limbs; she displays pride and does not restrain him as he departs;
and at the end of the kiss, she wipes her face.
She who was previously asleep rises afterwards.
A female mendicant, a female renunciant, a slave-girl, a nurse, a young maiden, a dyer,
a garland-maker, a wicked woman, a female friend, a barber’s wife, and female messengers— [these are the types of women].
77.10ab/ Since female messengers are the cause of the destruction of a family, therefore, for the sake of increasing the lineage, fame, and honor, women must be protected from them with great effort.

77.11ab/ Staying out at night, wandering about, staying awake, making excuses for illness, visiting the houses of others, and looking at things [belonging to others]; 77.11cd/ as well as vices and festivals—these are the causes for appointments, and they must be guarded against.
At first, she neither desires nor abandons talk of love, being languid with a mixture of bashfulness;

in the middle, having cast aside shame, she becomes dejected with her face bowed by modesty; and finally, she performs a manifold representation of emotion, becoming once more full of earnest interest.
Having understood both the person and their innate nature, she attends to them with behaviors that are either weary or otherwise.
77.13a The virtues of women consist primarily of youth, beauty, dress, courtesy, discernment, and grace;
77.13c and among those endowed with such virtues, a woman is designated as a "jewel."
Women and other diseases are the afflictions of a clever man.
77.14a One whose body is smeared with impurities should not use vulgar words; 77.14b nor should one engage in conversation concerning censurable bodily parts;
77.14c nor should one recall other matters while staying in private.
For the mind is indeed the root of him whose form was consumed by Hara.
Exhaling her breath in harmony with that of her man, skilled in using her arm as a pillow and offering her breast,
she whose hair is fragrant, who is deeply attached when close at hand, who falls asleep after he has slept, and who awakens before him.
77.16ab/ Those women who are of a wicked nature and who cannot endure the times of friction should be avoided.
77.16cd/ Those whose blood is red, black, blue, yellow, or copper-colored are not praiseworthy.
77.17ab/ She who is habitually sleepy, has excessive blood and bile, or suffers from discharges;
77.17cd/ she who eats excessively, has perspiring limbs, disfigured body parts, short hair, or is covered with grey hairs.
That woman whose flesh trembles,
who has a large belly, and who makes a "khikkhimi" sound;
One should not engage in sexual union with those women who have been described as possessing inauspicious female characteristics.
Blood that resembles the blood of a hare, or resembles the juice of lac, or which becomes free from color when washed— that blood shall be considered pure.
That blood which, devoid of sound and sensation, ceases after three days,
becomes the embryo through union with a man, provided it is free from deliberation.
For three days, one should not indulge in bathing, garlands, or ointments, nor with women;
on the fourth day, one should bathe according to the instruction prescribed in the scriptures.

77.22ab. With those medicinal herbs for the Puṣya-bath that have been mentioned, mixed with water, one should bathe; 77.22cd. likewise, the mantra to be used here is the very same one that was specified there.
77.23ab. It is said that human males are born on even nights, while females are born on odd nights.
77.23cd. Those born on widely separated even nights are long-lived, handsome, and happy.
On the right side there is a man, on the left a woman; both are situated as twins.
That which has entered the middle of the belly should be understood as a neuter being.
When the benefics are situated in the quadrants (kendras) and the trines (trikoṇas),
and the Moon is in the ascendant conjoined with benefics, while the malefics are located in the third, eleventh, or sixth houses, one should set out on a journey.
And [he should observe] the union during conjunctions that result in male births.
During the fertile period, a man should by no means inflict wounds with his nails or teeth upon a woman;
the fertile period (*ṛtu*) lasts for sixteen days.
The first three nights there are not to be passed.
Chapter 78: On the Characteristics of Beds and Seats.
Since this treatise is useful for everyone at all times, I shall therefore describe the characteristics of beds and seats, especially for kings.
78.02ab/ Asana, spandana, candana, haridrā, suradāru, tindukī, and śāla; 78.02cd/ Or kāśmarya, añjana, padmaka, śāka, and śiṃśapā are auspicious.
78.03ab/ Those struck down by lightning, water, wind, or elephants; those made into nests by bees or birds;
78.03cd/ And those bound to sacred trees, in cremation grounds, on roads, or to tall, withered creepers.
Those trees that are thorny, those that grow at the confluence of great rivers,
those born in the abodes of gods, and those that fall toward the southern direction are not auspicious.
78.05ab/ From the use of beds and seats made from prohibited trees comes the destruction of the family.
78.05cd/ There arise diseases, fears, losses, and quarrels, as well as manifold misfortunes.
If the wood for the post should be one that has been previously cut, it must be examined at the commencement;
if a young boy climbs upon it, that post brings sons and cattle.

78.07ab/ Seeing white flowers, an elephant in rut, curd, unbroken rice, a full water-pot, jewels, 78.07cd/ and other auspicious things at the commencement [of an undertaking], it should be known that there is good fortune.
78.08ab/ A finger-measure (*aṅgula*) consists of eight barley-corns (*yava*), free from husks and attached to the belly.
78.08cd/ A great bed of one hundred such finger-measures, when prepared, leads to victory for kings.
That same [number] ninety, when reduced by six, twelve, and eighteen respectively,
shall be the [lifespans] of the king’s son, the minister, the commander of the army, and the domestic priest.
78.10ab/ Half of this, diminished by one-eighth, is declared by Viśvakarman as the width (viṣkambha).
78.10cd/ The height of the base (pāda), together with its belly (kukṣi) and head (śiras), is equal to one-third of the length.
78.11ab/ A couch made entirely of *śrīparṇī* wood bestows wealth.
78.11cd/ One made of *asanā* removes disease, while one made from the heartwood of *tinduka* brings about riches.
78.12ab/ That which is fashioned from pure śiṃśapā wood brings manifold prosperity.
78.12cd/ One made of sandalwood destroys enemies and bestows merit, fame, and long life.
A couch made of *padmaka* wood bestows long life, prosperity, learning, and wealth;
one fashioned from *śāla* wood brings auspiciousness, as does one constructed with *śākara*.
Seated upon a couch fashioned entirely of sandalwood, encased in gold, and adorned with various jewels, the king is honored even by the gods.
A tinduka tree joined with another [tree], nor a śiṃśapā tree, bestows auspicious fruit;
likewise, neither a śrīparṇa, nor a devadāru tree, nor even an asana tree [does so when thus joined].
When the Śāla and Śāka [planets] are conjoined with one another, they bestow auspicious results both separately and together;
likewise, the Haridraka and Kadamba [planets] are praised when both separate and combined.
78.17ab/ Every movement that is contrived is inauspicious, and one performed by a single person destroys life.
78.17cd/ A swing made of other wood besides *asan* quickly produces many defects.
78.18ab/ From the shaking of *amba*, *spandana*, and *candana* trees, auspicious results follow for the feet. 78.18cd/ A bed or seat made from young fruit-bearing trees yields all desired fruits.
78.19ab/ Ivory is declared to be the most excellent for use with all other types of wood.
78.19cd/ The procedure for crafting ornaments should be performed using highly praised ivory.
78.20ab. Having subtracted twice the circumference of the root of the tusk from its length, one should determine the remainder.
78.20cd. It is somewhat greater for those that do not frequent marshy lands, and slightly less for those that roam the mountains.
When auspicious marks such as the śrīvṛkṣa (or śrīvatsa), the vardhamāna, the parasol, the banner,
and the fly-whisk appear in their proper form upon the cutting [of the hair], one sees health, victory, increase of wealth, and happiness.

78.22ab/ In a mark resembling a weapon, there is victory; in a Nandyāvarta, the recovery of a lost region. 78.22cd/ In the case of a clod of earth (loṣṭa), however, there is the acquisition of a region previously held.
If a woman appears in the form of a water-pot (bhṛṅgāra), there is loss of wealth; if it rises up, there is the birth of a son.
By means of a jar (kumbha), one attains a treasure; and by a staff (daṇḍa), there is an obstacle to the journey.
78.24ab/ When the forms of chameleons, monkeys, and serpents appear, there will be famine, disease, and subjugation by enemies.
78.24cd/ When the forms of vultures, owls, crows, and hawks appear, there will be a pestilence among the people.
Furthermore, if there is a noose or a headless trunk (kabandha), there is death for the king and calamity for the people; if blood flows, it is likewise ill-omened.
If it is black, dark-brown, rough, or foul-smelling, misfortune occurs.
78.26ab/ A cut that is white, even, fragrant, and glossy brings auspicious results.
78.26cd/ Whatever cuts are inauspicious or auspicious [in other contexts], they yield the same fruits when applied to beds.

78.27ab/ In the joining of the pole, wood with its tip pointing clockwise is praised by the teachers. 78.27cd/ If the tip points in a single direction counter-clockwise, there will be danger arising from spirits.
By one foot being turned downward, there indeed occurs a deficiency of a limb;
by two, food is not digested; and by three or four, there is the affliction of being bound by exhaustion.
If there is a hollow or discolored knot at the top of the foot, there will be disease;
if there is a "water-pot" (kumbha) mark on the foot or that same knot, there will be abdominal disease.
If a mark is made on the shank below the pitcher, it causes fear;
if it is made on the lower part of that [shank], it causes the loss of wealth.
78.31ab/ That knot on the hoof of animals which causes pain has been described.
78.31cd/ And one situated at the third part of the shaft and the head-piece would not be auspicious.
Niṣkuṭa, Kolākṣa, Sūkaranayana, Vatsanābha, Kālaka, and another called Dhundhuka— this is said to be the summary of the hollows (chidras).
78.33ab/ Hollow like a jar in the middle, narrow at the mouth, and with a small opening; 78.33cd/ the hole is the size of a flat bean, dark blue, and shaped like the eye of a jujube fruit.
78.34ab/ That which is shaped like a boar’s eye, uneven, discolored, and one and a half finger-joints long;
78.34cd/ which curls to the left, is split, and measures [only] a single joint—this is called the *vatsanābha*.
That which is known as *kālakasaṃjña*, black, and called *dhundhuka*,
when it is split open and has the color of wood, is not declared to be so sinful.
In the [asterism] named Niṣkuṭa, there is loss of wealth; in Kolekṣaṇa, the destruction of the family;
in Sūkaraka, fear of weapons; and in the one called Vatsanābha, fear of disease.
A hole known as *kālaka* or *dhundhuka*, or one pierced by insects, does not bring good fortune;
likewise, wood that is entirely full of knots is not auspicious in any respect.

A [house] made with a single tree brings wealth; one constructed with two trees brings even greater wealth. With three, it increases one's progeny; with four, it brings prosperity and preeminent fame.
78.39ab/ One who lies down there in a bed constructed from five trees meets his death;
78.39cd/ if it is fashioned from six, seven, or eight trees, there will be the destruction of the family.
Chapter 79: Examination of Jewels.
Through an auspicious jewel, there is prosperity for kings; through an inauspicious one, misfortune.
Therefore, those who know [the matter] must examine the divine power residing in jewels.
79.02ab. The term "jewel" (ratna) is applied to elephants, horses, women, and so forth, by virtue of their own specific qualities.
79.02cd. However, in this context, the reference is to stone-jewels, beginning with the diamond (vajra).
79.03ab. Others say that the jewels were produced from Dadhīci by force from the Daitya; 79.03cd. some say that the variety of stones arises from the inherent nature of the earth.
79.04ab/ Vajra, indranīla, marakata, karketara, padmarāga, and rudhira;
79.04cd/ Vaiḍūrya, pulaka, vimalaka, rājamaṇi, sphaṭika, and śaśikānta.
79.05ab/ Those known as saugandhika, gomedaka, śaṅkha, mahānīla, and puṣparāga; 79.05cd/ as well as brahmamaṇi, jyotīrasa, sasyaka, pearl, and coral.

79.06ab/ That from the banks of the Veṇā is pure and has the luster of a śirīṣa flower; that from Kauśala is copper-red; 79.06cd/ that from Saurāṣṭra is reddish-brown; and the diamond from Saurpāraka is black.
Slightly copper-colored, it is found in the Himalayas; resembling the *vallapa* flower, it is yellowish in Kaliṅga; and that which originates in Pauṇḍra is dark.
The [disc] of Indra is six-cornered and white; that of Yama is black and shaped like a serpent’s mouth;
and that of Viṣṇu resembles the trunk of a plantain tree—such is the configuration of all [the discs].
The water element (vāruṇa) is like the private parts of a woman and resembles the *karṇikāra* flower;
the fire element (*hautabhuj*) has the shape of a *śṛṅgāṭaka* and resembles the eyes of a tiger.
79.10ab/ And that which is of the nature of wind is declared to be like barley and to have the luster of an aśoka flower.
79.10cd/ The source of origin is threefold: from a stream, from a mine, or as scattered [in the earth].
Red and yellow are auspicious for kṣatriyas; white is for the twice-born (brāhmaṇas);
that made of śirīṣa wood is for vaiśyas; and for śūdras, one resembling a dark sword is recommended.

Eight white mustard seeds make one grain of rice; twenty grains of rice weigh as much as two hundred thousand [units] when measured on a scale, and this value is halved for each subsequent reduction by two.
79.13ab/ Less by one-third, one-half, and one-quarter; and one-third, one-fifth, and one-sixteenth;
79.13cd/ as well as one-twenty-fifth, one-hundredth, and one-thousandth.
79.14ab/ A diamond that cannot be pierced by any substance, which is light, floats on water, and is radiant;
79.14cd/ and which resembles lightning, fire, and the bow of Indra—that diamond is said to be for one's benefit.
79.15ab/ Those [arrows] marked with crow-feet, flies, hair, or minerals, pierced by gravel,
79.15cd/ those with double-edged points, smeared, turbid, trembling, or shattered— these are not auspicious.
And those which have tips crushed like bubbles, flattened like axes, or as long as a *vāsī* fruit—
for all of these, an eighth part of their value shall be deducted as a loss.
79.17a Some authorities maintain that not even a trace of a thunderbolt (vajra) should be worn;
79.17b those who know the truth desire it for women seeking sons.
79.17c That which is situated like a *śṛṅgāṭaka* or a triple-pulverized grain (*tripuṭa-dhānyaka*)—
And that which resembles the hips brings good fortune to those desiring sons.

A thunderbolt characterized by inauspicious signs brings about the destruction of one's kinsmen, wealth, and life; however, for kings, it is auspicious, destroying the fear of lightning, poison, and enemies, and bestowing great enjoyment.
Chapter 80: On the Characteristics of Pearls.
80.01ab/ Pearls are produced from elephants, serpents, oyster shells, conch shells, clouds, bamboos, whales, and boars.
80.01cd/ Among these, the pearl born from the oyster shell is the most excellent and abundant.
The Siṃhalaka, Pāralaukika, Saurāṣṭrika, Tāmraparṇī,
Pāraśava, Kaubera, Pāṇḍyavāṭaka, and Haima— these are the eight mines.
Those that have many shapes, are glossy, resemble swans, originate from Siṃhala, are thick,
slightly copper-colored, white, and free from dark spots are called *tāmra*.
80.04ab/ Black, white, yellow, and sandy-colored [stones] are for the next world and are uneven.
80.04cd/ Those from Saurāṣṭra are neither too large nor too small, and resemble fresh butter.
80.05ab/ Luminous, brilliant, heavy, and possessing exceedingly great qualities are the *pāraśava* [iron] swords;
80.05cd/ while those that are light, worn-out, resembling curd, large, and even having a double shape are of gold.
80.06ab/ That which is variegated, black-and-white, light, and possesses the proportions and brilliance of Kubera is from Kaubera.
80.06cd/ The powders of nimba fruit, tripuṭa, and dhānyaka should be those produced in Pāṇḍyavāṭa.
The [halo] belonging to Viṣṇu is dark like the flax flower; that of Indra resembles the moon;
that of Varuṇa is like yellow orpiment; and that which has Yama as its deity is black.
That which is copper-colored like a ripe pomegranate seed or a guñjā berry has Vāyu as its presiding deity;
that which possesses the luster of a smokeless fire or a lotus is to be known as belonging to Agni.
80.09ab/ Forty-three hundred [paṇas] are declared to be the price for one [piece] weighing four māṣakas, endowed with the quality of brilliance.
80.09cd/ These are stated to be kārṣāpaṇas as the value for that which possesses the quality of luster.
From that, by a reduction of one *māṣaka* at each stage, there are thirty-two, twenty, thirteen,
eight hundred, three hundred, and fifty-three.
80.11ab. "One hundred and thirty-five" means four *kṛṣṇalas* valued at ninety [paṇas].
80.11cd. Three and a half *guñjās* are the standard form of currency valued at seventy [paṇas].
The price for three guñjas of superior quality is fifty rūpakas;
for thirty-five rūpakas, it is three guñjas less half a guñja.
80.13ab/ A tenth part of a pala is a dharaṇa; if thirteen beautiful pearls [weigh that much], 80.13cd/ The price fixed is thirty-five rūpakas as the total value.
The sixteenfold [set] consists of two hundred and twenty; the twenty-fivefold [set] consists of one hundred and seventy;
that which is held as the twenty-fivefold [set] consists of one hundred and thirty.
80.15ab / Worth thirty or seventy [paṇas], or worth four hundred and fifty;
80.15cd / Or sixty minus five, or a dharaṇa worth five times eight [forty].
80.16ab/ That [amount] of one hundred and thirty, minus eighty pearls, is reduced by five rūpakas.
80.16cd/ Two, three, four, and five hundred; twelve, six, five, and three.
80.17ab. *pikkā*, *piccā*, *arghā*, *ardhā*, *ravaka*, and *siktha* are the names for the first thirteen [units].
80.17cd. Beyond those, the names for the [units] up to eighty are *nigara* and *cūrṇa*.

80.18ab/ This price has been proclaimed for those endowed with these qualities and maintained by the earth. 80.18cd/ For those of inferior quality, it should be calculated proportionately; a reduction must be made.

80.19ab/ For those that are black, white, yellow, or copper-colored, even if they are slightly irregular; 80.19cd/ [the value] is reduced by one-third for those that are irregular or yellow, and reduced by a sixth part for those that are pale.

Those born of the Airāvata lineage on the days of Puṣya, Śravaṇa, the Moon, or the Sun, as well as those born during the northern course [of the sun] or during an eclipse of the Sun or the Moon, are auspicious elephants.
80.21ab. From them, it is said, pearls are produced within water-filled shells;
80.21cd. they are numerous, large in size, of various shapes, and endowed with luster.
No price should be set for these, nor should they be pierced; for they are endowed with great luster. Worn by kings, they bring about the victory of sons, health, and great purification.
80.23ab/ At the base of the tusk is the boar-stone (vārāha), which possesses the luster of the moon and is endowed with many virtues.
80.23cd/ That which comes from the Timi fish, the Matsyākṣī, and the elephant is large, purifying, and possessed of many virtues.
Born like a rain-stone (diamond) and fallen from the seventh wind-sphere,
it is said to be carried through the sky by divine beings— possessing the luster of lightning and produced from the clouds.
The pearls found at the edge of the hoods of those serpents born of the lineages of Takṣaka and Vāsuki, who can travel at will, are glossy and possess a blue luster.
If it rains suddenly upon an auspicious region of the earth while [the water] remains in a silver vessel, that should be known as originating from the Nāgas.
Worn by kings, the serpent-gem removes misfortune and poison, destroys enemies, spreads fame, and grants victory even when its value has not been formally appraised.
That which resembles camphor or crystal, being flat and uneven, should be known as originating from bamboo;
that which originates from a conch shell resembles the moon, being circular, radiant, and beautiful.
80.29ab / Those produced from conch-shells, timi-fish, bamboo, elephants, boars, serpents, and clouds are not to be pierced [or: are beyond medical treatment].
80.29cd / And because of their immeasurable qualities, their value has not been specified in the treatise.
All these [omens] possess great virtues; they bring about sons, wealth, good fortune, and fame,
and they destroy the misfortune and grief of kings.
Pearls grant all desired wishes.
The *surabhūṣaṇa* consists of one thousand and eight vines, each four cubits long;
the *vijayacchanda* by name is half that length, following the *inducchanda* meter.
A *hāra* consists of one hundred and eight strings; *devacchanda* consists of eighty-one;
an *ardhahāra* consists of eight times eight (sixty-four); and a *raśmikalāpa* consists of ninety-six.
A *guccha* consists of thirty-two [verses], while one called an *ardhaguccha* is said to consist of twenty;
a *māṇavaka* consists of sixteen, and an *ardhamāṇavaka* consists of twelve.
80.34ab/ That which is known as *mandarasa* consists of eight [strings]; the *pañcalatā* and the *hāraphalaka* have been described.
80.34cd/ A *hasta* consists of twenty-seven pearls; this is called the *nakṣatramālā*.
80.35ab/ That which is joined with intermediate jewels, or has jeweled steps with golden beads;
80.35cd/ and has a swaying jewel in its center—that should be known as the *cāṭukāra* (the flatterer).
80.36a That which is called a *ekāvalī* consists of a desired number [of beads],
80.36b measuring one cubit (*hasta*) and devoid of gems; 80.36c but that which is joined with a gem in the middle [is also so called].
80.36d "It is called a *yaṣṭi* by those who know ornaments."
Chapter 81: Characteristics of Padmarāga and Other Gems The origin of the *padmarāga* (ruby) is from *saugandhika*, *kuruvinda*, and *sphaṭika*.
Those born from *saugandhika* possess the luster of a bee, collyrium, a lotus, or the juice of the *jambu* fruit.
Those originating from kuruvinda are variegated and dull in luster because they are pierced by mineral ores;
those originating from crystal are radiant, multicolored, and pure.
81.03ab/ Glossy, radiant, clear, luminous, heavy, and well-proportioned;
81.03cd/ internally luminous and intensely colored—these are the qualities of all precious gems.
81.04ab/ Tawny, dull in luster, streaked with lines, containing mineral inclusions, fractured, 81.04cd/ poorly pierced, unattractive, and gritty— these are the defects of gems.

81.05ab/ A gem that has the color of a bee, a peacock’s neck, or the flame of a lamp, and which belongs to serpents— 81.05cd/ that which is found upon the head of a *kika* should be known as priceless (*anargheya*).
81.06a That lord of men who bears it shall never suffer any afflictions caused by poison or disease;
81.06b and in his kingdom, the god shall constantly pour down rain.
And by the power of that jewel, he destroys his enemies.
Twenty-six thousand palas are the weight of a single *maṇi* of ruby;
twenty thousand are prescribed for a ruby weighing three *karṣas*.
For one *karṣa* of twelve *palas*, which is half a *pala*, the price is six thousand;
and for that which is held at eight *māṣakas*, the price is three thousand.
81.09ab/ Four māṣakas are worth one hundred and ten [paṇas], while two [māṣakas] are worth five hundred [paṇas].
81.09cd/ The price for those with qualities inferior or superior [to these standards] should be determined by interpolation.
81.10ab/ For one deficient in color, the value is half; for one deficient in brilliance, the value is an eighth part.
81.10cd/ One with few good qualities and many defects receives only a twentieth part of the value.
81.11ab/ One may obtain [a ruby] that is smoky-grey, full of flaws, and possessing very few good qualities for two hundred parts.
81.11cd/ Thus has the value of the *padmarāga* been declared by the ancient teachers.
Chapter 82: On the Characteristics of Emeralds 82.01ab:
An emerald that possesses the luster of a parrot’s wing, a plantain leaf, or a śirīṣa flower, and is endowed with excellent qualities, 82.01cd:
is ordained for men when used in rites for the gods and ancestors; it bestows exceedingly auspicious results.
Chapter 83: On the Characteristics of Lamps.
A lamp that turns counter-clockwise, has sooty rays, emits sparks, and is small in size, quickly goes out even when provided with pure oil and a wick.
A lamp that makes a sound and trembles indicates evil;
one whose flames are scattered and which is beset by moths and wind goes to destruction.
A lamp with a compact form, a long body, free from flickering,
radiant, silent, beautiful, moving clockwise, and possessing the luster of beryl or gold,
swiftly reveals prosperity for a very long time.
And that which is raised up and shines for a long time—
this remaining characteristic should be applied according to the appropriate logic, just like the characteristics of fire.
Chapter 84: On the Characteristics of Tooth-sticks (Dantakāṣṭha-lakṣaṇādhyāya).
84.01a There are thousands of types of tooth-sticks, distinguished as creepers (vallī), climbing plants (latā), shrubs (gulma), and trees (taru); 84.01b by means of which [these] tooth-sticks exist.
The results [of the mantras] should now be stated; however, lest there be an excessive prolixity regarding them, I shall therefore describe those that grant all desires.
One should not eat tooth-sticks that have not been used before,
nor those accompanied by leaves,
nor those with an even number of nodes, nor those that are split.
Nor [should one eat] those that are dried on top, nor those without their bark.

In the *vaikaṅkata*, *śrīphala*, and *kāśmarī* trees, there is the splendor of Brahmā; in the *kṣematara* tree, there are excellent wives; in the *vaṭa* tree, there is prosperity; and in the *arka* tree, there is abundant luster.
The sons [of the sage] are virtuous toward the *madhūka* tree (or *kakubha*), and they hold it dear.

If it falls on a *śirīṣa* or a *karañja*, there is prosperity; likewise, if on a *plakṣa*, the desired success of one's aims shall be attained. If it falls on a *jāti* tree, one attains honor among the people.
They say that preeminence resides in the Aśvattha tree.
Health and long life are obtained from the *badarī* and *bṛhatī*;
increase in sovereignty from the *khadira* and *bilva*;
and desired wealth is found in the *atimuktaka*.
He attains those very same [qualities] again in the Kadamba [world].
84.06a Under the *nīpa* (or *nimba*) tree there is the attainment of wealth; under the *karavīra*, the acquisition of food.
84.06b Under the *bhāṇḍīra* there is likewise abundant food.
84.06c Under the *śamī* one destroys enemies, and so too under the *arjuna*.
And when it is Śyāmā, there is the destruction of enemies alone.
They say that in the *śāla*, the *aśvakarṇa*, the *bhadradāru*,
and also the *āṭarūṣaka*,
one attains favor from people everywhere.
With *priyaṅgu*, *apāmārga*, *jambu*, and *dāḍima*.
Facing either north or east,
having placed his desire in his heart as he wishes for a year, he should eat while seated comfortably and without censuring [the food].
Having washed it, one should discard it in a clean place.
That which falls facing [the observer], situated in a calm direction, or stands upright, is auspicious and exceedingly beautiful;
otherwise, it is declared to be a bringer of inauspiciousness.
And it makes even stale food delicious.
Chapter 85: On Omens from Birds That which Ṛṣabha proclaimed from the treatises of Śakra, Śukra, Vāgīśa, Kapiṣṭhala, Garutmant, Bhāguri, and Devala.
Having observed the opinion of Bhāradvāja, the King of Avanti, Śrī Dravyavardhana, the great king and sovereign over kings, spoke.
Whatever is the opinion of the Seven Sages, both in the refined (Sanskrit) and the vernacular (Prakrit) languages, and whatever has been stated by Garga and many other authors on expeditions;
Having seen those [works], Varāhamihira, out of affection for his disciples, composed this Compendium of All Omens (Sarvaśākunasamgraha) as a supreme means of knowledge.
85.05ab/ The auspicious or inauspicious karma performed by men in other previous births,
85.05cd/ that [karma] the omen announces as it reaches its fruition for those who are traveling.
85.06ab/ Those that frequent villages, forests, water, land, the sky, or heaven, and those that move by day or by night;
85.06cd/ They are to be understood as male, female, or neuter according to their cries, gait, appearance, or speech.
85.07ab/ Because they do not abide as distinct universals, their manifestation is not perceived.
85.07cd/ Regarding the description of the general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), these two verses were composed by the Sage.
85.08ab/ Those men whose shoulders are thick, elevated, and well-spaced, who have broad necks and fine chests,
85.08cd/ and whose voices are low and deep, possess steady prowess.
Those women who have slender chests, heads, and necks, and possess subtle mouths, feet, and gait, and who speak with constant gentleness— other than these, one is a eunuch.

85.10ab/ One should learn from the world itself about the movements of villages, forests, and so forth. 85.10cd/ Desiring to be concise, I shall speak only for the purpose of providing a general outline of the journey.
85.11ab/ One should designate oneself as the one to be protected in the army, and the king as the deity in the city;
85.11cd/ In a caravan, the leader is the one to be designated; in a group of equals, the one superior by birth, learning, or age should be chosen.
85.12ab/ In the directions where the sun has departed, arrived, or is about to arrive, the results are likewise [of those three types].
85.12cd/ Those [directions] are respectively burning, smoking, and blazing; the others beyond them are tranquil.
85.13ab One should predict that the auspiciousness of those [planets] is equal to that of the fifth direction throughout the three periods of time.
85.13cd For the two remaining directions, one should declare the auspicious or inauspicious results according to their proximity.
85.14ab/ [One should declare] swift [results] from those situated near or in low ground, and after a long time from those situated high or far away;
85.14cd/ and likewise, one should state the result again according to the increase or destruction of the location.
85.15ab/ A planet is illuminated by the gods according to the sequence of the moment (kṣaṇa), lunar day (tithi), asterism (uḍu), wind, and sun;
85.15cd/ it is illuminated by its actions according to its motion, position, house (bhāva), tone, and activity.
Thus, although peaceful in ten ways, he who subsists on grass and fruit is gentle;
one who eats meat and impure substances is fierce; and one who eats mixed food is known as "mixed."
85.17ab/ Those situated on auspicious and pleasing sites such as mansions and palaces,
85.17cd/ And those on trees with sweet, milky sap, fruit, and flowers, are the most excellent.
85.18ab/ At their respective times, those moving on land, in water, and as nocturnal creatures are strong;
85.18cd/ they should be known as neuter, female, and male, and among these, they become stronger in successive order.

85.19ab/ Those endowed with speed, noble birth, strength, position, joy, courage, and voice; 85.19cd/ And those who are favorable in their own domain—these are [the favorable]; those lacking these qualities are to be avoided.
Kukkuṭa, ibha, pirilya, śikhi, vañjula,
chikkarā, balina, siṃhanāda, and kūṭapūri are located in the east.
Jackals, owls, hārītas, crows, koka birds, bears, and piṅgalās, as well as the cooing of pigeons and other harsh, wailing sounds from the south; 85.21.
85.22ab/ Cows, hares, curlews, woolly beasts, swans, cranes, and francolins;
85.22cd/ Cats, festivals, musical instruments, songs, and laughter—these belong to Varuṇa.
The hundred-petaled lotus, the deer, the rat, the wild animal, the single-hoofed horse, and the cuckoo;
the blue jay, the porcupine, the auspicious proclamation, the bell, and the conch—these are the sounds of water.
One who is domestic should not be taken when dwelling in the forest, nor one who is wild when established in a village;
one who roams by day should not be taken at night, nor one who roams by night during the day.

85.25ab/ Those birds that are terrified by being afflicted with dual diseases, those desiring quarrels or meat, those separated by a river, or those that are intoxicated— nowhere should such omens be accepted.
The Rohita deer, horse, goat, *vāleya*, *kuraṅga*, camel, antelope, and rabbit are known to be fruitless in the winter; likewise, the crow and the cuckoo are fruitless in the spring.

85.27ab/ However, in Bhādrapada, wild boars, dogs, wolves, and the like are not to be taken; 85.27cd/ water-fowl, fish-eaters, cattle, and cranes [are taken] in Śrāvaṇa, as are elephants and the cātaka bird in Bhādrapada.
85.28ab/ Tigers, bears, monkeys, leopards, buffaloes, and those that dwell in holes;
85.28cd/ these, as well as all children and non-human beings, are known to be fruitless during the winter.
Situated in three divisions between the directions of Indra (East) and Anala (South), the Superintendent of the Treasury, the Fire-attendants, and those devoted to austerity are stationed clockwise.

An artisan, a mendicant, a naked woman, and one who takes refuge in the law of the outcaste (mātaṅga) or the cowherd (gopa) appear in the intermediate directions between Yama and Agni; and beyond those as well, there are others who likewise rely on such laws.
Between the directions of Nairṛtī and Vāruṇī (the southwest and west) are women, childbirth, and thieves;
between Vāyavyā (the northwest) and the west are liquor-sellers, fowlers, and violent men.
85.32ab. After that, one who destroys poison, a cowherd, and a fraudulent knower;
85.32cd. then a wealthy man, an oculist, and after him a garland-maker.
The Vaiṣṇava and the Caraka, who is devoted to the protection of horses—
thus, thirty-two divisions are declared, including those from the eastern directions.
The king, the prince, the leader, the envoy, the merchant, the spy, the twice-born,
and the royal superintendent— these, beginning with the eastern direction, are Kṣatriyas and others situated in the four quarters.
Whether one is walking or standing, in whichever direction a bird cries while situated, a meeting with someone from that direction is to be predicted.
85.36ab/ Broken, terrifying, feeble, distressed, harsh, emaciated, and shattered—such sounds are not desired; 85.36cd/ Auspicious sounds are those that are calm, joyful, and full of natural vitality.
The jackal, the *śyāmā*, the *ralā*, the *chucchu*, the *piṅgalā*, the house-lizard, the sow, and the cuckoo— those with masculine names [are auspicious] when appearing on the left.
The female-voiced *bhāsa*, *bhaṣaka*, monkey, *śrīkarṇa*, and *dhikkaras*;
as well as the peacock, *śrīkaṇṭha*, *pippīka*, *ruru*, and hawk—these are auspicious when on the right.
The sounds of lion-roars, hand-claps, "Auspicious Day" chants, songs, conchs, and water-splashing;
the study of the Vedas accompanied by musical instruments; and other auspicious voices like those of men, as well as those like those of women.
The *grāmas* of Madhyama-ṣaḍja and Gāndhāra are auspicious;
furthermore, the notes Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, Gāndhāra, and Ṛṣabha are beneficial.

85.41ab/ Among those seen crying out, the peacock, the goat, and the peacock-feathered [peacock], 85.41cd/ as well as the mongoose and the blue jay, are auspicious; however, the chameleon portends evil when it appears in front.
The mention of the jāhaka, snake, hare, boar, and iguana is auspicious; however, the sound or the sight of monkeys and bears is not desired, nor is it favorable when they appear in opposition.
85.43ab/ Animals such as the mongoose and birds are auspicious when moving to the right;
85.43cd/ but the blue jay and the mongoose are auspicious on the left, according to Bhṛgu, in the afternoon.
The chikkara, the kūṭapūra, and the pirilī are auspicious when moving to the right during the day;
however, fanged animals and those that dwell in holes are always considered auspicious when moving to the left.

85.45ab/ When the horse is excellent and dark-colored in the east, and when there is a corpse and meat in the south; 85.45cd/ When a maiden and curd are in the west, and cows, Brahmins, and virtuous men are in the north.
85.46ab/ A net, a horse, and feet are not desired in the east; the south brings blows from weapons.
85.46cd/ In the west, liquor and eunuchs; and in the north, a rogue, a seat, and a plough.

In matters concerning action, association, battle, entry, and the search for lost objects, one should take the planets situated in the *yāna* (vehicle) and *vyasta* (opposite) positions; the specific details regarding this will be stated hereafter.

85.48ab/ Deer, ruru-deer, and monkeys are to be taken as [auspicious] when setting out during the day; 85.48cd/ and the blue jay, vañjula-birds, and cocks [are auspicious] in the first part of the day.
In the latter part of the night, the Naptṛkā, Ulūka, and Piṅgalā—
all of them being reversed— should be understood as belonging to women traveling in caravans.
85.50ab/ It should be observed when seeing the king, as well as upon entering [a city], just as at the time of departure;
85.50cd/ and also when entering mountains or forests, and when plunging into rivers.

Those two [planets] which are auspicious when situated on the left and right are, when situated at the front and rear, called *parigha*; when blazing during an action, they lead to the destruction of the traveler.
But those two very birds, with their cries and movements stilled according to their respective portions,
are known as the "Bird-Door" (śakunadvāra) for the accomplishment of one's purpose.
85.53ab Some, however, desire a "bird-gate" (śakunadvāra) formed by birds of a single species stationed on both sides, 85.53cd whose movements are calm and whose cries are auspicious.
If one person dismisses [the omen] while another prohibits it, that conflict is inauspicious for the traveler; whichever [view] is stronger should be accepted.
Having first been one who enters, he should again become one who departs;
this indicates success with ease through the entry, whereas the opposite of that indicates the reverse.
If that very same bird, having first flown away, then returns and obstructs [the traveler],
it foretells for the traveler the death of an enemy, or a riot, or even disease.
85.57ab/ But birds that fly to the left are "blazing" (dīpta) and announce danger.
85.57cd/ A blazing bird at the commencement of an undertaking brings fear at the end of the year.
85.58ab/ According to their sequence, the lunar day (tithi), wind (vāyu), sun (arka), asterism (bha), position (sthāna), movement (ceṣṭā), and brilliance (dīpta) [are considered];
85.58cd/ they become sources of fear for wealth, the army, strength, the limbs, desired objects, and actions respectively.
When [the quarters] are illuminated by the roar of clouds, there is danger from wind;
when they are illuminated at both twilights, they portend the danger of an uprising of weapons.
85.60ab/ Those situated on funeral pyres, hair, or skulls bring about death, imprisonment, and slaughter;
85.60cd/ those standing on thorny wood or ashes cause quarrels, exhaustion, and suffering.

85.61ab/ Birds situated on dry land, stones, or barren ground cause either failure or fear; 85.61cd/ if they are blazing, they produce these results, but if they are calm, their effects are merely palliative.
85.62ab/ One should know that [the two types of sounds] which cause the removal [of obstacles] and the bringing [of provisions] bestow non-attainment and attainment respectively.
85.62cd/ Crying from its place, it indicates a journey; otherwise, it foretells arrival.

85.63ab/ There is quarrel when [the planets] are strong by tone (*svara*), and conflict when they are strong by position (*sthāna*). 85.63cd/ Having placed a high [tone] first and a low one afterwards causes harm (*doṣa*).

85.64ab. Roaring in a single location while blazing, it causes the destruction of a village within seven days. 85.64cd. For cities, countries, and kings, [the effects occur] after six months, half a year, or a year.
85.65ab. All such [omens] bring about famine; they devour the flesh of their own kind.
They should be free from snakes, mice, cats, and thick-haired creatures.
Those who engage in sexual intercourse with other species are subject to rebirth in lower realms;
this is excepted only for the production of mules and for the non-procreative sexual acts of humans.
There will be dangers of imprisonment and blows caused by [planets] situated in the feet, thighs, and head;
and there will be afflictions from hunger, rain, and disease for those who eat young grass, water, meat, and grain.
85.68ab/ And from those who are cruel, fierce, corrupted by faults, and who have served as high officials or kings;
85.68cd/ and after a long time, there is the arrival of those men from the directions beginning with the radiant ones (the southeast).
He shall possess substantial wealth and be powerful; there will be an acquisition of property for him who possesses substance.
He is radiant, has a downward gaze, is gentle in nature, yet performs cruel deeds.

85.70ab/ A bird situated in a diagonal direction (vidiś) that is bright and called out to by one standing on the left [side] indicates the abduction of a woman; 85.70cd/ its origin is declared according to the direction [indicated by the bird].
A cry that is calm when uttered by one who is ablaze with the fifth note brings victory;
it causes the arrival of people from various directions, whereas its opposite produces faults.
Moving to the left or the right, the middle [cry] foretells danger for oneself and others; all of these, when crying out together in unison, announce death.

85.73ab/ The arrival of elephants, horses, and charioteers is indicated by the tips, middles, and bases of trees; 85.73cd/ the arrival of men, boats, and palanquins is indicated by the tips that are occupied by long lotuses.
85.74ab. Or, when [the moon] is situated in the Śakaṭa (Cart) configuration, elevated, in its own shadow, or joined with a parasol;
85.74cd. [The result occurs] after one, three, five, or seven days, in the first and subsequent intervals.
The lords of the directions starting from the east are, in order: the Lord of the Gods (Indra), Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Pavana (Vāyu), Indu (Soma), and Saṅkara (Śiva).
These are males for the cardinal directions and females for the intermediate directions.
85.76ab/ There should be [images of] trees, palms, bamboo, garments, lotuses, arrows, shields, and leather straps;
85.76cd/ these are to be placed within those thirty-two divisions of the circle of the directions.
85.77ab/ The sounds of physical exertion, the warbling of peacocks, quarreling, water, fetters, mantras, and the lowing of cattle;
85.77cd/ And the colors—red, yellow, black, and white—are located in the corners, while those that are mixed occupy the intermediate directions.
85.78a A mark, a banner, a burnt place, or a cremation ground; 85.78b a cave, water, a mountain, and the sound of a sacrifice— 85.78c one should recognize fears arising from association with these.
Or other places not previously specified.
Among women, those who are of large stature, young girls, deformed, foul-smelling, or dressed in blue garments; those who are wicked, excessively tall, or widows— these are the ones [to be avoided].
Those who contemplate union would be mere observers of the funeral pyre.
85.80 In inquiries concerning women distressed by silver or gold, or those seeking refuge in sheep, vehicles, sacrifices, or herds of cattle;
and [omens] known as the Nyagrodha, the Red Tree (Raktataru), the Rodhra, and the Kīcaka—
85.80d Mango trees, as well as *khadira*, *bilva*, and *nagārjuna* trees.

Chapter 86: The Inner Discourse on Ominous Birds (Śākune 'ntaracakrādhyāya) If a bird cries out in the eastern direction (Aindrī) when it is propitious, it announces the arrival of someone associated with a king;
[the bird] also indicates honor, gain, and the acquisition of jewels, gems, and wealth.
Immediately following that direction, there shall be the arrival of gold and the accomplishment of desired objects;
in the third division, there shall be the acquisition of weapons, wealth, betel nuts, and fruits.
In the fourth house, there is the sight of an affectionate Brahmin as well as one who maintains the sacred fires;
in a corner, there is the appearance of dependents and mendicants, and the acquisition of gold and iron.
86.04ab/ To the south of the first [asterism], there is the sight of a prince and the attainment of one's desired success.
86.04cd/ Beyond that, the acquisition of a woman’s virtue and the obtaining of mustard seeds and barley are also declared.
In the fourth division from a corner, there is the recovery of wealth previously lost;
furthermore, whatever result [is indicated], the traveler shall obtain it during the journey.
86.06ab. Success in one's journey, along with the acquisition of a peacock, a buffalo, and a cock, occurs through [the influence of] the southern quarter. 86.06cd.
In the second division from the south, there is association with wandering performers, auspiciousness, and joy.
86.07ab/ Success follows; there is meeting with fishermen and the acquisition of fish, partridges, and the like.
86.07cd/ One sees a wandering ascetic, and being intent upon that, there is the attainment of cooked food and fruit.

86.08ab/ In the southwest (nairṛtyā), there is the acquisition of a woman, as well as the receipt of horses, ornaments, messengers, and letters. 86.08cd/ Beyond that, there is the sight of leather-workers and craftsmen, and the gain of leather goods.
86.09ab/ Seeing monkeys, mendicants, or ascetics occurs from the southwest (Nairṛta) in the third division;
86.09cd/ And the arrival of fruits, flowers, or ivory-carved objects occurs from the corner (Vāyu) in the fourth division.
In the western quarter (Vāruṇī), there is the acquisition of jewels born of the ocean, such as vaidūrya gems;
beyond that, however, there is association with Śabaras, hunters, and thieves, and the obtaining of raw flesh.
86.11ab/ Even from others, there is the sight of those suffering from wind-diseases (vāta), and the acquisition of sandalwood and aloe-wood.
86.11cd/ Thereafter, there is the obtaining of weapons and books, as well as association with those who follow such occupations.
In the northwest, there is the acquisition of soap, chowries, and woolen goods; likewise, a scribe is obtained.
In another [direction], there is the gain of earthenware, as well as the vessels of bards and cymbal-players.
86.13ab. From Vāyavyā, in the third [period], there is a meeting with a friend and the acquisition of wealth.
86.13cd. Beyond that, there is the obtaining of clothing and horses, as well as union with beloved friends.
86.14ab/ The acquisition of curds, rice, and parched grain, as well as the sight of a Brahmin in the north;
86.14cd/ the attainment of wealth follows immediately thereafter, and one meets with a caravan leader.
86.15ab/ Meeting with a courtesan, a young student, or a slave; elsewhere, the acquisition of dry flowers and fruits.
86.15cd/ Beyond this, there is the sight of a painter and the obtaining of variegated garments.
86.16ab/ In the northeast, there is an encounter with a temple-priest (devalaka), and the acquisition of grain, jewels, and cattle.
86.16cd/ In the east, during the first watch, there is the acquisition of clothing and also a meeting with a prostitute.

86.17ab/ From this point forward, there will be association with a washerman and the acquisition of water-born goods from others. 86.17cd/ There will be a gathering of those who live by elephants, and from this, the acquisition of wealth and elephants.

86.18ab/ The circle of directions (dikcakra), divided into thirty-two parts, is said to be like a building site (vāstu), including its rim; [it is also stated in the section on the binding of the site].
86.18cd/ Within it, by means of the spokes and the hub, the results are to be conceived in nine ways.
86.19ab. When [the planet] is situated in the navel, there is a meeting with kinsmen and friends, and supreme satisfaction arises.
86.19cd. Furthermore, there is the acquisition of red silk garments and a swift union with the king.
86.20ab. In the southeast (Āgneya), there is a connection with artisans, carpenters, laborers, horsemen, and charioteers.
86.20cd. There is also the acquisition of goods produced by them, or the acquisition of horses.
86.21ab/ Having understood the portion of the rim and the portion of the hub, if the spoke is on the right side,
86.21cd/ there shall be association with righteous people and the attainment of merit (dharma).
The arrival of cowherds, players, and Kāpālikas is indicated in the southwest;
furthermore, there is the acquisition of a bull here, and food consisting of mung beans, horse gram, and the like.
If there is a depression in the western direction, farmers will have attachment to it;
furthermore, there will be the acquisition of maritime goods, high-quality glass, fruits, and liquor.
Furthermore, when situated in the direction of the wind (the northwest), there is the sight of a porter, a carpenter, and a mendicant;
and the obtaining of *tilaka* flowers, as well as *nāga* and *punnāga* flowers.
86.25ab. A bird situated in that quarter which is the north—the direction of Kubera—proclaims the acquisition of wealth when it is in a state of tranquility.
86.25cd. It also foretells a meeting with a devotee of the Lord (Bhāgavata) and with those wearing yellow garments.
86.26ab/ In the northeast, a woman engaged in religious vows comes into view.
86.26cd/ And the acquisition of black iron, weapons, or bells should be understood [as the result].

In the eighth part of the southern direction, the journey is unfavorable; in the second, sixth, third, seventh, and eighth parts from the west, it yields middling results; and in the second part from the north, as well as in the remaining directions, the expedition is highly auspicious.
Within the inner circle, [the asterism] situated at the navel and on the six spokes yields auspicious results; however,
a journey during both the northwest and southwest spokes brings only affliction.

86.29ab/ This result has been stated for the quarters when they are tranquil; therefore, I shall now declare it for those that are blazing. 86.29cd/ In the direction of Indra (the east), there is danger from the king and an encounter with enemies.
86.30ab/ Immediately thereafter, there is the destruction of gold and fear for the goldsmiths.
86.30cd/ In the third [period], there is loss of wealth, quarrels, and the outbreak of weapons.
In the fourth house there is fear of fire, and in the southeast (āgneya) there is also danger from thieves;
furthermore, in the second house from the corner (koṇa), there is loss of wealth and the destruction of the king’s sons.
In the third and fourth parts, there will be the destruction of women and embryos;
and in the latter part, there will be the ruin of goldsmiths and artisans, as well as an outbreak of weapons.
86.33ab. Now, in the fifth [year], fear of the king and the sight of pestilence and death are to be declared. 86.33cd. But in the sixth, fear from the Gandharvas and the Ḍombas is to be known.
When [the asterism] is blazing, there is danger for fishermen and bird-catchers from the seventh part;
thereafter, it is said that there will be an obstruction to food and fear of the Nirgranthas.
86.35ab/ In the southwest (nairṛta) quarter, there is quarreling, the shedding of blood, and the outbreak of weapons.
86.35cd/ In the western (apara) quarter, leather goods are destroyed and there is danger from leather-workers.
Immediately following that, there is danger from wandering mendicants and hearing [unpleasant news]; thereafter, the danger is from fasting.
In the region of Varuṇa, there is danger from rain, and beyond that, danger from dogs and thieves.
86.37ab/ In the subsequent [houses], there is destruction through seizure by wind for those who live by weapons, books, and trade;
86.37cd/ in the corner [house], there is destruction of books, and in the next, danger from poison, thieves, and wind.
86.38ab/ One should know that there will be loss of wealth from others and conflict with friends.
86.38cd/ When it is near, the death of a horse and even danger from the domestic priest (purohita) are declared.
86.39ab/ The theft of cattle, injury by weapons, and [death by] water occur at a distance; likewise, the destruction of a caravan and the loss of wealth occur nearby.
86.39cd/ And when near, there is danger from dogs for those who are outcaste (vrātya), twice-born men, slaves, and courtesans.
86.40ab/ Near the northeast (aiśāna), there is said to be fear from variegated garments and painters.
86.40cd/ In the northeast, however, there is danger from fire and even the defilement of excellent women.
86.41ab. Prior to that, suffering arises for him when he is near [the king], and there is the destruction of his wife.
86.41cd. After that, fear from washermen and from those who deal in leather goods is to be known.
86.42ab/ There shall be fear for elephant-riders and the destruction of elephants at the conclusion of the mandala.
86.42cd/ But if it blazes within, the death of one's wife is certain in the eastern quarter.
86.43ab/ In the Āgneya [quarter], there is danger from weapons, fire, and wrath; there is the death of horses and fear for artisans.
86.43cd/ In the Yāmya [quarter], there is the destruction of dharma, and in the other [directions], attacks by fire and the killing of those who are pure.
But others say that there is danger for those engaged in ritual acts; furthermore, in the northwest (Vāyu) direction, there is the slaughter of donkeys and camels.
In that very same place, humans face the danger of cholera and poison.
In the north, there is suffering for Brahmins; in the northeast, however, there is mental anguish.
There is also suffering for villagers and cowherds, and likewise, in the navel [of the diagram], there is self-destruction.
Chapter 87: On Birds The śyāmā, śyena, śaśaghna, vañjula, śikhin, śrīkarṇa, cakravāka,
cāṣa, aṇḍīraka, khañjarīṭaka, śuka, dhvāṅkṣa, and the three kinds of kapota;
The peacock, the potter-bird, the cock, the donkey, the harita-bird,
the vulture, the monkey, the pheasant, the cock, the *pūrṇakūṭa*, and the sparrow are declared to be creatures that roam by day.
The hair-eater (lomāśika), the one called the tawny scorpion (piṅgalacchippikā), the flying fox (valgulī), the owl (ulūka), and the hare (śaśaka) all roam at night,
departing from their own natural time.
It portends either the destruction of the country or the death of the king.
87.03a Horses, men, serpents, camels, leopards, lions, bears, iguanas;
87.03b wolves, mongooses, deer, dogs, goats, cows, tigers, and swans;
87.03c spotted deer, jackals, porcupines, partridges, and cuckoos.
Day and night alike, the cat, the crane, and the boar [are likewise].
Bhaṣā, Kūṭapūrī, Kurabaka, and Karāyikā are known by the name Pūrṇakūṭā;
the names of Ulūkaceṭī are Piṅgalikā, Pecikā, and Hakkā.

The *kapotakī* is the *śyāmā*, and the *vañjulaka* is said to be the *khadiracañcu*; the *chucchundarī* is the daughter of the king (*nṛpasutā*), and the *vāleya* is declared to be the donkey (*gardabha*).
87.06ab/ A female rat that breaks channels or tanks, has only one offspring, and causes quarrels;
87.06cd/ which cries out like a water-jar at night, and whose body is two fingers long.
87.07ab/ The *durbalika* and the *bhāṇḍīka* are auspicious for those of the East; this [latter] is especially praised for the South.
87.07cd/ The *dhikkāra* belongs to the deer species, while the *kṛkavāku* is declared to be the cock.

87.08ab/ That which is known as the *gartākukkuṭaka* is indeed named the potter’s cock (*kulālakukkuṭa*). 87.08cd/ The house-lizard (*gṛhagodhikā*) is to be understood by the designation "wall-fish" (*kuḍyamatsya*).
The celestial bow has been described; the boar is the *kroḍa*, and then the cow is the *usrā*.
The dog is called *sārameya* by birth, and the female sparrow is the *sūkarikā*.
87.10ab / Having thus obtained the names from those who know them in various regions, [one should compile them].
87.10cd/ For the purpose of knowing the cries of omens, these [rules] should be applied after having reflected upon them in the treatise.
The cry of the *vañjulaka* bird is "tittiḍ" when it is blazing, and "kilkili" when it is full.
Hawks, parrots, vultures, and herons are blazing when their voices differ from their natural ones.
87.12ab/ Whether it be a vehicle, a seat, a bed, a dwelling, or the entering of a pigeon into one's home;
87.12cd/ these bring misfortune to men, though the timing may differ according to the distinction of their birth.
The fruit of the pale pigeon (*āpāṇḍura*) ripens after a year, and that of the variegated dove (*citrapotaka*) after six months;
the fruit of the saffron-colored smoke-grey pigeon (*kuṅkumadhūmakapota*) ripens immediately.
The sound "ci-ci" uttered by a female partridge is full; the sound "śūli-śūl" is auspicious; the sound "cac-ca" is radiant; and the sound "cik-cik" leads to the attainment of one's own beloved.
The sound of Hārītī is like that of bdellium; others may be full and blazing. All varieties of tone in the case of Bhāradvājī are declared to be auspicious.
The sound "kiṣkiṣi" uttered by a female monkey is full and auspicious;
the sound "kahakaha" leads to security alone, but the sound "karakara" does not bring about the accomplishment of one's aims.
The sound "koṭukli" is auspicious, while "kaṭukli" portends rain for her;
"koṭikili" is fruitless, and the sound made by "guṃ" is indeed blazing.
87.18a When a divine weapon appears in the left hand,
87.18b success is to be known [to follow] when it rises to the height of one cubit (hasta). 87.18c When that very [weapon] stands raised above the body, [success is attained].
The earth, bounded by the oceans, comes under the control of the nurse.
87.19a A snake approaching from the front portends an encounter with enemies;
87.19b it also foretells the death or imprisonment of a kinsman for one who travels.
87.19c Or, if it approaches from the left side, [it likewise brings misfortune].
87.19d He is not skilled in success, nor in going and coming.
87.20a On the heads of elephants, horses, and serpents, [the sight of footprints] bestows sovereignty; 87.20b on pure, lush grassy meadows, it brings about welfare;
87.20c on ashes, bones, wood, husks, hair, and straw, it brings suffering.
Indeed, when the Khañjana bird is seen, it brings rain for one year.
87.21a The cry of the partridge, "kilikilikili," is auspicious; otherwise, it is of a different result. 87.21b If a hare appears on the left side at night, it is peaceful and brings praised fruit.
Crying out, it is declared that its fruit is auspicious.
87.22a They declare that the blazing "kilikili" cry of a monkey does not bestow auspicious results upon a traveler;
87.22b yet they also say that a "cuglu" sound is auspicious.
And that which resembles a monkey belongs to the potter's cock.
If a blue jay approaches from the right side of a man whose face is covered with worms, insects, ants,
and the like, or if it draws a swastika in the sky for one who is about to depart, [it portends success].
It brings about the acquisition of very great wealth for him before long.
If a blue jay quarrels with a crow,
the defeat belongs to the one on the right side;
then, for the man who has set out on his journey, there will be death.
In the opposite case, his victory is ordained.
If the blue jay (*cāṣa*) utters the cry "ke-ka" from its left side like a full vessel, it shall bring victory; however,
its cry "kre-ka" (or *krakre-ti*) is not auspicious when it is blazing.
The sight of him always brings auspiciousness to the traveler.
87.26a One filled with the cry "aṇḍīrakaṣṭī" is called *pūrṇa*; 87.26b one with the sound "ṭiṭṭiṭṭi" is said to be *dīpta*.
87.26c A pheasant (*pheṇṭa*) situated on the right side is auspicious.
No distinction was made regarding whether it had been barked at or not.
The cry of the Śrīkarṇa bird on the right is proclaimed as auspicious when it sounds "kvakva-kva"; likewise,
the sound "cik-ciki" is indeed considered neutral.
They maintain that everything else is fruitless.
Even for one who is weak,
if the sound "cirilvi-rilvi" is uttered from the left, it indeed bestows desired results;
and if [the breath] should move from the left to the right.
It bestows the accomplishment of one's purpose before long.
But having uttered a "cik-cikī" sound,
if it moves from the left side toward the right,
it brings security but does not accomplish one's goals.
If the movement is reversed, it leads to fear of execution or imprisonment.
If a sārikā bird cries out "krakra" quickly, or if a *vibhītaka* tree shrieks even when there is no fear,
it foretells that blood will soon flow from the limbs of one who intends to travel.
87.31ab/ To the left of the pheṇṭaka, the sound "cirilvirilv" is declared auspicious; another is said to be "pradīpta" (blazing).

87.32a They desire the excellent, firm, and desirable sound of the donkey; 87.32b by the sound of the syllable *oṃ*, it is beneficial for the traveler. 87.32c Beyond this, however, is that which is accompanied by the braying of a donkey.
They declare that blazing [light] to be the support of all.
The *kuraṅga* deer, accompanied by other deer, utters the sound "ā"; the *pṛṣata* deer, full of vigor, utters the sound "o";
and whatever other sounds there may be, they are said to be blazing.
Full [houses] are auspicious; those that are combust yield evil results.
Terrified, the red-crested cocks cry out "kuku-kukv" at night, abandoning their other fear-inducing calls;
yet at the end of the night, they resume their natural cries as they feel secure.
The stars bestow prosperity upon the kingdom, the cities, and the sovereign.
For there are various kinds of cries from the *chippikā* bird; its *kulukulu* call is auspicious, while the remaining ones are not.
The cry of a cat is never auspicious for one who is traveling.
But a sneeze on a cow brings about nothing less than death for the traveler.

87.36a Uttering "huṃ huṃ gu gu lug," the owl cries out joyfully, longing for its mate. 87.36b When it is full, there is a heavy sound; moreover, "kiskisi" should always be understood as a blazing [omen].
87.36c A quarrel is to be recognized when there is a repeated hooting of "balabala" from it (or her).
The sounds "ṭa-ṭa-ṭa-ṭa" lead only to misfortune and are not auspicious; however, all other vowels are radiant (*dīpta*).
87.37ab/ The cry of a pair of cranes (*sārasa*) uttered simultaneously brings about a desired result;
87.37cd/ but a single cry is not auspicious, nor is it so if, after one has cried, the other cries out only after a long interval.
The female jackal (piṅgalā) brings auspiciousness when she utters the sounds "cirilvi" or "rilvi" with the vowels;
however, those other vowels which follow are designated as "blazing" (pradīpta).
If the cry of the *iśī* bird prohibits departure,
and if the *kuśukuśu* bird causes a quarrel,
then its course regarding the desired undertaking is as follows.
He explains that procedure, and I shall explain it.
At the time of the evening twilight,
having come to that tree for his dwelling, he,
being purified, worshipped the gods, beginning with the Grandfather (Brahmā).
And he [honored] that tree with new garments and fragrant scents.
At midnight, standing alone in the direction of the fire (southeast),
having bound her with divine and other oaths,
he should ask about the matter exactly as it was thought of.
By means of this mantra, he hears according to his wish.
87.42ab. Know, O blessed lady, that you have been prompted by me regarding this matter; 87.42cd. O auspicious one, you are celebrated as one who understands the meaning of all words.
87.43ab. "I take my leave today; I shall depart, but I will let you know again.
87.43cd. Having returned in the morning, I shall ask you while situated in the southern direction."
87.44ab/ "I urge you; you ought to explain to me that which [you have done]. 87.44cd/ "O auspicious one, so that through your own account I may understand it clearly."
87.45a When this has been said, if those dwelling on the tops of trees utter the sounds "cirilvi" or "rilvi," there is success in one's purpose.
87.45b If the sound "diśikāra" is heard, there will be extreme agitation [or, according to another reading, lack of agitation].
Or when it is uttered thus: "kucākucā."
87.46a Even when [the query] is directed downwards, there is the accomplishment of the intended purpose;
87.46b other than this, there are the results of the previously mentioned wheel of directions.
87.46c And the result should be declared as superior, middling, or inferior.
87.46d When [the moon] is situated on a branch, it is excellent in the middle and low at the ends.
87.47 One should determine the results of the house-lizard (gṛhagodhikā) within the internal and external portions of the circle of the directions;
the *chucchundarī* (musk-rat) is [the deity] of the blazing quarter, known as *cicciḍ*.
But when it was full, it made the sound "tittiḍ."

Chapter 88: On the Dog’s Wheel (Śvacakra) When a dog urinates before a traveler as he proceeds, [the following objects indicate his success]: a man, a horse, an elephant, an elephant's frontal globe, a saddle, a milky tree, a heap of bricks, an umbrella, a bed, a seat, a mortar, a banner, a fly-whisk, a grassy field, or a place covered in flowers.
Then, if one urinates upon a fresh *ārdraka* root or cow dung, there will be the attainment of sweet food;
if one urinates upon dry [substances], there will be dry food, or else the acquisition of molasses and sweetmeats (modaka).
Furthermore, having urinated upon a poison tree, the thorny *kaṇṭakī*, wood, stone, a dry tree, bone, or a cremation ground, and then carrying it away—
Or if one who is traveling has a leader announce something undesirable; or if a dog urinates on beds, pottery, and other vessels while they are unused or unbroken—it causes defects in a maiden.

If it urinates on them while they are being used, it indicates the corruption of their mistress. Likewise, the result of urinating on shoes is the same; and if it urinates on a cow, there arises a mixture of castes born of dishonor.

88.01c When one should approach holding a sandal as a means for departure, then there is success; if the mouth is filled with flesh, there is the attainment of wealth; by holding a moist bone, there is auspiciousness; by holding a dry bone together with a firebrand, there is death;
by a firebrand whose flame has been extinguished, there is injury to a man; and by [holding] the head, hands, feet, and so forth, there is the arrival [of a guest] at the earth.
Some say that misfortunes arise from [the dog's mouth being filled with] garments, rags, and so forth; if it enters a house while wearing clothes, there will be good fortune.

However, if it enters a house with its mouth full of dry bones, there will be the death of the head of the household. Furthermore, if it should approach while carrying a chain, a withered vine, a leather thong, or the like, then it is a sign of imprisonment; shaking its feet, it licks them.

If a dog climbs onto its own ears, it portends obstacles for the traveler; likewise, if it fights in opposition, there will be conflict; if it scratches its own limbs, there will be strife; and if it sleeps with its feet raised upward, it always causes misfortune.
If a dog barks at sunrise while facing the sun in the middle of a village—
whether alone or gathered together in a group— [it portends misfortune].
They quickly proclaim another as the ruler of the land.
Facing the sun and situated in the direction of the south-east,
it causes fear of thieves and fire before long;
at the time of midday, it portends death by fire.
If it is bloody, there will be a quarrel in the afternoon.
Crying out while facing the sun at the time of sunset,
it quickly brings fear to farmers;
and if it cries toward the northwest at the time of dusk, [the same result follows].
