It brings fear arising from wind and thieves.
Facing north at the time of midnight, he portends distress to Brahmins and the theft of cattle;
at the end of the night and at the break of day, he is auspicious.
88.05d [He brings about] the defilement of virgins, fire, miscarriages, and abortions.
If they are situated on a heap of grass, or located upon an excellent palace or mansion, they produce loud sounds; in such cases,
they announce heavy rain during the rainy season.
Except for death, burning, and disease.
During the rainy season, when there is no rain, one should immerse oneself in water and repeatedly emerge with exhalations; or else,
shaking [the body], one should drink the water.
They cause rain to fall within twelve days.
88.08a If a dog, placing its head outside at the door while its body remains within, 88.08b barks repeatedly upon seeing the mistress of the house,
88.08c it shall bring disease; furthermore, if [it does so] inside the mansion...
Turning his face outward, he speaks of—that is, praises—that unchaste woman.
When it digs up the wall of a house, then there shall be danger from a thief;
when it digs up a cow-pen, one should predict the seizure of cattle; and when it does so on grain-fields, there will be the acquisition of grain.
With one eye full of tears and a dejected look, eating little and causing distress to that household,
[the planet] plays together with the cattle; this portends a time of plenty.
And it bestows security, health, and joy.
If one smells the left knee, it portends the acquisition of wealth; if the right, it indicates a quarrel with women. Smelling the left thigh signifies the enjoyment of sensual pleasures.
If one smells the left side, there will be conflict with beloved friends.
If one smells the feet of a traveler, it foretells that he will not go; if he smells the feet of one who is stationary, it indicates the attainment of desired wealth.
If one smells the sandals of someone standing in their place, [the same result follows].
The dog quickly makes for its journey.
For when both arms are smelled,
it should be understood as the conjunction of an enemy and a thief;
therefore, one should hide the food in ashes.
Flesh and bones [are consumed], and there is a rapid provocation of the fire element.
If, after barking in the village, they bark outside in the cremation ground, there will be the destruction of a preeminent man;
and if it howls facing one who desires to travel, [that too portends ill].
Whenever that occurs, the dog obstructs the journey.
88.15a When there is a cry with the color of the syllable *u*, there is the accomplishment of one's purpose;
88.15b and with the color of the syllable *o* on the left side [of the body].
88.15c One should recognize distraction from the sound of the syllable *au*.
And afterwards, one should perform the prohibition with all sounds.
Those dogs that repeatedly cry out loudly "khaṃ-kha" as if they were being beaten with sticks,
and run about in a circle—
They would cause emptiness and the fear of death.
88.17a If, having displayed its teeth, it licks the corners of its mouth, 88.17b then those who know [the signs] declare that the food will be sweet;
88.17c but when it licks the mouth itself and not the corners of the mouth, [it portends otherwise].
Even when the meal has already begun, he then creates an obstacle to the food.
If those dogs that bark repeatedly and in a pack in the midst of a village or a city,
they announce trouble for its lord.
Like a dog dwelling in the forest, he should be regarded as being like a wild beast.
If a cry is heard near a tree, there will be a fall of water; if at the *indrakīla* (the threshold pillar), there is suffering for the minister;
if in the house of Vāyu, there is danger to the crops; and if inside the house, [there is danger] to the household.
And there will be suffering for the city itself when [the planet] is situated at the gate.

If they bark at the beds of their masters, there is fear; if they bark from behind while traveling, they portend danger; and if they move counter-clockwise around a settlement of people, it is likewise ominous.
Barking in fear, they foretell danger for their enemies.
Chapter 89: On the Howling of Jackals.
Jackals are similar to dogs in their results; the distinction between them is that jackals attain intoxication during the winter season.
At the end of the *hūhū* cry is *ṭāṭā*;
the full vowel is followed by others which are said to be blazing.
The sound *kakka* indeed belongs to the *lomāśikā*;
it is full, arising from its own nature. Those other vowels are devoid of that fundamental nature.
And all these are declared to be "blazing."
A jackal howling in the northeast is auspicious; one that is calm is praised everywhere and honored.
One that is smoking or facing toward the observer brings death, and one that is loud and blazing destroys the lords of the directions.
The king, the prince, the leader, the envoy, the merchant, the spy, the twice-born,
and the elephant-keeper are the presiding deities of the eastern and other directions, starting with the Kṣatriyas and others in the four quarters.
89.05ab/ In all directions, the jackal is inauspicious when its cry is blazing; it is especially inauspicious during the day.
89.05cd/ When it circles to the left of a city or an army, or faces the sun, the jackal is a source of misery.
"Go!"—this portends danger from fire; "ṭāṭa"—this is a bier for the dead;
"Fie! Fie!"—this announces a wicked deed; and when it is flaming, it foretells the destruction of one's country.
89.07ab Some do not at all describe her as being fierce, like a blazing fire;
89.07cd for her mouth is of the nature of saliva, like the fire of the sun and other such fires.
89.08ab/ A jackal's howl facing south portends death by hanging;
89.08cd/ that same cry facing west foretells death in the water.
89.09ab/ Absence of agitation, hearing pleasant news, the acquisition of wealth, and the arrival of loved ones;
89.09cd/ Agitation, the division of leaders, and the prosperity of mounts.
89.10ab/ This result [is to be understood] up to the seventh [note]; beyond that, the sound is not to be grasped.
89.10cd/ In the southern quarter, the result is the reverse, except for the sixth and fifth notes.
That jackal which causes horripilation in men and the voiding of dung and urine in horses,
and produces terror with its howl, does not bestow auspiciousness.
When a female jackal remains silent after being answered by men, elephants, or horses,
that auspicious omen bestows prosperity upon the army or the city.

The jackal’s cry of "bhe-bhā" is auspicious, whereas "bho-bho" indicates misfortune; the sounds "mṛti," "bandha," and "nivedinī" portend death or captivity, while "phiphe" (or "phipha") and "hū-hū" are auspicious cries for one's own welfare.
89.14a But Śāntā, ascending further from the unvoiced [consonants], crying out "ṭā-ṭā-m," 89.14b thus uttering the raised sounds;
89.14c first "ṭe-ṭe" and afterwards "the-the."
That cry of hers arose from her own satisfaction.
Having first uttered a loud and terrible cry,
she should afterwards howl like a jackal;
for she is the one who foretells safety and the acquisition of wealth.
Or reunion with a beloved who has been away on a journey.
Chapter 90: On the Movements of Wild Animals.
Wild animals standing on the boundary, crying out, whether stationary, moving away, or charging toward [the army], [portend various outcomes].
Blazing and wandering about on all sides, they bring about the destruction of the present, the past, and the future, leaving everything empty.
90.02a When they are barked at by domestic animals,
they become a source of fear and obstruction for wild ones; 90.02b if they are barked back by both types, they [become even more formidable].
And deer cry out for the sake of capturing them for the hunters.
If a wild animal stands at the gate of a city, a siege is to be predicted; if it has entered, destruction [of the city] will occur.
If it is born there, death [to the ruler] shall happen; and if it remains stationary, there will be fear.
When [the planet] has gone to the house, imprisonment is ordained.
Chapter 91: On Bodily Gestures (Iṅgita) 91.01a Cows that appear dejected portend misfortune for the king;
91.01b And those that paw the ground with their hooves foretell diseases.
With eyes long and filled with tears, they bring about their husband's death, crying out in fear of thieves.
91.02ab/ If it barks without cause, there will be misfortune; at night, a bull portends fear, while a jackal portends welfare.
91.02cd/ If it is excessively swarmed by flies, then there will soon be rain, or else [death] from its own offspring.
Coming toward the house with the lowing of cows,
tending the cattle for the prosperity of the herd,
their limbs were moist and their hair bristling with joy.
Blessed indeed would be the cows and the buffalo-cows as well.
Chapter 92: On the Signs of Horses.
A fire [emerging] from the anus is not auspicious; likewise, one situated behind the seat is not favorable. However, a blaze on the left side is excellent.
92.01c If there is a flaming of all the limbs, it brings no prosperity to the horses; 92.01d for two years, sparks from a fire or incense [should be applied as a remedy].
If the fire blazes in the genitals, the harem goes to ruin; if it blazes in the belly, the treasury goes to exhaustion; and if it blazes in the anus or the tail, there shall be defeat.
And there is victory when the fire blazes from the mouth and the head.
The blazing of the shoulders, the seat, and the arms portends victory;
the blazing of the feet is declared to signify bondage;
and smoke appearing on the forehead, the chest, the eyes, and the arms [indicates the same].
The blazing fire leads to defeat; [the smokeless fire] leads to victory.
92.04a If there is a discharge from the nostrils, the lips, or the head,
and 92.04b if the eyes blaze at night, it leads to victory;
[this applies to horses] that are reddish-brown, copper-colored, black, or variegated.
It is always desired for one who is white with a luster like that of a parrot.
92.05a Hatred toward fodder and water, sweating without a cause, or trembling; 92.05b and the falling of blood from the mouth, or the appearance of smoke;
92.05c insomnia at night, hostility toward those who are not enemies, and daytime sleepiness, lethargy, or a state of vacant meditation.
Lassitude and hanging down of the head—this is known as undesirable behavior for horses.
92.06ab/ Mounting another horse, or a horse equipped with a saddle and gear; 92.06cd/ Or riding a mount intended for ceremonial processions, or one that is ill-proportioned or lacking in beauty.
92.07a Like a curlew, it neighs for the destruction of the enemy;
92.07b with an immovable neck and face upturned, 92.07c it is affectionate, loud, resonant, and joyful.
And with horses whose mouths were blocked by mouthfuls of fodder.
A full vessel, curd, a brahmin, or a deity; or else perfumes, flowers, fruits, gold, and so forth—
such may be the desired object, or even something more excellent.
If victory is at hand, one should not be afraid.
92.09a Or they delight in food, drink, and the bit; 92.09b or they rejoice in what is pleasing to their master;
92.09c or else their gaze is directed toward the left side.
92.09d Horses grant the fruits of one's desired objects.
92.10a Striking the earth with their left feet, they portend the departure of the husband; 92.10b likewise,
those who gaze at the radiant [sun] during the twilights [foretell the same].
If they neigh, it portends the defeat of the enemy's forces.
92.11a They neigh excessively and scatter their manes; 92.11b being fond of sleep, they announce a journey. 92.11c Shedding their hair, they have a wretched and harsh sound.
And dogs seen swallowing dust portend fear.
92.12a Lying on their right sides like a casket,
92.12b and standing with their right forefeet raised—
this [is the posture] for victory even among the remaining mounts.
The wise man should predict the result according to what is possible.
When the king, endowed with discipline,
mounts another horse following his procession, that horse neighs loudly; or else,
it touches its own right flank with its mouth.
That horse which [is thus] soon destroys the fortune of its master.
92.14a He voids urine and excrement repeatedly;
92.14b even when being beaten, he does not move in the direction of the blow;
92.14c he is afraid of what ought not to be done, and his eyes are filled with tears.
The horse did not announce anything auspicious for its master.
92.15ab/ This behavior of horses has been described; hereafter I shall declare that of elephants.
92.15cd/ [One should know it] by their actions such as the setting of their tusks, the breaking [of branches], and the withering [of flowers].
Chapter 93: On the Movements of Elephants.
One should subtract twice the circumference of the root of the tusk from its length and determine the remainder;
for elephants that frequent marshy lands, this is slightly more, while for those that roam the mountains, it is slightly less.
93.02ab/ When cuts are seen that correspond to the śrīvatsa, the vardhamāna, the umbrella, the banner, or the fly-whisk, 93.02cd/ there result health, victory, increase of wealth, and happiness.
In a [dream] resembling a weapon, there is victory; in a *nandyāvarta* [mark], the recovery of a lost region;
but in a clod of earth, there is the acquisition of a region previously held.
93.04ab/ If a woman appears, there is the destruction of one's own horse; if a water-pot (bhṛṅgāra) rises up, there is the birth of a son.
93.04cd/ By a water-jar (kumbha), there is the acquisition of treasure; and by a staff (daṇḍa), there is an obstacle to the journey.
93.05ab/ When the forms of a chameleon, a monkey, or a serpent appear, there will be famine, disease, and subjection to enemies.
93.05cd/ When the forms of a vulture, an owl, a crow, or a hawk appear, there will be a pestilence among the people.
93.06ab/ Furthermore, if [the blood] appears as a noose or a headless trunk (kabandha), there is death for the king and calamity for the people; if it flows as blood, [there is misfortune].
93.06cd/ If it is black, dark-brown, rough, and foul-smelling, it portends evil.
93.07ab/ A fracture that is white, even, fragrant, and glossy brings about auspiciousness.
93.07cd/ Furthermore, fruits that are shriveled or withered are equal to a broken tooth.
93.08a–c. Then, the gods, daityas, and humans are situated respectively at the root, the middle, and the tip of the teeth;
consequently, the fruit is abundant in the middle and very slight at the ends.
93.08d Arising after a short, intermediate, or long period of time.

93.09ab/ Here, the breaking of a tooth on the right side brings about the flight of the king, the country, and the army. 93.09cd/ On the left side, it destroys sons, the domestic priest, elephants, forest-dwellers, wives, and leaders.
93.10ab/ One should predict the total destruction of the king's lineage from observing the failure of both [the planetary and the astrological conditions].
93.10cd/ Through the moon, the ascendant, the lunar day, the asterism, and so forth, auspiciousness increases; one should declare the opposite for what is inauspicious.
If the tusks are broken by trees laden with milk, cleansed fruits, and flowers, or by the banks of rivers, it brings about the destruction of the enemy; otherwise, the result is the opposite.
With faltering gait, his ears suddenly pricked up in alarm and appearing deeply dejected,
he pants softly and for long intervals; with his forelegs cast upon the ground,
his eyes are rapidly closed, he is prone to sleep, and his disposition is contrary.
Causing fear and devouring what is harmful, he has repeatedly produced blood and excrement.
93.13a If, with a joyful gaze, it moves at its own will crushing anthills, stumps, shrubs, thickets, and trees;
93.13b if it proceeds with quick steps in the direction favorable for the expedition while holding its head high;
93.13c and if, at the time of girthing and armoring, it repeatedly emits spray or lets out a roar— [then it portends success].
Or at that time, the attainment of Madā is the bringer of victory; likewise, when it encircles the right tooth.
The elephant’s entry into the water may lead to the king’s destruction by a crocodile;
but if he seizes the crocodile and emerges, it will be the king’s [or the elephant’s] deliverance.
From water, dry land arises, bringing prosperity to the lord of men.
Chapter 94: On the Cawing of Crows. 94.01ab:
For those in the eastern regions, crows are auspicious when they are to the south, and *karāyikā* birds are auspicious when on the left.
94.01cd: In other regions, the opposite is true; the limit [of these rules] is established simply by popular consensus.

94.02ab. A nest in an undamaged tree during the month of Vaiśākha bestows abundance and auspiciousness. 94.02cd. In trees that are censured, thorny, or withered, there will be famine and fears for that region.
94.03ab/ If [the bird] is on the nest at the eastern branch in autumn, there will be the first rain; if on the western branch, [there will be rain later].
94.03cd/ If it is between the southern and northern branches, there will be moderate rain; if above the tree, there will be abundant rain.

94.04ab. If there is rain within the mandala in the direction of Agni (the southeast), there is the ripening of the autumn harvest; 94.04cd. in the southwest (Nairṛtya), there is abundance; in the remaining two directions, there is plenty of food, and in the northwest (Vāyavya), there is an abundance of mice.
94.05ab/ In regions abounding in reeds, darbha grass, thickets, creepers, grain, palaces, houses, or lowlands, 94.05cd/ that land becomes desolate, afflicted by thieves, drought, and disease.
94.06ab/ Having two, three, or four young ones bestows abundance; having five results in the replacement of the king.
94.06cd/ The scattering of eggs, having only one egg, or total failure to produce offspring does not bode well.
94.07ab/ One should indicate that thieves are present by the colors of thieves; death by variegated ones; and fear of fire by white ones.
94.07cd/ By deformed crows one should indicate fear of famine, and by their young, [the same].
94.08ab. When they are without a visible cause, not forming a flock, located in the middle of a village, and crying out in fear of hunger;
94.08cd. If they form a circle like a wheel, there will be a siege; if they stand in separate groups, there will be a localized assault.
94.09ab/ Frightening people with their beaks and wings and overwhelming them with the striking of their feet,
94.09cd/ they bring about the increase of enemies and the destruction of the people as they roam about at night.
When crows circle in the sky with their left wings, or move in reverse circles out of fear of themselves,
or whirl about in extreme confusion, there will be a storm of wind.
94.11ab / Those with upturned faces and fluttering wings portend danger on the road; those that steal grain portend the fear of famine.
94.11cd / Those stationed within an army's ranks portend war, while those with borrowed wings portend plunder.
94.12ab / By scattering ashes, bones, hair, and leaves upon the bed, one brings about the death of her husband.
94.12cd / By crushing jewels, flowers, and the like, there is the birth of a son for the woman, or otherwise, [the birth of another woman].

If a crow discharges its droppings on a full face, there will be the acquisition of wealth; however, if it does so with sand, grain, moist earth, or flowers, it brings fear from living among people, provided that the crow then carries away the goods.
94.14ab/ If one tramples upon a vehicle, a weapon, a sandal, a parasol, a shadow, or a limb, death occurs.
94.14cd/ If one offers worship to these, there will be honor; if one voids excrement upon them, there will be the acquisition of food.
94.15ab. Whatever substance one brings forward, the gain pertains to that; if it is stolen, there shall be a total loss.
94.15cd. With yellow substances, gold [is indicated]; with white cotton fabrics, silver.

94.16ab/ Roaring and frequenting both riverbanks, sandy shoals, and groves of milk-exuding Arjuna and Vañjula trees during the rainy season; 94.16cd/ [Omens are auspicious] when there is rain in the monsoon, but foul weather out of season, and when [the birds] have bathed in muddy waters.
A crow perched upon the hollow of a tree, uttering a harsh cry, portends great danger;
yet if it looks toward the water and caws, it brings rain, as does one that cries out in harmony with the clouds.
94.18ab/ One who is agitated by a blazing fire, striking at the branches, and shaking its wings; 94.18cd/ or one who places red substances, burnt grass, or wood within the house.
If one facing the direction of Indra (the east) and others, while speaking in the house of a householder with his face turned toward the sun,
there will be fear of the king, imprisonment by thieves, quarrels, and danger from cattle.
94.20ab/ Looking at a peaceful eastern quarter, one shall cry out; there will be the acquisition of royal servants, friends, and kinsmen.
94.20cd/ Furthermore, there is the gain of gold and the acquisition of rice-food and molasses.
94.21ab. In the southeast, there is gain of minerals from fire-tending women who are preeminent;
94.21cd. In the south, there is food consisting of black gram and horse-gram, and association with musicians.

In the southwest (nairṛtyā), there is the acquisition of messengers, horses, equipment, curd, oil, and food made of sesame paste. In the west (vāruṇyā), there is the acquisition of meat, wine, spirits, grain, ocean products, and jewels.
94.23ab/ Under Māruti, there is the acquisition of weapons, missiles, lotuses, creepers, fruits, and food;
94.23cd/ under Saumyā, the eating of excellent food and the acquisition of horses and garments.
94.24ab/ There shall be the acquisition of vessels filled with ghee and of oxen in the northeast;
94.24cd/ such is the fruit for the householder when [the planet] rests upon the roof of the house.
If it is equal to Karna in its motion during travel, it leads to safety but not to the accomplishment of one's purpose.
If it approaches facing the traveler while crying out, it shall cause the journey to be turned back.
If, after first crying out on the left, a jackal then cries on the right side of a traveler, it causes the loss of wealth;
the opposite of this brings about the attainment of wealth.

If a jackal, crying out repeatedly on the left, moves in a direction favorable to the traveler, it leads to the accomplishment of one's purpose; and the same applies to one moving toward the east or the south.
A crow moving to the left, crying out in a contrary direction, creates an obstacle to one's journey;
it foretells the very result desired by one staying there regarding the trip.

94.29ab/ If, after crying out on the right, it cries out on the left, there is the attainment of what is desired. 94.29cd/ If it cries out facing forward, one should proceed quickly; then there will be the acquisition of exceedingly great wealth.
If it cries out behind him and then swiftly moves away to the right, it portends bloodshed;
if it walks on one leg while looking at the sun and crying out in front, it is a cause for blood.
When the crow, having seen the sun, scratches its own feathers with its beak while standing on one leg before a great multitude of people, it then foretells slaughter.
If it cries out while perched on a field rich with grain during a period of calm, there will be the acquisition of land with crops;
if it cries out with agitated movements at the boundary of a field, it brings distress to the traveler.

In trees that are fragrant and sweet, bent down by very glossy leaves, sprouts, flowers, and fruits, and which possess milky sap, are free from wounds, well-established, and pleasing to the mind, there is the accomplishment of one's purpose.
When it cries out amidst green fields of ripened grain, verdant gardens, palaces, mansions,
and towers, or among auspicious heaps of grain, it brings the arrival of wealth.
If [the planet] is situated in Gopuccha or in Valmīka, there is the sight of a serpent;
if it is in Mahiṣa, there is immediate fever; and if it cries out in Gulma, the result is slight.
If the crow is situated on a heap of grass, or on the left side, or upon water (or bones), there is an obstruction to the task at hand;
and if the crow is scorched by fire from above or struck by lightning, death occurs.
94.37ab/ When the Moon is mixed with thorny plants, there is success in the undertaking, yet also quarrel.
94.37cd/ If it is among thorny plants, there is quarrel; if it is entwined by a creeper, there is imprisonment.
If the crow is perched on a withered tree, there will be the cutting off of limbs or the severing of members and strife;
if it is perched on a lump of cow dung either in front or behind, there is the acquisition of wealth.
If it stands upon the limbs or members of a dead man and cries out loudly, it causes fear of death;
if it breaks a bone with its beak and cries out, it portends the breaking of bones.
If a crow caws while perched on a rope, a bone, wood, a thorn, a worthless object, or its own head-hair,
there will be, respectively, fear of snakes, diseases, fanged beasts, thieves, weapons, fire, and fire.
If a crow has its mouth filled with white flowers, pure substances, or meat, the traveler attains his desired success;
however, if it flaps its wings and repeatedly caws while facing upward, it portends an obstacle.
94.42ab. If it barks while holding a chain, a leather thong, or a creeper, there will be confinement.
94.42cd. And if it is on a stone, there is danger, as well as distress and a journey with an unknown companion.
When their mouths are filled by feeding one another, there is supreme satisfaction. When a husband and wife both cry out simultaneously, it should be understood as a sign of obtaining a woman.
94.44ab/ When the full pitcher is situated upon the head of a woman, there is the attainment of wealth through women;
94.44cd/ when the pitcher is broken, there is misfortune for one's son, but when it is merely struck, there is the acquisition of food.
94.45ab/ At the time of encamping the army and its divisions, a bird with fluttering wings portends a change of location;
94.45cd/ but one with motionless wings indicates danger alone.
When vultures, herons, and crows enter the army and so forth without any flesh,
there will be friendship with those enemies who are not hostile, and war with those who are hostile.
94.47ab/ When [the Moon] is situated in a Boar sign, there is imprisonment; when it is a Boar smeared with mud, there is the acquisition of wealth.
94.47cd/ When it is situated in a Donkey or Camel sign, some say there is security, but others say there is death in the case of the Donkey.
If a crow caws while following behind as one travels on horseback, there will be the gain of a vehicle; if it falls [upon the rider], there will be a wound from blood.
Furthermore, other birds that follow the traveler like crows portend the same.

94.49ab/ Whatever has been specified for each of the thirty-two divisions of the circle of directions, 94.49cd/ that very thing should be applied accordingly as the result of merits and defects for those desiring to set out on their journey.
94.50ab/ The cry "kā" uttered by a crow while perched in its own dwelling is said to be fruitless.
94.50cd/ The cry "kava" is for one's own pleasure, and upon the cry "ka," there is the acquisition of affectionate friends.
The cry "karā" portends a quarrel; "kurukuru" brings joy; "kaṭakaṭa" indicates curd-rice; and the cries "keke" or "kuku" announce the acquisition of wealth for one who is traveling, so it is said.
The cry "kharekhare" announces the arrival of a traveler; "kakhākhā" foretells the death of one who is departing; "ā kakhalā" (or "ā khalakhala") prohibits departure;
and "ā khalakhala" indicates immediate rain.
"Kākā" indicates an obstacle; "kākaṭi" signifies the spoiling of food;
"kavakava" denotes a source of pleasure; and "kagāku" likewise signifies bondage.
If the sound "kara" or "kara" occurs, there will be rain; "guḍa" indicates fear; "vaḍ" signifies the acquisition of clothing;
and "kalaya" portends a union of Śūdras with Brāhmaṇas.
With the sound "kaḍ" (or "phaḍ"), there is the attainment of fruit; with "phala-da" (or "phala-vā"), it bestows fruit.
With the sight of a snake, there is the sound "ṭaḍḍi" (or "ṭaḍiti"), which indicates blows.
With the cry "strī," there is the gain of a woman.
"Gaḍ" is for cows; "puḍ" is for flowers.
If [the sound] is "ṭākuṭākv," there will be battle; "guhu" indicates fear of fire; "kaṭekaṭe" signifies quarrel;
and "ṭākuli," "ciṇṭici," "kekeka," or "puraṃ ca" lead to misfortune.
94.57 This same result that has been described through the cries, movements, and so forth of a pair of crows applies equally to other birds as well, just like the crow.
Wild animals and those with fangs above should be avoided like dogs.
94.58a When there is a reversal of land-dwelling and water-dwelling creatures during the rainy season, 94.58b it leads to an abundance of rain; at other times, it portends fear.
94.58c Honey that has settled in a dwelling quickly makes that place empty.
And even death [is indicated] when blue flies settle upon the head.
94.59a Ants depositing their eggs in the water 94.59b indicate that the rain will cease; 94.59c [if they do so] on a tree or dry land...
When they lead [the water] from a low place to a high ground or even to dry land,
then they announce rain.
94.60a But if a primary omen occurs within [the period of] an intermediate one on that same day,
94.60b one should know the result to be certain; thus these [omens] are to be considered at the time of commencement, departure, and likewise entry.
They maintain that a sneeze is not to be welcomed as auspicious anywhere at all.
94.61a A favorable fruition of the planetary period, success without obstacles;
94.61b protection of one's roots or else companions;
94.61c the accomplishment of what is desired, and freedom from disease.
They speak thus of the king who honors them.

Some say that the cry of a bird beyond the distance of one *krośa* is fruitless; however, if the first omen there is inauspicious, the king should perform five or six breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). If it is inauspicious on the second occasion, he should perform sixteen.
If the third [alternative] is undesirable, he should therefore return to his own abode.

Chapter 95: The Subsequent Chapter on Ominous Birds (Śākunottarādhyāya) One should consider the direction, location, movement, sound, day, lunar mansion (nakṣatra), auspicious moment (muhūrta), horā, karaṇa, rising sign (udaya), and degrees;
as well as whether [the bird] is moving, stationary, or long-staying.
Having understood the strength and weakness of the mixed *carasthira* [movements], the knower of cries should predict the results.
95.02a They declare that for those who are established, there are two kinds of effects: 95.02b that which is designated as future and that which is designated as stable;
95.02c [these concern] kings, messengers, spies, and things born in other lands.
95.02d Injury, as well as one's own kin and so forth, is designated as "coming" (āgama).
Hanging by a rope, adultery, eating, thieves, fire, rain, festivals, the death of a son, quarrels, and fear—
this group of calamities remains stable when the Moon is conjoined with a fixed sign at its rising.
One should know that what was stated as stable [is so] in a fixed sign, and as moving in a movable sign.
95.04ab/ In stable locations, on stone platforms, in temples, and in proximity to earth and water, one should perform fixed rites;
95.04cd/ whereas mobile rites for the sake of arrival [or attainment] should be performed in unstable locations and the like.
Those [planets] which are blazing at the rising of water-bearing constellations, at the moments and directions, in the waters, and at the ends of the fortnights—
all of them, when they cry out, bring rain.
Even when in its state of quiescence, the water-dweller produces rain.
If it cries while the sun is blazing in a region where the auspicious moment (muhūrta) is fixed upon the southern quarter (the direction of Agni), there is danger from fire;
likewise when the Viṣṭi karana, the asterism of Yama (Bharaṇī), or the Kaṇṭaka yoga has arisen.
And it would cause harm [or, according to K., theft] among the leafless creepers.

95.07a If it is domestic, blazing with its voice and movements; 95.07b fierce, crying out, and perched upon a thorny tree; 95.07c and if it occurs under a terrestrial nakṣatra or lagna in the southwest (nairṛtī).
If he is seen standing nearby, intent on quarreling.
95.08a If Venus is situated in the ninth part of the sign occupied by the Moon at the ascendant,
95.08b it cries out from a corner with its face turned downwards;
95.08c if it is blazing, it brings about a sexual union.
By that womb, she who was ordained in the intermediate direction [is established].
If the ascendant is a masculine sign and the lunar day is odd,
and the bird named Śukuna is situated in the eastern direction and is blazing,
then the abduction of men should be predicted.
In the case of a mixture, there would be union with a eunuch.
95.10a Thus, when the Sun is in the ascendant of its own sign, navāṃśa, or lagna; 95.10b or when the Sun itself is situated in the ascendant;
95.10c a bird that cries out while being "dīpta" (flaming/bright) indicates [a favorable omen].
For that is indeed the cause of the Puruṣa and the Pradhāna.
95.11ab/ When all undertakings are being commenced, one should calculate the ascendant from the sign occupied by the Sun.
95.11cd/ Just as "success" and "failure" are counted in sequence, so too should they be declared accordingly.

If the Sun is in the twelfth house from the ascendant with the right eye [occupied by a planet], one is blind in the right eye; if it is with the left [eye occupied], one is blind in the left eye. Furthermore, if the Sun is situated in the ascendant and aspected by malefic planets, one is indeed blind.
One born in one's own asterism may be humpbacked, deaf, or dull-witted.

If a malefic planet is situated in the sixth house from the ascendant and is aspected by a malefic, there will be a wound on that limb of the body which corresponds to the sign occupied by that planet. This is what I have declared regarding the time of birth.
95.13d One should contemplate each respective mark and form within this.
95. Hereafter, [the following] are determined according to worldly convention: various collections of syllables regarding substances, which have been desired, composed, and divided.
95. I shall now declare the names [of the planets] according to the sequence of the centers (kendras).

95. When the signs situated in the ascendant, the fourth house, the seventh house, and the tenth house are occupied by planets, one should take the letters corresponding to the degrees of the houses located in the ascendant; from these, the syllables are derived based on their own respective houses.
95. One should know [the results] of the planets according to the sequence of their own respective groups.
95. They declare that the *vargas* of Mars, Venus, and Mercury are preceded by the *ka*-group; those of Jupiter and Saturn are preceded by the *ya*-group;
and those of the Moon are said to be preceded by the *ya*-group.
95. Furthermore, the vowels ṛ, ṝ, and ḷ are derived from the letter *a* of the Sun.

95.4ab. They declare that by increasing the number of *dreṣkāṇas*, the name consists of three, five, or seven syllables in the case of an odd sign; 95.4c. but in an even sign, one should know it to consist of two, four, or six syllables.
95. The syllables of the name [are determined] by the increase in the aspects of the planetary aspects.
95.ṛ5a In a Vargottama [sign], there is a two-syllable [name] in a movable [navamśa]; 95.ṛ5b in a fixed [navamśa], that is four-syllabled;
95.ṛ5c and in odd [navamśas] other than these, there are an odd number of syllables.
95. But in the case of those with dual natures, they should be like [the lords] of the zodiac signs.
95.6ab One should state two names for a sign known as having two forms (dvimūrti),
when it is aspected by Mercury and possesses a dual nature. 95.6c Whatever the number of degrees [of the planets] situated in their own rising signs...
95. ṛ6d That much is the collection of syllables in the Saṃgrahaṇī.
95.7a One should recognize a conjunction at the beginning among the many [letters].
95.7b They say that in the case of *kūṭas*, it is followed by a conjunction. 95.7c In its own exaltation portion (*uccāṃśaka*), it is doubled due to its connection with the lunar mansion (*ṛkṣa*).
95. A heavy syllable (guru-akṣara) occurs in that [position] which is the portion of its house.
95. ṛ8a. When joined with the planets in a trine, it should be endowed with the measures (mātrā) and so forth, as in the case of the syllables corresponding to the Dreṣkāṇas.
95. ṛ8b–c. In the strengths of the sky, [the sequence is] from above; in the lotuses, from below.
95. The visarga should be known as being present in those [syllables] endowed with the eight powers (aṣṭabala).
95.9ab In the case of those [consonants] arising from the head (ūrdhva), they desire the *mātrā* to be above;
and for those designated as arising from the back (pṛṣṭha), it is below.
95.9cd One should understand that in the case of those arising from both [the head and the back], it is transverse (*tiryak*).
95. One should place a long [syllable] in the long [metres], and another in the remaining [short metres].

95. From the signs situated in the east, the ascendant, the water [the seventh], and the setting [the seventh from the ascendant] in the sky, the collection of syllables is derived from their degrees. A malefic planet situated in a quadrant destroys the syllable.
95. Or, by its aspect, [it gives results] according to its measure when situated in a trine.
95. A benefic planet, possessing powerful energy,
is said to bestow syllables equal in number to its house-position and its portion (navāṃśa),
provided it is situated aspecting [the lord] or in a quadrant or a trine.
95. Even when one's own [planetary] exaltation sign occupies its own portion, two signs [are considered] as its own part.
95. When the lord of the *kṣetra* (the house) has its strength exhausted and its *aṃśaka* (division) is likewise diminished, that which arises from it—the *mātrā-akṣara*—goes to destruction;
yet even when that [lord] is impossible [to find], it attains manifestation within it.
95. When the first of the Vargas (the sign) is joined with its own exaltation degree and aspected by the Lord (the ruler of the sign), [it is auspicious].
95.13a–c. Having understood the excellence of the strength of each according to its position in the angles (kendras), as well as that of the field and its lord,
the sequential application of the syllables should be performed.
95. And there is the conceptualization of the combination of measures and so forth.
95.14a–c. Therein, the four ascendants beginning with the first sign [Aries] are determined by the sequence of the first degrees and so forth,
from the degrees of the planets, according to the letters of their respective groups.
95.14d This attainment regarding the purposeful meaning is to be maintained.

95.15a In Aries, the letter *ka* [is the seed-syllable]; in Cancer, the letter *ya*. 95.15b In Libra, the letter *ca*; in Capricorn, the letter *pa*. 95.15c In Aries, the letter *cha*; and in Cancer, the letter *a*.
95. In Libra, the letter *kha*; in Capricorn, the letter *pha*.
In Aries, the letter *ṭa*; in Cancer, the letter *ṭha*;
in Libra, the letter *ta*; in Capricorn, the letter *tha*.
In Aries, however, it is the letter *ra*; in Cancer, the letter *ja*.
In Libra, the letter *ba*; in Capricorn, the letter *ga*.
95.17a. The letter *ā* [is assigned] when the Moon is in the first house; the letter *gha* when it has entered the fourth house;
95.17b. The letter *bha* when it is in the seventh house; the letter *jha* when it is in Capricorn (*makara*). 95.17c.
The letter *ḍa* when the Moon is in the ascendant (*lagna*); the letter *da* when it is in the fourth house (*hibuka*).
95. One should place the letter *ḍha* in the crocodile (*makara*) and the letter *ḍha* in the scorpion (*dhvaja*).

95.ṛ18a In the ascendant is the letter *ña*, and in the fourth house is the letter *ma*. 95.ṛ18b In Libra is the letter *ṅa*, and in Capricorn is the letter *la*. 95.ṛ18c In the ascendant is the letter *ka*, and in the fourth house is the letter *pa*.
In Libra, the letter *ca* is used; in Capricorn, the letter *i*.
95.19a The letter *na* is in the ascendant, and the letter *ta* is in the fourth house; 95.19b the letter *ṇa* is in Libra, and the letter *ṭa* is in Capricorn.
95.19c Thus has this been stated regarding that which is designated as "movable" (*cara*).
95. I shall now describe the fourfold [system] known as Sthira.

In Vṛṣa, the letter *pha* [is assigned] to the Hibuka; in Kīṭa, the letter *kha*; in Nṛghaṭa, the letter *va*; and in [the remaining] signs, the letter *cha*. From these initial portions, the wise man should assign [the letters].
95.20d In due order, among those designated as "stable" (sthirasaṃjñaka).

95.21a The letter *ba* is in the ascendant, and the letter *ja* is in the fourth house. 95.21b The letter *ī* is in the seventh house, and the letter *ga* is in the tenth house. 95.21c The letter *tha* is in Taurus, and the letter *ṭa* is in the fourth house.
In the word *kīṭa* (insect), there is the letter *ḍa*; in the word *nṛghaṭa* (man-pot), there is the letter *da*.
In Taurus, there is the letter *gha*; in Cancer, the letter *śa*. In Leo, there is the letter *jha*; in Virgo, the letter *bha*.
In Aries, there is the letter *ja*; in Cancer, the letter *u*.
In the word *kīṭa*, the letter *ṅa* [is present]; in the word *nṛghaṭa*, the letter *ma*.
95.23a If the letter *ḍha* is in the ascendant, and then the letter *ṇa* is in the water [the fourth house],
95.23b and the letter *dha* is situated in the sky [the tenth house], and the letter *na* [is there as well];
95.23c the letter *ṣa* is in Taurus [the second house], and the letter *ca* is in the hibuka [the seventh house].
In the word *kīṭa*, there is the letter *pa*; in the word *nṛghaṭa*, there is the letter *ka*.

95.24a They say the letter *ū* is in the Bull and the Water [signs], and *kha* is in the Lion; 95.24b the letter *pha* is in the Man [Aries] and the Jar [Aquarius], and *cha* is in the last [Pisces]; 95.24c they desire *ṭa* and *ta* in the final Bull [Taurus].
95.24d They declare that *ṭhaṃ* is in Leo and *thaṃ* is in Aquarius.
In Gemini, known as Dvimūrti, there are the letter *ja*s;
in the sixth sign, Cancer, the letter *ba* should be in the first division; and when Sagittarius has reached the eighth house, there is the letter *ga*.
95.25d When the two Pisces are situated in the sky, the letter *sa* [is used].
95.26a. The letter *gha* is in the ascendant, and the letter *bha* is in the fourth house;
95.26b. the letter *jha* is in the seventh house, and the letter *ī* is in the middle of the sky (the tenth house);
95.26c. the letter *da* is in the ascendant, and the letter *dha* is in the fourth house.
95.26d They know the letter ḍa to be in the heart and the letter ḍha in the ether.
95.27a The letter *ma* is in the ascendant, and the letter *ṅa* is in the fourth house. 95.27b The letter *ha* is in the seventh house, and the letter *ña* is in the tenth house.
95.27c The letter *pa* is in the ascendant, and the letter *ca* is in the fourth house.
The letter *ai* is in the chest; the letter *ka* is in the sky.
95.28a They say that when [the moon] is in the eastern ascendant, it is *na*; when in the water-sign, *ṇa*.
95.28b When it has set, it is *ṭa*; when situated in the sky, *ta*. 95.28c When in the eastern ascendant, it is *kha*; when in the water-sign, they say it is *ya*.
95. Ṛ when the sun has set, and Pha when it is situated in the sky.
95.29a. They know that *jam* is in the ascendant, *okāra* when situated in the fourth house, 95.29b. *gam* when situated in the seventh house, and *bam* in the tenth house (*ambare*).
95.29c. *ṭham* is in the ascendant, *ṇam* in the twelfth house, and *ḍam* when situated in the fourth house (*hibuka*).
95.29d When the sun has set and the moon is situated in the sky.
95. Thus has this collection of syllables, the method for the designation of names, been explained;
and in all [astrological] ascendants, some [authorities] speak thus.
95.30d However, they desire [it] according to the previously stated procedure.

95. Having multiplied each of the quadrants (kendrāṇi) separately by their respective degrees situated in the quadrants, and having divided [the sum] by three, they know that to be the syllable (akṣara).
95. The ownership [is determined] by the circumambulation of the portions of the field-lord.

95.32 In dreams concerning what has been thought of or longed for, or what has emerged [from the mind]; regarding things lost, wounded, women, sexual pleasure, or food; and in the case of groups such as bears, thoughts, men, and so forth—

95. One should observe the names among these [planets]: 95.14a. A two-syllable name [is appropriate] when the Moon is in a movable sign, a house, or a division; 95.14b. And his name should have four syllables when it is in a fixed sign.
Furthermore, among those with two forms, there is also a pair of names;
and its [name] consisting of three syllables occurs through five [syllables].
The consonant groups beginning with *ka* are assigned respectively to Mars, Venus, Mercury, Jupiter,
and Saturn;
the eight vowels beginning with *ya* belong to the Moon.
From the letter 'a' of Ravi, the vowels shall arise in succession.
Having reflected in due order on the names of Agni, Ambu, Kumāra, Viṣṇu, Śakra, Indrapatnī, and Caturānana, which are identical to those of the Sun;
One should compose [mantras] with two, three, or more syllables according to one's own intelligence.
95.17a Their birds are [divided] by suckling, infancy,
95.17b those established in vows, youth, middle age, and old age; 95.17c and those who are exceedingly old— thus [it is said regarding] the Moon and Mars.
95.17d Of Mercury, Venus, Jupiter, the Sun, and Saturn.
Chapter 96:

On Maturation (Pākādhyāya) The maturation of the Sun occurs after a fortnight; that of the Moon, monthly; that of Mars is said to be as stated by Vakra [after a month]; and that of Mercury and Jupiter occurs after a year from the time of their first appearance.

96.02ab. For Śukra, [the period is] six months; for Śani and the enemy of the gods (Rāhu), one year; for half a year for Sūrya; 96.02cd. For a solar eclipse, it is immediate; likewise for Tvaṣṭṛ and Kīlaka.
96.03ab/ By three months alone for Dhūmaketu, and at the end of seven nights for Śveta; 96.03cd/ [The effects of] halos, rainbows, twilight clouds, and comets [occur] after seven days.
96.04ab/ The inversion of cold and heat, the production of fruits and flowers out of season, and the burning of the quarters;
96.04cd/ the transformation of stationary and moving beings, and deformities at birth—these occur within six months.
96.05ab/ When that which is not to be done is performed, there will be earthquakes, lack of festivals, and ill-omened sacrifices.
96.05cd/ Furthermore, within half a year, there will be the withering of things that should not wither, and a change in the courses of rivers.

In three months, there will be trembling, sweating, and the speaking, weeping, shaking, and sweating of pillars, granaries, and images; as well as quarrels, rainbows, thunderclaps, and the ripening of fruits.
An abundance of insects, mice, flies, and snakes, the crying of wild beasts and birds,
and the floating of a clod of earth in water— these three portents ripen in exactly three months.
96.08ab/ The breeding of dogs in the forest, the entry of wild animals into the village,
and the appearance of honeycombs, arched gateways, and Indra’s banners [occur] when the rain exceeds its normal measure.
96.09ab/ A pack of jackals and vultures [portends] ten days; the sound of musical instruments [portends] immediate [danger].
96.09cd/ A cry of abuse yields fruit within a fortnight; an anthill and the cracking of the earth [yield fruit] immediately.
The spontaneous ignition of fires and the raining down of ghee, oil, fat, and the like—
these portents ripen immediately, or within one and a half months, as do public rumors.
The results for the umbrella, the funeral pyre, the sacrificial post, and the fire are obtained within seven fortnights;
however, some say that the result for the umbrella and the archway is attained after one month.
96.12ab/ There is an extreme mutual aversion among beings, yet there is affection and sound in the sky;
96.12cd/ and there is a union between a cat and a mongoose with a mouse for a month.
96.13ab/ A city of Gandharvas, a change in the taste of water, and a transformation of gold;
96.13cd/ And the quarters of the sky filled with banners, houses, dust, and smoke—these also have their results within one month.
The asterisms beginning with Aśvinī have ripening periods measured by nine, one, eight, ten, one, six, three, and three months respectively; Āśleṣā yields its fruit immediately.
96.15ab/ Six months, six, three, half [a month], and eight, three, six, one, and one [are the durations for the Pitrya rites].
96.15cd/ In the four-month period beginning with Āṣāḍha, the cooking [of the śrāddha] may be done immediately during the asterisms of Pāka (Pūrvaphalgunī) and Abhijit.
The fruition of the lunar mansions beginning with Śravaṇā occurs, respectively, in seven, eight, one and a half, three, three, and five months.
If it is not seen when the stated time has passed,
it ripens even more, doubling in intensity; this is unless [the debt] is cleared by the gift of gold, jewels, or cattle.
And it was pacified according to the rules by the twice-born with propitiatory rites.

Chapter 97: The Chapter on the Qualities of the Actions of the Lunar Mansions (Nakṣatra-karmaguṇādhyāya) Fire, quality, taste, sense-organ, fire, moon, object, quality, season, five, eight, fortnight;
object, one, moon, element, ocean, fire, Rudra, Aśvin, Vasu, and fire.
97.02ab/ One hundred, fifty, twenty-eight, and thirty-two—such is the measure of the stars.
97.02cd/ The duration for Aśvinī and the other constellations is determined respectively by the number of their stars.
97.03ab/ The results arising from the lunar mansion at marriage—whether good or bad—are to be declared after a number of years equal to its stars.
97.03cd/ The cessation of a fever or any other disease is to be predicted after a number of days [equal to its stars].
97.04ab/ Aśvin, Yama, Agni, Brahmā, the Moon, Śiva, Aditi, Jupiter, the Serpent, and the Pitṛs;
97.04cd/ Yoni, Aryaman, the Sun, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vāyu, Indra, Agni, and Mitra.
97.05ab/ Śakra, Nirṛti, Toya, Viśvedevas, Brahmā, Hari, Vasu, Varuṇa, 97.05cd/ Ajapāda, Ahirbudhnya, and Pūṣan are the presiding deities (īśvara) of the lunar mansions (bhā).
97.06ab/ The three Uttaras and Rohiṇī are fixed among them; with these, one should perform consecrations, rites for peace, planting trees, building cities, and the undertaking of the seeds of Dharma.
97.07ab/ Mūla, Śiva, Śakra, and Bhujagādhipa are the fierce [nakṣatras]; in them, these succeed:
97.07cd/ assault, mantras, vetālas, binding, killing, and causing dissension.
97.08ab/ The fierce [nakṣatras]—Pūrvabharaṇī and Pitrya (Maghā)—are to be employed for uprooting, destruction, and deceit;
97.08cd/ as well as for success in matters such as binding, poison, fire, and the stroke of a weapon.
97.09ab/ Laghu, Hasta, Aśvinī, and Puṣya are declared to bring success in trade, pleasure, knowledge, ornaments, and the arts; 97.09cd/ as well as in crafts, medicine, vehicles, and so forth.
97.10ab. The group of soft [asterisms]—Anurādhā, Citrā, Revatī, and Rohiṇī—is for the sake of friendship.
97.10cd. They are also beneficial for sexual union, garments, ornaments, auspicious songs, and so forth.
The three Śravaṇas, together with Āditya (Punarvasu) and Anila (Svāti), produce results that are mild, sharp, or a mixture of both; they are beneficial for mobile undertakings.
The three stars of Hasta, the three of Mṛgaśiras, the three of Śravaṇa, Pūṣan (Punarvasu), Aśvinī, Śakra (Jyeṣṭhā), Guru (Puṣya),
and Punarvasu are beneficial for the rite of shaving, whether at the time of sunrise or during the auspicious moment.
And they were joined by the lord of the stars (the moon) and by an auspicious star.

97.13a Not for those who have merely bathed and are eager to depart after adorning themselves; 97.13b nor for those who have anointed themselves, eaten, or are dismissed at the time of battle; 97.13c nor during the twilight, the night, on Saturday, Tuesday, Sunday, or on an inauspicious lunar day (rikta).
Shaving is beneficial on the ninth day, but not on a *viṣṭi* lunar day.
By the king’s command, with the consent of Brāhmaṇas, at the time of marriage, during the impurity caused by death or birth,
upon the release of one who is bound, and at the initiations for sacrifices— in all these instances, the practice of shaving is recommended.
Hasta, Mūla, Śravaṇā, Punarvasu, Mṛgaśiras, and Puṣya—
these lunar mansions are auspicious for undertakings designated as masculine.
97.15ab/ Under the asterisms of Savitṛ, Pūṣan, Anila, Mitra, Tiṣya, Tvaṣṭṛ, and likewise the lord of the host of stars (Jyeṣṭhā);
97.15cd/ one should perform the purificatory rites, initiation, vows, the girdle ceremony, and so forth, when Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, or the Moon are present.

If the third house of profit is occupied by benefics, devoid of malefics, and the ascendant is a benefic sign, the two ears should be pierced when the ascendant is Aries or Leo, and under the asterisms of Puṣya, Mṛgaśiras, Citrā, Hasta, or Revatī.

97.16 When the benefic planets occupy the twelve angles (kendras) and the eighth house, while the malefic planets are situated in the third, sixth, and eleventh houses; or when Jupiter—the preceptor of the gods—or even the one worshipped by the lord of the Daityas, is placed in the ascendant or in an angle; and when the sign rising at the time of action is auspicious for the doer, there is the successful attainment of the fruits of all undertakings.
97.16d And when there is the rising of a fixed sign associated with a village, a house should be built or one should enter it.
Chapter 98: The Chapter on the Qualities of the Lunar Days (Tithis) and Their Deities.
The presiding deities of the lunar days (tithis) are, in order: Brahmā (Kamalaja), Vidhātṛ, Hari, Yama, Śaśāṅka, Ṣaḍvaktra, Śakra, Vasu, Bhujaga, Dharma, Īśa, Savitṛ, Manmatha, Kala, and Viśve.
98.02ab/ On the new moon day (amāvāsyā), the ancestors are present; rituals should be performed by them according to their designations.
98.02cd/ Nandā, Bhadrā, Vijayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā—these are the five types [of lunar days], which are further divided into three categories.
98.03ab/ Whatever task is to be done under a particular lunar mansion (nakṣatra) should be performed on lunar days (tithis) presided over by that same deity.
98.03cd/ It is likewise conducive to success when performed during the specific Karaṇas and Muhūrtas associated with that deity.
Chapter 99: On the Qualities of the Karaṇas The lords of those known as Vava, Bālava, Kaulava, Taitila, Gara, Vaṇija,
and Viṣṭi are, respectively, Indra, the Lotus-born (Brahmā), Mitra, Aryaman, Bhū (Earth), Śrī (Lakṣmī), and Yama.
From the half of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the fixed [periods] are Śakuni, Catuṣpāda, Nāga, and Kiṃstughna;
their lords are Kali, Vṛṣa, Phaṇin, and Māruta.

99.03a One should perform auspicious, stable, and nourishing rites during the Karana called Vava; 99.03b likewise, religious acts and those beneficial for the twice-born should be done during the one named Bālava.
99.03c During Kaulava, there should be acts of mutual affection, making friends, and choosing [a spouse].
And in that which is called Taitila, there are houses that are the refuge of good fortune.
In the *gara* yoga, there arise matters concerning agriculture, seeds, houses, and shelter; in the *vaṇij* yoga, there are constant undertakings and associations with merchants.
Indeed, the *viṣṭi* yoga does not bring about anything auspicious.
It brings success against the attacks of others, poisons, and the like.
99.05a In Śakuni, one should perform rites for prosperity, such as medicinal herbs and the like, as well as root-mantras;
99.05b in Catuṣpada, rites concerning cattle, and kingdoms dedicated to the twice-born and the ancestors;
99.05c in Nāga, rites involving immovable objects and those that are cruel, as well as seizure and acts leading to misfortune.
In Kiṃstughna, there is auspiciousness, the performance of sacrifices, the rites for nourishment, and the accomplishment of auspicious deeds.

If the third house from the ascendant is the house of gain (the eleventh), and it is occupied by benefics while being devoid of malefics, and the ascendant is a benefic sign; and if the two ears (the first and seventh houses) are pierced [by planets] while the ascendant is that of a deity (a sign ruled by a planet), and the birth occurs under the asterisms of Puṣya, the Moon (Mṛgaśiras), Citrā, Hari (Śravaṇa), or Pauṣṇa (Revatī).
99.07a–c. Marriage is auspicious when the moon is rising in Rohiṇī, Uttarā-revatī, Mṛgaśiras, Mūla, Anurādhā, Maghā, Hasta, or Svāti; or when it is in the sixth, Libra, or Gemini signs;
provided that the seventh, eighth, twelfth, and outer houses are auspicious, and the moon is in the first, second, or third house.
If malefic planets occupy the third, sixth, and eighth houses, there is no [auspicious] result; however, this is not the case if Venus is in the sixth or Mars is in the eighth.

When the Sun is favorable in its course and free from the two, nine, and eight signs for the couple; when the Moon is free from the Sun, Mars, Saturn, and Venus, or situated between two malefic planets; and having avoided the days of Vyatīpāta and Vaidhṛti, as well as the Viṣṭi karana and the Riktā lunar days; [then the marriage should be performed].
99.08d When the cruel [planets] are absent from the Āyana, Pauṣa, and Caitra [months], and when the human [sign] occupies the degree of the ascendant.
100.01ab/ One born under Aśvinī is fond of ornaments, handsome, fortunate, skillful, and wise.
100.01cd/ One born under Bharaṇī is resolute, truthful, free from disease, capable, and happy.
One born under Kṛttikā is a great eater, devoted to the wives of others, and renowned for his brilliance.
One born under Rohiṇī is truthful, pure, pleasant-spoken, steadfast, and handsome in form.
In Mṛga, one is fickle, clever, timid, skillful, energetic, wealthy, and a seeker of enjoyments;
in Raudra-Ṛkṣa, one is deceitful, arrogant, fierce, ungrateful, violent, sinful, and cruel.
A person born under Punarvasu is self-controlled, happy, virtuous, yet dull-witted, subject to disease, and thirsty; furthermore, such a person is content with very little.
Under Puṣya, one is peaceful in soul, fortunate, wise, wealthy, and devoted to the Dharma;
under Bhaujaṅga, one is deceitful, a consumer of all things, sinful, ungrateful, and a rogue.
One who has many dependents and wealth, an enjoyer of pleasures, devoted to the gods and ancestors, and possessed of great effort, is described in the *Pitrya* [Navāṃśa].
One who is pleasant of speech, generous, radiant, a wanderer, and a servant of the king is found in the *Bhāgya* [Navāṃśa].
Under the second Phalgunī, one is fortunate, endowed with learning and wealth, a possessor of enjoyments, and a partaker of happiness;
under Hasta, one is energetic, bold, a drinker of liquor, pitiless, and a thief.
100.08ab/ One who wears variegated garments and garlands and possesses beautiful eyes is born under Citrā.
100.08cd/ One who is self-controlled, a merchant, compassionate, sweet-spoken, and devoted to righteousness is born under Svātī.
One born under Viśākhā is envious, greedy, radiant, eloquent in speech, and a maker of quarrels.
In Anurādhā, one is wealthy, a resident of foreign lands, hungry, and a wanderer.
100.10ab/ Under Jyeṣṭhā, one has many friends, is contented, performs righteous deeds, and is prone to great anger.
100.10cd/ Under Mūla, one is honorable, wealthy, happy, non-violent, steadfast, and a enjoyer of pleasures.
In the house of Jaladeva, one is a hero with beloved and joyful wives and firm friendships;
in the house of Vaiśva, one is humble, righteous, possesses many friends, is grateful, and is fortunate.
Under Śravaṇā, one is illustrious, learned, noble in wife, and endowed with wealth;
under Dhaniṣṭhā, one is famous, a donor, wealthy, fond of songs by heroes, and greedy for riches.
One born under Śatabhiṣaj has clear speech, is addicted to vices, slays enemies, is impetuous, and is difficult to restrain.
One born under the Bhadrapadas is anxious, dominated by women, skillful with wealth, and a non-giver.
One born under the second lunar mansion becomes an eloquent speaker, happy, possessed of offspring, a conqueror of enemies, and righteous.
Under the asterism of Puṣya, one is complete in all limbs, fortunate, heroic, pure, and wealthy.
Chapter 101: The Division of the Zodiac Signs 101.01ab.
Aries is declared to consist of Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and the first quarter of Kṛttikā (Bahulā). 101.01cd.
Taurus consists of the remainder of Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, and half of Mṛgaśiras.
The half of Mṛgaśiras, Raudra (Ārdrā), and three quarters of Punarvasu constitute Gemini;
one quarter of Punarvasu, Tiṣya (Puṣya), and Aśleṣā constitute Cancer.
101.03ab. Leo consists of Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, and one quarter of Uttaraphalgunī;
101.03cd. the remainder of that [quarter], Hasta, and half of Citrā constitute the sign known as Virgo.
101.04ab/ In Libra, there is the latter half of Citrā, Svātī, and three quarters of Viśākhā.
101.04cd/ In Scorpio, there is one quarter of Viśākhā, as well as Anurādhā and Jyeṣṭhā.
101.05ab/ Mūla, Aṣāḍhā, Pūrvā, and the first portion of Uttarā belong to Sagittarius (Dhanvī).
101.05cd/ Capricorn (Makara) consists of the remainder of that [portion], Śravaṇa, and the first half of Dhaniṣṭhā.
101.06ab/ The sign of Aquarius (Kumbha) consists of the latter half of Antyadhaniṣṭhā, three quarters of Śatabhiṣaj, and the remainder of Pūrvabhadrapadā;
likewise, Uttarabhadrapadā and Revatī constitute Pisces (Jhaṣa).
101.07ab/ Aśvinī, Pitrya (Maghā), Mūla, and the others [beginning with] Meṣa (Aries), Siṃha (Leo), and Haya (Horse = Aśvinī) are the odd asterisms;
101.07cd/ they return [to their starting points] by increasing one quarter (pāda) for each subsequent one.
In the first house (the Ascendant),
the Sun makes [the woman] a widow, Mars likewise; Rāhu makes her one whose sons have perished, and Saturn makes her poor.
Venus, the son of the Moon (Mercury), and Jupiter likewise cause the ruin of a virtuous wife; then the Lord of the Night (Mars) brings about the end of her life.
The Sun, Saturn, Rāhu,
and Mars cause incomparable misery of poverty when situated in the second house;
whereas Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury [bestow] a wealthy mistress who is not a widow.
The Moon makes a woman one who has many sons.
If the Sun, Moon, Mars, Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury are in the third house,
they always make [the woman] possessed of many sons and a sharer of wealth;
Saturn makes her manifest and fortunate.
Indeed, Rāhu, by his very nature, bestows death through the observance of this rule.
When Mercury is in the fourth house, very little milk flows;
the Sun and the Moon cause misfortune;
Rāhu causes a co-wife; and Mars makes one possess little wealth.
Bhṛgu, the preceptor of the gods, and Budha bestow happiness.
If the Sun and Mars are indeed situated in the fifth house, one's children are lost;
however, Mercury bestows many sons, as do Jupiter and Venus. Rāhu brings about death, and Saturn grants severe disease.
The Moon brings about the destruction—or, according to another reading, the birth—of a maiden before long.
Saturn, the Sun, Rāhu, Jupiter, and Mars, when situated in the sixth house,
will make [the wife] fortunate and devoted to her father-in-law;
the Moon makes her a widow, and Venus makes her poor.
The son of the Moon (Mercury) [rules] over prosperity and those who are fond of quarreling.
102.07a Saturn, Mars, Jupiter, Mercury, Rahu, the Sun, the Moon, and Venus—
102.07b these seven planets, when situated in the seventh house, will indeed forcibly bring about 102.07c widowhood, imprisonment, death, ruin, and the destruction of wealth.
102.07d Illness, exile, and death, respectively.
If Jupiter and Mercury are certainly in the eighth house from the ascendant, there is separation;
likewise, the Moon, Venus, and Rāhu cause death. The Sun makes [the woman] non-widowed, while Mars makes her diseased.
The son of the Sun [married] Dhanavatī, who was beloved by her husband.
When Mars, Jupiter, Saturn,

and Rāhu are situated in the ninth house (the house of Dharma), they respectively cause one to be established in righteousness, devoted to the law, free from disease, or barren; whereas the son of the Sun (Saturn) makes her barren.
The Moon causes the birth of a daughter and brings about wandering.
Rāhu, situated in the vault of the sky, makes her a widow;
the Sun and Saturn make her devoted to sin;
Mars brings death; and the Moon makes her a wanton woman destitute of wealth.
The remaining planets would make her wealthy and fortunate.
If the Sun is in the eleventh house, she will have many sons; the Moon, wealth; Mars, sons; Saturn, abundance of wealth;
Jupiter, long life; and Mercury, prosperity.
Rāhu makes her not a widow; Bhṛgu makes her possessed of wealth.
102.12a At the end [of the period], Jupiter makes her wealthy; the Sun makes her poor;
102.12b the Moon makes her a spendthrift; and Rāhu makes her unchaste; 102.12c Venus makes her a virtuous wife; and Mercury makes her possessed of many sons and grandsons.
The son of the Sun (Saturn) and Mars [afflict] one whose heart is addicted to drinking.
The dust raised at the end of the day by cowherds struck with sticks and trampled by the hooves of cattle brings,

upon the marriage of beautiful women, abundant wealth, sons, health, and good fortune; at that time, neither the lunar mansion, nor the lunar day, nor the *karana*, nor the *lagna*, nor the astrological conjunction (*yoga*) matters at all.
Renowned for the sake of men's happiness, the dust raised by the cows pacifies all misfortunes.
103. Chapter on the Sphere of the Planets (Graha-gocara-adhyāya) 103.01ab:
Generally, ancient works, though devoid of a formal aphorism (sūtra), possess openings for illumination; 103.01cd:
like jewels and scriptures, they are capable of being adorned by being joined with new qualities.
103.02ab/ Generally, this is the domain of worldly practice; therefore, I shall describe its fruits.
103.02cd/ Due to various meters, we may have exhibited verbal fickleness; may the noble ones forgive us.
103.03ab/ Having heard the words of Māṇḍavya, [it was said: "Neither does my own [wife] please me, nor indeed is it otherwise.
103.03cd/ For a virtuous woman is not as dear to men as one who is restless in her hips."

The Sun is situated in the sixth and thirteenth houses; the Moon is in the third, tenth, sixth, seventh, and first; Jupiter is in the seventh, ninth, second, and fifth; Venus and Saturn are in the sixth and third;
Mercury is in the sixth, second, fourth, eighth, and twelfth. All these are auspicious when near the Sun.
Venus, when conjoined with the seventh, sixth, or tenth lunar mansion, causes terror like a tiger.

In the first year, the Sun causes exhaustion; in the second, it brings about loss of wealth like a digestive ailment or a long journey, as well as the destruction of fortune, lack of happiness, deception, and eye disease. In the third year, it grants the attainment of status, a joyful accumulation of wealth, health, and the destruction of enemies.
In the fourth house, it bestows diseases and repeatedly causes obstacles to the enjoyment of garlands.
If the Sun is situated in the fifth house, there will be manifold afflictions arising from disease and enemies.
In the sixth house, the Sun destroys diseases, subdues enemies, and dispels sorrows.
Situated in the seventh house, it causes travel, fear of abdominal ailments, and wretchedness.
And when Rukṣa is situated in the eighth house, even a beautiful-faced woman does not become one's own wife.

In the ninth house, there is distress from calamities and illness; in the tenth, there is opposition to one's thoughts and actions, yet one attains fierce victory and success in undertakings in due course. In the eleventh house, there is a position of victory, honor, prosperity, and the destruction of disease.
In the twelfth house, the actions of those who follow virtuous conduct become fruitful, but not so for others.

103.08a If the Moon is in the first house at birth, it provides excellent food, bedding, and clothing. 103.08b In the second house, it causes honor and wealth to wither, and one becomes beset by obstacles. 103.08c In the third house, one obtains garments, women, wealth, victory [or accumulation], and happiness.
In the fourth [stanza], there is distrust in the Śikhariṇī meter, which is like a serpent.
In the fifth house, the Moon produces dejection, disease, and grief;
in the sixth, it generates wealth, happiness, and the destruction of enemies and diseases;
and in the seventh, it brings vehicles, honor, beds, food, and the acquisition of riches.
In the Mandākrāntā meter, with the *phaṇi* (naga) and *himaga* (snow-goer) [syllables] in the eighth position, who would not feel fear?
103.10a When situated in the ninth house, the Moon causes bondage, anxiety, fatigue, and diseases of the stomach.

103.10b And in the tenth house, the Moon brings about the accomplishment of commands and actions. 103.10c Occupying the penultimate (ninth) house, it bestows prosperity, association with friends, wealth, and joy.
And in the end, he renders those faults, which follow the conduct of a bull, along with their consequences.
103.11ab/ If Mars is in the first or second house, there is a violent assault, and suffering for the king due to quarrels and the faults of enemies.
103.11cd/ Even one who resembles Upendra (Viṣṇu) will suffer greatly from bile, fire, thieves, and diseases.
And when Mars is in its third house from the son of the thief (the fifth house), it bestows results from his presence:
brilliance, authority, wealth, and woolen garments.
103.12d It is said that there are others known as repositories of mineral ores.
If Dharaṇija is in the fourth house, there arises fever, abdominal disease, and blood-born ailments;
moreover, it forcibly brings about misfortune from association with wicked men.
In the fifth year, O daughter of the Earth, there shall be fear of enemies, weapons, and anger, as well as sorrows caused by one's children;
moreover, his splendor shall not remain stable for long.
Just as a *mālatī* flower is placed upon the head of a monkey.

103.15ab/ Free from fear of enemies and strife, possessing gold, coral, and copper, he attains his desires. 103.15cd/ When the son of the Earth has gone to the house of an enemy, what other facial contortion does one observe?
When Mars is situated in the seventh house, it causes discord with one's wife, eye disease, and abdominal ailments;
in the eighth house, it results in the loss of blood, emaciation, and the depletion of wealth and honor;
and when Mars is placed in the ninth house, it brings about humiliation, the destruction of wealth, and other such misfortunes.
One's gait becomes languid due to the exhaustion of the body's strength and constituent elements.
103.17ab When Mars is in the tenth house, there is equal acquisition of various kinds of wealth; when it is in the penultimate house, there is victory.
103.17cd Standing above his own country, he enjoys it like a bee enjoying a forest with its blossoming tops.
When Mars is in the twelfth house, a person is tormented by various expenses and hundreds of misfortunes,
as well as by the anger of women, bile-related ailments, and pains in the eyes.
103.18d Even he who was proud of his lineage in the family of Indra.
103.19ab/ Deprived of his wealth by wicked speech, slander, malice, and dissension, as well as by imprisonment and quarrels;
103.19cd/ one who travels on the road during the birth-period of Mercury does not hear even a "welcome" or news of well-being.

103.20ab. When Mercury is in the second house, there is humiliation; when in the third house, there is the acquisition of wealth and the gaining of friends. 103.20cd. With his mind apprehensive due to fear of the king and enemies, he walks with quick steps because of his own misdeeds.
When the Moon is in the fourth house, there is prosperity for one's own kin and family, as well as the acquisition of wealth;
when it is situated in the fifth house, there is conflict with children and wife.
And he does not pursue even a woman who is pleasing to him.
In the sixth house, Mercury bestows good fortune, victory, and prosperity;
in the seventh, extreme discoloration and quarrels; and when situated in the eighth, there is the gain of victory, sons, clothing, and wealth.
103.22d Skillfulness arises that gladdens the mind.

Chapter 105:
Conclusion Having churned the ocean of the science of astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra) with the mountain of my intellect as the churning rod (mandara),
I have now raised up this moon of a treatise that provides illumination for the world.
105.02ab/ While composing this treatise, I have not discarded the works of the former teachers.
105.02cd/ Having examined them as well as this [work], you, O virtuous ones, should apply yourselves to it according to your desire.
Alternatively, a virtuous person, even when [the fault is] great, proclaims the merit [of another] after seeing it, having emerged from an ocean of faults;

therefore, it should be recited with great effort before malicious people.
Whatever of this work currently in circulation has gone to ruin through the process of being transcribed from the mouths of the learned,

Therefore, a wise person should act here by setting aside passion.
This treatise has been compiled by one whose mind has been graced by prostrating at the feet of the Sun, the Sage, and the Guru;

106. Table of Contents of the Treatise:
First, the introduction to the treatise, the Sūtra on the Year, and the motion of the Sun;
[followed by] those of the Moon, Rāhu, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and Ketu.
106.02ab/ The movement of the sage Agastya, the conjunction of the Seven Sages, and the configuration of the constellations;
106.02cd/ The distribution of the constellations among the planets, and the planetary conflicts.
106.03ab/ The conjunction of the planets with the moon, the correct annual results of the planets,
and the characteristics of the embryos of clouds situated in the shape of a rhombus (śṛṅgāṭa).
The yogas of Dhāraṇa, Varṣaṇa, Rohiṇī, Vāyavya, Āṣāḍha, and Bhadrapada;
sudden showers, flowering creepers, the signs of twilight, and the burning of the quarters.

106.05ab/ Earthquakes, meteors, halos, the characteristics of Indra’s bow (rainbows), and comets; 106.05cd/ Solar halos, atmospheric thunderclaps, and the section on the prices of crops and commodities.
The consecration of Indra’s banner, the *khañjanaka* bird, portents, and the variegated peacock;
the measurement of the turban for the Puṣya-consecration, and the characteristics of the sword—these constitute the section on architecture (*vāstu*).
106.07ab/ Water-gates, park-keepers, the characteristics of celestial abodes, and the application of diamond-paste;
106.07cd/ Images, entry into forests, and the consecration of divine temples.
106.08ab/ Furthermore, the marks of cows, dogs, cocks, tortoises, goats, and men;
106.08cd/ the classification of the five types of men, the female mark, and the cutting of garments.

106.09ab/ Examination of yak-tail whisks, praise of women, and charms for making oneself beloved; 106.09cd/ The chapter on aphrodisiacs, ointments, and the "man-woman" (pūṃstrika), and the rules for the bedchamber.
106.10ab/ The examination of diamonds, the characteristics of pearls, and then those of rubies and emeralds;
106.10cd/ The characteristics of lamps, the cleaning of the teeth, and the mixed section on omens from birds.
106.11ab/ The inner circle, the cry [of animals], the behavior of dogs, and then the cry of the jackal.
Then follows the conduct of deer, horses, and elephants, as well as the science of crows (*vāyasa-vidyā*).
106.12ab / The ripening [of karma], the qualities of the lunar mansions, the qualities of the lunar days and the karaṇas, and the qualities of birth together with the constellations;
106.12cd / furthermore, the planetary courses (gocara) of the planets and the man of the lunar mansions (nakṣatrapuruṣa) have been explained.
106.13ab. These one hundred chapters have been set forth in their sequential order. 106.13cd. Herein, three thousand four hundred verses have been composed.
106.14ab / Within this very [work] are included the *pariśeṣa* and that which has been declared regarding journeys (*yātrā*).
106.14cd / The *jātaka* has been described as full of wonders, and the *karaṇa* as containing many points for inquiry.
